title: A cyclic analogue of Schur multiple zeta values
abstract: In this paper we introduce a cyclic analogue of Schur multiple zeta values. For a diagonally constant index on a periodically extended skew Young diagram, it is a sum over semi-standard cyclic Young tableaux. It includes the cyclic multiple zeta values of Hirose, Murahara and Murakami as a special case. The first two main results are a cyclic analogue of the Maesaka--Seki--Watanabe formula for truncated sums and an {integral--series identity} under an admissibility condition. As an application, we give a proof of $4^nζ(\{1,3\}^n)=ζ(\{4\}^n)$ by counting linear extensions of a poset. The third main result expresses a cyclic Schur multiple harmonic sum as a finite signed sum of Schur multiple harmonic sums with the same number of boxes and the same multiset of exponents.

title: XRISM view of a featureless cluster Abell 1060: Revealing the advection of a diffuse radio source by ICM motions
abstract: Abell 1060 is a nearby, dynamically relaxed galaxy cluster hosting the extended radio structure Flying Fox (FF) near its center. We used high-resolution XRISM/Resolve spectroscopy to measure intracluster medium (ICM) motions and velocity dispersion. Spatially resolved analysis reveals a velocity gradient of approximately 100 km/s along FF and enhanced velocity dispersion near the brightest cluster galaxy NGC 3311, suggesting turbulence generated by galaxy-ICM interactions. These results and the compact extent of FF favor fossil plasma supplied by past activity of the brightest cluster galaxy and transported by ICM motions. We also tested whether the measured turbulence could generate or maintain the nonthermal components of FF. For a velocity dispersion of $96.7^{+23.9}_{-24.6}$ km/s and an assumed turbulence scale of 50 kpc, comparable to the Resolve field of view and approximately half the cluster core radius, the turbulent energy flux is approximately $3.49 \times 10^{-28}$ erg cm$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$. Although this flux may weakly reenergize pre-existing relativistic electrons, the acceleration timescale of approximately 2.5 Gyr exceeds the synchrotron and inverse Compton cooling timescale of approximately 210 Myr. The present turbulence is therefore insufficient to accelerate electrons to high energies. In situ turbulent reacceleration is unlikely to dominate the generation of FF, although it may help maintain fossil electrons supplied by past AGN activity. These results link ICM dynamics to the origin of nonthermal emission and support a time-evolutionary picture of particle acceleration in galaxy clusters.

title: A Deterministic Polynomial-Query Protocol for Envy-Free Cake Cutting
abstract: We give a deterministic protocol that divides a heterogeneous cake completely and without envy among $n$ agents using $O(n^6\log n)$ Robertson--Webb queries in the worst case. Valuations may be arbitrary nonnegative, nonatomic measures, and bundles may be disconnected. The protocol makes $O(n)$ calls to certified trimming, which uses $O(n^5\log n)$ queries on $n$ pieces. In a certified trim, each agent receives the end part, or suffix, of a different piece without envy, and every shortened piece has a witness tie leading back to a whole piece. At each step, the witness values the shortened suffix exactly as much as her own. For pieces of positive interval length with strictly increasing suffix values, the retained suffix lengths are unique, although their holders may differ. Candidate assignments share a table of value and cut queries. If the coordinatewise median of their value estimates fails a matching test, the test identifies an agent whose value is underestimated, ruling out at least half the remaining assignments. A weighted median of cut marks lets one repair step remove a small envy while allocating almost all of the residue. For complete envy-free chore allocation, the query bound is $O(n^7\log n)$.

title: Statistically Optimal and Near Linear Time Hypothesis Selection
abstract: In hypothesis selection we are given $n$ distributions $q_1,\dots,q_n$ on a countable domain $\mathcal{X}$ and samples from an unknown distribution $p$. The goal is a distribution $q$ with $\mathrm{TV}(p,q)\leα\min_i\mathrm{TV}(p,q_i)+ε$. The factor $α=2$ is optimal for algorithms using a number of samples from $p$ that is independent of $|\mathcal{X}|$, and in general only improper learners achieve it. We give a learner that achieves $α=2$ with $O(\log(n/δ)/ε^2)$ samples of $p$, with probability at least $1-δ$. This matches the sample complexity of Yatracos's factor-$3$ estimator, and it removes the logarithmic factors in the factor-$2$ bound of Bousquet et al. (FOCS 2021). The learner accesses the $q_i$ only through sampling and pointwise comparisons. We measure its running time by its oracle complexity, the number of oracle calls. In expectation it makes $O((nε^{-2}+ε^{-4}\log(1/ε))\log(n/δ))$ oracle calls, independent of $\mathcal{X}$. It runs multiplicative weights over the constraints $\mathrm{TV}(q,q_i)\le\mathrm{TV}(p,q_i)$ and uses at most one sample of $p$ per round.

title: EnvTrap: Revealing the Environment-Only Attack Surface in Embodied AI via Consequence-Blind Action Execution
abstract: As AI models evolve from text and vision to physical agents, embodied AI faces a fundamentally different attack surface. Prior attacks on embodied systems have used crafted instructions, adversarial visual inputs, and training-time policy modifications; we study environment-only object rearrangements with unchanged models and instructions. We reveal an attack surface in safety-critical spatial relations among existing objects. An adversary who rearranges objects, without modifying instructions or accessing models, can cause hazardous consequences. In this work, we propose EnvTrap, a diagnostic pipeline that constructs paired safe, trap, and null-trap (benign but misleading) embodied scenarios. We demonstrate that environment-only perturbations raise hazardous-action rates to an average of 83.4% across the five evaluated action policies, with similar vulnerability patterns confirmed in world models. On a consequence-prediction task, model accuracy remains near chance, while human evaluators achieve high accuracy. We further propose a consequence-aware defense that reduces trap trigger rates by an average of 76.3 percentage points across action policies in simulation and by 62.9 percentage points pooled across physical backends. Together, these findings link environment-only attacks to a broader deficit in physical reasoning: embodied models recognize task-relevant objects yet fail to anticipate how spatial relations change the consequences of acting on them. EnvTrap makes this gap directly testable and turns hazardous layouts into training scenarios for safer embodied action. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/INKSIR/Envtrap.

title: Training Dynamics of Large State-Transition Models
abstract: Next-token prediction relies on learned token embeddings whose dimension $d$ is much smaller than the vocabulary size $V$. Existing analyses of training dynamics either fix the embeddings with $d\ge V$ or train them only in restricted settings. It remains unclear whether jointly training the embeddings by gradient-based methods from random initialization leads to accurate prediction when $d<V$. In this paper, we study this question in the simplest setting where it is already nontrivial, namely next-token prediction with a one-token context, which we refer to as a state-transition model. The model consists of an input embedding and an output embedding, either untied or tied, and is trained from Gaussian initialization by perturbed gradient descent with weight decay on the population cross-entropy loss. We consider ground-truth transition laws whose centered log-probability table has low rank and bounded entries, and measure the prediction quality by the relative prediction gain (RPG). It is zero for the uniform predictor and one for the optimal predictor. For the untied model, we show that when $d=Ω(\sqrt V)$, with probability at least $1-e^{-cd}$ for some constant $c$, the RPG is above $7/8$ at every iterate in the final $1-1/d$ fraction of training iterations. For the tied model trained on a subset of states, we prove that the RPG on the observed states is $1-O(V/d^2)$, and under a coverage condition on the ground truth and a bound on the learned embeddings, we further prove a prediction guarantee on the unseen states. Our analysis is based on the bounded trace of the Hessian of the softmax cross-entropy loss, which implies that the approximate second-order stationary points reached by training have high prediction gain. Numerical experiments with practical parameter choices illustrate the persistent training gain and the transfer of the tied model.

title: Sequential Selection against an Adaptive Opponent
abstract: Selecting a strategy by testing it against an opponent is common in game-playing AI, red-teaming of language models, and safety evaluations of AI agents. In many of these settings, the opponent adapts to what it observes, so a strategy that keeps winning in practice may already have stopped working by the time it is used. Motivated by these settings, we study a player who tries strategies in practice games against an adaptive opponent, decides when to stop, and then either selects one strategy for the next game or abstains. The goal is to select a strategy that meets a target win probability while rarely selecting one that has already fallen below it. For a single strategy, we propose the Sequential Private Accumulated-excess Rule (SPAR), which accumulates evidence through a capped likelihood ratio and selects the strategy once this evidence reaches a privately drawn uniform threshold. We show that the stopping time must involve such private randomness. The number of games SPAR needs is inversely proportional to the error tolerance, and this rate is optimal even when the opponent happens not to adapt. To select among multiple strategies, we introduce Screen-then-SPAR, which screens candidates in stages before applying SPAR. The procedure adapts to the best strategy's unknown initial margin above the target and achieves the minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. The performance of Screen-then-SPAR is demonstrated through simulations and two real-data studies, one using recorded coding-agent attacks from MonitoringBench and the other using rock-paper-scissors matches between human players and an adaptive bot.

title: One Latent World for Heterogeneous LiDARs: A Scan Pattern Agnostic 4D World Model via Direct Ray Decoding
abstract: LiDAR world models generate and predict metric 3D observations in the form of LiDAR scans. They typically synthesize scans following the scan pattern of their training sensor or render them from an intermediate 3D surface or field. However, following one scan pattern limits transfer to LiDARs with other patterns, and rendering from intermediate geometry can cause incorrect depths and false returns. In this paper, we propose a scan pattern agnostic 4D LiDAR world model that decouples the scene from sensor observation, so one spatial latent can be observed by heterogeneous LiDARs at the same mounting position without regeneration. Our decoder predicts the hit probability and depth of each ray directly from the latent, combining global scene context with local features retrieved at a preliminary depth. Without an intermediate surface or field, it reduces incorrect depths and false returns, and as each ray is decoded independently from one latent, LiDARs that share a ray receive the same return and observe one consistent scene. Finally, a diffusion transformer generates scenes in this latent and predicts 4D sequences from observed latents warped by the given ego and object motion. On KITTI-360 and nuScenes, our model generates realistic scenes and reduces the registration error between predicted frames by about 70% relative to the best compared world model. Its decoder yields 19 to 28% lower depth error than the rendering used by other world models, and generated scans benefit several downstream tasks. Our code will be open-sourced. More details are available at https://minwoo0611.github.io/OneLatentWorld.

title: SA-GLRT-D: Sidelobe-Aware GLRT-Based Detector for FMCW Radar
abstract: This paper investigates adaptive detection for frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar in multi-target complex scenarios, where reference-cell contamination, spectral leakage from the cell under test (CUT), and the resulting sidelobe interference severely degrade detection performance. A sidelobe-aware detector based on the generalized likelihood ratio test (GLRT), termed SA-GLRT-D, is proposed. Unlike conventional filtering-then-constant false alarm rate (CFAR) schemes, the proposed method explicitly accounts for the non-ideal frequency-domain energy spreading of the CUT induced by the finite-window effect. Accordingly, conventional single-cell target detection is extended to local-region detection, and decision statistic construction, CUT-related parameter estimation, and sidelobe interference suppression are jointly accomplished within a unified hypothesis-testing framework. Furthermore, to reduce computational complexity, a fast implementation of SA-GLRT-D is developed, together with a dedicated parameter initialization strategy to enhance the stability of numerical optimization. Simulation and real-measurement results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves high-accuracy target detection while maintaining a constant false alarm rate, with favorable computational efficiency.

title: Tableau Consequence under Positive Contexts: A Reconstruction of Walukiewicz's Completeness Proof
abstract: We establish a positive-context lifting theorem for tableau consequence in the modal $μ$-calculus: under explicit syntactic hypotheses, $\mathcal T_B\Rightarrow\mathcal T_C$ induces $\mathcal T_{A(B)}\Rightarrow\mathcal T_{A(C)}$. The proof orders instances of the given relation by birth time and assigns overlapping formula occurrences to the oldest supporting instance. A corollary gives bidirectional replacement by automaton normal form inside positive contexts. Together with a separate unfolding consequence lemma and ANF bisimulation, the lifting theorem yields a self-contained reconstruction of Walukiewicz's completeness proof for Kozen's axiomatisation and makes its least-fixpoint step more transparent. We also give a finite parity-game proof of regular-refutation existence and a two-sided transfer from tableau consequence to thin refutations.

title: Hierarchical randomized neural networks for efficiently and accurately finding multiple solutions of semilinear elliptic equations
abstract: Being able to find multiple solutions of a semilinear elliptic equation is a fundamental problem in scientific computing. In this paper, fully taking the advantages of randomized neural networks, we propose a new efficient and accurate method for identifying potentially as many solutions as possible. The new method is constructed from three aspects--initialization, optimization, a technique for acceleration and improving accuracy, two of which are innovative developments. Firstly, based on the basis functions of a randomized network and the sampling points, a characteristic matrix is introduced so that its singular value decomposition can be used to determine weakly variant search directions, followed by a newly developed algorithm to generate effective initial candidates. Then the good deflated Gauss-Newton method [see {\em A. Riley, et al., SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 47~(5) (2025) A2963-A2987}] using an exponential deflation operator is adapted as the optimization to search for all multiple solutions. Local error estimate of a particular solution under some proper condition is given in terms of the neurons in the hidden layer and the sampling points for this newly designed method. Furthermore, to accelerate the computation and improve the solution accuracy, a new multilevel method based on hierarchical networks is designed. Without using any {\em a priori} information, several numerical tests show together with the multilevel method, the new method can not only accurately find multiple solutions with relative errors reaching $10^{-16}$ only in less than one-tenth computational cost for the best case, but also preserve the inherent symmetries of multiple solutions.

title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research
abstract: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.

title: FlexGaze: Weakly Supervised Gaze Estimation at Scale
abstract: Most gaze estimation models are trained on data collected using specialized equipment. The limited diversity of subjects, scenes, and head poses in these datasets hinders generalization to new conditions. We present FlexGaze, a family of 3D gaze estimators pretrained with weak supervision from gaze labels (pseudo-labels) automatically generated from in-the-wild images. We use off-the-shelf models to predict 2D gaze targets and scene depth, then combine these predictions to generate 3D gaze labels for approximately 3.24 million head instances. At inference, FlexGaze predicts gaze from a head crop alone and can handle profile and rear views without requiring face detection or head pose estimation. We use data augmentation during training to improve robustness to variations in crop position and scale. Pretrained using only these generated gaze labels, FlexGaze generalizes to unseen benchmarks. After supervised fine-tuning on public gaze datasets, we evaluate FlexGaze on eight benchmarks under a unified evaluation protocol. Our models match or outperform publicly available gaze estimators with several times as many parameters on most benchmarks. We release our dataset of generated gaze labels, all trained models, and code via https://github.com/ihp-lab/FlexGaze.

title: 3AGameFactory-Motion: Agentic Rigging and Reliable Complex Motion Generation for Diverse 3D Assets
abstract: Animating arbitrary 3D assets from instructions requires both structural inference and motion control, yet existing motion benchmarks mostly cover conventional human or animal skeletons with simple instructions. We introduce DivDynBench, which evaluates rigging and motion generation across six morphology categories, with instructions requiring multi-phase part coordination and explicit timing, angle, repetition, and trajectory constraints. With large language models, we systematically compare three common paradigms: specialized motion generation, video generation followed by motion recovery, and direct agent-driven generation. We analyze their control capabilities, cross-morphology adaptability, and generation costs. Guided by this comparison, we propose an Agentic Motion Framework in which an agent writes compact parametric skeleton and motion programs, and a deterministic executor performs rigging, kinematic solving, and geometric correction. Compact parameter control reduces generation overhead and improves rigging reliability and motion-control accuracy, providing practical guidance for deploying complex 3D motion generation.

title: Spin-adapted state preparation for quantum chemistry
abstract: Quantum phase estimation for strongly-correlated molecules requires an initial state of high overlap with the true ground state, and preparing one is a significant fault-tolerant cost. Matrix product states (MPS) produced by the density matrix renormalisation group (DMRG) are a leading choice, yet existing circuits treat their tensors as dense or do not use the full symmetries present in molecular electronic Hamiltonians. In quantum chemistry, DMRG also exploits total spin, a non-abelian symmetry, storing one amplitude per spin multiplet instead of one per state. We show that the reduced tensors of such a spin-adapted MPS, labelled by the steps of the unitary group approach, form an abelian-symmetric MPS, which existing block-sparse preparation protocols can load at a cost set by the multiplet count. One state-independent rotation per site, determined by a Clebsch-Gordan coefficient, then returns the state to the occupation basis. We provide resource estimates for our circuits on singlet ground states of active space models of iron-sulphur clusters, finding improvements in Toffoli count up to $135\times$ compared to dense methods and $4.9\times$ compared to block-sparse methods applied to the same states, with up to $3.7\times$ fewer ancilla qubits required.

title: Nonmonotonic In-Plane Thermal Transport in Metal-Embedded Graphitic Carbon Nitride
abstract: Embedding metal atoms within the intrinsic cavities of graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) modifies its local bonding and vibrational properties, yet its consequences for lattice thermal transport remain poorly understood. Here, we combine a machine-learned potential (MLP) with homogeneous nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (HNEMD) to investigate in-plane thermal transport in Cu-embedded g-C3N4 across the full range of cavity occupation. The thermal conductivity exhibits a pronounced nonmonotonic dependence on Cu occupation, decreasing at intermediate occupation and partially recovering as the cavities approach full occupation. Frequency-resolved analysis reveals that this behavior originates from the competition between two phonon contributions. The low-frequency vibrations introduced by Cu couple to the intrinsic modes of g-C3N4, reconstructing the phonon dispersion and suppressing thermal transport below 10 THz. With increasing Cu occupation, the collective mechanical response of the N atoms surrounding the cavities is enhanced, accompanied by increased phonon group velocities in the 20-30 THz range and a corresponding recovery of the high-frequency thermal contribution. The competition between the saturating low-frequency suppression and the increasing high-frequency contribution gives rise to the nonmonotonic thermal conductivity. A similar occupation dependence and spectral redistribution are observed for Ag-embedded g-C3N4. These results identify competing phonon contributions as the microscopic origin of nonmonotonic thermal transport in metal-embedded g-C3N4 and suggest that occupation of intrinsic cavities provides a route to redistributing phonon transport in porous crystalline materials.

title: ReplaySAM: Zero-Shot 3D Particle-Pack Segmentation with SAM 2
abstract: X-ray computed tomography (XCT) provides non-destructive three-dimensional (3D) images of particle packs, making their internal structure accessible for quantitative analysis. Extracting particle-level measurements from these volumes first requires identifying and separating individual particles, a task that remains challenging in dense, irregular packs. Existing workflows often require manual correction or task-specific training, while promptable models need a strategy for automatically locating individual particles and recovering their instance masks. We present ReplaySAM, which adapts the pretrained Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) to three-dimensional particle-pack segmentation without additional training. It generates point prompts from foreground geometry and fuses SAM2 predictions across orthogonal slice sequences to recover particle instances. On XCT volumes of real quartz and iron-ore particle packs, ReplaySAM achieves higher mean instance Dice scores than expert-assisted watershed and nnInteractive under the evaluated protocols. ReplaySAM thus provides a training-free framework for 3D particle-pack instance segmentation, with geometry-based prompting that eliminates manual prompt placement.

title: OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering
abstract: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.

title: Radiation-Hydrodynamical Modeling of Accretion Columns in Ultraluminous X-ray Pulsars
abstract: Ultraluminous X-ray pulsars (ULXPs) provide a unique laboratory for studying accretion-column physics under strongly magnetized super-Eddington conditions. In this work, we employ a one-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamical model to investigate the vertical structure of ULXP accretion columns, applying it to NGC 300 ULX-1, Swift J0243.6$+$6124, and SMC X-3. We solve the coupled conservation equations for the inflowing gas and radiation field in a dipole-funnel geometry, allowing the velocity, density, gas pressure, radiation pressure, total energy transport rate, radiation sonic surface, and thermal mound location to be determined self-consistently. We find that radiation pressure naturally produces an extended sinking region above the stellar surface, where the inflowing gas is gradually decelerated and its kinetic energy is converted into radiation energy that partly escapes through the column walls. Despite their different luminosities, magnetic fields, and column geometries, the radiation sonic surfaces are tightly clustered near $15$ km, indicating a similar large-scale radiative deceleration structure. These results show that ULXP accretion columns develop extended radiation-dominated structures regulated by the mass accretion rate, magnetic scattering opacity, and column geometry. The dynamical profiles obtained here provide a physical basis for interpreting radiation-dominated accretion columns in ULXPs and for future physics-based spectral modeling.

title: Optimization of a Solar-Grid Water Supply System with Hydraulic Energy Storage: A Case Study
abstract: Given the high cost of grid-scale batteries, other energy storage approaches are needed for developing and low-income regions. Elevated volumes of water are often more economically feasible energy storage options than batteries in these contexts. This paper presents a dual-framework modeling approach for one such energy storage setup: a solar-grid hybrid water supply system in the arid Afar region of Ethiopia. By utilizing an elevated 1,900 m3 water reservoir as a "hydraulic battery," the system replaces traditional electrochemical storage, significantly reducing capital expenditures. Using Python for high-resolution technical simulation and Xendee for economic optimization, the study shows a 55.1% solar fraction and a 10% Internal Rate of Return (IRR). The results confirm that hybrid systems with hydraulic storage offer a financially viable and reliable solution for water access in energy-constrained regions.

title: Automated Neural Network Auditing (ANNA) for Energy Market Settlements: A Machine and Reinforcement Learning-Based Approach
abstract: The integration of segmented energy markets into Independent System Operators (ISOs) like CAISO and MISO has increased settlement complexity. Automated transaction processing creates challenges for evaluating accuracy, compliance, and financial integrity. Traditional rule-based manual auditing is inefficient, error-prone, and cannot handle the data volume from automated markets.This research proposes Automated Neural Network Auditing (ANNA), a machine and reinforcement learning framework for settlement auditing via anomaly prioritization. ANNA integrates statistical anomaly detection, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), clustering, and Deep Q-Network (DQN) reinforcement learning to flag potentially anomalous transactions from historical market data. The approach is evaluated as an analyst-support tool for prioritizing transactions needing further audit review.ANNA was tested against traditional statistical methods, clustering-based techniques, and supervised/reinforcement learning models. The study used three years of CAISO settlement data over 63 million source records across 32 charge codes and multiple counterparties. After preprocessing, approximately 2.9 million labeled transactions formed the working dataset, with model-specific subsets used for training and evaluation. Performance was assessed using precision, recall, computational efficiency, and false-negative detection.ANNA outperforms traditional methods by identifying hidden relationships in settlement data, while standard deviation thresholds, K-Means, KNN, and Q-Learning performed poorly across key metrics. The result is a scalable solution integrating machine and reinforcement learning for automated auditing of energy market settlements, contributing computationally efficient anomaly prioritization to settlement-auditing workflows.

title: StatClaim: Study Designs as Types, Protocols as Programs and Statistical Claims as Proof Obligations
abstract: Statistical guarantees depend on the compatibility of a study's model, hypotheses, sampling plan and analysis. StatClaim is a declarative domain-specific language for encoding research protocols and statistical analysis plans as programs built from objects whose types encode their statistical roles within the study design. The compiler checks type compatibility and applies contracts to check additional requirements on the values and relationships of these objects. When verification is requested, StatClaim's backend constructs and checks proofs of supported statistical claims using Lean under stated assumptions. These claims concern Type I error, familywise error, power and interval coverage, including supported combinations of analyses and procedures with planned stopping rules. Reports distinguish formally proved, conditional, cited and author-declared guarantees and provide replayable certificates for verified claims. The same specification supports sample-size searches, power calculations and interval-precision assessment using exact calculations, analytical approximations or reproducible simulation. A command-line interface, editor integration and graphical block editor use a shared compiler and execution layer. Validation reproduces 102 optimal and minimax two-stage designs from Simon's published tables and verifies their error and power bounds in Lean. A clinical trial case study illustrates partial encoding of a published analysis plan using cited methods and conditional proofs. The open-source implementation includes runnable tutorials and examples for specifying and checking study designs before outcomes are collected.

title: MOVER: Planning Beyond Motion
abstract: Residual world models forecast a driving scene through its temporal change, so feature components that stay constant over time vanish from the residual pathway. We ask whether evidence with weak temporal change, such as a waiting pedestrian or a stopped vehicle, can be used more effectively for planning, and introduce MOVER, a complementary event-routing mechanism. A training-time teacher measures how each spatially grounded event query responds when a past frame is removed from shared history and contrasts that sensitivity with the event's pooled temporal residual, prioritizing events that depend on history but receive weak residual evidence. A student predicts the resulting priorities from unperturbed history, so the teacher adds no inference cost. Under fixed total routing mass, one distribution scales a low-rank future bird's-eye-view update and biases trajectory-conditioned event reading. On nuScenes, MOVER reduces ResWorld's UniAD-style average L2 from 0.65 to 0.55 m and its collision rate from 0.23% to 0.12% without direct planner ego status (0.50 m and 0.09% with it), adding 4.1 ms per frame. Matched controls show that the complementary teacher outperforms either signal alone and that the allocation acts mainly during training. Adapted to BridgeDrive-LEAD, MOVER reaches a 96.52 +/- 0.65 driving score over three seeds on the 220-route Bench2Drive closed-loop benchmark, exceeding matched controls in each paired seed by a margin within seed variation.

title: QSRadar: Query-Conditioned Sparse Radar-Camera Fusion for Efficient 3D Object Detection
abstract: Reliable 3D object detection for autonomous trucks requires both the semantic detail provided by cameras and the geometric and motion cues measured by 4D radar. Existing radar-camera detectors commonly construct global radar bird's-eye-view (BEV) representations, whose computational and memory costs grow with the perception range. Sparse query-based detectors offer greater efficiency, but global feature construction can obscure point-level radar geometry and motion information. We present QSRadar, a query-conditioned sparse radar fusion framework for efficient long-range 3D detection. Built on a Sparse4Dv3-style visual-temporal detector, QSRadar retrieves a compact set of raw radar points around each evolving object hypothesis. The selected points are represented in an anchor-aligned coordinate frame, augmented with motion residuals, radar cross section, and sweep timing, and aggregated by a query-conditioned set encoder. Radar neighborhoods are retrieved again after each anchor refinement, coupling evidence selection with object estimation. Under the official MAN TruckScenes validation protocol, QSRadar achieves 38.09 mAP and 52.20 NDS, compared with 37.08 mAP and 50.78 NDS for our reproduced Sparse4D-Radar global Radar-BEV baseline. In matched tests on an RTX 4090 D, QSRadar reduces latency by 45%, peak memory usage by 49%, and GFLOPs by 43%.

title: FlexWAM: Learning Flexible Visual Routing for World Action Models
abstract: Humans dynamically adjust their reliance on sensory modalities across manipulation stages. Although existing World Action Models (WAMs) fuse multi-camera observations, they struggle to adapt their reliance on individual views based on the current observations. This raises a central question: how can the action expert integrate complementary visual evidence while prioritizing the views most relevant to the current action? FlexWAM addresses this challenge through three modules. First, we alternate within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and complementary cues. For action prediction, View-Routed Action Attention uses an observation-conditioned router to prioritize relevant views. To calibrate routing, we train a critic using counterfactual view credit, estimated from action loss sensitivity upon suppressing each view's contribution to action attention. We evaluate FlexWAM with two video backbones on five challenging real-world manipulation tasks across two robot platforms. The two variants improve mean task success by 16.4 and 23.0 percentage points over the strongest baseline. Project website: https://flexwam.github.io/.

title: Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neurons (DAWIN): A Universal Primitive for Continuous-Time Spatiotemporal Learning
abstract: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neuron (DAWIN), a continuous-time primitive for replacing standard neural layers in MLPs, Transformers, and graph neural networks. DAWIN couples spatial projection with elapsed-time-dependent wave excitation and integrates it into a local complex state through closed-form damped evolution, avoiding numerical differential equation solvers. We show that DAWIN generalizes static sinusoidal and memoryless wave neurons on interval-augmented inputs, derive closed-form gradients, and establish bounded-input bounded-output stability for positive damping and sampling intervals bounded away from zero. An associative Triton prefix-scan implementation, DAWINLinear, uses FP32 accumulation and achieves O(log L) parallel depth for sequence length L. Across 11 parameter-matched tasks covering irregular oscillators, MuJoCo dynamics, pedestrian trajectories, and PhysioNet 2012 clinical sequences, DAWIN outperforms Neural CDE on 9 tasks and ReLU-MLP on 8. It achieves the lowest error on dense clinical dynamics (0.9531 NRMSE, winning across all 10 seeds) and ties for the best mortality prediction (0.9993 AUROC). Shuffling elapsed intervals increases error by 58.2%-77.4% on selected dynamics tasks, versus 0.06% on a time-irrelevant control, supporting reliance on physical timing. On NVIDIA B200 GPUs, parallel wave integration accelerates inference by up to 2,630 times over its serial implementation and reduces peak GPU memory by up to 97.6% relative to Mamba in the tested configurations.

title: Design of a Compact Cable-driven 4-DoF Salamander Robotic Limb with Large Range of Motion and High Load Capacity
abstract: A compact yet agile and powerful limb is essential for amphibious legged robots that transition between spine-based swimming and leg-based terrestrial walking, as salamanders do. Salamander limbs combine large ranges of motion (ROM), multiple degrees of freedom (DoFs), and high load capacity. These features enable swinging and body-weight support during walking, as well as folding alongside the body during swimming. Their proximal kinematics can be represented by three rotational DoFs at the hip and one at the knee. Replicating these capabilities within a compact robotic limb is challenging with direct-drive architectures, because multiple joint-mounted actuators must be sufficiently spaced or placed distally to avoid self-collision, increasing limb size and rotational inertia. Here we present a cable-driven 4-DoF salamander robotic limb with a spatial cable-routing architecture that relocates actuators proximally while preserving large ROM and load capacity. Transmission-induced coupling is mitigated by mechanically compensating multi-segment cable paths, model-based feedforward decoupling, and output-side joint angle feedback. Compared with a direct-drive limb, the proposed design reduces mass by 20.4%, projected envelope area by 20.5%, and estimated effective yaw-axis inertia by 31.9%. Experiments verify independent, decoupled control over joint-angle ranges of 45 deg, 118 deg, 118 deg, and 135 deg for hip pitch, yaw, roll, and knee flexion/extension, respectively. During lifting tests, the limb supported an equivalent vertical load of at least 5.4 times its own weight. The proposed limb provides a compact, biologically representative platform for future studies of salamander locomotion and neural control.

title: Fast 4-bit KV-Cache Decoding on Hopper GPUs: Why Existing Kernels Are Slow and How to Fix Them
abstract: A 4-bit KV cache reads about half the bytes of FP8, but Hopper GPUs have no FP4 hardware and little instruction-issue capacity per byte of memory bandwidth, so 4-bit values must be decoded in software. On H200, vLLM's NVFP4 KV path (FlashInfer's decode) reaches 10-20% of memory bandwidth and is up to 1.7x slower than FP8. NVBit instruction counts show two causes: the kernels behind vLLM's 4-bit paths (FlashInfer NVFP4, Triton UltraQuant) execute 2-6x Hopper's issue budget per byte and serialize loading, decoding and matrix multiplies. Our Hopper-native decode kernel overlaps a TMA producer warp with two compute warpgroups, lays the cache out at write time so decoded values feed the tensor cores from registers, and swaps the matrix operands so small query groups need no padding. On H200 it reaches 67-75% of peak bandwidth at batch 32-128 and at all 11 shapes is 1.12-1.49x faster than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4's proposed native FP8. Inside vLLM, with an accuracy recipe (K mean removal and rotation, 4 BF16 sink tokens, BF16 layer 0), it decodes 1.12-1.64x faster per step on Llama-3.1-8B than vLLM's FlashInfer FP8 path at batch 8 and above (1.04-1.24x over FlashAttention-4's FP8), is level at batch 1, and holds 1.63x as many tokens. On one H200 under a reasoning-like request stream, the highest rate at which 99% of requests meet the latency targets is 1.23-1.32x FP8's on Llama-3.1-8B and 1.67-2.20x on Qwen2.5-72B, as the cache becomes the limit; prefill-heavy streams are worse (7% slower prefill). On five 7B-32B models, repeated runs show no significant accuracy difference from BF16 KV. In Qwen2-family models, whose reasoning variants collapse under FP8 KV, layer 0's key mean is almost entirely the key-projection bias identified by prior work, seen through RoPE and computable from the weights alone; keeping that layer in BF16 restores FP8 KV and, with K mean removal, 4-bit KV.

title: Quantum Amplitude Estimation for Ligand and Pose Index Retrieval
abstract: Structure-based virtual screening spans a combinatorial configuration space, motivating a quantum screening framework that targets threshold-qualified configuration indices without reconstructing a complete interaction-score table. Quantum amplitude estimation based on quantum phase estimation (QAE/QPE) supplies finite-resolution phase information to a reversible comparator that writes its decision to FLAG, while optional Grover-style quantum selection (QSEL) amplifies FLAG-selected outcomes and selector measurements identify the ligand, receptor state, rotation, and translation. In an ideal logical benchmark using AutoDock grid interactions as a proof-of-concept model, we evaluated initial FLAG acceptance probability, classification precision, shots required for 95% FLAG detection, and logical Q-operator calls across eight receptor systems and nested libraries of up to 1,024 ligand occupancies. Higher QAE/QPE resolution generally improved classification precision at additional evaluation cost, whereas suitably chosen QSEL iteration counts reduced required shots without improving classification precision, revealing selection and resource trade-offs for extending coherent index retrieval to more physically detailed molecular evaluation models.

title: An Exact Vertex Localization of Zykov's Theorem
abstract: We establish a vertex-based localization of the exact form of Zykov's theorem. For a graph $G$ of order $n\geq1$, let $N(G,K_t)$ denote its number of copies of $K_t$, and let $c(v)$ be the order of a largest clique containing $v$. Write $Z_t(n,s)=N(T_s(n),K_t)$, where $T_s(n)$ is the balanced complete $s$-partite graph on $n$ vertices. We prove that, for every integer $t\geq2$, \[ N(G,K_t)\leq \frac1n\sum_{v\in V(G)}Z_t(n,c(v)). \] Equality holds if and only if $G$ is $K_t$-free or $G\cong T_s(n)$ for some $t\leq s\leq n$. Moreover, the coefficients $Z_t(n,s)$ are pointwise best possible among all bounds of this form. Our result strengthens the previous vertex-localized bound \[ N(G,K_t)\leq n^{t-1} \sum_{v\in V(G)} \frac{\binom{c(v)}{t}}{c(v)^t} \] by accounting for the integer part sizes of Turán graphs. The comparison between the two upper bounds is strict precisely when some vertex $v$ satisfies $c(v)\geq t$ and $c(v)\nmid n$. As consequences, we recover the exact Zykov and Turán bounds without divisibility assumptions.

title: Evidence Toward a Conjecture in List Recoverability of Folded Reed--Solomon Codes
abstract: This paper investigates the list-recoverability of folded Reed--Solomon codes and provides new evidence toward a recent conjecture. Chen--Zhang (STOC 2025) established that for any $\ell,a \ge 2$ and $L = \ell^a - 1$, if a folded Reed--Solomon code of rate $R$ is $(ρ,\ell,L)$-list-recoverable, then $ρ\leq \frac{L+1-\ell}{L+1}(1-\frac{aR}{a-1}).$ It is conjectured that this upper bound is tight. We provide two pieces of evidence concerning this conjecture. First, we prove that explicit folded Reed--Solomon codes of rate arbitrarily close to $\tfrac{a-1}{a+\ell-2}$ are $(0,\ell,L)$-list-recoverable, which confirms the conjecture in the special case $ρ=0$ and $\ell=2$. Second, we show that for any $R\in(0,\tfrac{a-1}{a})$, there are rates arbitrarily close to $R$ at which attaining the conjectured bound requires exponentially large alphabets. This mirrors the phenomenon observed by Alrabiah--Guruswami--Li (SODA 2024), where achieving the generalized Singleton bound in the list-decoding setting also necessitates exponential alphabet size.

title: Discovery-Targeted False Discovery Rate Control
abstract: In exploratory multiple testing, the false discovery rate (FDR) is a commonly used error criterion, and existing methods typically take an FDR level and return a set of discoveries. However, scientists often begin with a target number of discoveries, and accept any FDR level below a reasonable upper limit. Motivated by this practical need, we develop an FDR control approach with a data-driven, discovery-targeted level, which uses synthetic null p-values to split the p-value information between level selection and multiple testing. For independent p-values, the proposal controls finite-sample FDR given the reported level, which can therefore be interpreted in the standard way of a prespecified level. Asymptotically, the number of discoveries and the reported FDR level converge to the target and the optimal value. We also extend the approach to conformal p-values and to include a null proportion estimate. In simulations and real-data examples, the procedure yields a number of discoveries close to the target and smaller FDR levels compared with methods based on e-values or simultaneous false discovery proportion bounds.

title: Model-Assisted Probability of Detection Studies for Image-Based Human Inspection
abstract: Establishing a probability of detection (POD) curve is important for assessing the reliability of components in aging systems. Traditional POD studies rely on physical specimens containing representative flaws and human inspectors who record detection results, making such studies costly. This paper demonstrates how appropriately validated physics-based simulation can substantially reduce, and in suitable applications potentially replace, physical POD experiments. We use XRSIM, an X-ray radiographic simulator, to generate weld images containing cracks of varying size, morphology, and location. Flaw characteristics, locations, and the number of flaws per image were randomized, with images containing zero to three flaws. Each simulated flaw is treated as an observational unit contributing flaw-level hit-miss responses. To capture human inspection variability, the images were presented in random order to five inspectors, each of whom inspected the images twice. The resulting data were analyzed using a repeated-measures binary-regression model accounting for flaw-to-flaw, inspector-to-inspector, flaw/inspector-combination, and inspection-to-inspection variability. Bayesian inference was used to estimate the population-mean POD curve, inspector-specific POD curves, and associated statistical uncertainty. Results show that flaw-to-flaw variability dominates, with appreciable differences among inspectors. The study provides a framework for combining physics-based image simulation with controlled human inspection to estimate POD while reducing the experimental burden of physical specimen fabrication.

title: One UWB Radar, Many Views: Comparing and Fusing Signal Representations for Human Activity Recognition
abstract: IEEE 802.15.4z-compliant impulse-radio ultra-wideband (IR-UWB) transceivers are increasingly built into consumer devices, enabling contactless, privacy-preserving human activity recognition (HAR) in healthcare. Before activity classification, the signal is typically converted into range-time, range-Doppler, or time-Doppler maps, each exposing different spatial and motion cues. Existing comparisons often apply shared processing across representations, leaving it unclear whether their rankings hold after independent tuning. It is also unknown whether rankings and fusion gains generalize across environments and activities, and at what computational cost. Consequently, practitioners lack guidance on which representation and processing suit a given HAR deployment. We release an open dataset of raw IR-UWB measurements collected by a ceiling-mounted radar from 44 participants during scripted activity sequences in 12 layouts across two bedrooms. Using a statistically guided, staged search, we independently tune each representation across five processing and deployment settings. We then compare individual and fused performance under layout and room shifts and quantify computational cost. Across over 1{,}000 cross-validated models, independent tuning proves essential, as optimal processing differs per representation and processing choices shift macro-F1 by up to 26 points, four times the gap between representations. Once tuned, the range-Doppler map leads for unseen layouts (85.1\% macro-F1), while time-Doppler map does for unseen rooms (72.7\%). Fusing all three maps raises these scores to 89.1\% and 80.0\%, respectively. Lower sampling rates and narrower Doppler bands reduce latency by 38--51\% with at most a 1.5-point macro-F1 loss. The best representation for UWB HAR is therefore a deployment decision, not a fixed property.

title: STUN-Bench: Truly Unseen Tools for Evaluating Shared Tool Experience
abstract: A tool router retrieves a few candidate tools per request and lets a language model choose. Methods that share experience across organizations add past requests about each tool to what the router retrieves. StableToolBench calls some of its test groups tests on "unseen" tools, yet the ToolBench instruction pool, which retrievers and experience-sharing methods learn from, contains every test query and labels every gold tool of the two single-tool groups among them. We release STUN-Bench (StableToolBench, Truly UNseen), a split whose experience pool has no item that labels or names 172 held-out tools. Unseen here means absent from shared experience and retriever training data, not from pretraining. On the split we find crowding: experience pooled from five simulated clients, added to an index of tool descriptions, outranks the descriptions of tools no client has used, which then often drop out of the candidate list. Under the Jina-v2 retriever, routing accuracy on held-out tools falls from 0.534 to 0.278. Retrievers trained for tool retrieval lose much less, and keeping experience in a separate index recovers most of the loss under Jina-v2. The split also reverses a conclusion: with every test tool labeled in the pool and our default leak filter applied, shared experience beats descriptions alone; on STUN-Bench it falls below them. The split, leak filter and evaluation harness are available at https://github.com/<org>/STUN-Bench.

title: TRAE: Trustworthy Automated ESG Annotation via Multi-Agent Consensus and Confidence Assessment
abstract: With the growing demand for ESG disclosure and evaluation, constructing high-quality datasets for automatically extracting ESG-related information from large-scale documents has become essential. However, ESG annotation remains challenging due to strong context dependence, ambiguous label boundaries, and the need for domain expertise, resulting in high annotation cost and limited scalability. To address these challenges, we propose TRAE (TRustworthy Automated ESG annotation), a multi-agent framework for scalable and reliable ESG data construction. Unlike direct LLM-based annotation, TRAE evaluates annotation reliability by modeling agreement, confidence, and reasoning consistency among multiple agents through a structured multi-step reasoning process. Experimental results demonstrate that TRAE improves annotation performance compared with existing automated annotation strategies. Furthermore, TRAE supports a hybrid human-AI annotation strategy that assigns expert labeling only to uncertain samples, reducing annotation cost while preserving data quality. Using TRAE, we construct a high-quality ESG dataset containing approximately 20,000 instances with complete reasoning traces, intermediate agent outputs, and reliability information to enhance transparency and reproducibility. Overall, this work provides a practical and scalable framework for trustworthy ESG data construction. The code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/nowzer0/TRAE.

title: On the extension of non-faithful and non-normal traces of von Neumann algebras to their affiliated operators
abstract: Let $τ$ be a positive tracial functional on a finite von Neumann algebra ${\mathcal{M}}$, not necessarily normal. For a positive self-adjoint operator $A$ affiliated with ${\mathcal{M}}$ we define ${τ_{\mathrm{Y}}}(A)=\lim_{h\downarrow0}τ(A(\mathrm{I}+hA)^{-1})\in[0,\infty]$. We show that $τ_{\mathrm{Y}}(A)=\sup_Rτ(\min(A,R \mathrm{I}))$. We prove that ${τ_{\mathrm{Y}}}$ is additive on positive affiliated operators, by a form--resolvent comparison valid for arbitrary positive traces. As a consequence, $τ$ has a positive linear extension to the span $\mathscr D_τ$ of the positive affiliated operators of finite extended trace, and $τ_{\mathrm{Y}}(T^*T)$ defines a pre-Hilbert structure for every positive trace. For every trace, $τ_{\mathrm{Y}}(|S+T|)^{2/3}\le τ_{\mathrm{Y}}(|S|)^{2/3}+τ_{\mathrm{Y}}(|T|)^{2/3}$; hence the operators $T$ with $τ_{\mathrm{Y}}(|T|)<\infty$ form a ${\mathcal{M}}$-bimodule $\mathscr L_Y^1$, on which the linear extension is defined and cyclic. It turns out that $\mathscr L_Y^1=\mathscr D_τ$; $d(S,T)={τ_{\mathrm{Y}}}(|S-T|)^{2/3}$ is a translation-invariant pseudometric on $\mathscr L^1_Y$ and is a metric iff $τ$ is faithful. On the approximation side, a Chernoff family in ${\mathcal{M}}$ forces affiliation of its generator. Trace defects of Chernoff families need not converge to ${τ_{\mathrm{Y}}}(A)$, even for faithful normal traces, while two-sided resolvent comparison suffices. For faithful normal traces, ${τ_{\mathrm{Y}}}$ is the canonical extension and the associated space $\mathscr L_Y^p$ coincide with the classical $L^p({\mathcal{M}},τ)$ as well as their norms ($1\leq p<\infty$).

title: CSI-Agnostic End-to-End Neural Decoding of LDPC Codes under Synchronization Errors
abstract: Correcting synchronization errors (insertions, deletions, and substitutions) in concatenated coding schemes, typically comprising an inner marker code and an outer Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) code, poses a significant challenge. Traditional algebraic decoding fails entirely under sequence misalignment. While recent neural pipelines attempt to resolve this, they typically demand exact channel state information (CSI) for inner synchronization and suffer from error propagation caused by premature syndrome binarization before outer decoding. In this paper, we propose ASDecoder, a data-driven, CSI-agnostic end-to-end neural decoding architecture specifically designed for LDPC codes over insertion-deletion-substitution (IDS) channels. ASDecoder features a CNN-Transformer front-end that implicitly aligns variable-length sequences and fuses multi-read redundancies without requiring explicit CSI. Tightly integrated into this pipeline is a novel \emph{syndrome-free} BiDecoder back-end. By mapping continuous soft features directly into a sparse-masked graph attention network, it strictly avoids intermediate hard decisions and effectively captures topological constraints. Experiments demonstrate that a single universal ASDecoder outperforms the BCJRFormer baseline, providing consistent error correction across highly asymmetric channels. Furthermore, it generalizes robustly to real-world deployment scenarios, including the industrial CCSDS $(128,64)$ QC-LDPC standard and non-linear DNA biological constraints.

title: Super-Multiplicativity of the Noncommutative Minimum and Applications to Quantum Privacy and Hypothesis Testing
abstract: The hockey-stick divergence is a fundamental distinguishability measure in quantum information theory. It characterizes quantum differential privacy and determines the optimal error probability of binary quantum hypothesis testing with arbitrary priors. We study how it behaves on tensor-product states. To this end, we consider the noncommutative minimum $m(A,B):=(\mathrm{Tr}[A]+\mathrm{Tr}[B]-\|A-B\|_1)/2$ of positive semidefinite operators, which reduces to $\sum_x\min\{a_x,b_x\}$ when $A$ and $B$ commute, and we prove that it is super-multiplicative, i.e., $m(A\otimes C,B\otimes D)\ge m(A,B)\,m(C,D)$. As a consequence, we establish a sub-additivity property of the hockey-stick divergence on product states, in which the parameters of the individual systems are multiplied, and no additional prefactor appears. We show that this bound is tight, also for noncommuting states, and that it is strict for faithful states whenever at least two of the divergences are positive. Using this, we obtain sub-additivity of the Datta-Leditzky divergences, a parallel composition theorem for quantum differentially private channels under product neighboring inputs with at most linear degradation of the privacy parameters, and a sharp sub-additivity property of the hypothesis-testing relative entropy normalized by the acceptance probability. Finally, we apply the same tools to symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing. We determine the exact prefactor of the quantum Chernoff bound for every pair of noncommuting states satisfying mild conditions including a nonlattice condition and, under a quantitative version of this condition, the full asymptotic expansion to every fixed order in $1/n$, with explicitly computable coefficients. As a consequence, we determine the sample complexity of symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing up to one sample, as the error probability tends to zero.

title: Geometric Polarization-Virial Theorems for Field-Induced Dipolar Interactions and Force Reversal
abstract: Electric fields can turn attraction into repulsion between far-separated atoms, yet the complete angular mechanical structure governing this reversal has remained unknown. Here, we uncover an entropy-like geometric structure: the cubically weighted interaction free energy, r^3 F(r), is nondecreasing under physical dilation. This structure unifies two exact polarization-virial theorems for arbitrary stable quasistatic dipole assemblies and fully retarded dipole pairs under stated conditions. Consequently, the free energy has at most one zero and energetic cancellation precedes mechanical cancellation. A force zero retains strictly positive energy, whereas an energy zero retains an attractive force. The resulting analytical angular fine structure is resolved by a quantum harmonic oscillator pair, yielding the complete arbitrary-angle interaction energy and radial force that recover quantum-perturbative results. The conventional dipolar magic angle splits into strictly ordered energy- and force-zero angles; the latter uniquely bounds the radially repulsive sector and carries a positive energy barrier. Derived scaling laws and finite-sphere calculations provide experimentally testable signatures from microscopic dipoles to macroscopic polarizable bodies.

title: Teaching How to Reason, Beyond What to Answer: Evidence-Faithful On-Policy Distillation for streaming video understanding
abstract: Moment Retrieval (MR) aims to localize the temporal segment in a video that corresponds to a given textual description. However, a textual query often provides only a sparse semantic description of the target event, whereas the video contains rich and fine-grained visual variations. This mismatch creates an inherent gap between textual semantics and visual content, making a single textual input insufficient for precise cross-modal alignment. As a result, when multiple temporally adjacent or semantically similar segments exist, the model may struggle to distinguish the target moment from confusing candidates. To address this challenge, we propose a Multi-Perspective Auxiliary Representation (MPAR) framework, which aims to bridge this alignment gap by enriching a single textual input with complementary visual cues from multiple perspectives. Specifically, MPAR consists of three key components: (1) Auxiliary Representation Initialization (ARI) constructs multiple learnable representation slots from the original query, preserving the query intent while preparing flexible carriers for subsequent visual cue injection; (2) Visual-Induced Semantic Structuring (VISS) injects target-specific visual attributes into each representation while preserving semantic coherence with the original query; and (3) Multi-Perspective Semantic Aligner (MPSA) aligns each auxiliary representation with corresponding video regions to enhance discriminative localization. By constructing multi-perspective auxiliary representations and guiding the model to attend to relevant visual regions across these representations, our model achieves more accurate moment localization. Extensive experiments on MR benchmarks demonstrate that our MPAR outperforms state-of-the-art methods, validating the effectiveness of MPAR.

title: Spiking World-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how the world responds to actions and offer a promising path toward general embodied intelligence, but they are large and run the network many times per plan, so they are hard to deploy on robots. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) compute with sparse binary spikes and use additions instead of multiplications, which saves power. However, existing WAMs use dense videos as the world state, so a spiking version would spend most of its computation on the background. We therefore introduce SpikingWAM, the first spiking WAM, which uses a sparse task skeleton as the world state. Inspired by biological motor control, which attends only to the key positions of a task, the Task Skeleton State (TSS) keeps the keypoints of the arm and the task objects, and a small spiking front end estimates the object keypoints from images. Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA) keep millimetre precision, and the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR) runs the network once per plan. On the simulated benchmarks LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, SpikingWAM achieves competitive success rates with far less energy than ANN methods and surpasses all compared methods on LIBERO-Plus. Real robot experiments further confirm its effectiveness. These results show that a task skeleton lets spiking networks implement WAMs at very low energy, offering a new solution for low power embodied intelligence. Project page: https://wxqnl.github.io/spikingwam/

title: SWAM: State-aware World Action Model for Multi-Agent 3D Environments
abstract: Interactive world models generate virtual environments autoregressively from player actions and visual history. However, visual history alone cannot reliably capture the evolving states of independently acting non-player characters (NPCs) in real games, particularly when they are outside the camera view. Recent multi-agent world models address this challenge through joint multi-view generation or persistent shared state, but often rely on external observations, like maps or scene geometry, or predefined state transitions. We present SWAM, a State-aware World Action Model that separates agent-state evolution from autoregressive visual generation in interactive 3D environments. A lightweight state model propagates character dynamics from actions without consuming generated frames, combining motion priors with learned scene-dependent corrections. The predicted states then guide an autoregressive diffusion transformer alongside visual history through a novel conditioning scheme. Rather than requiring an explicit scene geometry map or visibility tests, the conditioning indicates where characters may appear, allowing the diffusion model to learn their appearance and occlusion. This design enables NPCs to evolve independently of visual generation while maintaining consistent observations across visibility changes, interactions, and respawns. Evaluations in a custom Godot-based first-person shooter game demonstrate improvements in visual fidelity, NPC consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing approaches.

title: Domain advantage in two-dimensional quantum-device design with multi-modal agentic harness
abstract: High-quality two-dimensional quantum devices are commonly fabricated from mechanically exfoliated crystals, whose irregular shapes and placement require a lithographic layout tailored to each specimen. Drawing these layouts remains largely manual. We introduce qlaybench, a benchmark that tests whether language-model agents can turn microscope images and experimental requirements into device layouts that fit the specimen. Agents with conventional tools often construct devices when material outlines are supplied, but struggle to identify those outlines from images. Modelled on the human workflow, qlaybot, a multimodal agentic harness, connects image interpretation to the tools used to align images, draw device features and inspect the resulting layout. We evaluate each layout with checks drawn from practical design experience, asking whether it fits the specimen and connects its intended components. With greater computational effort, an agent using qlaybot passes 81.5% of the benchmark tasks, compared with 24.1% when it uses conventional tools. This domain advantage highlights the importance of connecting scientific interpretation of a specimen to geometric design and provides a route towards reducing manual effort in two-dimensional quantum-device fabrication.

title: The response field approach to path integral control
abstract: This paper investigates non-linear path integral control problems within the response field formalism of nonequilibrium field theory. The aim of this work is exploratory, based on the identification of correspondences between backward adjoint processes and the response field of non-equilibrium statistical physics, whose properties have not been set out in an optimal control setting. The response field is found to play an analogous role to the backward adjoint process under the stochastic maximum principle. In particular, the gradient of the optimal cost-to-go at the initial time, which is proportional to the optimal control, is given by the average of the response field at the initial time. In contrast to the case of non-equilibrium dynamics, the response function is found to be acausal in the control setting. The linear-quadratic case of path integral control is studied, confirming it as the free theory, meaning that solving the control problem is equivalent to completing the square and determining the propagator for a two point boundary value problem. The developments presented here are a necessary prelude to applications based on field theoretic approximation, for both path integral control and their dual inference problems.

title: The Entangled Veil: Why Redistribution Requires a New Language
abstract: The Rawlsian veil of ignorance requires choosing principles of justice without knowing which position-temporal, spatial, social, or personal one will occupy. We argue that this object cannot be represented faithfully within standard economic models. A faithful representation must satisfy three requirements: it must treat all generations symmetrically, capture non-separable correlations among positions, and allow mobility costs to vary across locations and occupations. We show that standard optimal-tax models violate at least one requirement, and that the minimal framework satisfying all three is a geometric framework adapted from string theory, in which the veil is an entangled state over a space of possible life situations. We derive full equalization as a first-best benchmark, the emergence of separated clusters when correlations reward distinction, a symmetry between intraand inter-generational equity, and a tunneling mechanism by which correlations reduce institutional barriers. The model generates four inequality profiles and four inequality types. The estimates are quantitatively important: the framework changes the ranking of redistributive policies, and ignoring the margins it identifies leads to systematically biased policy evaluation.

title: Wasserstein Penalisation as an Endogenous Breadth Constraint in Penalised Mean-Variance Portfolio Selection
abstract: A manager who wants a long-only book and has read that Wasserstein-robust mean-variance selection improves risk-adjusted performance faces two decisions: how much robustness to buy, and how diversified to be. In the long-only problem, and for the penalised scalarisation of the robust objective, these are the same decision: the robustification term depends on the weight vector alone, so on the simplex the radius prices effective breadth and nothing else. The equivalence is specific to that scalarisation; it fails for the return-floored form, where the radius also raises the return threshold, and for the exact robust risk-minimisation problem. Two consequences follow. First, a negative one needing no alpha: positive definiteness of the covariance does not imply breadth, since no bound on the dispersion of the mean and no positive spectral floor prevents the long-only optimum from collapsing onto a single asset, so the breadth of the minimum-variance benchmark is an irreducible input. Second, identification: matched to a benchmark with the same effective number of holdings, the robust portfolio attains the same mean-variance value to solver precision, so the radius carries no in-sample information beyond breadth selection, and the residual weight difference lives in near-null directions of the covariance. On fourteen A-share panels the ex post comparison is exact by construction, hence no evidence. The informative test fixes breadth before the window is used: a cap set to the historical level of the robust portfolio's realised breadth recovers about five sixths of its gain, leaving a residual of seven to eleven basis points per day across five tracking rules, whereas a fixed target recovers only a quarter to two fifths. The robust portfolio is thus a breadth rule, not a fixed breadth choice. We close with a reporting standard that makes the attribution checkable.

title: RoboLiveMem: Is Robot Memory Solved When the World Does Not Wait?
abstract: Robot agents built on frontier vision-language models now solve most robot memory benchmarks. Does this mean they can remember what they need in a home, where people and machines keep moving things? Existing memory benchmarks cannot answer this question, because they pause the simulator while the model thinks: nothing can change during a decision, so whatever the robot remembers is still true when it acts. We introduce RoboLiveMem, a benchmark that runs the same memory tasks twice, once with the world paused while the model thinks and once with the world running. It contains 29 task families in three tiers, from 16 realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes of homes, workshops and a restaurant to controlled ManiSkill tasks. Every task mixes real changes with harmless look-alikes and runs without any change, so that no fixed strategy succeeds, and most tasks have a twin that keeps the change in view, which separates forgetting from acting too late. Testing 16 models on 34,176 episodes, we find three surprises. (1) Paused results hide the problem: when a remembered object changes in a realistic scene, the 8 Claude and GPT models succeed in 97% of episodes on average with the world paused, but in only 50% with the world running, and their ranking changes: Claude Opus 5.5, which never fails when paused, succeeds in 44%. (2) Speed is not the fix: slower models do no worse, and models given only 2 s per decision still fall at least 36 points below their paused success. (3) Models see the change but act on camera frames from before it ended. Looking again just before acting closes most of the realistic gap, yet when identical objects are swapped several times, all nine models we test still lose points to memory.

title: On Self-orthogonal MDS Codes
abstract: Both self-orthogonal codes and MDS codes are of great interest for coding and combinatorial theory. In this paper we consider the existence problem of self-orthogonal MDS codes, i.e, codes satisfying self-orthogonality and achieving the Singleton bound. More precisely, we investigate for which length $n$ and dimension $k$, there exist $q$-ary $[n,k]$ self-orthogonal MDS codes. We completely solve this problem for even prime power $q$ except for the case where $[n,k]=[q+2,3]$. For odd prime power $q$, we solve this problem for the cases where $n=q+1$, $n|q$ or $n|(q-1)$ except for two cases where (i) $[n,k]=[q+1, (q-1)/2]$; and (ii) $[n,k]=[q-1,(q-1)/2]$ and $q\equiv 1\pmod{4}$. Furthermore, we conjecture nonexistence of self-orthogonal MDS code for the first case. For odd $q$, we also show existence of self-orthogonal MDS codes for some other cases. Note that in general a self-orthogonal MDS code can not be derived from self-dual MDS codes (see the detailed discussion in Section 1). Our technique is to make use of the language of algebraic geometry codes. An advantage of using the language of algebraic geometry codes is that the Euclidean dual code of a functional algebraic geometry code is a differential code which can be turn into a functional code again. Thus, by choosing an appropriate differential, one can give an explicit construction of self-orthogonal MDS codes.

title: AIRPiano: Piano Score Following with Tabletop Hand Gestures
abstract: AIRPiano aims to bring sound to the common practice of rehearsing piano music on a tabletop. Guided by a known score, users make piano-like finger movements on a flat surface without reproducing absolute keyboard positions. The score supplies pitches, while hand motion determines which score events to play and when. We formulate this interaction as online alignment between tabletop hand motion and symbolic score events. To address the ambiguity of tabletop motion, its differences from piano-playing motion, and the scarcity of aligned motion-score data, we develop motion and score representations, build a data processing pipeline, and train a Transformer with supervised attention on existing piano performance recordings. We further design a streaming inference framework that combines local alignment predictions with sequence tracking for real-time interaction. We construct two evaluation sets, VSF-Piano and VSF-Tabletop, to assess alignment on piano and tabletop performances, respectively. After a post-hoc global timing adjustment, AIRPiano achieves a mean chord alignment rate of 74% within a 133 ms tolerance on the paired subset of VSF-Tabletop, compared with 79% on VSF-Piano.

title: PsyDrift: Healthy-Reference Latent Diffusion for Anomaly Scoring in Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract: Individual heterogeneity and acquisition-site variability complicate neuroimaging-based characterization of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We propose PsyDrift, combining ASD/healthy-control-supervised functional-connectivity representations with healthy-reference latent diffusion. An encoder produces 128-dimensional representations, and a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) learns exclusively from healthy training latents. Distance from a diffusion-denoised reconstruction provides a continuous deviation score. We evaluate 1,102 subjects from all 20 ABIDE-I sites using five-seed leave-one-site-out cross-validation. The classifier and DDPM achieve mean-site AUROCs of $0.798 \pm 0.003$ and $0.718 \pm 0.013$, respectively; uncertainties denote seed standard deviations. Matched healthy-reference scorers on the same representation achieve 0.68-0.71; the statistical significance of diffusion's modest numerical advantage remains unestablished. Within ASD, scores show weak associations with ADOS Total (Spearman $ρ= 0.108$, $p = 0.038$) and full-scale IQ ($ρ= -0.138$, $p = 0.002$), without adjustment for age, sex, site, or head motion. Frozen evaluation without retraining or hyperparameter adaptation yields pooled AUROCs of 0.69 on ABIDE-II and 0.61 on ADHD-200, providing preliminary evidence of cross-cohort and cross-disorder transfer. These results demonstrate healthy-reference deviation scoring within an ASD-supervised representation; incremental predictive and clinical value remains unestablished.

title: MIMO Integrated Sensing and Communications: A Fisher-based Local Mutual Information Approach
abstract: Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) beamforming requires a sensing utility that is compatible with the communication rate and aligned with per-target angle estimation. Fisher information (FI)/Cramér--Rao bound (CRB) criteria depend on the angular units and generally involve coupled multi-target matrices, whereas sensing mutual information (SMI) is typically defined on aggregate response variables. This paper proposes Fisher-based local mutual information (F-LMI), a prior-aware bit-domain utility for multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) ISAC. F-LMI linearizes each target-specific range-compressed statistic around the angular prior mean and yields a closed-form local information gain.
