In the single-target case, it admits a Bayesian CRB (BCRB) log-ratio interpretation and is a locally consistent surrogate for the nonlinear parameter MI. For multiple targets, the prior-induced variations of the non-intended targets are marginalized into a beamformer-dependent interference-plus-noise covariance in each branch. We derive a fractional-programming algorithm with linear-system updates and scalar bisection. Monte Carlo simulations with nonlinear target-wise posterior-mean receivers show that F-LMI reduces the root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 5.0--14.7\% relative to a target-indexed Bayesian-bound baseline at two matched rates in a closely spaced layout. Under a common basis-selection protocol, it also attains lower branch RMSE than aggregate and joint criteria.

title: ESGPT: A Data-Centric ESG Language Model with Unified Instruction and Benchmark Resources
abstract: ESG analysis requires complex language understanding across diverse sources, including corporate reports, news, and disclosures, for tasks such as ESG relevance detection, action interpretation, impact analysis, and question answering. However, existing ESG datasets are fragmented by task and source, with heterogeneous formats and annotation schemes, limiting their use for training general-purpose ESG LLMs and unified evaluation. In this work, we construct ESG-Instruct, a 30,000-instance ESG instruction dataset built from public ESG resources, and ESGU-Bench, an ESG understanding benchmark covering six representative ESG tasks. Based on these resources, we further develop ESGPT, an 8B ESG-specialized LLM, and evaluate it against diverse open-source and API-based LLMs. Experimental results show that general-purpose LLMs exhibit substantial performance variation across ESG tasks, while ESGPT, despite its relatively small scale, achieves the best performance on multiple ESG tasks. This work provides unified data and benchmark resources for training and evaluating ESG-specialized LLMs.

title: Trajectory arclength reveals thermodynamic criticality
abstract: Thermodynamic criticality arises at continuous phase transitions, where collective interactions produce non-analytic behavior in equilibrium thermodynamic quantities in the thermodynamic limit. We show that this criticality also leaves an analytically predictable signature in the arclength of microscopic Hamiltonian trajectories. For the attractive Hamiltonian mean-field model, we derive the thermodynamic limit of the equilibrium-averaged arclength, formulated as a normalized Lagrangian descriptor, and demonstrate that it develops a kink precisely at the phase transition. We trace this non-analyticity to spontaneous magnetization and derive the leading critical finite-size correction, scaling as $N^{-1/2}$ with an explicit analytical prefactor. Simulations with up to $10^5$ degrees of freedom confirm both predictions without adjustable parameters. Requiring neither tangent-space evolution nor prior specification of an order parameter for its computation, trajectory arclength provides a simple, quantitative link between microscopic Hamiltonian motion and collective thermodynamic criticality.

title: Environmental dependence of the properties of H$α$ emitters in the extremely massive galaxy protoclusters BOSS1244 and BOSS1542 at $z = 2.24$
abstract: Protoclusters, the progenitors of galaxy clusters, provide ideal laboratories for studying how high-density environments influence galaxy formation and evolution at early cosmic epochs. It remains unclear whether environmental effects on galaxy properties over scales of $>30$ cMpc are already in place at $z > 2$ and how these effects depend on the evolutionary stage of large-scale structures. We investigate the physical properties of H$α$ emitters (HAEs) in two extremely overdense protoclusters, BOSS1244 and BOSS1542, at $z = 2.24$, and explore the environmental dependence of galaxy properties at this redshift. In BOSS1244, we find a clear color-density and stellar mass-density relation. HAEs in higher-density regions are significantly redder in $z_{\rm s}-K_{\rm s}$ and more massive than those in lower-density regions. In contrast, BOSS1542 shows weak or no such correlations. Red HAEs $(z_{\rm s}-K_{\rm s}>2.5)$ in both fields are preferentially located in the densest cores, have high stellar masses $(>10^{11}\,M_{\odot})$, high SFRs, and are $4-7$ times more abundant than in general fields. The irregular morphologies observed in some red HAEs are consistent with ongoing mass assembly and may be associated with dust-obscured star formation or galaxy interactions. Both protoclusters broadly follow the star-forming main sequence, but BOSS1542 exhibits a steeper slope, indicating more active star formation in massive galaxies. Our results demonstrate that environmental effects on galaxy properties operate over scales of $\sim39$\,cMpc at $z=2.24$, but their manifestation is strongly dependent on the evolutionary state of the large-scale structure. BOSS1244 appears more evolved, with ongoing galaxy merging and possible quenching, while BOSS1542 remains in an early, filamentary, gas-rich phase.

title: Bi-Refine: Semantic Verification-Guided Progressive Refinement for Moment Retrieval
abstract: Moment Retrieval (MR) aims to identify the temporal segment in an untrimmed video that corresponds to a natural language query. Existing approaches commonly refine temporal predictions within the localization pathway, without explicitly verifying candidate-level semantic consistency. Moreover, directly reusing semantic scores as feedback can cause over-correction when the verification signal is unreliable. To address these issues, we propose Bi-Refine, a semantic verification-guided progressive refinement framework that formulates MR as a closed-loop verification-and-refinement process. A Heuristic Localization Branch first generates candidate moments, while a Semantic Verification Branch evaluates their query consistency in a semantically enriched latent space. Query supervision further trains the verifier with the same candidate moment but different queries, encouraging it to distinguish the matched query from semantically similar mismatched queries. The resulting verification features are incorporated into a Progressive Refinement Loop that updates both query representations and multimodal features. To suppress potentially harmful updates, a lightweight reliability estimator gates query updates and reweights candidate contributions in feature feedback. A convergence-based adaptive stopping strategy additionally terminates unnecessary refinement during inference. Experiments on three standard MR benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and state-of-the-art performance of our method.

title: H(n)-Gordian graphs of knotoids and their quotients: Gromov hyperbolicity
abstract: In this paper, we study $H(n)$-moves on knotoid diagrams and the corresponding $H(n)$-Gordian graphs. We establish that the $H(n)$-Gordian graphs of knotoids are not Gromov hyperbolic. We also consider quotient graphs of the $H(n)$-Gordian graph of knotoids by the following knotoid invariants: the height of a knotoid, the span of the affine index polynomial, the $y$-span and $z$-span of the invariant $H_K(t, y, z)$, and the span of the Jones polynomial. We prove that in all these cases, the quotient graphs are Gromov hyperbolic.

title: FireDesmoke: Fire Smoke Removal via Real Smoke Transfer and Semantic Rectification
abstract: Fire smoke removal must restore dense and medium smoke regions while preserving the clear (smoke-free) content. Existing methods either leave the smoke or alter the visible content, and generative models may hallucinate people or remove flames. Real fire smoke is spatially local: the degradation and its corruption of semantic features are both concentrated in the smoke regions. We propose FireDesmoke, built on this locality: Real Smoke Transfer calibrates smoke fields on real-fire recordings and transfers their spatial layout onto clean images to synthesize training pairs, and Semantic Rectification uses pixel features to rectify the tokens of a frozen foundation encoder where smoke corrupts them. With matched training budgets, replacing the transferred pairs with SmokeBench pairs lowers dense-smoke PSNR by 0.74 dB, and removing Semantic Rectification leaves clear regions 1.31 dB below the input. On what is, to the best of our knowledge, the first paired dataset of real fire smoke for image restoration, with 1,500 test frames from a held-out viewpoint, FireDesmoke improves dense- and medium-smoke PSNR by 3.73 and 2.63 dB while keeping clear regions at the input level (+0.41 dB); no other compared method gains at least 1 dB in dense smoke without lowering clear-region PSNR, and no hallucinated person is found in its outputs. It achieves state-of-the-art overall results on this benchmark and, trained on SmokeBench, the highest PSNR with the second-best SSIM and LPIPS.

title: Solids activated by multi-body nonreciprocity
abstract: Field-mediated forces between particles can be both nonreciprocal and irreducibly multi-body, giving rise to emergent activity in systems of individually passive particles. While prior work extensively studied how multi-body nonreciprocity can activate few-body systems, fuel intermittency, and drive liquid-like behavior, the effect on the solid state of large particle ensembles is less explored. Here we use two-dimensional, close-packed rafts of identical, athermal, acoustically levitated microspheres to show how multi-body nonreciprocity injects activity in solids. At the level of both individual particles and collective dynamics, crystalline rafts exhibit persistent circulations with no net handedness. The rafts also exhibit a phonon-like dispersion relation corresponding to a large Poisson ratio, indicating an induced softness to shear. Within the bulk, lattice symmetry masks microscopic nonreciprocity, although it can manifest in renormalized, reciprocal elastic coefficients. At dislocations and raft edges, where this symmetry is broken, multi-body nonreciprocal interactions act as local generators of activity. A coarse-grained microscopic model of multi-body nonreciprocity, calibrated on three-particle simulations, recovers the rafts' experimentally observed dispersion relations and localized activity. Using these findings, we illustrate how to harness defect-induced activity for programmable movement by arranging microscopic dislocations to drive macroscopic propulsion and rotation of a whole raft.

title: Beyond Binary Correctness: A Surrogate for Confidence Learning in Large Language and Vision-Language Models
abstract: Confidence estimation for large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) aims to assess how likely a particular generated response is to be correct. We investigate how learning this assessment can benefit from the model's predictive reliability on the underlying query. Binary correctness supervision, however, assigns identical labels to occasional errors and frequent failures, as well as isolated successes and consistent success. These outcomes can arise from substantially different predictive behavior under stochastic decoding. We propose a confidence-learning framework that supplements realized response correctness with query-level predictive reliability. We estimate reliability through repeated generations under a fixed model and decoding configuration, then combine the empirical success rate with individual correctness to construct a graded confidence surrogate. The surrogate differentiates responses sharing the same correctness label while preserving the average predictive reliability of the sampled response pool. To learn this target, we condition an independent confidence estimator on the query and its full generated response, and optimize backbone LoRA adapters together with a projection and scalar confidence head using mean squared error. Repeated sampling is required only for supervision construction; inference scores an individual response without additional generations. We establish ordering and mean preservation properties of the surrogate and derive a selective-risk bound connecting population surrogate prediction error to the error rate among accepted responses. We evaluate the framework across language and vision-language models, examining confidence calibration and selective prediction.

title: Growth versus boundedness for viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equations with a forcing term: a Fujita-type dichotomy
abstract: We study the Cauchy problem $u_t=Δu+|\nabla u|^q+a(t)w(x)$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$, where $q>1$ and the integrable forcing has positive total mass. Unlike classical Fujita problems, regular solutions exist globally, so the relevant dichotomy concerns boundedness versus grow-up. We identify the critical exponent $q_c=N/(N-1)$ for $N\geq 2$, with $q_c=\infty$ for $N=1$. For stationary forcing, every solution grows at least linearly on a fixed ball when $1<q\leq q_c$. In two dimensions, solutions tend to infinity locally uniformly for every $q>1$, with an explicit logarithmic lower bound. For $q=2$, the Cole--Hopf transformation relates the exact growth rate to the spectrum of $-Δ-w$. Conversely, when $N\geq 3$ and $q>q_c$, bounded solutions exist for sufficiently small nonnegative data and forcing. We also establish growth criteria for time-dependent forcing, including decaying profiles.

title: EVD-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for EEG-to-Image Decoding
abstract: EEG-to-image decoding recovers visual information from non-invasive brain recordings, providing a window into human perception. However, comparisons across systems are confounded by a variable that is rarely reported as such: which participants' data the system was allowed to use. The same Top-1 score on a 200-way gallery may come from a per-participant system, a pooled model over all participants, or a model that never saw the test participant---cases that differ by more than most architectural changes between the methods being compared. We present \bench, a benchmark on THINGS-EEG2 that standardizes the gallery and EEG input, matches training budgets across systems within each regime, and compares three participant-access regimes: within-subject, joint-subject, and strict leave-one-subject-out, with unlabeled target calibration reported separately. All three settings evaluate concept-level zero-shot retrieval: the 200 test concepts are disjoint from the 1,654 concepts used for EEG--image fitting and validation. We compare retrieval across access regimes and use zero-EEG and matched-wrong EEG controls to assess dependence on correct EEG--stimulus pairing. We vary trial averaging, gallery size and difficulty, and training data coverage, and compare target adaptation and visual feature targets. We also assess sensitivity to EEG window length and channel count, robustness to input perturbations, and confidence calibration. These results establish participant-access regime as a necessary reporting dimension alongside gallery, repetition, and visual target.

title: What Do Co-Folding Models Learn? Insights from Enhanced Transition Path Sampling
abstract: Co-folding models are diffusion-based generative models that sample biomolecular complexes from distributions learned on a large corpus of experimental data. Although these models are powerful for structure prediction, it remains unclear whether the conformational ensembles they learn resemble physically meaningful statistical ensembles. To understand what these models learn, we introduce transition path sampling (TPS), which uses Markov chain Monte Carlo over denoising trajectories to sample the learned distribution. Because its Monte Carlo trajectories resemble biomolecular dynamics, TPS couples directly with enhanced-sampling techniques to recover the full conformational ensemble. Applied to Boltz-2, enhanced TPS reveals physical conformational changes biased toward crystal-like states near the training data, indicating both learned physics and memorization. These results suggest new ways to evaluate and improve co-folding models by jointly assessing structural recovery, proximity to training data, and conformational ensembles.

title: LaTSEC: Lattice-Based Threshold Signatures with Native Non-Interactive Identifiable Abort and Compact Per-Party Storage
abstract: We present $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$, a three-round lattice-based threshold signature scheme with native non-interactive identifiable abort. Each party holds one small-norm signing share and is associated with one public abort key, against which its partial signature is verified directly, without zero-knowledge proofs or an additional interactive protocol. Prior lattice-based threshold signatures that identify misbehaving parties rely on one of three mechanisms: zero-knowledge proofs, an additional interactive protocol, or an everywhere-short secret sharing scheme in which each party holds multiple signing shares, each with its own public abort key. Compared with schemes that use the third mechanism, $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$ substantially reduces per-party storage. The construction uses $\mathsf{SEC}$, a recent ramp everywhere-short secret sharing scheme based on lossless expanders that gives each party a single short share. We prove correctness, identifiable-abort security, and threshold unforgeability under the standard $\mathsf{MLWE}$ and $\mathsf{MSIS}$ assumptions. The unforgeability proof introduces the Repeated-$\boldsymbol{A}$ Matrix Hint-MLWE problem, a new variant of $\mathsf{MLWE}$ with hints that captures the complete tuple of correlated public abort keys. We rigorously prove that this new variant admits a reduction from the standard $\mathsf{MLWE}$ problem. For 60 parties at 128-bit security, $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$ tolerates up to 6 corrupted parties, and, empirically, a randomly chosen set of at least 46 parties can sign with probability at least 0.99. Each party holds one signing share of about 14.3 KiB and is associated with one 24-KiB public abort key.

title: How Latent Transition Geometry Matters for Planning in World Models
abstract: World models support planning by predicting how the environment evolves under candidate actions. However, one-step predictive accuracy alone does not characterize multi-step planning utility, which depends on distinguishing candidate futures. This raises a natural question: How does latent transition geometry shape planning? We investigate this through an action-conditioned transition-field view, using curvature regularization as a controlled intervention. Across four continuous-control tasks, appropriately tuned regularization improves planning, while excessive regularization can be detrimental. By decomposing the transition field into affine and non-affine components, we find that regularization reduces action sensitivity mainly through the non-affine component. To assess its role in planning, we directly manipulate the non-affine action response in frozen models and show that it affects candidate selection and closed-loop success. Further analysis shows that curvature generally brings predicted futures closer together, while preserving more of the differences along the goal direction. This helps explain why the planning effects vary across tasks. We observe broadly consistent planning trends across five sampling- and gradient-based solvers on LeWM and similar rollout-geometry trends on DINO-WM. Qualitative attention visualizations reveal accompanying shifts toward task-relevant visual structure. Together, these findings clarify how latent transition geometry influences multi-step planning.

title: Regularizing Hard Examples Improves Adversarial Robustness
abstract: Recent studies have validated that pruning hard-to-learn examples from training improves the generalization performance of neural networks (NNs). In this study, we investigate this intriguing phenomenon -- the negative effect of hard examples on generalization -- in adversarial training. Particularly, we theoretically demonstrate that the increase in the difficulty of hard examples in adversarial training is significantly greater than the increase in the difficulty of easy examples. Furthermore, we verify that hard examples are only fitted through memorization of the label in adversarial training. We conduct both theoretical and empirical analyses of this memorization phenomenon, showing that pruning hard examples in adversarial training can enhance the model's robustness. However, the challenge remains in finding the optimal threshold for removing hard examples that degrade robustness performance. Based upon these observations, we propose a new approach, difficulty proportional label smoothing (DPLS), to adaptively mitigate the negative effect of hard examples, thereby improving the adversarial robustness of NNs. Notably, our experimental result indicates that our method can successfully leverage hard examples while circumventing the negative effect.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy Is Not Deployment Value: Decision-Aligned Reliability Evaluation for Foundation MLIPs in Materials Discovery
abstract: In AI-guided materials discovery, machine-learning models increasingly decide which candidate materials should receive expensive first-principles or experimental evaluation. Standard reliability metrics such as uncertainty, calibration, novelty, and ranking accuracy evaluate properties of the predictions, but success on these metrics does not necessarily imply a better downstream screening decision. We study this mismatch for foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MACE-MP, CHGNet, Orb V3) used to rank candidate crystal structures before DFT verification. We evaluate three representative reliability interventions (novelty detection, sparse DFT calibration, and chemistry-level ranking audits) using a deployment objective that measures how much DFT can be avoided while maintaining a required recall of near-hull candidates. Across all three, a reliability signal can succeed on its immediate target without improving the final screening decision: novelty detects distribution shift but weakly ranks failure severity; calibration can improve pooled ranking metrics while leaving screening unchanged or degrading it; and sparse audits identify MLIP-chemistry combinations with poor ranking reliability without yielding a robustly beneficial routing policy. A two-oracle analysis further shows that the source of failure depends on the screening decision itself: under formation-energy screening, even perfect knowledge of average ranking reliability can select the wrong model, whereas in the evaluated hull-aligned variant the oracle target becomes decision-aligned but finite-budget audits still fail to realize the value. Reliability should be evaluated relative to the decision it supports: the relevant question is not whether a model is uncertain or inaccurate, but whether acquiring and acting on additional information will improve the final discovery decision enough to justify its cost.

title: FolioWeaver: A LayerGraph-Grounded Agent for Layered Image Generation and Editing
abstract: Layered image generation separates images into compositable layers, allowing users to manipulate individual elements independently. However, such asset-level editability does not enable the generation system to interpret successive feedback, perform targeted edits, and preserve unaffected content. We introduce FolioWeaver, a LayerGraph-grounded agent that unifies layered-image generation and iterative editing through a persistent Executable Scene State. FolioWeaver constructs a LayerGraph and generates independent visual assets conditioned on a shared scene reference. An Editing Agent performs feedback-driven modifications and self-repair through scoped actions, selective layer execution, and visual verification, enabling targeted updates while reusing unchanged assets. We also publicly release LayerFolio, a dataset of 100,377 human-reviewed layered scenes spanning six visual domains, together with two evaluation protocols: AtomicQA for measuring requirement satisfaction and CBLP for assessing layer organization. Experiments demonstrate that FolioWeaver achieves superior layer organization and composite fidelity compared with direct layered-generation methods. Analyses validate the contributions of component adaptation, execution-grounded repair, and cross-domain training. FolioWeaver advances layered-image generation toward persistent, controllable, and iterative visual creation. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/FolioWeaver/LayerFolio.

title: Reconstructing Pure-State OTOCs from Forward-Time Linear Response
abstract: We show that the connected out-of-time-ordered correlator (OTOC) of any pure state can be reconstructed exactly from commutator linear responses alone. The protocol requires no time reversal, no ancilla, no double copy, and no weak measurement: a unitary string pulse, forward many-body evolution, and a single local readout suffice. An average over a complete basis of pulse generators yields the OTOC exactly. We further show that the measurement can be made sparse by restricting the pulses to a fixed operator weight, which turns the truncation into an analytically controlled spectral filter: the deterministic bias can be computed before the experiment and cleanly separated from the statistical sampling variance. For Gaussian states, the finite-weight response is exactly proportional to the full OTOC after a known combinatorial rescaling. For quantum chaotic systems, the typical residual is suppressed as a power law in the sector size. Exact-diagonalization benchmarks in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model and a nonintegrable Ising chain confirm these predictions.

title: Pixel as the Common Language: Unified Multimodal Embedding via Visual Rendering
abstract: Multimodal embedding models map heterogeneous inputs into a shared representation space, yet text-only, image-only, and composed inputs are still presented in distinct formats and follow different routes through the model. This fragmentation prevents heterogeneous tasks from jointly optimizing the same end-to-end encoding process, limiting supervision transfer across input configurations. To address this issue, we propose unification before encoding and instantiate this paradigm in RenderEmbed. The framework uses Visual Substrate Rendering to convert heterogeneous inputs into a common visual substrate for encoding with a VLM. From the resulting visual tokens, Progressive Hierarchical Anchor Encoding produces compact retrieval representations by interleaving learnable anchors and fusing their states across layers, retaining broad context and fine-grained cues. Interventional Rendering Learning trains these representations to remain sensitive to content changes and stable across rendering variations through complementary semantic and rendering interventions. Extensive experiments on MMEB and ViDoRe v2, spanning diverse retrieval tasks, show that RenderEmbed outperforms prior state-of-the-art models at the same scale and exhibits strong out-of-domain generalization. Compared with MetaEmbed, RenderEmbed improves MMEB Overall Precision@1 by 1.7 points, with a larger 2.1-point gain on out-of-domain tasks. Transfer and scaling analyses further show that a shared visual pathway enables more effective learning from heterogeneous supervision.

title: Stable but Hidden: Identifiability and Experimental Design under Missing Compositional Support
abstract: AI-guided scientific discovery often uses inexpensive predictors to allocate scarce verification measurements. We study a structural failure when relevant components have been observed separately but never jointly: distinct admissible response functions can agree on all observed compositions while disagreeing on the missing combinations. Additional same-support data cannot resolve this ambiguity, and agreement among fitted models need not expose it. We characterize the unresolved directions as an invisible subspace $\mathcal{N}_T(\mathcal{F}) = \ker \mathcal{R}_T$, whose geometry determines oracle zero-shot ambiguity and minimax risk under a symmetric, bounded ambiguity class. When the missing response lies in an $r$-dimensional, well-conditioned linear basis, optimally designed joint measurements achieve minimax integrated risk $Θ(σ^2 r/m)$, with classical $I$-optimality the fixed-design criterion. We validate on materials. In electrocatalysis, a six-dimensional support-derived structural basis (a prior on candidate directions, not an identified physical model) reduces held-out MSE against a dimension-matched generic basis (median paired ratio 0.75, improving 98% of 60 element pairs at $m = 15$), while $I$-optimal and same-basis posterior-variance acquisition show no detected difference. In Materials Project, removing joint property labels reduces $E_{\text{above hull}}$ ranking on 90% of 30 element pairs, more than matched data-removal controls, under a frozen pretrained representation. Pair difficulty is reproducible across learners but poorly predicted by zero-label ensemble disagreement; 20 joint measurements enable transferable pair-level rankings without reliable absolute calibration. In practice, experiment selection should ask which relationships the observed support leaves unidentified before asking where a fitted model is least certain.

title: SalivaryHSI-Seg: A New Challenging Benchmark for Ex Vivo Salivary Gland Hyperspectral Tissue Segmentation
abstract: Salivary gland tumors are common lesions in oral and maxillofacial practice, and accurate identification of tumor regions and surrounding salivary gland tissues is important for tissue assessment, pathological sampling, and clinical decision support. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) records continuous spectral responses together with spatial imaging information, providing a promising way to capture fine-grained tissue-discriminative information. Nevertheless, the development of salivary gland HSI tissue segmentation remains limited due to the lack of standardized benchmarks with pixel-level annotations and unified evaluation protocols. To address this issue, we introduce SalivaryHSI-Seg, a hyperspectral tissue segmentation benchmark for ex vivo salivary gland specimens, containing 119 HSI samples from 31 patients with multi-class pixel-level annotations. We establish a patient-level five-fold cross-validation protocol and evaluate different input representations, model architectures, and challenging subsets with small tumor and complex boundary. Based on this benchmark, we further propose HyBSD, a hyperspectral boundary-guided spectral-difference network for full-HSI salivary gland tissue segmentation. HyBSD exploits boundary-guided spectral-difference cues to improve tissue delineation in ambiguous transition regions. Extensive experiments show that full-HSI input provides more discriminative information than sampled spectrums, and that HyBSD achieves 74.97% mDice and 87.76% Tumor Dice, with further advantages on the challenging subsets. Dataset and code will be released.

title: HERO: Hierarchical Region-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Exploration
abstract: Autonomous exploration is widely used to map unknown environments, yet maintaining both path efficiency and low online computation remains difficult as environment scale increases. Hierarchical planners reduce global search through coarse regional representations but often rely on handcrafted local viewpoint-selection rules. Graph-based reinforcement learning can improve local decisions, but its inference cost grows with the exploration graph and global direction is usually represented only implicitly. To address these limitations, we present HERO, a hierarchical framework that assigns distinct responsibilities to global planning and learned local decision-making, enabling each level to focus on the function it is best suited to perform. To reduce the growing inference cost of graph-based policies, HERO restricts learned target selection to reachable candidates within the current region while using region-level planning to provide long-horizon guidance. To avoid informative targets causing excessive deviation from this global direction, the proposed Dual-Branch Graph Policy balances Frontier Utility with guidance toward the next region, improving both local exploration and global progress. Experiments on unseen 2D maps show the lowest overall mean path length and target-decision cost among the evaluated methods. MARSIM simulations and deployments at three real-world sites further demonstrate the framework's applicability with LiDAR-based mapping and chassis dynamics.

title: SF-Flow: Spectral Flow Matching with High Structural Fidelity for Hallucination-Suppressed Scientific Image Generation
abstract: Scientific image generation focuses on reproducing experimental appearance while following a prescribed spatial layout. A key challenge is acute data sparsity, which requires operating with unpaired collections of materials (real images and prescribed layouts), where no direct supervision is feasible. Work on unpaired translation has shown that it is possible to reproduce the texture and intensity variations of real images, but it is extremely hard to retain the intended phase boundaries in the prescribed locations. This paper tackles this challenge and introduces SF-Flow, a flow-matching model trained only on real material images that imposes spectral constraints during generation, producing images that are high-fidelity and consistent with the prescribed layouts. Because layouts enter only at generation time, the approach extends to layout maps outside the distribution of any available training layouts. We evaluate the method on synchrotron tomography of concrete, lens-coupled laboratory microCT of powders, and industrial XCT of additively manufactured metal. Without instrument-specific modeling, we show that SF-Flow achieves substantially higher template agreement and joint fidelity--structure score than previous methods, including contrastive unpaired translation.

title: A Steady Theory for Highly Unsteady Thin Airfoil Motions
abstract: A generalized steady thin airfoil theory is built not from steady flow, but from flows in which there exists a frame of reference where the absolute vorticity field is steady. We specialize this general idea to construct a foliation of a domain of phase space for thin airfoil motions in which staying on a leaf of the foliation maintains zero absolute vorticity in the fluid indefinitely. The phase space is described by the airfoil's total rotation rate, speed, and angle of attack. It is found using this definition that one of the preeminent unsteady stall conditions is equivalent to the traditional steady stall condition for this class of flows, various other classical results can be re-interpreted as steady in the absolute vorticity field, and insight is also provided into the surprising experimental results of McGowan et al. (AIAA J. 49, 2011). We show parts of existing quasi-steady flow and Theodorsen unsteady flow theory can be built from a planar approximation of our foliation, making the quasi-steady extension of our theory trivial, and suggesting how an unsteady extension can be created as well. Furthermore, pure unsteady effects in the new theory amount to a transversal of the leaves, occupying just one dimension, inviting interesting prospects for future experimental and theoretical work.

title: Context-Grounded Skill Internalization for Vision-Language Agents
abstract: Skill internalization offers a way for agents to learn useful behaviors from skills and use them without explicit guidance in context at inference time. A common approach is to generate demonstration trajectories with the skill in context and then fine-tune the same model on its own trajectories with the skill removed. However, this leads to the problem that the model may learn to reference the removed skill, which we named as context misalignment (CoMi). In this work, we first analyze agent behaviors related to CoMi under this common pipeline. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ARC-AGI-1, skill-removed fine-tuning consistently results in CoMi: 12.2-46.0% of test trajectories reference the removed skill. To address this problem, we develop Context-Grounded Skill Internalization (CGSI). CGSI uses a sentence detector to identify unsupported references and then masks or rewrites the selected sentences before fine-tuning. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of CGSI and reveal two key findings. (i) Compared with directly fine-tuning with the skill removed, CGSI reduces CoMi at test time by 72.5-94.6% while preserving task success. (ii) Compared with existing reinforcement learning-based skill-internalization baselines, CGSI achieves comparable performance with substantially less training time. CGSI also significantly reduces processing costs compared with large-scale trajectory auditing and correction.

title: NEP-Spin: A spin-dependent neuroevolution potential for large-scale spin--lattice simulations
abstract: NEP-Spin is a \glsentrylong{nep} for coupled atomic motion and variable-length magnetic moments. Local bond and spin tensors give an energy invariant under independent spin and spatial rotations without \glsentrylong{soc} and under joint rotations with it. We benchmark energies, atomic forces, and magnetic forces on public datasets for collinear Fe--Al and noncollinear Fe. In multiferroic \glsentrylong{bfo}, the predicted zero-field cycloid period is 69.7~nm, compared with 62--63~nm from neutron scattering. An electric field of 20~mV/Å opposite to the polarization lengthens the period to 93.2~nm, while imposing the same polar displacement at zero field gives 85.1~nm. In a uniform antiferromagnetic cell at fixed lattice vectors, 6~T magnetic fields along orthogonal basal axes reorient the Fe moments and give opposite signs of the ionic polarization change $ΔP_y$. First-principles ionic relaxations at the predicted moment vectors reproduce both signs. In a 2.79-million-atom ferroelectric twin, the cycloid rotation planes tilt by different amounts from their shared initial plane and remain distinct over 10~ps at 100~K. At 10~ps the propagation axes lie within about $7^\circ$ of their initial directions. With inertial spin dynamics, GPUMD advances a 5.93-million-atom BiFeO$_3$ cell at 21.8 million atom-steps per second on four RTX 4090 GPUs.

title: PushMimic: Learning Adaptive Humanoid Box Pushing via Dynamic Motion Augmentation and Reference Distillation
abstract: Humanoid box pushing is challenging when the physical properties of the task, such as the box mass and the ramp inclination, are unknown before the push begins. This paper presents PushMimic, a framework that learns adaptive humanoid box pushing from a single level-ground kinematic reference motion. The learned policy adapts its pushing posture to these properties without observing them. PushMimic augments the reference motion into a dynamically feasible motion dataset over these properties with sampling-based trajectory optimization, and distills the dataset into one motion tracking policy in one stage of training. Simulation results over box masses from 5 to 15 kg and ramp inclinations up to 15 degrees show that PushMimic raises the success rate from 57.8% to 88.8% compared with a baseline that tracks the original reference motion. It also reduces the cost of push of the arms by 22%. Hardware experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid show that the policy adapts its torso pitch during continuous pushing on an inclined treadmill, with box masses up to 19 kg and ramp inclinations up to 12.6 degrees. PushMimic therefore needs only one reference motion, instead of one for every box mass and ramp inclination.

title: RadarOSV: Unified 3D Scene and Motion Perception from mmWave Radars
abstract: Millimeter-wave radar offers weather-resilient sensing for 3D occupancy prediction. Existing radar occupancy methods mainly model geometry, with limited joint modeling of semantics and motion. Cascaded imaging radar provides fine spatial detail but has a limited unambiguous velocity range, whereas single-chip radar offers a wider range but coarser spatial resolution. We propose RadarOSV, to our knowledge the first radar-only framework that jointly predicts occupancy, dynamic object semantics, and ground-relative velocity from raw radar data in unified voxels, by exploiting complementary measurements from both radars. Its Polar-to-Cartesian Geometry (PCG) backbone maps polar imaging-radar features into Cartesian voxels through fixed and deformable sampling, guiding cross-radar fusion for geometry and attribute prediction. Single-chip detection outputs provide class evidence, while raw Doppler spectra supply motion features and radial-velocity candidates. The velocity readout selects from these candidates using fused features to resolve aliasing, then combines the selected radial estimate with learned motion. Ego-motion compensation uses radar-estimated velocity, so inference requires no external odometry or other sensors. On K-Radar, single-frame PCG achieves 40.7% mIoU within 12.8 m, compared with RadarOcc's reported 34.3%. On the BRIDGE-Liv dataset, compared with a cascaded-radar baseline predicting the same outputs with external ego velocity, RadarOSV improves macro-averaged accuracy across four dynamic object classes within annotated object regions from 63.1% to 75.5% and reduces object radial-velocity MAE against manual Doppler annotations from 1.03 to 0.51 m/s, while maintaining geometric occupancy mIoU.

title: Designing Incoherent Multispectral Diffractive Optical Networks for Satellite Image Classification
abstract: Optical neural networks and diffractive optical computing provide a promising route for performing task-specific inference with high parallelism and lightweight electronic post-processing. These advantages are especially attractive for multispectral satellite imaging, where conventional workflows rely on transmitting high-dimensional image cubes to the ground for downstream electronic analysis. Here, we introduce a computationally efficient surrogate model-guided framework for designing incoherent multispectral diffractive optical networks that directly output class probabilities onboard, eliminating the need to capture and transfer the full multispectral data cube for ground-side inference. We first train a physically compatible surrogate model, represented by a non-negative fully connected model that accommodates a generalized detector readout, yielding a task-specific non-negative multispectral intensity transformation that can be transferred to an optical processor. We then synthesize its diffractive counterpart through data-free point-spread-function-based optimization under spatially incoherent illumination. Using this approach, we numerically demonstrate a six-spectral-channel diffractive classifier for tri-class satellite-scene recognition, achieving a blind-testing accuracy of 79.8% for artificial surface, water body, and vegetated land images, closely approaching the 81.8% accuracy of its surrogate. We further demonstrate a more compact three-spectral-channel design that numerically achieves 72.7% blind-testing accuracy, compared with 75.1% for its corresponding surrogate model. This surrogate model-guided strategy provides a practical pathway for designing compact, task-specific incoherent multispectral optical processors for resource-constrained remote-sensing inference.

title: Integrable discretization of the Maxwell-Bloch equations
abstract: Numerical schemes for the Maxwell-Bloch equations keep the length of the Bloch vector but not the integrable structure, so that solitons are only approximate solutions. We write an integrable discretization, in both time and space, of these equations for a complex field in a resonant two-level medium in the physical variables and use it as a numerical scheme. The lattice follows from a discrete Lax pair with the analytic structure of the continuous one; an auxiliary field variable is fixed by an isospectral normalization, and the resulting scheme is explicit, a $2\times2$ similarity transformation of the density matrix per grid node. It conserves the length of every Bloch vector and satisfies an exact energy balance between field and medium. The lattice coincides with a known fully discrete integrable system, which we use to obtain closed-form solitons and breathers; they are reflectionless potentials with energy $16\sum_j\mathrm{Im}\,λ_j$ and converge to the McCall-Hahn soliton and Lamb's breather. Inhomogeneous broadening is included through ordered sublayers that keep integrability. On a finite time window the scattering data evolve by a closed map, with the final state of the medium given by the data at one point of the spectral plane. On the infinite line, if the medium returns to its ground state behind the pulse (which we show on the first row and observe numerically on later rows), the transmission coefficient is conserved and the reflection coefficient evolves linearly, with the multiplier of the linearized lattice. As a numerical method the lattice is explicit and second order, with a cost per accuracy comparable to that of Cayley and exponential-midpoint schemes, and an area-preserving input map with a calibrated medium coupling makes it exact for a chosen soliton.

title: The Growth Path Is the Missing Half of Neural Networks
abstract: An artificial neuron computes and learns, but it does not live: the units of a network are fixed when it is designed, and every one of them is kept and paid for whether it is used or not. We give each neuron a second pathway. Beside its Task Path, the usual computation and gradient learning, a dual-pathway neuron has a Growth Path: a nutrient flows from the outputs back through the network, every layer receives the same fixed budget, and each unit is fed in proportion to how much the units above it use it. A well-fed unit divides and a starving unit dies. This allocation is not a separate analysis or pruning step: it runs throughout training and reads only activations and weights. The task is still learned from labels with the ordinary loss, and the training procedure gains no phase, no schedule and no target size. Because the budget is conserved, the competition is zero-sum and a single number sets the size of the network. Switched on in a pretrained network that is deployed on a narrower domain, the Growth Path shrinks the network while it keeps learning. With Adam the network ends 1.0 to 1.2 points more accurate on the domain than the same network trained ordinarily, at 24% to 60% of its compute, and at 12% of the compute it is still ahead; a random choice of the same number of units gives no gain. Letting starving pretrained units sleep instead of die keeps 1.2 to 4.6 points more of the rarely used content. Over 800 changing tasks a network with the Growth Path holds its accuracy while ordinary networks decline. With plain SGD the gains are smaller: at deployment the method trades compute against rarely used content, and on one of the two continual-learning streams it only ties networks of equal size. The experiments are small (three-layer perceptrons on MNIST-like data); what they show is that a conserved, loss-free second pathway can decide by itself which units a network needs.

title: Obstructed Harvey--Lawson cones and logarithmic special Lagrangian singularities
abstract: We construct two exact embedded special Lagrangian germs with the same unique multiplicity-one tangent cone, the Harvey--Lawson cone in $\mathbb C^9$. A quadratic obstruction and a corrected cubic obstruction yield the distinct sharp $C^1$ convergence rates $\lvert\log r\rvert^{-1}$ and $\lvert\log r\rvert^{-1/2}$, respectively. These rates distinguish the germs under unitary transformations and dilations. We also prove Jacobi nonintegrability of the Harvey--Lawson cones in $\mathbb C^8$ and $\mathbb C^9$, and realize the sharp rate $\lvert\log r\rvert^{-1/2}$ at the eight-dimensional cone.

title: MotionServe: Efficient Multi-Robot Serving by Exploiting Robot Execution Slack
abstract: As robotic arms undertake diverse manipulation tasks, a deployment may need to serve many task-specific vision-language-action (VLA) policies concurrently. Dedicating a GPU to each robot is costly, motivating shared-GPU inference. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone with lightweight policy-specific adapters, reducing model-weight memory and enabling cross-policy batching. However, robot inference must keep pace with physical execution. With action chunking, robots continue executing buffered actions while awaiting new predictions, and the remaining buffered time provides each robot's execution slack for serving its next request. Once this slack is exhausted, the robot stalls until new actions arrive, interrupting task progress. Observing earlier preserves more slack but can lead to disruptive replanning and lower task success, whereas delaying dispatch to form larger batches can improve GPU efficiency but consumes slack and risks stalls. To balance these competing demands, we present MotionServe, a shared-GPU serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with server-side batch formation. MotionExec selects observation triggers based on motion structure in predicted action chunks, allowing inference to overlap with remaining buffered execution. SlackBatch combines the resulting per-robot execution budgets with estimated outstanding GPU work to determine when to wait, which requests to batch, and when to dispatch them. We evaluate X-VLA on LIBERO and SimplerEnv's WidowX tasks and OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, with up to 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU. At 96 robots, MotionServe reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively, over each model's lowest-stall baseline. Backbone sharing also reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.

title: Relativistic Harmonic Generation in Spatiotemporal Plasma Photonic Crystals
abstract: Spatiotemporal photonic crystals offer a route to controlling the frequency, momentum, and energy of light. Extending this capability to relativistic laser intensities calls for a plasma-based platform. Here we propose a spatiotemporal plasma photonic crystal (SPPC) formed at a solid surface driven by intense pump pulses, with a separate probe interacting with the resulting modulation. The spatial and temporal periodicity of the SPPC determines the allowed harmonic frequencies and emission angles, while its complex Floquet bands explain how the probe draws energy from the modulation. Beyond harmonic generation, this picture predicts wavelength-dependent probe amplification as the probe accesses amplifying modes of the SPPC, providing an experimentally testable connection between the band structure and energy transfer. Agreement with particle-in-cell simulations supports this interpretation.

title: Coalescence and the Two-Point Covariance in the Directed Landscape
abstract: In the directed landscape with Brownian terminal data, we express the spatial derivative of the two-point height covariance in terms of the probability that two geodesics coalesce before the terminal time and the exit law of a single geodesic. This formula arises as the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang scaling limit of a zero-temperature Brownian last-passage identity from our earlier work on the O'Connell-Yor polymer. To pass the coalescence probabilities to the limit, we show that two paths sharing an optimal exit almost surely lose total weight if they must stay disjoint before reaching it. At stationarity, we determine when two zero-direction semi-infinite geodesics first coalesce. We recover this distribution by differentiating the height-increment variance first in the starting separation, then in the boundary strength. When the terminal reward is zero everywhere, the starting points with the same leftmost optimal exit as the origin form an interval. The probability that this interval extends past given distances on both sides equals the rate at which the height covariance decreases at their sum.

title: A Novel Multi-Target Approach for simultaneous enhancement of brightness, intensity, and bi-spectral performance of cold neutron sources
abstract: Increasing the brightness of cold neutron beams is a central objective in modern cold neutron source development, since it largely governs the sample intensity for high-resolution neutron instruments. Raising accelerator beam power is constrained by the target heat-removal limit of 0.5-1 kW/cm2, and increasing the moderator length beyond about 20-30 cm becomes inefficient owing to the finite mean free path of cold neutrons. We propose reversing the conventional design logic: rather than tailoring the cryogenic moderator to a fixed target-premoderator source, we tailor the thermal-neutron source geometry to a high-performance moderator configuration. The concept is realized as a staircase moderator assembly of several shorter compressed moderators, each with its own target-premoderator unit, which distributes neutron production among multiple units and thus enables higher accelerator powers while preserving the brightness advantages of compressed moderators. This approach can provide additional brightness and intensity gains relative to a single low-dimensional or conventional voluminous moderator at the desired transverse beam size and may naturally generate bi-spectral neutron beams, thereby extending the dynamic range of neutron instruments.

title: Correlated by Construction: Endpoint Choice and the Validation of Protein Screening
abstract: Machine learning for protein engineering depends on functional measurements collected at screening scale, but the designs those measurements rank are deployed in processes that run elsewhere. Whether a miniaturized assay remains informative under the conditions of use is usually assumed rather than demonstrated. We describe an automated production and screening platform and test the transfer of its solution-phase metal-affinity measurements to immobilized rare-earth separation. Primary pKd-derived separation factors tracked those measured on covalently immobilized protein across 82 protein-metal-pair measurements from 35 proteins, with pairwise Spearman correlations of 0.878 to 0.923 (pooled Pearson $r$ = 0.836; Spearman $ρ$ = 0.869). Separation factors at a fixed metal pair are insensitive to the ordering shared across the lanthanide series, so these coefficients report protein-specific correspondence directly; permutation of protein identity confirms it, giving a mean scrambled correlation of 0.003 and, for the 17 proteins measured on all three pairs, $r$ = 0.917 against 0.001 ($p \approx 0.001$). Profiles compared as profiles behave differently. An independent comparison against published LAMBS profiles for the same protein backbones (417 proteins, 5,212 paired measurements) reproduced normalized raw elution at $r$ = 0.870, but reassigning protein identity still reached 0.840. High profile-level agreement across assay formats is largely attributable to metal preferences shared across the series rather than to protein identity. Transfer can be demonstrated, but the endpoint decides whether a correlation shows it: a pairwise contrast removes the shared ordering; a normalized profile retains it, and needs a null that reassigns protein identity.

title: Valence band, electron correlation, and possible temperature dependent change in the electronic structure near $E_F$ of a candidate of ambient-pressure nickelate superconductors Sr$_3$Ni$_2$O$_5$Cl$_2$
abstract: Photoemission spectroscopy (PES) studies of Sr$_3$Ni$_2$O$_5$Cl$_2$ (Sr3252), a candidate ambient-pressure bilayer nickelate superconductor, have been performed to investigate the electronic structure. Valence band spectra, which are compared with DFT and DFT+U calculations, reveal dominant Ni 3$d$ $t_{2g}$-derived states located around 0.6 eV binding energy with a shoulder around 0.2 eV that can be attributed to states with a dominant Ni 3$d_{3z2-r2}$ character. The overall valence band shape is better reproduced by the simulated spectrum of DFT+U (= 3 eV), providing an experimental estimation of the strength of electron correlation. High-resolution PES near the Fermi level ($E_F$) exhibits marked temperature dependence, which cannot be fully understood by a broadening due to coupling of a photo-hole to phonons alone and suggests change in electronic structure. The results provide fundamental electronic structure information of Sr3252, which is useful to further explore the superconductivity of Sr3252.

title: GIT-thresholds for K-moduli spaces of Hypersurfaces
abstract: In this note, we confirm the first wall $c_1(d)$ of K-moduli of hypersurfaces of degree $d$ in $\mathbb P^n$ for $n\geq 3$ and $d\geq n+1$, where $c_1(d)=\frac{n+1}{nd}$ if $d$ is even; and $c_1(d)=\frac{n+1}{nd-(n+1)}$ if $d$ is odd. Before this wall, the K-moduli is identical to the GIT-moduli for degree $d$ hypersurfaces, so we also call this number the GIT-threshold.

title: Post-Training Agents for Long-Document Reasoning
abstract: Professional documents are a long-context workload that retrieval-style benchmarks do not capture. In a ten-domain enterprise collection, a task's evidence is spread across a source document of median length 27 pages (mean 48.8, maximum 873); a third of tasks rest mainly on charts, drawings, and maps; and 70.9% require two or more reasoning hops. We post-train Kimi-K2.7, an open-weight foundation model, at its full context window on 1,465 expert-authored tasks with atomic rubrics from that collection, training rank-32 adapters with one round of privileged-context on-policy self-distillation followed by two rounds of rubric-reward reinforcement learning. We render each PDF as text for training and as extracted text plus selected page images at evaluation. The smoothed RL training reward rises from 0.37 in the first tenth of the run to 0.67 in the last. On the 100-task GDP.pdf holdout, served in a 262,144-token window, strict pass (all rubric criteria met) more than doubles after the second round, from 11.0% to 24.5%, with gains across input lengths up to 240K tokens. Mean tokens generated stay flat (9,803 to 9,733), so the gain does not come from longer outputs. GPT-5.6 Sol's leaderboard strict pass is 30.7% at a measured 3,422 tokens. On 220 out-of-domain GDPval tasks, where the model runs as a long-horizon tool-using agent, mean rubric reward rises from 0.571 to 0.746 after the third round and zero-credit tasks fall from 54 to 10, while messages per task fall 18%, from 70.9 to 58.2. In paired trajectories, the third round replaces a context-thrashing retry loop with one up-front check of all sources, and verification extends from checking that files exist to checking what they contain. We argue that long-context evaluation of agents should report accuracy jointly with tokens and turns, and that datasets of long documents should ship text and image renderings alongside each PDF.

title: Flow-induced vibration of an array of circular cylinders in a square enclosure due to thermal buoyancy
abstract: Flow-induced oscillations of heated cylinder arrays in a square enclosure driven solely by natural convection are investigated in the current study at Prandtl number of 7 and Raleigh number of $10^7$ (based on side of square enclosure). This is accomplished by a coupled thermal-fluid-structure-interaction formulation based on body-fitted arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian framework, implemented using variational finite element methodology. Study on stationary array shows asymmetry in the $3\times 3$ configuration, along with a non-dimensional wall-gap plume oscillation frequency of 0.183 on the left column cylinders. When elastically mounted, these cylinders synchronize and lock-in with the frequency at reduced velocity of 15.7. The remaining cylinders undergo broadband buffeting that grows monotonically with reduced velocity and exceeds the synchronized response. The $4\times 4$ array shows symmetric behavior with no synchronization. The response is observed to be forced buffeting for all the cylinders, and dominated by the slow plume forcing for the inner column cylinders. The motion of the cylinders also influence the heat transfer characteristics. The $3\times 3$ array shows negligible change in heat transfer for the whole array, while measurable enhancement is observed for $4\times 4$ array.

title: Boundary spectroscopy of hidden near-horizon reflection
abstract: A classical black hole horizon absorbs completely, and any deviation would be hidden in the bulk. For a scalar field in a rotating Bañados-Teitelboim-Zanelli exterior, we derive an exact boundary response of a corotating passive wall near the horizon. An Airy filter gives its spectrum, and positive energy excludes growing modes. On any frequency band the response identifies a constant wall impedance and the wall position, which enter orthogonally with weights determined by the spectral function. The boundary thus sees a reflecting wall, whereas a perfect absorber is exponentially hidden.

title: AEGIS: Evidence-Guided Set Decisions for Requirement-to-Code Traceability
abstract: Requirement-to-code traceability recovery identifies code artifacts that implement a requirement, but manual review costs limit how many candidates developers can inspect. Code relations can reveal candidates missed by textual retrieval, yet can also introduce code unrelated to the requirement. We propose AEGIS, which combines retrieval evidence and code relations to construct and revise trace sets under a project-wide review budget. Grouped retrieval and semantic retrieval supply candidates. A set objective combines relevance to the requirement with structural compatibility. Local search constructs sets of different sizes, and dynamic programming selects one set per requirement within the budget. Call-context admission then compares replacements using evidence from arguments and return values in calls involving protected members, while bounding retrieval-score loss. Across 13 projects, AEGIS achieves the highest project-macro average on nine of ten evaluation metrics among the compared methods. Relative to same-corpus adaptations of TAROT-VSM and FTLR+MC, it improves F$_1$@5 by 33.21% and 52.28%, and MAP by 38.58% and 49.08%, respectively.

title: Character Information in Language Models: A Prompt-Independent Word Store and a Late, Question-Driven Signal That Grows With Scale
abstract: Linear probes recover character properties of a word from a language model's hidden states, but a probe at the answer position cannot say whether the property was stored with the word or produced because the prompt asked for it. We separate the two with a word-position baseline: the same held-out-word probe applied to the query word's own tokens in a sentence that asks nothing. Across 16 open-weight models from seven families (0.6B--14B) and eleven character tasks, the word tokens encode \texttt{first\_letter}, \texttt{last\_letter} and \texttt{most\_frequent\_letter} above a word-only nuisance floor in all 16 models, and about 70\% of that signal is already present in the token embedding. Asking the question adds a second signal at the answer position. Its size grows with model scale for all four prompt-sensitive tasks (Holm-corrected permutation $p \leq 0.018$, also within model families), and the growth is confined to the late layers: restricted to the first quarter of the network, the slope is indistinguishable from zero. Small models' answer positions hold less linearly decodable signal than their word-level store; large models' hold more. Four controls bound these claims. Measured against the nuisance floor, the question-free signal that a majority-baseline analysis counts as retained largely disappears (\texttt{last\_letter}: $-0.01$). Count tasks become measurable only after length, repetition and query-letter shortcuts are removed by design. A pre-registered test finds that a question placed before the word does not change the word's own encoding beyond what an arbitrary prefix change does. Representation--readout gaps show no robust scaling once probe saturation is accounted for. Pre-registered criteria, a fixed estimator (held-out layer selection, cold-start folds) and all analysis code accompany the paper.

title: A complete knot invariant from grid diagrams
abstract: Using grid diagrams, we define an infinite graph associated to each knot type. We prove that the isomorphism class of this grid graph is a complete invariant of the knot, up to mirroring. Even more, we prove that algorithmically determinable finite parts of this graph are enough to determine the knot type.

title: When "A or B" Is Less Likely than A: Coherent Probabilities for Vision Decision Models
abstract: Vision decision models answer a multiple-choice question about an image with one probability per option, and software uses them directly. We show that the probabilities depend on how the options are grouped: a merged option "A or B" receives on average 11.5 points less probability than the sum of A and B. This under-additivity appears at every model size from 0.85B to 26B and remains after fine-tuning on labels. We propose CORE, which asks each training question with its options regrouped and trains the answers to all these questions toward one target distribution over the original options, summed into each question's groups. On 1,050 items from seven benchmarks, CORE reduces the total variation distance between the answer to a regrouped question and the original answer summed into the same groups from 14.8 to 5.8 points on the 0.85B model, against 9.4 for the best baseline trained on the same questions. At all five model sizes, CORE reduces this distance without lowering accuracy.

title: Positive-partial-transpose structure of completely entangled subspaces and their complements
abstract: A completely entangled subspace (CES) contains no product vectors, so every state supported on it is entangled. Whether such a subspace can support states with positive partial transpose (PPT) is a more subtle question. The normalized projector onto a CES may be NPT even if there exist PPT states supported on the CES. We investigate this distinction using a semidefinite criterion that optimizes the smallest partial-transpose eigenvalue over all supported density operators. For two- qutrit states supported on CESs, this leads to a complete characterization: a CES supports PPT states exactly when it is four-dimensional and related by invertible local transformations to the complement of an unextendible product basis (UPB). We also establish restrictions on PPT states whose ranges contain only vectors of Schmidt rank at least three, ruling out their existence in $3\otimes n$, $4\otimes4$, and $4\otimes5$, and showing that any such state in $4\otimes6$ must have rank eight. An interesting structure emerges when two orthogonal completely entangled subspaces together span the full Hilbert space, which we term \textit{complementary CESs}. Explicit constructions in $3\otimes4$ demonstrate that both subspaces can support PPT entanglement even when their normalized projectors are NPT. In $4\otimes4$, we construct a complementary pair whose normalized projectors are themselves PPT entangled. These constructions offer an alternative route to obtaining PPT entangled states, beyond the familiar approach based on UPB complements.

title: Plasma-enabled magnet-free LSW search for eV-scale axions with laser-stimulated regeneration
abstract: In conventional light-shining-through-a-wall (LSW) experiments, strong magnetic fields mediate the conversion of photons into axions and their subsequent reconversion into photons. At eV-scale axion masses, however, photon--axion phase mismatch causes these conversions to lose coherence, substantially reducing the experimental sensitivity. We propose a magnet-free LSW scheme that addresses this limitation via plasma-based axion generation and laser-stimulated regeneration. At low laser intensity, a two-color dispersion-matched source generates axions in a narrow mass range set by the plasma dispersion. At relativistic laser intensity, a single-pulse plasma-broadened source generates axions over a broad mass range, as shown by particle-in-cell simulations. The Fourier spectrum of the source term $\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{B}$ broadens around the laser branch, consistent with mixing between the laser and low-frequency plasma waves. For axion detection behind the wall, a counter-propagating laser stimulates axion decay into a detectable signal photon and a second photon emitted into the laser mode, with the laser frequency chosen to satisfy phase matching. For representative parameters, the requirement of at least one regenerated photon yields projected upper limits on the axion-photon coupling on the order $10^{-7}\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$ over $m_a=0.1$--$1\,\mathrm{eV}$.

title: Policy-intrinsic Demonstration Curation
abstract: Fine-tuning a robot policy for a new target task requires target demonstrations, but only a few are available. Demonstrations of other tasks can fill this gap, and demonstration curation selects the useful ones among these candidates. Retrieval-based curation selects the candidates that are most similar to the target demonstrations. Since it does not use the policy, any candidate that looks similar receives a high score. Performance-aware curation therefore estimates the effect of each candidate on the policy. However, this requires training on the candidates and takes a long time. We propose a third branch, policy-intrinsic curation, which uses the policy and still takes little time. It estimates this effect with forward passes of the pretrained policy and needs no training. We instantiate this branch with PICKER (Policy-Intrinsic Curation from Known Errors). It selects the candidates on which the policy makes errors that agree with those on the target demonstrations. PICKER reaches success rates comparable to those of performance-aware curation and takes about as long as retrieval-based curation. Its selection is also stable across seeds.

title: Silver rate is sharp for gradient descent
abstract: We determine the minimax convergence rate of gradient descent with predetermined real stepsizes on smooth convex functions up to an absolute constant factor. Let $p=\log_2(1+\sqrt{2})\approx 1.2716$. We prove that for every $L>0$, every integer $n\ge1$ and every stepsize schedule $h\in\mathbb{R}^n$ there exist a convex $L$-smooth function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ in some finite dimension $d$, a minimizer $x_\star$ of $f$ and an initial point $x_0\neq x_\star$ such that the iterate $x_n$ of gradient descent with stepsizes $h$ satisfies $(f(x_n)-f(x_\star))/(L\|x_0-x_\star\|^2)\ge c\,n^{-p}$ with an absolute constant $c>0$. This lower bound matches the $O(n^{-p})$ upper bounds achieved by silver-type stepsize schedules and establishes the optimality of the silver rate up to an absolute constant factor. Previous lower bounds reached the optimal polynomial exponent for both nonnegative and signed schedules but retained subpolynomial losses. We remove these losses for all predetermined real stepsize schedules. The proof combines a quantitative stability estimate for a splitting inequality at the silver proportions with Moreau-envelope constructions that join prescribed gradient descent trajectories and with multiscale averaging over stepsize thresholds.

title: Agent on Guard: Self-Improving Runtime Intervention for Robust Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Robot foundation policies provide learned execution capabilities, while programming agents can reason about failures and construct recovery behaviors. Combining them effectively requires learning when intervention helps and when the policy can reliably resume. This challenge is inherently temporal: the physical world continues to evolve during reasoning, and a useful recovery may become infeasible before a decision takes effect. We introduce Agent on Guard (AoG), a hierarchical framework that improves collaboration between a frozen base policy and a programming agent through physical experience. An evolving outer planner allocates control as the physical state evolves, aligning decisions with the physical clock with attention to observation freshness, remaining recovery windows, and the time required for reasoning, recovery, and subsequent execution. Coupled inner loops jointly refine intervention timing, recovery skills, and handoff conditions. Rather than judging recovery by local correction alone, AoG uses downstream task progress, failure recurrence, final outcomes, and resource consumption to improve both recovery behaviors and scheduling. This turns temporary agent solutions into reusable collaboration capabilities that complement the frozen policy. On RoboDojo-Sim, AoG achieves a success rate of 50.57% and a task score of 57.26, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 11.22 percentage points and 10.68 points, respectively. It also reduces end-to-end episode latency by 80.4% and online token consumption by 85.1% relative to the GPT-6 Astra agent.

title: LMnOP: Pruning 3D Gaussian Splatting via Leave-Many-Out Importance
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting renders photorealistic views in real time. However, a single scene often needs millions of Gaussians, so these models are costly to store and render. Pruning reduces this cost by keeping a subset of the Gaussians. A common score is the leave-one-out importance, which is the loss increase when a Gaussian alone is removed. At high pruning ratios, many Gaussians are removed together, so Gaussians that are redundant alone but essential together are lost. We present LMnOP (Leave-Many-Out Pruning), which estimates the importance of each Gaussian under the removal of the other Gaussians. This leave-many-out importance is the average loss increase when a Gaussian is removed while the others are also removed at random. We compute the exact mean and variance of each pixel's color under random removal in closed form, and approximate the importance from them without sampling removal patterns. We refine each Gaussian's probability of remaining with its importance and prune once at the end. Without fine-tuning, LMnOP achieves the best results in 16 of 18 metrics on three datasets at 90% and 99% removal. It improves SSIM and LPIPS over GaussianPOP in all 13 scenes.

title: Difference estimates for Chern connections on homolomorphic vector bundles
abstract: This paper investigates the uniqueness issue of Chern connections from the Cheng-Yau type estimate point of view. We establish local difference estimates for Chern connections on holomorphic vector bundles over complete noncompact Kähler manifolds with Ricci curvature bounded from below. These local estimates not only enable us to obtain uniqueness results for Hermitian-Einstein connections on complete noncompact Kähler manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature, but also apply to study the Liouville theorem for complex Monge-Ampère equation on $\mathbb{C}^n$ as well as the Chern flatness and Kählerness for Hermitian metrics on complete noncompact Ricci flat Kähler manifolds.

title: A Polynomial-Time Best-of-Both-Worlds Algorithm for Matroid Semi-Bandit Problems
abstract: Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) offers a computationally attractive framework for online learning, with recent advances establishing Best-of-Both-Worlds (BOBW) guarantees for various bandit settings. For matroid semi-bandits, existing methods offering such guarantees primarily rely on Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL), which requires solving an optimization problem at each round. We establish BOBW guarantees for FTPL with Fréchet and Pareto distributions with a certain parameter with geometric resampling in the matroid semi-bandit problem, showing that FTPL can simultaneously achieve the minimax-optimal $O(\sqrt{mdT})$ regret in adversarial setting and a logarithmic regret in stochastic setting. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first polynomial-time algorithm for matroid semi-bandits that achieves BOBW guarantees.

title: Remote Charging of Quantum Batteries via a Multimode Resonator
abstract: We study the remote charging of a qubit battery by a qubit charger coupled through a finite multimode resonator. The charging protocol uses time-shifted coupling pulses that account for the spatial phases of the resonator modes. We compare the energy stored in the battery with its ergotropy, the maximum work extractable by a local unitary operation. In the single-excitation regime considered here, the battery stores energy at any nonzero excited-state population, but its ergotropy is positive only when that population exceeds one half. In the absence of loss, stronger coupling brings the battery above this threshold earlier, while the final charge remains nearly complete across the coupling range studied. For the parameters considered, qubit relaxation suppresses ergotropy more strongly than resonator loss at comparable decay rates. After the battery is disconnected, relaxation causes its stored energy to decay exponentially, yet its ergotropy vanishes at a finite time while half of its energy capacity remains occupied. For a fixed storage interval, disconnecting at the population maximum therefore preserves the most extractable work.

title: Ultrasound Watermark: Real-time Acoustic Watermarking against Voice Scams on Smartphones
abstract: Recent advances in text-to-speech (TTS), voice conversion (VC), and AI-driven speech synthesis enable adversaries to convincingly impersonate trusted individuals during phone calls. Existing defenses often rely on offline analysis, degrade under telephony distortions, or remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks. To address these limitations, we present Ultrasound Watermark, a real-time, smartphone-native framework that protects live calls by binding speech to the caller's physical articulatory motion through acoustic watermarking. During a call, the smartphone emits ultrasonic signals and captures reflections from facial articulatory movements using only its built-in speaker and microphone. Ultrasound Watermark extracts motion features from these reflections and fuses them with outgoing speech to generate a dynamic watermark. Because the ultrasonic measurements are physically and temporally coupled with speech production, they are difficult to spoof without the underlying articulatory motion. A synchronized generator-detector architecture enforces cross-modal speech-motion consistency against replay, synthesized speech, and articulation-mimicking attacks. Ultrasound Watermark operates continuously with less than 200 ms latency overhead and requires no additional hardware. We implement Ultrasound Watermark on iOS and Android and evaluate it using over 2.5 hours of synchronized speech-ultrasound recordings from 22 speakers across eight smartphones and four real-world environments. Results demonstrate robustness to diverse attacks and telephony distortions while preserving perceptual audio quality.

title: Quantum-Resilient, PUF-Based, and Anonymity-Preserving Authentication and Key Agreement Scheme for UAV Networks
