Second, to run an offline 2 s flow-matching gesture model on live audio, we reformulate inference as sliding-window continuation with overlapped look-ahead ensembling, which removes seam jitter. Third, we show that the remaining streaming gap comes from errors accumulating in the self-generated motion history rather than missing future speech; our Drift-Aware History Perturbation (DAHP) reduces this gap in about 50 min on one GPU by injecting inference-like drift into ground-truth training histories, and transfers to a second generator. On BEAT2, streaming BASE reaches an FGD of 0.342, on par with the tightly coupled MIBURI (0.333), and viewers prefer its body motion over MIBURI's in 82% of forced-choice judgments. Without retraining, the same layer drives a cascaded pipeline, three open full-duplex models, and a cloud API in real time.

title: AgentMoT: An Agentic Mixture-of-Transformers for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
abstract: Driving models need to choose which capabilities to use and when to reconsider their decisions. We introduce AgentMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers with built-in agent reasoning and system scheduling. Combinations of agent, world, and action experts form three jointly trained pathways for direct-action, vision-language-action, and world-action computation. The Router selects a native pathway, while the agent expert supplies reasoning and selects skills. Execution feedback raises wake-up requests, and the agent self-scheduler learns whether to reconsider the task decision or keep it. Mandatory requests invoke the agent directly. The relative-capability principle guides these choices by relating the benefit of additional computation or intervention to its cost. After open-loop initialization, dual-loop evolution trains the Router, agent, and self-scheduler from closed-loop experience while failure-driven updates refine skills and execution feedback. AgentMoT achieves state-of-the-art results on Bench2Drive v0.0.3 and v0.0.4, with 94.48/92.33 driving score and 85.45/82.73% success rate, respectively. With skills disabled, learned routing improves over the strongest fixed pathway by 1.79 driving-score points and 4.09 percentage points of success rate on v0.0.3. Ablation studies further show gains from closed-loop agent learning, two-view queries, and event-triggered wake-up.

title: Trustworthy Speech-Based Autism Screening under Class Imbalance with Uncertainty-Aware HuBERT Ensembles
abstract: Early screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is critical for timely clinical intervention, although establishing reliable speech based screening systems remains problematic due to limited clinical data, class imbalance, and the need for reliable uncertainty estimation. We propose an uncertainty-aware ASD screening framework based on self-supervised HuBERT representations, combining Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) crossvalidation, balanced k-bagging, and Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout. Multiple HuBERT models are fine-tuned on balanced subsets, with predictions combined through probability-based ensemble averaging and aggregated at the subject level. Experiments on the Child Pathological Speech Database (CPSD) show strong performance, achieving 86.30% balanced accuracy and 93.74% ROC-AUC at the utterance level, and 95.04% and 96.30%, respectively, at the subject level. Furthermore, predictive entropy effectively reflects classification reliability: incorrectly classified segments show higher entropy than correctly classified ones (0.4605 $\pm$ 0.2314 vs. 0.1717 $\pm$ 0.1830), with a significant correlation with errors (r = 0.3981, p = 7.38 x 10 -170 ) and an error-detection ROC-AUC of 0.8359. These results demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework as a robust and uncertainty-aware computer-aided tool for ASD screening.

title: Imprints of quantum space in the ringdown phase of Kerr black holes
abstract: We investigate quantum-space corrections to the gravitational quasinormal modes (QNMs) of Kerr black holes within the framework of noncommutative geometry. The analysis employs a pseudo-semi-Killing Drinfeld twist, which preserves the classical Kerr geometry as an exact background solution while introducing nontrivial quantum corrections to linearized gravitational perturbations. Working to first order in the black hole spin and the quantum deformation parameter, including their mixed contribution, we derive a Schrödinger-like master equation for axial gravitational perturbations with a frequency- and spin-dependent effective potential. We compute the fundamental QNM frequencies using the WKB approximation and Leaver's continued-fraction method. Our results reveal corrections to the QNM oscillation frequencies and damping rates arising from rotation, pure quantum effects, and their interplay. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic analysis of gravitational metric perturbations in a noncommutative Kerr black hole spacetime using a Drinfeld twist, extending prior work beyond the Schwarzschild case. Our findings demonstrate that quantum deformation effects alter both the oscillation frequencies and damping rates of quasinormal modes, with spin-quantum coupling introducing additional spin-dependent corrections to the Kerr QNM spectrum. Using a Kerr-anchored phenomenological prescription, we estimate the fractional frequency and damping-time shifts for selected merger remnants from the GWTC-3 and GWTC-5.0 catalogs. These estimates illustrate the potential signatures of quantum corrections in gravitational-wave ringdown.

title: LiquidGazeNet: Towards Event-Based Near-Eye Gaze Estimation under Low-Light Conditions
abstract: Near-eye gaze estimation under low-light nighttime conditions is challenging because the quality and effective temporal resolution of conventional intensity frames can be reduced. This paper presents LiquidGazeNet, an event-only gaze-estimation framework that combines polarity-aware spike-latency encoding with a custom LTC-based recurrent module. Positive- and negative-polarity events are represented in separate channels, while exponentially decayed time surfaces retain per-pixel temporal recency across successive event windows. A shared convolutional encoder extracts spatial features from each window, and a two-layer recurrent module composed of LTC-inspired cells integrates them causally over short temporal sequences. The network is trained using a hybrid objective that combines screen-space coordinate regression with centre-referenced directional consistency. The framework is evaluated on Gaze-FELL under cross-subject and cross-scene protocols and is further assessed through event-representation, temporal-module, window-duration, and computational ablations. LiquidGazeNet achieves mean errors of 3.75 degrees and 2.41 degrees under cross-subject and cross-scene evaluation, respectively. The results indicate that polarity-aware temporal-recency encoding, together with recurrent integration, is effective for event-only gaze estimation under the evaluated low-light nighttime conditions.

title: Dynamical calibration of a metallicity-dependent stellar mass--luminosity relation from Gaia wide binaries
abstract: The mass of a main-sequence star is usually estimated from its luminosity through a mass--luminosity relation (MLR). This relation depends on metallicity, and its empirical calibration relies on few stars with measured masses. We calibrate the MLR of single main-sequence stars in the Gaia $G$ band as a function of metallicity with $10\,559$ wide binaries. The projected relative speed and separation of a wide binary constrain its total mass statistically. We describe the stellar mass as a monotone function of absolute magnitude and metallicity and fit this function to all pairs. The metallicities come from Gaia low-resolution (XP) spectra and are calibrated by requiring that both stars of a pair have the same metallicity. The likelihood includes the measurement noise, the selection of the sample and pairs with an undetected close companion. The data constrain the MLR over $3.7\lesssim M_{\mathrm{G}} \lesssim11.8$\,mag and $-0.5\lesssim\ \mathrm{[M/H]} \lesssim0.4$, with a median statistical uncertainty of $2.5\%$ in mass. Tests of the model assumptions indicate an additional systematic uncertainty of up to $5\%$. At solar metallicity the MLR agrees with the PARSEC models to within $5\%$. At the faint end, the MIST, BaSTI, Dartmouth and BHAC15 models predict masses 8 to $22\%$ below our MLR. Published masses from orbits, eclipsing binaries and asteroseismology lie within about $10\%$ of our MLR for $M_{\mathrm{G}}<10.5$ mag. For fainter stars they are about $17\%$ lower. The origin of the difference at the faint end is not yet understood. Because a shift of $0.1$ dex in metallicity changes the mass by up to $5\%$, MLRs should be compared on a common metallicity scale.

title: FGPA-based advanced muon trigger algorithms for long-lived particle detection at the High-Luminosity LHC
abstract: The CMS Level-1 trigger must reconstruct muons in real time under stringent latency and hardware resource constraints. Conventional algorithms lose efficiency for high-energy muons undergoing radiative energy losses and can be suboptimal for displaced trajectories, limiting sensitivity to exotic signatures such as long-lived particles (LLPs). The Phase-2 upgrade introduces advanced FPGAs that enable more sophisticated reconstruction algorithms. This work presents two complementary developments addressing these challenges. In the barrel region, a dedicated algorithm detects showers from Drift Tube hit patterns at the first processing stage. At the subsequent filtering stage, shower primitives are correlated with conventional trigger primitives, currently targeting radiatively showering high-momentum muons, with LLP signatures as a broader objective. Simulation studies yield approximately $80\%$ shower-classification accuracy and an estimated matching efficiency above $80\%$ for radiating muons. Firmware prototypes demonstrate a shower-detection latency of approximately $20\,\mathrm{ns}$ and sub-bunch-crossing latency for preliminary matching logic. In parallel, a hardware-oriented optimization methodology is investigated for future graph neural network based displaced-muon reconstruction in the barrel--endcap overlap region. Using a GraphSAGE proxy on a benchmark dataset, a workflow combining integer quantization, power-of-two scaling, and data-driven bit-width optimization achieves $(75.0 \pm 1.1)\%$ accuracy and a deterministic latency of $19$ cycles ($52.8\,\mathrm{ns}$ at $360\,\mathrm{MHz}$), with only $20\%$ digital signal processor utilization. These results establish a basis for implementation studies using CMS muon data.

title: Neutron Spin Resonance as Probe of Triplet Pair Density Waves in CeCoIn$_5$
abstract: Spin resonance modes are among the most characteristic collective excitations of unconventional superconductors, yet their microscopic origin remains unresolved. Although commonly interpreted as purely magnetic excitations, this picture does not explain the rich magnetic field evolution of these modes observed in heavy-fermion superconductors. Here we combine inelastic neutron scattering and symmetry analysis to investigate the evolution of the spin resonance modes in the heavy-fermion superconductor CeCoIn$_5$ under an in-plane magnetic field. At high fields, approaching the upper critical field of the superconductor, we discover a third resonance mode with relatively high intensity. We demonstrate that the resonance branches observed experimentally can be interpreted as collective modes of the superconducting condensate involving transitions to excited superconducting states. This framework provides a unified interpretation of the field-induced splitting of the resonance, the newly observed mode at high fields, the relative neutron scattering intensities of each mode, and provides the first direct evidence that a spin resonance mode can be associated with a singlet-triplet excitation of a superconductor.

title: WEPWAWET-CORE: A Hardware-Resident ML-DSA Architecture with Fabric-Generated, Fabric-Sealed Keys for Post-Quantum Avionics
abstract: Spacecraft that exchange commands over crosslinks need quantum-resistant signatures, for which the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA, FIPS 204) is the standard, yet a software signer runs its data-dependent rejection loop, and keeps its key, on cores and memory shared with attitude control and payload processing. This paper shows that for a hardware-assisted signer the cost that matters is not the arithmetic but the number of times the processor crosses into the fabric, and that the boundary which minimizes those crossings is also where the key can be sealed. A gem5-supported analysis of three control granularities over the same kernels shows that only one job per signature, with the whole rejection loop on chip, takes the processor off the critical path. WEPWAWET-CORE realizes that boundary on an XCZU3EG at 300 MHz: a ROM microsequencer runs Sign, Verify, and key generation as three programs over one datapath and a banked scratchpad, and keeps the key, the on-die entropy, and the mask seed off the processor bus. The processor-side cost of a signature falls from over a second under per-kernel control to 0.53 ms, fixed whatever the number of rejections, and the fabric's time per attempt varies by less than 0.1% under a saturating workload. Under NASA JPL's F Prime with attitude-control and imaging loads, two nodes with fabric-generated, ground-certified keys exchanged 3,575 signed frames, every frame was accepted, and no attitude deadline was missed. A cycle profile places the remaining distance to dedicated cores in two serial units.

title: Event-Driven Parameter Dynamics for Spatiotemporal Parameter-Update Application in Deep Learning
abstract: Standard neural network training typically applies optimizer-generated update signals to model parameters at every iteration. This work introduces a spatiotemporal view of parameter updating and proposes Event-Driven Parameter Dynamics (EPD), which separates candidate-update generation from their application through an intermediate state with accumulation, event-triggered release, and reset. In a canonical coordinate-wise instantiation, accumulation produces temporal integration, release imposes a spatial budget, and reset separates successive inter-release intervals, while conventional dense updating is recovered as a boundary case. Across four model--optimizer configurations on CIFAR-100, EPD maintains final performance close to conventional training even when only a small fraction of coordinates are released at each step, including the 1\% regime. Matched-control experiments further show that temporal accumulation, state-dependent selection, and post-release reset each contribute to the observed behavior. Together, these results identify parameter-update realization as a controllable dimension of optimization and provide a concrete basis for studying its temporal and spatial organization separately from candidate-update generation.

title: New applications for optimal adaptivity
abstract: We introduce an explicit time-stepping scheme for ODEs, together with a residual-based a posteriori error estimator. Using this estimator, we show a new approach to proving optimality and linear reduction of adaptive algorithms for time-dependent problems that works in $H^1(0, t_{\rm end})$ and $W^{1,\infty}(0,t_{\rm end})$ norms, does not require quasi-orthogonality, and poses no restrictions on the marking parameter $θ$. The key idea is to use the Lipschitz continuity of the semi-discretized operator to obtain a stronger form of estimator reduction. Numerical experiments illustrate the benefits of this explicit scheme coupled with adaptive refinement over uniform time stepping for classical evolution problems, regularized dynamical approximation, and neural ODEs.

title: Cost-Sensitive Reversibility of Non-Deterministic Actions
abstract: Determining action reversibility requires checking whether the effects of an action can be undone. Recent work has extended reversibility to fully observable non-deterministic (FOND) planning. It distinguishes weak reversibility, where reversal may succeed, from strong-cyclic reversibility, where reversal is guaranteed under fairness. These notions are qualitative: they say whether reversal is possible, but not how costly it is. We introduce cost-sensitive reversibility for non-deterministic actions. Given positive action costs, we define weak and strong reversal budgets, $k$-bounded reversibility, and a distinction between finite strong reversal and strong-cyclic reversal with unbounded worst-case cost. We relate the resulting notions in a reversibility lattice, prove cost-aware policy-merging results, and show how to compute restricted weak and strong universal uniform reversal budgets using cost-optimal classical planning and worst-case-optimal FOND search, respectively. We also give an admissible lower-bound test for rejecting $k$-bounded reversibility. These notions support finer-grained safety decisions: a small finite strong budget bounds recovery cost, whereas a small weak budget certifies only a cheap possible recovery path. Actions without an acceptable strong bound may therefore warrant human approval, as in tool-using agent systems.

title: Morita equivalence classification for irrational noncommutative solenoids
abstract: Given a prime integer $p$, we define a $p$-angle to be an element of the $p$-solenoid ${\mathcal S}_p$ or equivalently an element of $\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{Q}_p$ modulo $\mathbb{Z}[1/p]$. Noncommutative $p$-solenoids, or equivalently $p$-rotation algebras, are $C^*$-algebras defined by a $p$-angle in the same way as non-commutative tori or usual rotation algebras are defined by an angle. We give a complete classification, in terms of their $p$-angles and in the irrational case, of these $C^*$-algebras up to strong Morita equivalence, but also the associated groupoids up to Morita equivalence; more precisely, we obtain the following classification result: two irrational $p$-angles define strong Morita equivalent noncommutative solenoids if and only if they define isomorphic dimension groups if and only if they are congruent modulo $GL_2(\mathbb{Z}[1/p])$ if and only if they define Morita equivalent groupoids. This generalises, with a different proof, the classification up to isomorphism, previously obtained by Latrémolière and Packer. We also give a geometrical construction of projective $C^*$-modules in terms of proper $G$-spaces which exhaust the dimension group up to a shift and implement all relevant Morita equivalences by groupoid equivalences.

title: Algorithms for Detecting Shape Defects in Concentrated Solar Power Plant Components
abstract: Concentrated solar power (CSP) technology offers a dispatchable renewable energy solution, capable of bridging the gap between intermittent generation and grid demand through high-capacity thermal energy storage. However, the overall thermodynamic efficiency and cost-effectiveness of CSP plants depend crucially on the optical quality and precise geometric alignment of thousands of reflective surfaces spread across vast solar fields. Shape defect detection algorithms have become essential tools for automating mirror profilometry, tracking the flow spot and diagnosing alignment issues. This paper presents a novel framework for geometric shape detection techniques tailored to CSP applications. It introduces the notion of \emph{parabolicity}, which motivates a class of optimisation problems in this setting and suggests a possible direction for further work in computational geometry. Both exact and approximate algorithms are proposed, together with an experimental study on synthetic datasets generated via simulation.

title: GeLiFiSH: Recursive LiDAR Keypoint Estimation with Ground and Moving Object Segmentation
abstract: LiDAR registration and loop closure often rely on sparse keypoints, which must remain repeatable across sessions, viewpoints, and sensors. To handle differing scan patterns, detectors typically operate on accumulated submaps, which introduces latency and processes each submap independently, so repeated observations are never fused. Height-based detectors also reference structure to an estimated ground, so its inconsistency across sessions propagates into the keypoints. Moreover, dynamic objects leave ghost trails that can be mistaken for static structure. We present GeLiFiSH (Geometric LiDAR Filtering with Sequential Hypothesis testing), a learning-free filter that recursively estimates persistent keypoints at scan rate. A height-structure detector runs on a rolling voxel map, and detections initialize tracks with a position, covariance, and existence probability, accepted or rejected by a sequential probability ratio test. Ground segmentation provides a sensor-agnostic height reference, and moving object segmentation removes dynamic points before map insertion. On SemanticKITTI, HeLiMOS, and HeLiPR, spanning five LiDARs and multiple sessions, GeLiFiSH attains the highest average keypoint repeatability among the compared detectors and the second-highest cross-session registration recall from keypoints alone, behind ISS which extracts four times as many keypoints. With one parameter set and no sensor-height prior, both ground and moving object segmentation modules outperform their baselines on average.

title: Quantum walks and conformal mappings
abstract: We study the most elementary discrete model of an electron moving along a line, known as Feynman checkers, quantum walk, or the six-vertex model with special complex weights, and provide a uniform asymptotic formula for the wave function in the whole xt-plane. In addition to the well-known appearance of the Airy function that describes the transition between the oscillating and exponentially decaying regimes, we observe a second transition governed by the gamma function when the electron speed approaches the speed of light. We prove two general theorems producing uniform asymptotic formulae involving the Airy and gamma functions, using conformal mappings associated with the underlying integral representations. They are applicable in several other situations as well.

title: Time Series Foundation Models on the Edge
abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast zero-shot with accuracy exceeding that of task-specific models, and the smaller ones fit on edge devices. Operational deployments must refresh their forecast as new observations arrive, and privacy and latency requirements often force this refresh onto resource-constrained edge devices. To serve as a forecasting system there, a TSFM must refresh quickly, keep latency and peak memory bounded as the stream grows, and retain its accuracy as the observed history accumulates. Refreshing incrementally without altering the forecast requires temporal causality: non-causal models recompute at every update, causal attention admits a KV cache that grows linearly, and causal recurrent models update a fixed-size state in constant time and memory. We make these states persist across refreshes for every causal architecture and verify equivalence to full recomputation. We evaluate nine TSFM configurations on univariate forecasting against all three requirements, measuring accuracy as a function of context length, single-refresh latency, and latency and memory on streams of up to one million time steps on a server-grade GPU and three edge devices. No model gains on average accuracy beyond its trained context and most lose it well before the full history is reached, while KV caches leave latency and memory growing linearly with the retained history. TiRex-2 is the only one of the nine configurations meeting all three requirements: it refreshes in 14 ms on the GPU and 120 ms on a Raspberry Pi 5, keeps latency, energy and peak memory constant over a million steps, and retains its accuracy on the untruncated history.

title: Optimistic Online Learning for Coding Agents with Aggregate Feedback
abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents operating on Web development platforms can interact with repositories, issue trackers, and continuous integration services to carry out long-horizon software engineering tasks. However, behavioral drift remains a major bottleneck in such multi-turn reasoning and action trajectories. To mitigate this, activation steering has emerged as a promising approach for regularizing agent behaviors by intervening on the LLM's transformer residual streams. Nonetheless, existing methods typically apply a static steering policy across all tasks, overlooking the fact that a single policy is rarely effective across heterogeneous tasks and varying execution turns. This limitation motivates dynamic online selection among candidate steering policies. Yet, doing so in long-horizon agentic settings is challenging: verifiable task-level feedback is only revealed upon task completion, leaving the contributions of individual steering turns unobserved. To address this challenge, we formulate online steering-policy selection as a multi-armed bandit problem with delayed task-level feedback and turn-level predictive hints derived from residual-stream activations. Within this formulation, we introduce Online Optimistic Activation Steering, a meta-framework that uses hints to guide within-task steering policy selection and leverages terminal task-level feedback to correct cumulative reward estimates. Theoretically, against the best fixed policy in hindsight, we prove regret bounds that tighten with increasing hint accuracy and establish a matching lower bound with respect to prediction error and candidate policy count. Empirical evaluations on realistic coding benchmarks demonstrate that our framework outperforms both static steering policies and naive online adaptive baselines.

title: TAP: Policy Interfaces for Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion language models denoise a masked canvas, making them a natural setting for selective generation decisions such as answering, waiting, clarifying, or refusing. We introduce TAP-DiLM, which adds a typed policy variable to masked diffusion LMs, and study how this policy should be attached to the denoising process. Across BERT-base, MDLMOWT, LLaDA-8B, and Dream-7B, we compare shared-vocabulary slots, dedicated slot heads, and CLS-based external heads. The results reveal a clear interface-backbone interaction: dedicated heads provide robust policy learning across scales, while sharedvocabulary heads can be effective when the LM-head geometry is favorable. A simple LMhead sharpness probe predicts when sharedhead policy internalization is reliable, giving a practical diagnostic for interface selection. Causal clamp and slot-injection tests show that dedicated policy slots can influence body denoising through feedback, especially at 8B scale. Safety-refusal experiments further show that TAP-DiLM supports competitive typed refusal behavior when trained with diverse unsafe prompts.

title: Universal thermodynamics and BKT transition of the planar Bose gas from weak to strong interactions
abstract: We compute the universal thermodynamics of the dilute two-dimensional Bose gas at weak and strong coupling using the functional renormalization group (FRG). We employ an approximation that retains the full field dependence of the effective potential and spatial derivative terms, extending previous FRG calculations. We find that the equation of state is remarkably insensitive to the approximation scheme, with differences of only a few percent even at strong coupling. By contrast, the improved approximation substantially improves the description of the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition, reproducing the universal jump of the superfluid density and the critical anomalous dimension to within a few percent. At weak coupling, our results agree very well with classical-field Monte Carlo simulations, while at stronger coupling we observe deviations from classical-field scaling, valid at weak coupling. Our approach thus provides a quantitative description of the thermodynamics and superfluid density across the BKT transition, including in the strong-coupling regime where classical-field methods are no longer reliable.

title: Interactions with hidden traits induce diversification and conceal its origin
abstract: Adaptive diversification is often inferred from a small number of measurable traits, even though evolutionary dynamics arise from many interacting phenotypic dimensions. Unmeasured traits may therefore do more than bias inference: through their interactions, they may determine whether diversification occurs at all. Here we develop a theory of the onset and attribution of adaptive diversification by partitioning phenotype space into focal and hidden sectors. Eliminating the hidden sector yields an exact effective operator. Coupling to hidden traits that are stabilizing in isolation can destabilize an otherwise stable phenotype and generate a diversifying composite mode: the interaction creates diversification rather than merely strengthening it. Conversely, when the hidden sector is itself diversifying, the focal traits diversify as a correlated response to a hidden-driven process: no effective description in the focal traits, not even the exact one obtained by eliminating the hidden sector, predicts the variation they display, and stabilizing the focal traits reduces it without removing it. These effects become strongest near the hidden sector's own threshold, so a weakly stabilized hidden trait can have a large effect even with modest coupling to the focal traits, and they can generate correlations between focal traits that have no direct interaction. Onset and observability are distinct: systems with the same leading eigenvalue can project very differently onto the measured traits, so the theory tracks both the full operator and the focal-hidden partition. Individual-based simulations recover the predicted threshold and variance law, coupling-induced trait splitting, and the reversal of induced correlations. Interactions with unmeasured traits can both create adaptive diversification and determine whether the diversification seen in measured phenotypes can be attributed to them.

title: Newton iterations and semi-Lagrangian schemes for mean field games of controls
abstract: We study Newton methods for second-order mean field games of controls (MFGC), in which agents interact through local averages of their controls. We prove local quadratic convergence of full Newton iterations, and of Newton iterations on reduced unknowns, near stable classical solutions. Stability holds under weak control interaction and under an infinitesimal monotonicity condition of Lasry--Lions type. We propose a semi-Lagrangian (SL) scheme for second-order MFGC, in which the average-control relation is solved by a convergent Chebyshev iteration, and two matrix-free solvers: a full Newton--SL method with block Gauss--Seidel preconditioning, whose spectrum we characterize in the absence of control coupling, and a reduced Jacobian-free Newton--GMRES method whose density iterates are nonnegative and mass-preserving by construction. We also construct an exact, time-dependent, coupled MFGC solution for use as a benchmark. In the experiments, the reduced solver converges quadratically in its final iterations, also in a strong-alignment test in which full Newton updates lose positivity. On the benchmark, the SL scheme and a finite-difference scheme both converge at first order with errors of comparable size, and our SL implementation is faster.

title: Disclosure Bias in AI Reviewers
abstract: AI models increasingly help to review papers, and many conferences and journals now require authors to state how they used AI. Does this AI-use statement change how an AI reviewer rates a paper, and could it change which papers are accepted? In a preliminary study, we varied only the AI-use statement of 150 ICLR 2027 submissions, in up to nine versions adapted from real statements: from no AI, through writing help and coding, to an AI research agent and an AI author. Six AI reviewers rated the versions: the decision model Jev and the language models Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 4 Argon. Across 23,652 reviews, we find that every reviewer rates papers lower on average when the statement says AI did all the work than under a statement of no AI use. The AI research agent statement lowers the rating significantly for Jev, Sonnet and Argon. We find no evidence of a disclosure bias for AI assistance: for writing help, coding and research help, no reviewer's rating differs significantly from its rating under a statement of no AI use. Whether the observed penalty changes which papers are accepted depends on more than the size of the penalty: on how finely and how consistently the reviewer separates the papers near the acceptance boundary, on whether the penalty is spread over all papers or concentrated on a few, and possibly on how many other papers disclose AI use.

title: Assumptions, Modeling and Risks: Applying ICH M15 to Statistical Modeling
abstract: In many instances in phase II and III clinical trials, critical assumptions underlying statistical analyses require discussion with regulators and other stakeholders. Such discussions benefit from a guiding process to promote consistency and clarity, but no widely and consistently applied framework currently exists. In January 2026, the International Council for Harmonisation released the ICH M15 Guideline on General Principles for Model-Informed Drug Development, which proposes a systematic framework for evaluating mechanistic models to support regulatory and development decisions. Although it focuses on mechanistic modeling, its structured assessment of model risks and benefits may be equally applicable to other approaches typically requiring a thorough appraisal of methodology and alignment among stakeholders, such as external data use and parametric longitudinal data analysis, and novel methodological approaches more generally. We illustrate and discuss how systematic risk-benefit evaluation of statistical models under the ICH M15 framework could work and propose its use to support acceptance of context-specific modeling strategies and to enhance decision-making transparency.

title: DMC-5: Dual-Model Collaboration with Cache-aware Context Compression for Long-horizon Agents
abstract: Long-horizon agents repeatedly feed an ever-growing interaction trajectory to a specialized agent model. Prefix caching reuses computation over repeated history, but cannot prevent context growth or remove information irrelevant to the current decision. This is especially costly when the specialized agent lacks the cached-input discounts available to general-purpose models, making trajectory compression a natural alternative. However, existing compression methods on selective context risk losing global information, recursively rewriting summary leads to semantic drift, while repeatedly recompressing the full history shifts the growing cost to the compressor. Therefore, we introduce DMC-5 (Dual-Model Collaboration with CaChe-aware Context Compression), an asymmetric framework that assigns full-history integration to a general compression model and action generation to a specialized agent model. DMC-5 maintains the raw trajectory as an Append-only Canonical View, preserving global access while allowing the compressor to reuse a stable historical prefix instead of recursively rewriting or recomputing prior context. The agent operates only on a compact Decision View with recent raw interactions, reducing repeated input while retaining the information needed for the next action. DMC-5 further incorporates YAMATO (integritY-Aware Memory Abstractions for Tool Operations) to preserve execution-critical information during lossy compression. Experiments on AppWorld, OfficeBench, and 8-objective QA show that DMC-5 reduces agent model input by 38.5-57.0% and end-to-end cost by 14.5-28.0% with 78.0-85.0% compressor cache-hit rates, while improving task performance by 1.0-5.8% over the uncompressed baseline.

title: Complex Oscillation and Non-Oscillation Results of Second-Order Linear Differential Equations
abstract: In this paper, we investigate oscillation and non-oscillation results of second order differential equations \begin{equation} f''+(H_1e^z+H_2e^{αz}+q)f=0,\tag{+} \end{equation} where $H_1,H_2\in\C\setminus\{0\}$, $0<α<1$, and $q$ is an entire function of order less than $1$. First, we show that if equation (+) has a zero-free non-trivial entire solution, then either $α=1/2$ or $α=3/4$, which settles the Problem 9 posed in \cite{HITW}. Second, we prove that if either $q$ is transcendental, or $α=(2m-1)/(2m)$ for some integer $m\geq 2$ and $q\equiv 0$, then every non-trivial entire solution $f$ of $(+)$ satisfies $λ(f)=\infty$.

title: Extreme Mass Ratio Inspirals: accessing generic orbits
abstract: Extreme Mass Ratio Inspirals (EMRI) are a significant gravitational wave source and a target for the upcoming LISA mission. Computations of the fluxes of conserved quantities, such as energy and angular momentum, are a critical part of modeling EMRI waveforms and can be performed using a frequency domain formalism to solve the Teukolsky equation. This requires computations of large numbers of mode amplitudes, many of which are negligible. However, it is unknown ex ante which can be safely skipped. We present a machine learning approach to estimate the dominant radial mode number as a function of the remaining mode numbers and apply it to reduce the number of unnecessary computations in EMRI flux calculation.

title: Computing $ab+cd$ and other expressions with correct rounding in binary floating-point arithmetic
abstract: We introduce two ``high-level'' algorithms that make it possible to evaluate the sum $(x\_h+x\_\ell) + (y\_h+y\_\ell)$ of two double-word numbers with correct rounding in binary floating-point arithmetic. These algorithms allow one to evaluate expressions of the form $ab+cd$, $a+b+cd$, $a+b+c+d$, and $abc$ with correct rounding, where $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$ are floating-point numbers.

title: Luminosity function of millisecond pulsars in globular clusters from their gamma-ray emission
abstract: Millisecond pulsars (MSPs) are widely believed to be responsible for the gamma-ray emission of globular clusters (GCs), yet the underlying MSP gamma-ray luminosity function remains uncertain. Existing GC-based determinations of the latter often rely on external prescriptions for the number of MSPs in each cluster. In this work, we constrain the MSP gamma-ray luminosity function in Milky-Way GCs directly from gamma-ray spectral energy distributions (SEDs), establishing an inference strategy that remains computationally viable for joint analyses of large GC samples. We construct a forward model in which each GC hosts a population of MSPs whose luminosities are drawn from a universal log-normal luminosity function. Synthetic GC SEDs are generated by summing individual MSP spectra, and we infer posterior distributions using first a likelihood-based nested sampling method and then a simulation-based inference (SBI) approach. We show how the likelihood-based method becomes rapidly impractical as the number of jointly modelled clusters (and cluster-specific latent parameters) increases, whereas the SBI approach scales mildly with sample size and reproduces the likelihood-based posteriors in regimes where direct sampling is feasible. We then apply the SBI pipeline to Fermi-LAT SEDs from the 4FGL-DR4 catalog for a sample of 36 GC-associated sources, augmented by dedicated phase-resolved ON/OFF SEDs for two clusters hosting individually detected MSPs. For the real data sample, we obtain informative constraints on the luminosity-function parameters consistent with previous analyses that constrain the cluster-specific MSP counts via complementary multi-wavelength information.

title: ANOR: Scaling Sparse Attention with a GPU-PNM Computing Hierarchy
abstract: Serving large language models with long contexts requires keeping the key-value (KV) cache of every request, which can exceed GPU memory capacity. Sparse attention reads only a small, query-dependent subset of this cache at each decoding step, yet must retain the full cache because later steps may select other entries. Processing-near-memory (PNM) devices attached through Compute Express Link (CXL) can hold the full cache and compute attention where it resides. Prior GPU-PNM systems for sparse attention are PNM-centric, processing most of the attention on the PNM. As existing CXL-PNM devices provide far less memory bandwidth than GPU HBM, this PNM-centric execution makes the PNM the bottleneck and leaves the GPU idle waiting for attention results. We present ANOR, a GPU-PNM joint acceleration system that exploits the selection locality of sparse attention by computing most of the attention on the GPU from a cache of recently selected entries and processing only the misses on the PNM. As the PNM processes cache misses directly, GPU cache updates can be decoupled from current-step execution. We develop a bounded cache-update policy that limits updates to the point where the hit ratio of later steps saturates, reducing GPU-facing link traffic. We add a small on-chip Early Streaming Buffer (ESB) that captures KV data during PNM attention and streams it to the GPU, avoiding most redundant DRAM reads despite the bandwidth mismatch between PNM memory and the GPU-facing link. We also propose an adaptive cache-factor mechanism that adjusts GPU cache size to the serving load, balancing hit ratio and batch size. Across two models and three long-context agentic workloads, ANOR improves decode throughput by 2.3x over HiSparse and 2.0x over a PNM baseline on average. These results show that PNM is most effective not as the primary attention engine but as a computing tier of the GPU memory hierarchy.

title: Uniform Ionization Bounds in Molecular Thomas--Fermi--Dirac--von Weizsäcker Theory
abstract: We study the molecular Thomas--Fermi--Dirac--von Weizsäcker theory. For each fixed number $K$ of nuclei, we prove that every minimizer of mass $N$ satisfies $N\leq Z+C_K$, where $Z$ is the total nuclear charge, and $C_K>0$ is independent of the nuclear charges and positions. This answers the molecular large-charge ionization question posed in [R. L. Frank, P. T. Nam and H. Van Den Bosch, CPAM, 2018]. For $N\geq Z$, we also compare the screened potentials and electronic radii of Thomas--Fermi--Dirac--von Weizsäcker minimizers with those of the corresponding neutral molecular Thomas--Fermi minimizers and establish a uniform bound on the ionization energy.

title: TamperCert: A Benchmark for Detecting Text Tampering in Degree Certificates
abstract: Degree certificates play a critical role in high-stakes decisions such as university admission, immigration, and hiring. The issuing institution vouches for the holder, so a forged certificate may let its bearer pass these checks. Degree certificate forgery is increasingly prevalent. Yet, many assume that it is easy to spot. Reported cases show otherwise: in 2024, the business school of the University of Hong Kong found that about 30 master's students had enrolled with forged academic credentials. Few studies have looked at how to detect forged degree certificates, partly because public benchmarks are scarce. We present TamperCert, a benchmark built from 400 real degree certificates issued by 38 universities. Each certificate was subjected to 11 publicly available tampering methods to alter the holder's name and further processed with four additional post-processing techniques, resulting in over 20,000 forged images. We evaluate 13 detectors, a commercial multimodal large language model (MLLM), and detectors trained on TamperCert.Our findings reveal that no detector is reliable for every tampering method. Consequently, a determined forger may still evade detection. Moreover, the commercial MLLM misses most forgeries made by general-purpose generative models, and post-processing, such as resizing an image or photographing it with a camera, severely degrades detection.

title: Safety-Tiered ISAC Scheduling with History-Aware Value of Information for V2X Networks
abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) assisted vehicle-to-everything (V2X) networks prioritize safety-critical radar sensing over communication. However, existing scheduling methods overlook the varying criticality of vehicles, long-term fairness in service quality, and information staleness. Considering this, we propose a low-complexity sensing-prioritized allocation for radar and communication (SPARC-V) to maximize the value of information (VoI) in V2X networks. SPARC-V addresses these challenges with a two-stage hierarchical resource scheduling framework. For sensing, vehicles are first categorized into safety tiers based on a risk metric. Safety-critical vehicles receive orthogonal resources, while others can reuse resources under specific constraints. Sensing resources are allocated based on a sensing priority metric that balances safety significance and long-term fairness. In the next stage, communication resources are allocated to vehicles with the most outdated information. Performance is measured using a unified VoI metric that considers sensing quality, safety relevance, and information freshness. Monte Carlo simulations show that SPARC-V achieves the highest network VoI of 26.5 among all baselines, with its advantage over baselines widening as vehicle density increases.

title: Confidence-Aware Discriminative Readout of Neutral-Atom Arrays
abstract: Fast and reliable detection is a central requirement for neutral atom quantum computers, yet fluorescence imaging remains a limiting step for rapid experimental cycling, large-scale array operation, and quantum-error-correction protocols. In this work, we demonstrate confidence-aware readout of $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$ atoms in optical tweezers using a discriminative classifier. Rather than forcing each atom-site image directly into a hard binary outcome, the proposed readout produces a measurement reliability score. This score is produced by a logistic-regression classifier trained on features derived from both the total photon count and the spatial pattern of fluorescence at each site. The resulting classifier achieves the same readout fidelity with approximately half the imaging time. At an exposure of 10 ms, it achieves $99.83\%$ readout fidelity, comparable to the $99.82\%$ achieved by conventional photon-count thresholding at 20 ms. Importantly, the classifier score enables low-confidence outcomes to be converted into measurement-level erasures, leaving fewer residual unflagged errors at a fixed erasure budget. This improvement is further accompanied by strong false-positive suppression, which is important for downstream operations such as atom rearrangement where false positives can create target defects. Monte Carlo rearrangement simulations show that the reduced false-positive rate and confidence-based erasure conversion improve predicted defect-free assembly performance. This work establishes confidence-aware readout using a discriminative classifier as a practical paradigm for fast and scalable neutral-atom quantum computing.

title: HWRE-Bench: Can LLM Agents Understand Hardware They Did Not Design?
abstract: Hardware benchmarks for LLM agents all run the design flow forward, from a specification to RTL, a layout or a bug fix. We ask the reverse question: given an implemented artifact, such as a layout, a gate-level netlist or a protected simulation model, can an agent work out what it does well enough to act on that knowledge? We introduce HWRE-Bench, a benchmark for agentic hardware reverse engineering built on one observation. Each step of the forward flow discards information (names, hierarchy, word-level structure, generator parameters, the programming model), and a reverse-engineering task asks the agent to recover what was lost and to prove it with an executable deliverable that the artifact alone cannot supply. Since layout extraction is now mechanical and a correct netlist is already a cycle-exact model, every task carries a mandatory copy-the-netlist control that must score zero. HWRE-Bench spans five tracks (Extract, Abstract, Audit, Interoperate, Modify), four information-loss levels and white- versus black-box access, all on original designs. We report a pilot of 148 rollouts from two agents on four seed tasks under 16 conditions, with stage-annotated trajectories. Agents built their own layout extractors and audited a sanitized layout as reliably as a netlist, at about 27% more turns. Keyless, equivalence-preserving obfuscation changed neither pass rates nor defect-repair scores. Whether agents read the structure at all depended on task framing rather than on necessity, so pass rate alone does not show understanding. Provider safety filters stopped 16% of one agent's runs on the audit tasks. These results argue for deliverables beyond equivalence and for reporting run validity explicitly.

title: Automated Call for Action: RAG-Based Environmental Law Enforcement Screening System
abstract: Environmental law inspectors face a structural issue in identifying potential violations from data: they often do not have the capacity to deal with large volume of data present in the emission events. This paper examines to what extent an LLM-based system can support evidence assembly and permit-based screening of such events, using the coke plants of a steel producer and a regional environmental service as a case. A simple puff-trajectory model aligns air quality measurements, weather and citizen complaints with each emission event. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline then retrieves facility-specific permit conditions and generates event reports and a period report with an investigation recommendation. Across 74 events from March 2025, plant-aware re-ranking reduced reports citing the other plant's conditions from 58.1% (hybrid retrieval) to 0% by rule-based plant labels, while maintaining high RAGAS and LLM-judge metrics. GPT-5-mini performed comparably to GPT-5.1, whereas GPT-5-nano scored lower on legal grounding and legal faithfulness. In an evidence ablation, removing air quality (AQ) data changed judge scores and period recommendations most; citation overlap changed only slightly under any removal, and removing complaint details had no measurable effect. This suggests a need for rules and guidelines that link complaints to incidents and permit conditions, so that community reports can count as evidence. The results support screening of events that may need further investigation. Design implications for involving environmental service experts are derived.

title: Spatial-Zero: Self-Evolving Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models from Zero Data
abstract: Spatial reasoning requires a vision-language model~(VLM) to understand metric distances, three-dimensional relationships, and viewpoint-dependent geometry. Learning these capabilities typically requires externally curated training data. This paper introduces Spatial-Zero, a VLMs' training framework that can self-evolve through autonomous spatial exploration with zero data. Spatial-Zero addresses two key challenges in autonomous spatial exploration: reliably generating valid spatial interaction tasks and providing accurate supervision for learning from these tasks. Specifically, a proposer specifies object configurations and questions, and a Coder turns them into executable scene programs that produce multi-view images and explicit scene geometry. A Geometric Oracle checks spatial constraints, visibility, and answer uniqueness and derives ground-truth labels from executed geometry; these labels supervise the Solver and ground difficulty feedback, while validation outcomes guide subsequent task generation. Across six spatial reasoning benchmarks and three VLM backbones, Spatial-Zero yields consistent gains through iterative self-evolution. After three iterations, Qwen3.5-9B improves average accuracy by 3.23 percentage points; with Qwen3.5-4B, Spatial-Zero also outperforms existing VLM self-evolution methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/YutongLi2024/Spatial-Zero

title: Non-Perturbative Analysis of Resonances by a Contraction Mapping on Complex Domains
abstract: In this paper, we consider a perturbation problem of embedded eigenvalues for an abstract Friedrichs--Lee Hamiltonian and analyze its spectral properties. By deforming the contour and constructing a contraction mapping on complex domains, we prove the existence of resonance poles.

title: Exact finite-sample and loss limits of squeezed-vacuum phase estimation
abstract: We settle the dispute over squeezed-vacuum phase estimation by exact computation of the finite-sample errors, resource-fair scaling, phase window, and loss ceilings. A fixed overhead of ten repetitions sets the attainable finite-sample frontier; the repetitions cancel from the resource-fair bound, so Heisenberg scaling survives; the operating window holds a repetition-set number of resolvable points and needs one bit of branch prior; and fixed loss caps the per-photon advantage at a value set only by transmissivity, already reached by the reported record.

title: Scanning nanowire quantum dot with radio-frequency read-out
abstract: Scanning single-electron transistors (SETs) are highly sensitive local probes of charge and electric potential, but their integration with robust height control for scanning probe microscopy remains challenging. Furthermore, readout bandwidths are limited to tens of kHz, while characterizing faster charge dynamics is often of interest. Here, we present a scanning SET in the form of a nanowire (NW) quantum dot (QD) integrated at the apex of a non-contact atomic force microscopy (NC-AFM) cantilever. We demonstrate NC-AFM topographic imaging and local electrometry capability by mapping the electrostatic potential generated by a set of nanoscale voltage-biased gate electrodes. Comparison with electrostatic simulations shows agreement with the measured potential profiles. We demonstrate radio-frequency (rf) reflectometry read-out of the sensor, by embedding the QD in an LC-resonator. This platform establishes a route towards high-bandwidth scanning electrometry with simultaneous topographic contrast.

title: Combining Physical Layer Security and Symmetric Encryption to Secure Rate-Splitting Multiple Access
abstract: The demand for increased spectral efficiency (SE) in downlink multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) systems has led to the development of various multiple access techniques. Among these, rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) can improve SE over space division multiple access (SDMA) and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) by splitting each user's data into common and private parts. The common parts from all users are then encoded into a single common message, which is transmitted alongside the private messages using an RSMA-specific precoder. Recent results showed that the precoder can be modified to enable physical layer security (PLS) by integrating secrecy rate constraints into the design. However, this approach only secures the private messages, while the common part of each user remains unprotected. To address this limitation, we propose a hybrid-PLS RSMA scheme that symmetrically encrypts all user data and embeds key information within the PLS-secured private messages. Additionally, the RSMA precoder is adapted to ensure that the private messages are sufficiently sized to carry the key information. The precoder design is formulated as a non-convex SE maximization problem and solved using successive convex approximation (SCA). Analytical and numerical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed hybrid-PLS RSMA can significantly improve SE compared to partially secure RSMA and secure SDMA, when complete user data security is required.

title: Revealing Nuclear Shape through Identified-Hadron Flow Decorrelations
abstract: Relativistic nuclear collisions encode nuclear shape in collective flow, yet the potential of identified hadrons to disentangle deformation modes remains largely unexplored. Using event-by-event viscous hydrodynamics coupled to hadronic transport, we investigate momentum-dependent elliptic-flow decorrelations of pions, kaons, and protons in central $^{238}$U+$^{238}$U collisions at 193 GeV and $^{20}$Ne+$^{20}$Ne collisions at 5.36 TeV. The identified species exhibit distinct momentum- and deformation-dependent responses, with nuclear-shape information persisting in their relative correlations even when individual deformation effects are weak. We introduce crossing coordinates $(P_{\rm cross},R_{\rm cross})$, defined by the intersection of pion-kaon and pion-proton flow-factorization ratios. Variations of quadrupole deformation and triaxiality generate distinct trajectories in the crossing plane, offering complementary constraints on both nuclear-shape parameters. The corresponding behavior persists in higher-moment correlations, while an energy comparison in Ne+Ne reveals the influence of collision dynamics. Our findings establish identified-particle flow decorrelations as a complementary approach to probing and constraining intrinsic nuclear geometry.

title: Signed Admissible Regions and 2-adic Area Obstructions for Perfect Triangles
abstract: A perfect triangle is a triangle whose sides, medians and area are all integers; whether one exists is an open problem. We study Buchholz's rational parametrization of triangles with two rational medians on the whole $(θ,ϕ)$-plane, allowing the generated side lengths to be negative. We factor its Heron polynomial $H(θ,ϕ)$ into ten explicit factors and show that the points whose componentwise absolute values form a triangle are exactly those with $H>0$; the points giving positive side lengths directly form three open quadrilaterals, one of which is the region used by Buchholz and Rathbun. Every triangle with two rational medians arises from sixteen signed parameter points, given by explicit rational functions. Rational area forces $H$ to be a square in $\mathbb{Q}_2$, and the valuation and the unit part of $H$ yield parity and modulo-8 conditions in three valuation ranges. Since a triangle is excluded as soon as one of its sixteen parameter points fails a test, these conditions exclude infinite families of signed admissible parameters, including non-integral ones. The conditions are necessary only and do not settle the existence of perfect triangles.

title: Angular characteristics of attenuation and temporal dispersion introduced by single deciduous bush in winter conditions at FR2 band
abstract: Vegetation-induced attenuation and temporal dispersion remain important impairments in millimeter-wave radio propagation, particularly in the frequency range 2 (FR2) band, where highly directional links are employed. Existing vegetation attenuation models, including ITU-R P.833, predominantly address scenarios involving trees or vegetation clusters and are typically derived for the main radiation direction of the transmitting antenna. This paper presents an experimental study of angular-dependent attenuation and temporal dispersion introduced by a single deciduous bush under winter conditions. Measurements were conducted on a university campus at 28 GHz and 38 GHz using a wideband channel-sounding testbed operating from 1 MHz to 44 GHz. The bush, approximately 3 m in height, was located at the center of a circular measurement trajectory with a radius of 10 m, along which the receiver was positioned at angular intervals of approximately 8 deg. Directional antennas with 7-9 deg half-power beamwidth were employed, and reception angles from 0 to 200 deg relative to the transmitter-bush axis were investigated. The results demonstrate significant angular variability in both excess attenuation and temporal dispersion, indicating substantial contributions from scattering outside the main propagation direction. Differences between the two carrier frequencies are analyzed, highlighting frequency-dependent attenuation mechanisms even in leaf-off conditions. The presented findings extend existing single-vegetation models by incorporating angular characteristics and temporal effects, providing valuable insights for the design and modeling of FR2 wireless links in sparse-vegetation environments.

title: Optimal XOR Lemmas for Information Complexity
abstract: Information complexity studies how much information the parties to a communication protocol must reveal to each other about their inputs to accomplish a given task. For a Boolean-valued communication problem $F$, let ${\rm IC}_ε(F)$ denote its information complexity with error $ε$, and let $F^{\oplus n}$ denote the XOR of $n$ independent instances of $F$. A fundamental question is whether information complexity obeys an XOR lemma, ${\rm IC}_{1/3}(F^{\oplus n})=Ω(n\cdot{\rm IC}_{1/(3n)}(F))$, which would match the trivial upper bound. Previous work either established the $n$-fold increase in information cost without the $n$-fold decrease in error (Bar-Yossef et al., FOCS 2002) or proved a lower bound with a subtracted penalty proportional to the input length of $F$ (Sawettamalya and Yu, STOC 2025). In particular, the question has remained open even for the XOR of $n$ or fewer copies of a function $F:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$. We completely resolve the question of XOR lemmas for information complexity, for every error $0\leε\le1/3$. For total functions $F$, we prove that ${\rm IC}_ε(F^{\oplus n})=Θ(n\cdot{\rm IC}_{ε/n}(F))$ unless $F$ has the degenerate form $F(x,y)=a(x)\oplus b(y)$, in which case ${\rm IC}_ε(F^{\oplus n})=O(1)$. For the richer class of partial functions, we obtain the characterization ${\rm IC}_ε(F^{\oplus n})=Θ({\rm IC}_ε(F)+n\cdot{\rm SIC}_{ε/n}(F))$, where ${\rm SIC}$ is the information complexity of protocols in which Alice and Bob privately output bits whose XOR is the answer. Finally, we prove an optimal distributional XOR lemma, for every function $F$ and every distribution. We obtain an optimal direct sum theorem to accompany each of our XOR lemmas. All implicit constants are absolute. Our work contributes a novel combination of information-theoretic and geometric techniques.

title: Darboux transformation for the ASDYM equations: Solitons and instantons
abstract: Using a one-fold Darboux transformation for the anti-self-dual Yang--Mills equations, we express the Yang--Mills Lagrangian density in terms of $τ$-functions. For solitons constructed from exponential functions, we show that the associated $τ$-functions admit a parametrization by arbitrary points in the Grassmannian Gr(N,M;$\mathbb{C}$), and construct the corresponding Yang--Mills fields. For instantons arising from the Atiyah--Drinfeld--Hitchin--Manin (ADHM) construction, we reinterpret the ADHM construction in terms of a one-fold Darboux transformation, recover Osborn's formula for the Yang--Mills Lagrangian density, and obtain the corresponding gauge connection.

title: Effect of dark matter and scalar-cut potential on the macroscopic properties of neutron stars: A chiral quark mean field approach
abstract: We investigate the effects of fermionic dark matter (DM) and scalar-cut potential ($U_{\text{cut}}(ϕ)$) on the equation of state (EOS) and macroscopic properties of neutron stars. The baryonic matter consists of neutrons, protons, electrons, and muons under the $β$-equilibrium and is described within the chiral SU(3) quark mean-field (CQMF) model. In this framework, quarks are confined within baryons, whose properties are modified through the exchange of scalar fields $σ$, $ζ$, and $δ$, and vector fields $ω$ and $ρ$. The DM is modelled as a self-interacting fermionic fluid with scalar $φ_D$ and vector $V_D^μ$ mediators. The baryonic and DM fluids interact only through gravity and are treated within a two-fluid Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff formalism. We examine the resulting mass-radius relation and tidal deformability, along with the gravitational redshift, to investigate the effects of DM on neutron star structure and observable properties. The inclusion of $U_{\text{cut}}(ϕ)$ stiffens the EOS, whereas increasing the DM fraction generally softens the EOS and modifies the mass-radius relation, tidal deformability, and gravitational redshift. The magnitude and nature of these modifications depend on the DM particle mass and mediator interactions, which determine whether the resulting configurations exhibit compact DM cores or extended DM halos.

title: Tensor Recovery with Heterogeneous Mode Structures
abstract: Tensor recovery methods often impose a common structural assumption across modes, even when different modes may exhibit distinct forms of regularity. We propose a unified convex framework that treats each mode according to its structure. Smoothly varying modes form an indexing domain and are handled by local kernel weighting, whereas retained modes may receive low-rank, group-sparse, graph-Laplacian, or autoregressive regularization in distinct and potentially overlapping combinations. The framework also covers ordinary tensor recovery without local smoothing. A consensus HM-ADMM algorithm separates the active penalties into tractable proximal and linear-system updates. For the population-quadratic estimator, we derive deterministic oracle inequalities and high-probability bounds under independent trace regression. The bounds disentangle stochastic error, rank and support complexity, smoothing bias, and quadratic mismatch. They also identify when quadratic penalties sharpen the Frobenius-error bound. For regular smooth domains, the theory characterizes the bias-variance trade-off and yields an optimal bandwidth order, with a specialization to uniform tensor completion. Simulations and two applications illustrate the gains from matching regularization to mode-specific structure, especially under severe undersampling.

title: MF-EDA: Joining Membership Functions to Adapt the Number of Distributions in Gaussian Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithms
abstract: An estimation-of-distribution algorithm (EDA) usually samples from one Gaussian, whose peak sits where most selected individuals are. On a landscape with two funnels that is not where the best solutions are: the wider funnel supplies most of the selected individuals, and the deeper funnel, which holds the global optimum, is lost early. This paper builds the search distribution as a neuro-fuzzy system builds a model: from Gaussian membership functions joined by membership degrees. In every generation the proposed MF-EDA searches the principal directions of the selected individuals for the direction along which they are bimodal, describes them on that direction by one or two membership functions according to the Bayesian information criterion and a separation test, joins each membership function to a local Gaussian in the other directions, and samples from the normalised union. A membership function has height one whatever the number of individuals under it, so a detected funnel receives samples according to its width. A two-region selection model shows that sampling shares proportional to the head count, as in a Gaussian mixture, compound the early disadvantage of the deeper funnel, and that the union does not. With one membership function the algorithm is its single-Gaussian baseline; the steps cost no fitness evaluations but make a generation 8 to 17 times slower to compute. On 36 double-funnel settings the component raises the successful runs of a rank-weighted Gaussian EDA from 805 to 1712 of 1800. On the Lunacek double funnel in 30 dimensions it raises that EDA from 4 to 49 and AMaLGaM from 0 to 47 successes in 50 runs, while results on single-funnel functions and on ten multimodal BBOB functions do not change. Restarted CMA-ES remains cheaper in evaluations on the standard double funnel, and the component stops helping when the global funnel is much narrower than the other.

title: Post-Newtonian expansion of the energy and angular momentum flux radiated to infinity: Eccentric-equatorial orbits about a Kerr black hole
abstract: We present analytical expressions for the energy and angular momentum fluxes radiated to infinity by a (nonspinning) point mass in an eccentric-equatorial orbit about a Kerr black hole. These results build upon our previous work involving point masses on eccentric orbits about a Schwarzschild black hole. We now adopt the Teukolsky formalism in first-order black hole perturbation theory to extend our methods to Kerr. We obtain the expressions using the method of Mano, Suzuki, and Takasugi, which provides infinite-series analytical solutions to the Teukolsky equation that we generate using Mathematica. The expressions presented are obtained as a double expansion in the post-Newtonian (PN) compactness parameter $1/p$, where $p$ is the dimensionless semi-latus rectum, and in the eccentricity $e$, up to 10PN and $e^{20}$, extending beyond prior 6PN and $e^{16}$ results available for generic orbits. We characterize how the PN flux coefficients depend on the black hole spin $a$ and $e$, and find a set of spin-dependent components that can be resummed as closed-form expressions in $e$. The analytical expressions are then validated with numerical comparisons against high-precision sample results from an independent Teukolsky code and with a broader set of numerically interpolated values derived from a flux data set produced with the same code. For $a=0.9M$, the numerically evaluated 10PN fluxes match current interpolated flux grids ($\sim10^{-7}$) for $p\gtrsim20$ to $75$ as $e$ ranges from $0.1$ to $0.7$, where they could replace Teukolsky-code results.

title: ROSE-Drive: Runtime Orchestration and System Evolution for Autonomous Driving
abstract: End-to-end driving models have made substantial progress, yet reliable closed-loop driving in complex traffic remains challenging. Beyond improving individual models, system-level orchestration offers a complementary approach by coordinating driving capabilities and computation. We introduce ROSE-Drive (Runtime Orchestration and System Evolution), a model-agnostic framework that jointly orchestrates driving execution and computation. It coordinates frozen driving models with driving skills, perception tools, and feedback controllers. A distilled vision-language model (VLM) proposes driving tasks and scene relations. Shared physical state and persistent tasks support capability composition, task continuity, and adaptive scheduling. The orchestrator combines model and skill outputs across control channels, maintains task responsibility through handover, and uses execution feedback to select controllers, reuse valid motion references, and schedule model inference. Offline revisions use execution records to refine skills and their coordination through a stable task interface. Successive system stages inherit these revisions while model, perception, and VLM weights remain fixed. Evaluations with four driving models on Bench2Drive v0.0.3, Bench2Drive v0.0.4, and Fail2Drive show accumulated capability and transfer before target-benchmark revision. On held-out Longest6, driving score (DS) rises from 25 to 52 for AutoMoT and from 22 to 47 for SimLingo across system stages, while both systems skip new model inference on over 71% of control steps.

title: Bypassing the Nanoampere Limit: A Thick-Target Methodology for Ultra-Low-Energy Resonances in the $^{11}$B(p,$α$)2$α$ Reaction
abstract: Precise measurements of the low-energy cross section for the $^{11}$B(p,$α$)2$α$ reaction is critical for nuclear astrophysics and fusion energy research, yet such measurements are experimentally demanding due to the reaction's extremely small cross section. Conventional thin-target experiments are fundamentally limited to nanoampere beam currents, which restrict count rates to impractical levels at ultra-low proton energies. To overcome this limitation, we report a correction-free thick-target methodology capable of operating at beam currents of 20-60 microamperes, corresponding to a gain of over three orders of magnitude. Monte Carlo simulations of the full reaction kinematics are employed to determine the absolute reaction yield, eliminating the requirement for empirical normalization factors. At the well-known 148~keV (c.m.) resonance peak, our extracted resonance energy ($E_{\mathrm{r}} = 148.0$~keV) and level width ($Γ_{\mathrm{cm}} = 5.3$~keV) are demonstrated in good agreement with published data. A scheme via comparing the measured reaction probability with a theoretical extrapolation result is furtherly presented to probe low-energy resonances below 100~keV region. Preliminary measurements at proton energies of 75~keV and 100~keV reveal no evidence for additional low-energy resonances. This work provides a robust new methodology to measure cross section and resonance parameters for the p$^{11}$B reaction and offers a highly efficient tool for systematic resonance searches in the ultra-low-energy regime.

title: Spectral Regularization Beyond Ridge Regression
abstract: We study Inclusive Ridge (IR), a two-parameter spectral regularization family that contains ridge regression as well as iterated Tikhonov regularization. We derive its exact finite-sample coefficient risk and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for increasing or decreasing the additional filter-shape parameter around the ridge baseline to locally lower risk. We show that oracle-tuned ridge is generically suboptimal within the IR family. Under joint divergence of the penalty and filter order, we show that a nondegenerate spectral limit exists precisely when their ratio converges to a positive finite constant, yielding a continuous exponential filter. Along the fixed effective-scale path, we also obtain an exact risk-difference comparison and explicit sufficient conditions under which both higher-order estimators and the exponential limiting filter strictly outperform oracle-tuned ridge. In this regime, IR becomes progressively less sensitive to perturbations in the absolute penalty parameter while retaining sensitivity to its effective spectral scale, and a plug-in coefficient-risk first-order condition coincides with a degrees-of-freedom-adjusted discrepancy equation. Numerical examples based on the Fredholm inverse problem, tomographic reconstruction, a regression design, and synthetic difference-in-differences donor-weight estimation illustrate both the potential gains and the limitations of feasible tuning, distinguishing oracle improvements from gains attainable with estimated tuning parameters.

title: Liouvillian Quasiparticle Spectroscopy
abstract: Quasiparticles play a central role in understanding closed quantum many-body systems, as they reduce complex many-body problems to effective single-particle descriptions and connect directly to spectroscopic measurements. In open quantum systems, the interplay between coherent dynamics and dissipation gives rise to unique phenomena, such as the Liouvillian skin effect and strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking. This raises a fundamental question: how can the quasiparticle picture be extended to open quantum systems to account for such phenomena and enable the experimental probing of quasiparticle spectra? Here we introduce coherent and incoherent Liouvillian quasiparticles, defined by responses to perturbations acting on one side and both sides of the density matrix, respectively. We propose spectroscopy protocols that couple the system to auxiliary levels, either coherently or via a dissipative pulse, to measure the corresponding complex quasiparticle energies. Numerical simulations of Liouvillians with skin effects validate these protocols, revealing nontrivial spectral winding associated with unidirectional transport in real space. Notably, coherent and incoherent quasiparticles can propagate in opposite directions within the same system. Furthermore, in models exhibiting weak and strong-to-weak $U(1)$ spontaneous symmetry breaking, our results unveil gapless Nambu-Goldstone modes in the coherent and incoherent quasiparticle spectra, respectively; the other quasiparticle spectrum remains gapped in each case. Our work provides a unified framework for theoretically describing and experimentally probing coherent and incoherent quasiparticles in open quantum many-body systems.

title: Approximate L_r-factorization of \ell_p-strictly singular operators on L_p
abstract: For \(1<p<2\), we study norm approximation of operators on \(L_p(0,1)\) by operators that factor through \(L_r(0,1)\), where \(p<r<2\). Using a sharp factorization estimate for finite diagonal blocks, we show that the corresponding norm-closed factorization ideals form a strictly decreasing chain as \(r\) increases. We also construct a strictly singular operator \(T_p\) at positive distance from the closed linear span generated by these ideals and all finitely strictly singular operators on \(L_p(0,1)\). In particular, \(T_p\) is \(\ell_p\)-strictly singular, yet its distance from the \(L_r\)-factorization ideals has a positive lower bound independent of \(r\). This answers a question due to Johnson and Schechtman in the negative.

title: Cross Correlation of Binary Niho-type Sequences and Related Constacyclic Codes
abstract: Let \(q=2^m\), where \(m\ge3\) is odd, and let \(d=(q-1)(q+4)/6+1\). We study the cross correlation between a binary \(m\)-sequence of length \(q^2-1\) and its \(d\)-decimated sequence of length \(3(q-1)\). We prove that the cross correlation is exactly four-valued and determine its distribution explicitly. For shift decimated sequence, we obtain at most five cross correlation values and express their frequencies in terms of a specified cubic root count over \(\F_q\). We also determine the complete value distribution of the associated exponential sums. As an application, we construct \(q\)-ary constacyclic codes with parameters \([q+1,4,2(q+1)/3]_q\) and determine their weight distributions.

title: A Cross-Domain Simulator and Benchmark for Uncertainty Quantification in Global 21-cm Inference
abstract: End-to-end uncertainty propagation in scientific inference often requires repeated evaluation of coupled simulators spanning multiple physical domains, often at prohibitive computational cost. Global 21-cm cosmology is an extreme example: a millikelvin cosmological signal must be separated from radio foregrounds and instrumental effects four orders of magnitude larger, making inference acutely sensitive to model misspecification. Reliable recovery is therefore contingent on an exceptionally accurate model that jointly propagates uncertainty through the complete observational chain. We present a differentiable, GPU-accelerated hybrid forward model combining neural emulation of the cosmological signal, a physics-informed multi-resolution parameterisation of the galactic foregrounds, and a linear surrogate model of the antenna. This unifies simulators spanning astrophysics and computational electromagnetics while reducing evaluation time by a factor of $7.2\times10^{7}$. Using GPU-accelerated Nested Slice Sampling, we benchmark the framework across 100 unseen signal realisations and find that 94 injected profiles lie entirely within their corresponding 95% credible bands.
