Together, the simulator and reference Nested Slice Sampling results provide a demanding benchmark of posterior calibration, mode coverage, and evidence accuracy across next-generation stochastic samplers, simulation-based inference, and variational inference frameworks.

title: Implicit Neural Representation for 3D Radio Map Compression in Low-Altitude Environments
abstract: Low-altitude wireless networks require accurate 3D radio maps (RMs) to support environment-aware communication. However, due to the extensive spatial coverage and multi-modal channel representations, 3D RMs usually incur prohibitive storage and transmission overhead, making efficient compression highly desirable. In this paper, we propose NeRM3D, an implicit neural representation (INR)-based framework for compact 3D RM compression. Specifically, NeRM3D represents the entire 3D RM as a lightweight neural network that maps discrete height values to corresponding RM slices, thereby encoding the RM into a compact neural network. To effectively model the volumetric spatial structure of 3D RMs, NeRM3D jointly integrates horizontal embeddings with height-aware modulation, enabling efficient extraction and fusion of spatial correlations across different vertical layers and channel modalities. Experimental results demonstrate that NeRM3D achieves competitive compression performance with low complexity and decoding latency, making it suitable for resource-constrained devices.

title: Pudding: A Retargetable Compiler for Processing-Using-DRAM Systems
abstract: Processing-Using-DRAM (PUD) architectures exploit the physics of DRAM arrays to perform Boolean operations directly in memory, eliminating the data movement bottleneck in memory-intensive workloads. Several PUD architectures have been recently proposed which differ in their primitive operation sets, row allocation models, and execution metrics. These architectural differences are today hard-coded in emerging PUD-aware compilers, making crossarchitecture reuse impossible. We present a retargetable, end-to-end compilation framework for PUD architectures. The central idea is to make the architecture description a first-class object in the compilation pipeline: retargeting to a new PUD architecture only requires supplying its description. Built upon the MLIR framework, our compiler operates at two coupled levels. At the tensor level, it lowers high-level programs through bit-slicing, mixed-precision assignment, and integer-linear-programming (ILP) based placement to reduce the number of PUD commands and inter-bank data movement. At the logic level, it employs equality saturation to explore Boolean network implementations, with rewrite rules and cost functions derived directly from the architecture description. Evaluated on representative workloads across multiple PUD targets with the same compiler passes, our framework matches (and in several cases surpasses) architecture-specific hand-optimized compilers, while delivering retargetability and extensibility.

title: The Computational Complexity of Concurrent Stochastic Games: Exact Value and Approximation
abstract: We consider two-player zero-sum concurrent stochastic games played over a finite state space for an infinite number of stages. In every stage, both players simultaneously and independently choose an action. Then, given the current state and chosen actions, the successor state is selected according to a stochastic transition function. We consider limit-average objectives, where Player 1 maximizes the long-run average of rewards assigned to every transition. The value from an initial state is the maximal expectation that Player 1 can ensure. We study the two basic computational problems: (a) the approximation problem of computing the values within an arbitrary additive error, and (b) the exact problem of deciding whether the value at a state is at least a given threshold. The previous results in the literature establish: (a) the approximation problem belongs to TFNP[NP], and (b) the exact problem belongs to PSPACE, via the theory of the reals, and is SQRT-SUM-hard. Our contributions are as follows. (a) Our main result shows that the approximation problem is in TFNP, and that the associated gap or promise problem is in NP $\cap$ coNP. (b) We also show that the exact problem is in $\exists\mathbb{R} \cap \text{co-}\exists\mathbb{R}$, i.e., it reduces to both the existential and the universal theory of the reals, and that it is PosSLP-hard.

title: Equivalence and origin of discrepancies between transfer matrix method and multiple reflection model of surface induced second harmonic generation
abstract: Second harmonic generation (SHG) spectroscopy is a sensitive tool to study surfaces and interfaces in thin films. To understand the layer boundaries and interpret the measured data, it is essential to use a theoretical model describing the SHG generation in the thin film. The transfer matrix method and multiple reflection model are two numerical techniques which have been commonly utilized in the calculation of surface-induced SHG. Here, we demonstrate that, despite the expected equivalence of the approaches, the two methods can lead to controversial results for the same input properties and second-order susceptibility tensors. The discrepancies resulting in different SHG intensity from both methods are caused by inconsistent numerical implementation of the interface SHG. We describe the conditions for the implementation to achieve the equivalence between the two models. Moreover, we identify the physical constraint that has to be imposed in numerical implementation to get identical results from both methods.

title: CHAMP: Coordinated Humanoid Loco-Manipulation with Whole-Body Motion Priors
abstract: Coordinating locomotion and dexterous manipulation is fundamental to humanoid robots operating in human environments. A key challenge is learning motion priors from diverse data and using them effectively for coordinated robot control. We present CHAMP, a unified framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that combines whole-body motion pretraining with adaptive feature extraction. CHAMP pretrains a vision-language model to predict future body and hand motion from approximately 2,298 hours of heterogeneous human and robot data. A shared motion representation enables unified whole-body motion learning across embodiments from datasets with body annotations, hand annotations, or both. To ground these motion priors in robot control, we introduce a Coordination-oriented Action Expert (CAE) and train it on replay data generated using the target controller. Through sparse routing, CAE adaptively selects, transforms, and fuses features from multiple layers of the pretrained model to jointly generate body and hand actions. In experiments, CHAMP achieves overall success rates of 84.8% on seven simulated tasks and 91.4% on seven real-world tasks with a Unitree G1, outperforming the evaluated baselines in both settings. In particular, CHAMP achieves 70.0% success on the long-horizon popcorn-serving task, compared with 40.0% for the best-performing baseline.

title: Does coverage explain core-set active learning? Mean, max, and the choice of distance
abstract: Core-set selection casts batch active learning as a covering problem, in which the points to label minimise the covering radius of the pool. Its main argument is a generalization bound in which this radius controls the gap between the loss on the pool and on the labelled sample. We examine what this bound requires and what it says in practice. We first state it with the assumption that its proof uses at the labelled points, a zero conditional risk, and show that it then holds for any dissimilarity and any selection rule that uses no label outside the sample. The proof works point by point and involves two averages, the mean distance of the pool to the labelled sample and the purity of the cells attached to the labelled points. Keeping them gives, when labels are deterministic at the labelled points, a bound on the pool loss with no zero-loss assumption and without the factor C, the number of classes, of the original constant. We then compare scales, for deterministic labels and a regression function Lipschitz on the whole pool. With the original constant, the bound can be informative only if the radius is below the smallest distance between two classes divided by C. Without C, its radius form can be informative only once the nearest-neighbour rule built on the sample is exact on the pool. Finally, a misalignment criterion measures whether a quantity ranks selections as the gap or the test error do. Experiments on a Gaussian pool and on two image pools, digits and MNIST, the latter under eight distances, and with a network retrained at each cycle, show that the radius does not rank selections consistently with the gap and, on the image pools, that the bounds that do not use the labels of the pool are never informative and that covering in mean rather than in maximum, as greedy k-medoids does, gives a higher purity and accuracy than random sampling.

title: Estimating M Dwarf Ages using their Transiting Brown Dwarf Companions
abstract: Determining M dwarf ages remains challenging because of their slow main-sequence evolution. We investigate using transiting brown dwarfs to constrain system ages through their measured masses and thermal emission. We report Palomar/WIRC secondary-eclipse observations of two close-in brown dwarfs, LP 261-75C and AD 3116B, measuring eclipse depths of $6.1 \pm 0.3$ parts per thousand (ppt) in $K_s$ and $9.1 \pm 0.6$ ppt in $J$, respectively. Combining these observations with space-based transit photometry, radial velocities, and host star spectra, we infer brown dwarf internal luminosities and, assuming coevality, host star ages using five sets of atmospheric and evolutionary models. For LP 261-75C, model-dependent median ages span 1.3-2.9 Gyr, substantially older than the previously proposed age of 0.1-0.2 Gyr based on presumed membership in the AB Doradus moving group. This result, the host star's high metallicity, and the companion's measured radius disfavor AB Dor membership. The revised age implies a mass of $\approx 62$-$68$ $M_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ for the wide-orbit companion LP 261-75B, compared with an earlier estimate of $\approx 21$ $M_{\mathrm{Jup}}$. AD 3116B, a member of the 0.6-0.8 Gyr Praesepe cluster, provides a test of brown dwarf evolutionary models through independent constraints on its mass, age, and luminosity. Its inferred age depends strongly on cloud treatment, spanning 0.4-0.6 Gyr for cloudy models and 1.0-1.3 Gyr for cloudless models. Among the models considered, Sonora Diamondback, which includes cloud condensation and cloud clearing across the L/T boundary, provides a plausible simultaneous match to the observed eclipse depth and radius. These results demonstrate a new method to constrain M dwarf ages using emission observations of their brown dwarf companions, while highlighting the sensitivity of the inferred temperatures and ages to evolutionary model differences.

title: SCAN: Neural Additive Networks for Scalable High-Order Component Selection and Estimation
abstract: Functional ANOVA models express a prediction as a sum of main effects and interactions, but existing neural functional ANOVA models require the interactions to be specified in advance, which forces a trade-off between missing higher-order structure and the cost of enumerating many interactions. We propose SCAN (Scalable Component Additive Networks), which learns which features each basis function combines, so that components of different orders are selected and estimated jointly without enumerating candidates. The learned component index sets form a small candidate collection on which post-hoc identification is carried out efficiently. A global component-selection parameter shares information across basis functions, and truncating negligible component-selection weights gives a sparse model that is identified after training. We establish universal approximation, a minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor, and component selection consistency, which together imply that the discovered components contain all identified true components with probability tending to one. In synthetic experiments, SCAN learns components whose maximum order is close to the true one, and recovers higher-order components more accurately than the baseline models, with post-hoc identification taking a few seconds for 100 inputs. SCAN also outperforms most neural functional ANOVA models in prediction on the benchmark datasets and trains at a much lower cost than exhaustive second-order models. We also apply SCAN to predict treatment response in breast cancer from 12,502 gene-expression variables.

title: PLATRS: A Lattice-Based Linkable Accountable Ring Signature for Permissioned Blockchains
abstract: Permissioned-ledger cross-domain data sharing needs anonymity and accountability: an endorsement hides its author, but a regulator must identify it on authorization reuse. Existing lattice-based schemes give these only separately: public traceability exposes signers to collision detectors; linkable non-tracing schemes cannot open; threshold schemes solve another problem. None gives post-quantum security, a signer-chosen ring, a publicly comparable per-event tag, and one-authority opening together. We propose \textsf{PLATRS}, a module-lattice linkable accountable ring signature for permissioned blockchains. Consortium-CA enrollment binds the key returned by an opening to a registered identity. The signer chooses the ring; verification is index-free; each signature has a per-event tag any verifier can compare. Tag noise derives from the signer's tracing secret and event, so linking is one comparison for honest signatures while the tag remains M-LWE without the secret. Detection is two-tier: tag mismatch is immediate; different tags on two accepted signatures for one event trigger an opening; the authority publishes the recovered public opening component, and any member recomputes the verdict against the ring. We prove CPA anonymity from M-LWE, linkability, authority-only traceability, and unforgeability from M-SIS with M-LWE in the random oracle model. At \(N=1024\), our open-source implementation: sign 9.886~ms, verify 3.919~ms, link 0.7~\(μ\)s, open 480~\(μ\)s; signature 107.3~KiB (log in ring size); adjudication 4.867~ms. Hyperledger Fabric: 60.5 signature submissions/s at 7.87~MB/s with 16~MiB blocks, commit-bandwidth limited. Common-harness: fastest of 5 schemes to sign/verify, second in size; vs FLLL\(^+\)21, signing is 3188\(\times\) faster and signatures 133\(\times\) shorter.

title: Tidal effects of bulk viscosity in neutron stars
abstract: Bulk viscosity in neutron-star matter provides a temperature-dependent mechanism for tidal dissipation. In this study, we investigate the impact of bulk viscosity on the dissipative tidal response of neutron stars composed of neutrons, protons, and electrons. Employing cold equations of state derived through the momentum-dependent interaction model, we examine the bulk viscosity arising from the direct Urca process, which acts to restore chemical equilibrium. The temperature dependence is incorporated through the weak-interaction rate, allowing us to explore the behavior of bulk viscosity in the neutrino-transparent regime at temperatures up to a few MeV. To account for the spatial distribution of bulk viscosity within neutron stars, we introduce the effective bulk viscosity, a volume-averaged quantity over the region where direct Urca process operates, and establish a connection with the bulk viscosity. Specifically, we investigate its implications for tidal quantities, including the lag time and dissipative deformability, highlighting their dependence on temperature and stellar compactness. We find that the dissipative tidal effects become maximal at a temperature approximately coinciding with the one of maximum bulk viscosity on the onset of direct Urca. Additionally, these effects are more pronounced in intermediate neutron star masses compared to maximum ones. Finally, for both canonical $1.4\;M_\odot$ and maximum-mass neutron star configurations, we derive causality-based upper bounds on these quantities, providing theoretical benchmarks for assessing the potential observability of bulk-viscous effects in gravitational-wave signals from binary neutron star inspirals.

title: CGSpec: Consistency-Guided Speculative Decoding with Overlap-Aware Verification Scheduling for Edge-Cloud Inference
abstract: Collaborative speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by enabling edge clients to draft tokens locally and a shared cloud model to verify them. However, draft target disagreement wastes communication and verification resources, while heterogeneous client return times complicate shared verifier scheduling. We propose CGSpec, a consistency guided framework for multi client edge-cloud speculative decoding. CGSpec uses draft target distribution divergence to adapt the speculative budget and introduces a nomination and competition mechanism to construct candidate trees through global growth control and local token selection. An overlap-aware scheduler further estimates remaining verification work and client return times to prioritize requests and improve verifier utilization. We evaluate CGSpec using four model pairs and three datasets under heterogeneous network conditions. Across 24 configurations with 8 and 16 clients, CGSpec achieves the highest mean system and client throughput among the evaluated methods. Compared with current SOTA methods, it improves system throughput by 12.2\% and 10.2\%, and mean client throughput by 14.0\% and 33.0\%, respectively.

title: Oceanic Surface Waves from Wind-Drift-Layer Instability: Exponential Growth to Finite-Amplitude States
abstract: Oceanic wind-wave genesis via shear-induced linear instability and the propagation and breaking of finite-amplitude waves have traditionally been studied as decoupled problems. While experimental evidence indicates connection between the two regimes, a first principles demonstration that the latter can emerge from the former remains challenging. Here, we bridge this gap by investigating gravity-dominated surface waves arising from an inviscid, shear-driven Holmboe instability. The background state comprises a uniform air current and a constant-vorticity water drift layer of finite thickness overlying deep irrotational water. In the high-Bond-number and low-Froude-number regime, this configuration supports Holmboe-unstable modes beyond a critical Froude number. Two-phase simulations of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, initialised with the fastest-growing eigenmode, exhibit initial exponential growth in excellent agreement with linear theory. In the subsequent nonlinear stage preceding breaking, finite-amplitude propagating waveforms develop. Spatio-temporal spectral analysis reveals bound harmonics locked to the primary carrier wave, coexisting with residual free-wave components. This indicates that an infinitesimal, linearly unstable mode can evolve into a nonlinear propagating waveform of approximately permanent form under background shear. To characterise these waveforms theoretically, we formulate an exact nonlinear boundary-value problem for steady-state propagating waves including background shear. The resulting wave profiles show very good agreement with time-averaged profiles extracted from the transient simulations in the nonlinear stage. These findings extend the existing theory and complement the wind-wave observations, demonstrating that sheared Stokes-like waves, can naturally emerge during the nonlinear evolution of a wind-drift-induced linear instability.

title: Interactions between the magnetised jets in the twin radio galaxy J104455+354055
abstract: Pairs of galaxies in which both objects host kiloparsec-scale radio jets are extremely rare. Such systems provide unique opportunity to study the formation of relativistic jets and their resistance to side-way collisions with each other prior to their eventual merger. We analyse the radio data for the twin radio galaxy J104455+354055 associated with a pair of distant elliptical galaxies (z=0.163). The radio jets of both sources avoid disruption/merging for the initial tens of kiloparsecs. We investigate the role of the magnetic fields in the propagation of these radio jets. We used VLA radio data at high frequencies in both compact and extended array configurations to obtain sensitive high-resolution polarimetric data and study the properties of the magnetic fields in all jets. Polarisation data suggest shearing of the magnetic fields at points where the jets bend. The orientation of the magnetic field parallel to jet axis helps confine the jet. Such field configuration in two adjacent jets seems to prevent them from merging. The strength of the magnetic field slightly increases in jet bends and the associated shearing enhances the ordered component of the magnetic field. The more diffuse radio plumes at the end of each jet have comparable strengths and energies of the magnetic field. The twin radio galaxy J104455+354055 provides a unique possibility to study the interplay of radio jets of two radio galaxies. The analysis of the properties of the magnetic fields observed along the radio jets suggests that the wiggles and bends of these jets, caused by the likely interactions of the host galaxies, could be also governed by the magnetic fields that may prevent them from merging. The derived strengths and energies of the magnetic field in different parts of the jets should allow us to improve the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of radio galaxies.

title: Decompose and Describe: Narrowing the Diagnosis-to-Report Gap in 3D CT Report Generation
abstract: Automated 3D CT report generation could support radiology workflows, yet medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) often omit diagnostic findings from generated reports. We ask whether the diagnostic ability of these models carries over to free-form reporting. Across five MedVLMs, diagnostic VQA achieves higher macro-F1 than reports generated from the same CT studies and evaluated on the same disease categories. We call this task-dependent discrepancy the diagnosis-to-report gap. Conventional Report Adaptation improves reporting for most models but does not close the gap. To investigate and narrow it, we introduce DeCAD (Decompose CT Analysis and Describe), which progressively decomposes CT report generation at diagnostic, regional textual, and regional visual levels. The model identifies positive findings before writing a report, organizes diagnosis and description into regional tasks, and restricts each task to visual tokens from the corresponding region. Diagnostic and regional textual decomposition improve report-level diagnostic performance across the five MedVLMs, whereas regional visual decomposition provides limited additional gains. In a standard VLM without medical VQA pretraining, the first two levels remain effective; regional visual decomposition also provides further gains with a region-level contrastively pretrained encoder. Full DeCAD achieves state-of-the-art performance on CT-RATE and Merlin. Analyses show greater CT-token attention during diagnosis and higher recall of reference-positive findings in both the diagnostic output and final report than with Report Adaptation. These results show that explicitly organizing diagnosis improves diagnostic reporting and helps narrow the diagnosis-to-report gap.

title: Cross-calibration of Hera/HyperScout-H with MRO/CRISM and MEx/OMEGA based on Mars observations
abstract: On March 12, 2025, Hera, the European Space Agency's planetary defense mission, performed a Mars flyby en route to the asteroid system (65803) Didymos-Dimorphos. During this event, HyperScout-H (HS-H), the spacecraft's hyperspectral imager, acquired five high spatial resolution images over the southern hemisphere of Mars. These observations provide an opportunity for systematic cross-calibration of HS-H with two established Mars orbital instruments, Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM) on board the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (Murchie et al., 2007), and Observatoire pour la Minéralogie, l'Eau, les Glaces et l'Activité (OMEGA) on board Mars Express (Bibring et al., 2004). This study evaluates the performance, reliability, and readiness of HS-H for the forthcoming asteroid observation phase by comparing it with CRISM and OMEGA data. We selected 21 surface regions spanning diverse terrain types from three HS-H images in which the Martian surface fills the entire field of view. These images were corrected, calibrated, and co-registered to associate each pixel with latitude and longitude. The relative inter-channel correction factors are close to unity for bands 3-25 (0.688-0.952 μm), with standard deviations of 0.52% for OMEGA and 0.62% for CRISM, indicating good agreement in spectral shape. Bands 1 and 2 show a systematic mismatch of 4.7% and 3.6%. The absolute flux correction factors reveal offsets of 8% relative to OMEGA and approximately 0.7% relative to CRISM, with mean inter-image standard deviations below 2%. These results confirm the radiometric stability of HS-H and establish a calibration framework for future Didymos-Dimorphos observations.

title: CONCOR: Benchmarking Contrastive Decoding for Visual Hallucination Mitigation Beyond Final-Output Performance
abstract: Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.

title: LiveMirror: Real-Time Diffusion Virtual Try-On on a Consumer GPU and Its Self-Supervised Adaptation to Indian Ethnic Wear
abstract: Diffusion virtual try-on (VTO) models produce convincing garment transfers from a single product photograph, but at hundreds of milliseconds to seconds per image every deployment today is offline or falls back to AR mirrors that need a rigged 3D asset per product. We present LiveMirror, a live-camera try-on mirror that renders a flat garment photograph onto a moving person with a diffusion model on one 16 GB consumer GPU. Its core is asynchronous keyframe try-on: generation never blocks the display, every displayed frame is an optical-flow warp of the latest generated keyframe, and keyframes are replaced only through a cross-fade. The display runs at camera rate (25 FPS at 720p) while a new try-on arrives every 370-490 ms; we measure the residual flicker, give a stage-by-stage latency budget, and report which accelerations (step count, consistency LoRA, tiny decoder, compilation) keep garment prints intact. We then show that the same GPU fixes the model's biggest cultural blind spot: try-on models trained on VITON-HD and DressCode render a knee-length kurta or sherwani as a torso-length top or a dress over bare legs. A thigh-covering mask, self-supervised pairs built automatically from 24.9k on-model e-commerce photographs, and 3.2 GPU-hours of attention-only fine-tuning of CatVTON halve the perceptual error on ethnic wear (LPIPS 0.137 to 0.077 on IndoFashion, 0.135 to 0.073 on Atlas; 200 held-out pairs per source) with no regression on Western tops. A two-pass hem-aware mask then removes the remaining failure, recoloured trousers below the hem, on all but 3-4% of pairs at no training cost; in the mirror the hem comes from the previous keyframe for free. The adapted model beats FASHN VTON 1.5 on every aggregate ethnic-wear metric at about $20\times$ lower inference cost, and its weights drop straight into the mirror.

title: Consecutive sums and Reconstructing Problems
abstract: We study several problems concerning consecutive sums of integer sequences and their relationship with Sidon sets. We also provide new lower bounds for an extremal function related to sequences with distinct consecutive sums, and consider reconstruction problems from multisets of consecutive sums.

title: Autonomous UAV Navigation in an Unknown Environment via Multi-Trajectory Model Predictive Control
abstract: A novel model predictive control (MPC) formulation, named multi-trajectory MPC (mt-MPC), is presented and applied to the problem of autonomous navigation of an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) in an unknown environment. The UAV is equipped with a LiDAR sensor, providing only a partial description of the surroundings and resulting in time-varying constraints as the vehicle navigates among the obstacles. The control system layout is hierarchical: the low-level loops stabilize the vehicle's trajectories and track the set-points commanded by the high-level, mt-MPC controller. The latter is required to plan the UAV trajectory trading off safety, i.e. to avoid collisions with the uncertain obstacles, and exploitation, i.e. to reach an assigned target location. To achieve this goal, mt-MPC considers different future state trajectories in the same Finite Horizon Optimal Control Problem (FHOCP), enabling a partial decoupling between constraint satisfaction (safety) and cost function minimization (exploitation). Recursive feasibility and, consequently, persistent obstacle avoidance guarantees are derived under the assumption of a time invariant environment. The performance of the approach is studied in simulation and compared with that of a standard MPC, showing good improvement.

title: Cyclic changes of frame for designing non-retracing verification cases for numerical interface tracking
abstract: A forward-backward deformation test supplies an exact final interface, but retracing can allow errors from the two halves to cancel. We construct alternative tests by superposing a cyclic change of frame on the same base deformation. The frame returns to its starting pose, preserving the exact final phase and the deformation history up to rigid placement. A small returning translation can keep trajectories close to the retraced ones. A full rotation about a fixed centre or axis gives closed paths with nonzero winding for material labels that stay off that centre or axis. For incompressible base fields the transformed velocity is divergence-free. We construct discretely solenoidal face fluxes for geometric volume-of-fluid advection by circulating the transformed potential. In three TwoPhaseFlow benchmarks, with a shared time grid for each pair, a full-turn frame increased the final cell-average shape discrepancy in all 30 comparisons, with a median factor of 1.50. The fitted convergence exponent decreased in each of the six benchmark-reconstruction comparisons over the tested grids.

title: Pesticide mixtures may compromise ecosystem services provided by an egg parasitoid of soybean pest stink bugs: a comprehensive ecotoxicological risk assessment
abstract: Tank mixtures of crop protection products are widely used in agricultural systems, yet their integrated effects on biological control agents remain poorly understood. We evaluated the lethal, sublethal, and transgenerational effects of four synthetic insecticides, applied alone or in binary mixtures with three fungicides and two herbicides, on adults and pupae of Telenomus podisi (Hymenoptera: Scelionidae), an important egg parasitoid of pest stink bugs. In adult bioassays, LC50 values ranged from 28.26 mg a.i. L-1 for isocycloseram + lambda-cyhalothrin to 265.88 mg a.i. L-1 for acephate. Overall, mixtures increased adverse effects relative to the individual products, reducing survival, parasitism, and longevity. The lowest parasitism rates occurred with isocycloseram + lambda-cyhalothrin combined with chlorothalonil or glyphosate SL formulation. Transgenerational effects were also detected, including reduced F1 emergence and an increased proportion of males in some treatments. Following pupal exposure, several mixtures reduced F0 emergence, whereas ethiprole + fenpropimorph and acephate + bixafen + prothioconazole + trifloxystrobin also reduced parasitism and longevity of the emerged adults. Integration of lethal and sublethal responses using the reduction coefficient (Ex) revealed increased toxicity for several mixtures and shifts in IOBC risk classification; notably, all insecticide + glyphosate mixtures reached Ex = 100% after pupal exposure. These findings show that assessing pesticides individually may underestimate ecotoxicological risk to T. podisi and highlight the need to consider pesticide mixtures in integrated pest management programs.

title: Dissipative Tidal Love Numbers of Neutron Stars from Viscous Heating
abstract: We compute the leading low-frequency dissipative tidal response of nonrotating relativistic neutron stars. We formulate the response in a worldline effective field theory. We determine the linear dissipative Love number in two complementary ways: from the redshifted viscous entropy production inside the star and from the imaginary, frequency-odd part of the exterior metric. The first method reduces the calculation to an integral over the static equilibrium tide; the second provides an independent check. We apply our approach to publicly available equations of state and assess the corresponding correction to the gravitational-wave phase of neutron-star binaries. For an equal-mass $1.4+1.4M_\odot$ binary with both stars at a redshifted temperature $T_\infty=10^5\,\mathrm K$ and a standard electron shear viscosity, tidal dissipation shifts the gravitational-wave phase by less than $10^{-3}$ cycles between $20\,{\rm Hz}$ and $1\,{\rm kHz}$ for the four equations of state considered. Including the resulting rise in the stars' temperature in a simple thermal model reduces the shift below $10^{-6}$ cycles. For the viscosity model considered here, shear-viscous tidal dissipation in cold neutron stars is negligible for gravitational-wave phasing. This suggests that a measurable dissipative tidal signature would have to come from a different mechanism.

title: SGD Selects Initialization-Dependent Representation in Overparameterized ReLU Networks
abstract: Overparameterized neural networks can represent the same function through many different hidden configurations, raising the question of which representation is favored by a given training algorithm. We study how stochastic gradient descent (SGD), jointly training both layers, resolves this ambiguity in finite-width, bias-free, two-layer ReLU networks trained to learn a linear teacher under Gaussian inputs. At width two, exact fitting leaves no choice: the neurons must align with the teacher directions. At every width $m \ge 4$, however, infinitely many non-aligned exact fits are possible. Despite this ambiguity, we prove that joint batch-size-one SGD from sufficiently small initialization drives every neuron arbitrarily close to one of the two teacher directions while reaching arbitrarily small population error in finite time. This occurs without explicit regularization, layerwise training, gradient clipping, or a learning-rate schedule. The dynamics additionally select an initialization-dependent allocation of the fitted function across neurons, providing a finer characterization of the representation selected by SGD. Numerical experiments reproduce the predicted alignment, fitting, and initialization-dependent allocation. Our results identify sufficient conditions under which standard SGD exhibits a strong implicit bias toward a highly structured internal representation, even when overparameterization creates infinitely many qualitatively different exact representations.

title: For whom the Bell tolls: joint measurements and state updates in quantum field theory
abstract: State update rules and their behaviour in Bell tests play an important role in the study of measurement schemes and quantum information. We consider the state updates of the Fewster-Verch measurement framework for quantum field theory using their connection to the probability distribution of measurement outcomes. We focus on a set of observables of the form $A(f_i)^*A(f_i)$, where $A(f)$ is the (complex) smeared field operator for any theory induced by a formally hermitian, Green hyperbolic differential operator, and where the $(A(f_i))_{i=1, \dots, m}$ are assumed to be normal and mutually commuting. Under the assumption that these operators have a sufficiently nice representation on a bosonic Fock space, we derive the joint moment generating functional and the unique joint probability distribution for the observables $(A(f_i)^*A(f_i))_{i=1,\dots,m}$. As an application of these results, we construct a model of a Bell inequality test within quantum field theory using a recently developed coupled Proca-scalar model for polarization measurements. We show that our Bell test model can violate the CHSH inequality, approaching Tsirelson's bound for maximally entangled states in the limit where vacuum effects are perfectly rejected. These results show that the state update rules derived in the Fewster-Verch framework are compatible with strongly quantum correlations. They also support a viewpoint in which state updates should be understood in relation to available information.

title: Struct2Det: Grounding Category Structure in Visual Evidence for Few-Shot Object Detection
abstract: Few-shot detectors struggle to distinguish categories that look alike but differ in local components, because a few examples rarely reveal which differences determine category identity. Category descriptions specify components and relations but do not establish their presence in an image. We propose Struct2Det, which uses category structure to guide detection and verify candidates in three stages. Relational Structure Encoding maps category graphs to component embeddings and a global condition. Component-Grounded Detection uses component queries to retrieve multi-scale image evidence that, with the global condition, modulates category text embeddings for initial detection. Verification-Guided Refinement matches candidate regions with components expected by their top-scoring categories; when class scores are close and matches are reliable, matched pairs correct region features before the shared detector predicts again. Category structure informs both classification inputs: text embeddings integrate image-wide component evidence, while region features incorporate candidate-specific matches. We also construct InduSym, with 88,912 symbol instances across 275 categories from 674 engineering drawings and a structural graph per category. Struct2Det improves few-shot-category AP over the strongest baseline by 6.02 points on InduSym and 9.68 on Digitize-PID, with the highest base-category AP on both. InduSym ablations show few-shot gains from correct category structure, image-level retrieval, and candidate verification. Further tests show gains in few-shot natural-object detection and zero-shot Chinese character recognition.

title: One-shot identification of analytic systems
abstract: We study when the coefficients of a linearly parameterized analytic system can be identified from a single input-solution pair. Given a finite dictionary of analytic operators, each admissible input induces a finite-dimensional linear recovery map from coefficients to observed outputs. Coefficient recovery is possible exactly when this map is injective. We define the degenerate input set as the set of inputs for which injectivity fails and prove a zero-one law: either every admissible input is degenerate, or the degenerate set is negligible in the sense that it is compactly slice-null and has zero measure under every nondegenerate Gaussian measure. We then apply this framework to the recovery of matrices, analytic continuous-time dynamical systems, and differential operators. For several ODE and PDE classes, we further characterize the degenerate sets explicitly and identify deterministic choices of inputs that guarantee recovery.

title: Inclusion of obstacles in ground point classification in ALS data for terrain models used for analysis of vehicle traversability
abstract: Classification of ALS point clouds has been studied for decades, but it remains challenging in forest contexts due to the great variety of terrain types, sensor equipment, flight parameters, and resulting point densities. Point cloud density has increased significantly in recent years, and existing algorithms, developed for lower density point clouds, may no longer be effective. It is beyond the scope of most existing algorithms to classify obstacles, such as boulders, while also distinguishing non-obstacles, such as bushes and undergrowth. We evaluate the performance of different algorithms for ground point classification in ALS data in a context where obstacles are included in the ground class, resulting in terrain models useful for offroad machinery route planning and navigation. The evaluation is performed using metrics directly on the point clouds (Precision, Recall, $F_1$-score) and on resulting terrain models (RMSE and maps of differences). The results show that there are several algorithms that perform well, but performance is highly affected by the parameters used. The best results in terms of terrain model RMSE are obtained with the CSF-algorithm, with an average RMSE of 0.08 meters. The results indicate that existing algorithms can be adapted to include obstacles in the ground class under the tested conditions.

title: Target-Part Preference Optimization for Part-Aware 3D Generation
abstract: Part-aware 3D generation requires not only globally plausible objects but also complete, well-separated semantic parts, yet high-quality part decompositions remain too scarce to support large-scale supervised fine-tuning. We study whether preference fine-tuning based on Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) can adapt a pretrained part-aware generator from limited part-annotated data without architectural changes. We rank candidates generated with different random seeds against ground-truth (GT) geometric metrics, and select the (object, target-part) examples with the largest across-seed quality gap. Each selected example stores a seed pair whose two flow trajectories share one clean GT compositional latent and differ only in Gaussian noise. We derive a reference-relative target-block preference loss from FlowDPO that compares the two trajectories against a frozen reference model. GT flow-matching losses on the target block and complete part set provide absolute supervision, while only the diffusion transformer (DiT) is updated. Human-ranked controls test an alternative ordering source, and synthetic cropping provides controlled loser targets that are incomplete by construction. Among the three training-set scales, the medium-scale setting gives the strongest result on held-out Objaverse and outperforms both the pretrained generator and the reported direct supervised fine-tuning baseline on the multi-part aggregate. Further analysis shows sensitivity to pair ordering, target-part coverage, and the balance between pairwise and GT supervision. Cross-dataset experiments show less consistent gains under distribution shift.

title: What Information Survives Authenticated Byzantine Communication?
abstract: Two principals independently approve actions for a delegate that can choose a route to a goal and carry it out under current policy. A stable work-order receipt records the routes authorized at issuance. For intersection policies, we characterize the leading number of reachable joint configurations under overlapping updates. The lower bound uses the first writer's ability to finish before its peer invokes an update. The matching protocol checks an older route against the changed principal's policy because the unchanged principal already approved each of its steps. When each route has a command unique to it, the count has a closed form in terms of unions of route supports. Two three-command workflows with four possible receipts each have leading counts of $360$ and $328$ under encoded overwrite, and both have append count $1024$. Exact policy read-back forces at least six bits per block in both cases. Route overlap affects the count even when route lengths are fixed. The construction preserves authorization, withdrawal, stable recovery, and progress after stabilization with one coordinator crash.

title: Exact solution of the long-range voter model in arbitrary dimensions: correlations and effective-dimensional scaling
abstract: Long-range interactions can profoundly alter collective ordering and critical behavior, yet exact ana- lytical results for non-equilibrium systems with such interactions remain scarce. We obtain an exact analytical solution for the spatial correlation function of the voter model with long-range interac- tions in arbitrary spatial dimension. Starting from the evolution equation for the Fourier modes, we identify the long-wavelength dispersion generated by the interaction kernel and derive the resulting coarsening and stationary scaling regimes. The solution yields the critical condition separating these regimes, the characteristic coarsening length, and the asymptotic decay of stationary correlations. These results establish an exact effective-dimensional correspondence: the long-range model in dimen- sion d, with interaction exponent \b{eta}, exhibits the same scaling exponents as a short-range voter model in the effective dimension deff = 2d/\b{eta}. The correspondence holds across the coarsening, marginal, and stationary regimes, while the associated scaling functions need not coincide

title: Pion scattering in finite volume within the Inverse Amplitude Method: Extension to moving frames
abstract: We study the leading exponentially suppressed finite-volume corrections to $ππ$ scattering near threshold in moving frames. Using the one-loop Inverse Amplitude Method (IAM), we compute the $I=0$ and $I=2$ amplitudes in a box with total momentum $\vec P=2π\vec d/L$, including the left-hand cut and the $t$-, $u$-channel and tadpole contributions neglected in Lüscher's quantization condition. We derive the resulting correction to the near-threshold energy levels and measure its size relative to the Lüscher term. We find that it becomes comparable to the latter for $m_πL\lesssim 1.5$--$1.7$ at rest, and that it is larger in moving frames, reaching $m_πL\lesssim 2.8$ for $\vec d=[002]$. The corrections become negligible only for $m_πL\gtrsim 5$.

title: Weighted Numerical Homological Regularities over Positively Graded Algebras
abstract: Let A be a noetherian positively graded algebra. We investigate several weighted numerical homological regularities: weighted CM-regularity, weighted Tor-regularity (Ext-regularity), and weighted Ex-regularity, defined in terms of the weighted supremum or infimum degrees of canonical complexes associated with graded A-modules. Introduced by Kirkman, Won, and Zhang, weighted regularities provide finite invariants even when their unweighted counterparts are infinite. Through parametrized degree reweightings, they unify classical homological invariants, including unweighted numerical regularities, sup, inf, depth, projective dimension, and local cohomology dimension. This framework clarifies the behavior of homological regularities under degree shifts and reveals intrinsic relationships among these invariants, particularly those involving the a-invariant. We establish several inequalities and equalities relating these weighted regularities to the weighted supremum or infimum degrees of derived Hom and derived tensor complexes. These results recover their unweighted counterparts and yield new relations involving the a-invariant for a fixed weight. Some of these results generalize the inequalities of Kirkman-Won-Zhang between weighted CM-regularity and Tor-regularity by allowing the weight to range over the entire plane R^2. We also give conditions under which these inequalities become equalities, thereby answering a question posed by Kirkman-Won-Zhang. We use weighted AS-regularity to study the Artin-Schelter regularity of A. Under mild conditions, we prove that the weighted AS-regularity of A vanishes if and only if A is an N-graded AS-regular algebra. This generalizes an unweighted result of the present authors and a weighted result of Kirkman, Won, and Zhang.

title: OVOGO: Offline Value-Guided On-Policy Generative Optimization for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action models can benefit from robot experience collected during deployment, but repeatedly acquiring new physical interactions for policy improvement is costly. Offline reinforcement learning provides a natural way to reuse collected experience, while flow-based policies offer an additional opportunity because fresh generation trajectories can be cheaply resampled from the current policy at replay observations. This motivates separating offline value learning from on-policy optimization of the generative process. We propose OVOGO, an offline reinforcement learning framework that realizes this separation for flow-based VLAs. A central challenge in this formulation is to learn a critic that remains grounded in logged robot experience while providing useful value signals for newly generated actions. OVOGO introduces a Return-Anchored Ranking Critic that combines in-sample distributional value learning with guarded local ranking, improving discrimination among generated actions without assigning them artificial return targets. The frozen critic then provides group-relative value signals for selected-transition optimization of fresh action candidates sampled from the current flow policy. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and LIBERO, as well as a real-robot dexterous manipulation task, show that OVOGO improves the initial VLA across all four settings and achieves higher success rates than the evaluated offline adaptation and value-guided baselines. These results suggest that offline robot experience can be repeatedly reused for value learning while inexpensive generative sampling supports policy optimization, providing an effective approach to experience-based post-training of flow-based VLAs.

title: Asymptotic approximation for a certain class of statistics associated with generalized urn models
abstract: The generalized urn model is defined in terms of a collection of random frequencies, which is treated as a collection of conditionally independent random variables given their sum. We consider a class of random variables that can be represented as series of functions of these frequencies. The general results concern asymptotic normality, estimates of remainder terms, and Edgeworth-type asymptotic expansions for such random variables. We then consider random variables defined in various versions of the generalized urn model. These models include the random allocation of particles of several types into finite or infinite numbers of cells, random sampling without replacement from a finite population, random coverage of a circle, random forests, and random permutations.

title: Weitzenböck curvature estimates in arbitrary degree and sectional-scalar curvature pinching
abstract: For each odd dimension $n\ge7$ we give an explicit constant $B_n<(n-1)/(n+2)$ such that a closed, connected, nonflat Riemannian $n$-manifold with $K_{\min}\ge B_n S_0$ is a rational homology sphere, where $S_0=\operatorname{Scal}/[n(n-1)]$. For example, $B_7=28/43<2/3$. This answers the question of Li, Matinpour, and Petersen about lowering the sectional curvature coefficient in the remaining odd dimensions. The same argument recovers their five-dimensional endpoint $B_5=10/19$. The proof starts with a four-frame inequality for two-forms. Contracting forms and averaging over hyperplanes propagates a Ricci-weighted estimate whose coefficient depends on the parity of the codimension. For an algebraic curvature tensor with nonnegative sectional curvature, we obtain lower bounds for the Weitzenböck curvature endomorphism in every degree. When the dimension and degree are both even, we classify all nonzero equality pairs for the sharp bound by powers of Kähler forms. For three-forms the optimal coefficient in the scalar curvature bound is $1/3$ in dimensions five and six and lies between $4/9$ and $5168/11253$ in dimension seven. On the cone of strongly nonnegative curvature tensors we determine the optimal coefficient in every degree.

title: Test-Time Latent Computation to Improve Visual Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Recent work on Large Language Models (LLMs) suggests that reasoning capabilities can be enhanced at test time not only through longer token-level reasoning traces, but also through additional computation in latent space. This raises a natural question for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs): can additional computation in latent space improve visual perception at test time? In this work, we first verify that MLLMs contain stable reusable layers that can be re-forwarded at inference time without disrupting normal generation. Based on this observation, we propose \textbf{Lo}ok \textbf{Ba}ck in the \textbf{L}atent \textbf{S}pace (\textbf{Lobals}), a training-free decoding method that identifies the contiguous layer window with the strongest visual-token attention and re-forwards through it, allowing the model to revisit visual evidence in latent space. We demonstrate that this latent-space revisit strategy can improve MLLMs' performance across diverse multimodal settings, including general vision-language tasks, visual hallucination tasks, and vision-centric tasks.

title: QED theory of scalar hyperfine interactions in HD$^+$
abstract: HD$^+$ is the simplest heteronuclear molecular ion. It has been used to determine the proton-to-electron and deuteron-to-electron mass ratios, to test quantum electrodynamics, and to search for new interactions. All these applications rely on an accurate knowledge of its hyperfine structure, for which theoretical predictions have disagreed with several precise measurements. Here we calculate the two dominant hyperfine interactions, namely the couplings of the electron spin to the proton and deuteron spins, including the complete nonrecoil electronic relativistic and leading radiative corrections of relative orders $α^2$ and $α^3$, respectively, evaluated in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation. Nuclear-structure effects are suppressed by using the measured hyperfine splittings of atomic hydrogen and deuterium. The resulting couplings for 40 rovibrational states are about 18 times more accurate than the previous ones. They agree with the recent Penning-trap measurement in the ground state within the combined uncertainty of 65 Hz, i.e., 7 parts in $10^8$, and with a recent measurement in a rotationally excited state, whereas a discrepancy of $7.4(9)$ kHz persists for a vibrational overtone transition. Our results provide improved theoretical input for future determinations of the proton and deuteron masses from HD$^+$ spectroscopy.

title: Optimal first eigenvalue estimates for positive holomorphic sectional curvature
abstract: Let $(M,ω_g)$ be a compact Kähler manifold with holomorphic sectional curvature $\geq 2$. We prove that the first positive eigenvalue of the Laplacian $Δ_d$ satisfies $$λ_1\geq 4, $$ and $λ_1=4$ if and only if $(M,ω_g)$ is holomorphically isometric to $(\mathbb{P}^1,ω_{\mathrm{FS}})$.

title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
abstract: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.

title: Weakly Nonlinear Whitham Modulation and Dispersive Shock Waves in the Modified Gardner Equation
abstract: We investigate weakly nonlinear Whitham modulation and dispersive shock waves (DSWs) in a modified Gardner equation. A three-equation modulation system is derived through a Stokes expansion and averaged conservation laws. Perturbative analysis of its characteristic structure provides explicit conditions for hyperbolicity and genuine nonlinearity, and identifies a wavenumber-dependent transition between real and complex characteristic splitting. The dispersive resolution of compressive Riemann data is examined using DSW fitting, yielding analytical predictions for the harmonic- and solitary-wave edge velocities. The solitary-wave prediction is further supported by a traveling-wave energy analysis. Numerical continuation of the modulation characteristics identifies the limitations of the weakly nonlinear approximation, while direct numerical simulations using a Fourier pseudospectral method confirm close agreement with the predicted leading-edge velocity and the leading solitary-wave amplitude for the resolved cases. These results clarify the weakly nonlinear characteristic structure and the edge dynamics of dispersive shocks for the modified Gardner equation.

title: Universal stabilizer correlations in chaotic eigenstates
abstract: Entanglement and nonstabilizerness provide complementary perspectives on quantum-state structure. In this work, we find that the stabilizer correlation, defined as the difference between the Rényi-$2$ mutual information and the mutual stabilizer Rényi entropy, approaches a universal constant for chaotic eigenstates. This constant is determined solely by the symmetries, and quantifies the correlation that does not contribute to nonstabilizerness. We identify this universal stabilizer correlation analytically via random-state ensembles, which give $\log_2 7$ (GOE) and $\log_2 4$(GUE) without extra symmetries, $\log_2 14$ and $\log_2 8$ under spin-inversion parity or half-filling magnetization. While imposing reflection or translation symmetry leaves these values unchanged. Exact calculations for a chaotic mixed-field Ising chain confirm the predicted plateau and finite-size approach. Integrable free-fermion and strongly disordered eigenstates behave qualitatively differently. This universal stabilizer correlation reveals a characteristic structure of chaotic eigenstates beyond entanglement or nonstabilizerness alone.

title: Characterization of solar background signatures in IXPE gas pixel detectors through laboratory measurements
abstract: We present a laboratory to in-flight comparison of the IXPE background signatures, using the spare Detector Unit (DU), identical to the three flight units, exposed to a Co-60 radioactive source, historically adopted as a proxy for solar-induced X-ray background. Co-60 emits 1.17 MeV and 1.33 MeV photons which undergo Compton scattering in the DU structures, producing a degraded spectrum extending down to the keV range after ADC counts to keV conversion via Fe-55 (charging measurement) calibration. The source was placed on the top and side of the DU; event tracks were reconstructed to extract spectral and morphological observables (track size, energy fraction in the track's main cluster, number of pixel triggered per event). Laboratory spectra and parameter distributions are compared with IXPE in-flight in-eclipse (Earth occultating the sun) and in-sun backgrounds from two observations (NGC 2110, RCW 86). We discuss how the in-flight and on-ground spectral and modulation properties of the background compare to each other.

title: Constraints on ultralight dark matter couplings from orbital perturbations of binary pulsars
abstract: Ultralight dark matter coupled directly to ordinary matter perturbs the orbits of binary pulsars, and the perturbation grows secularly when its frequency matches a harmonic of the orbital motion. We use this effect to constrain three couplings with the wideband timing data for the $50$ binary pulsars of the NANOGrav 15 yr data set: a linear and a quadratic universal coupling of a scalar field to matter, and a vector field coupled to baryon minus lepton number ($B-L$). For every system and for masses between $10^{-23}$ and $10^{-18}\,$eV, we build the timing signature from the perturbed orbital elements. We then sample the coupling together with the local amplitude, phase and direction of the field and the red noise of the pulsar, marginalizing analytically over the timing model, and combine the single-pulsar likelihoods into $95\%$ credible upper limits at each mass. For a universal linear coupling, the orbital resonances of the eccentric systems bring the limit close to the Cassini bound. For the quadratic coupling, treating the neutron star as a point particle, the limits are the strongest available between $2\times10^{-22}$ and $2\times10^{-21}\,$eV. In the case of vector ultralight dark matter, the limit is comparable to the PPTA and Eöt-Wash bounds between $3\times10^{-22}$ and $10^{-21}\,$eV and reaches or beats the Eöt-Wash bound at isolated orbital resonances, while MICROSCOPE remains stronger over the entire mass range.

title: Do learned image captioning metrics generalize? Auditing duplicated samples in human-judgment benchmarks
abstract: Learned image captioning metrics are trained and tested on human judgments, so their reported correlation is a claim about generalization. We audit this claim for the three most recent collections of such judgments, Polaris, Nebula, and Spica, matching images at the pixel level. First, test samples reappear in training sets: the Spica training set contains about two-thirds of the Polaris test set, with identical human ratings. Second, controlled retraining shows that duplicates can inflate a metric: for Pearl, the gain is confined to the duplicated samples and grows with every epoch; for DENEB, it stays below one point. The gain depends on the learner and on how often a training set repeats a sample. Third, Kendall's $τ$ over all samples is the sum of two terms, detecting captions with the lowest human score and ranking the others; the first supplies most of the reported correlation and is nearly saturated. The recent test sets cannot order Polos, DENEB and Pearl consistently, and a ridge regression on frozen features matches or exceeds all three. Fourth, we propose a protocol that ranks a learned metric only with a model trained without test samples, reports both terms, and compares metrics by paired tests. Under it, zero-shot vision--language judges rank first on the three recent test sets, and a fine-tuned judge ranks first on the three earlier benchmarks. The same analysis applies to any evaluator learned from human judgments; filter lists and code are released at https://github.com/morninghut/ic-dataset-audit .

title: Non-invertible Duality Defects in Four-Dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_N$ Lattice Gauge Theories
abstract: We consider four-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_N$ lattice gauge theories with generalized plaquette actions. These theories are known to exhibit dualities. We construct topological interfaces implementing these dualities by assigning a weight to each building block and proving topological invariance. At self-dual couplings, these interfaces become duality defects representing non-invertible symmetries. We also study center symmetry defects and their junctions with the duality interfaces and derive several crossing relations.

title: EgoStudy: How Does Scaling Egocentric Data Affect VLA and WAM Pretraining?
abstract: Egocentric human manipulation data offer a scalable resource for training dexterous robot policies. However, how effectively robots can learn and benefit from these data remains unclear due to the embodiment gap between humans and robots. We present EgoStudy, a systematic, controlled study of egocentric data for robot learning. Holding the robot dataset fixed, we vary the scale and diversity of egocentric data, data processing strategies, and co-training configurations. We investigate three questions: (1) Which data processing and pretraining choices most effectively exploit egocentric data? (2) Which components of robot action prediction benefit most from scaling these data? (3) How do scaling effects differ between vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs)? Our experiments yield three main findings. First, data diversity, alignment between trajectories, and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Second, scaling egocentric data yields larger gains in predicting end-effector translation than in predicting fine-grained finger movements. Third, WAMs perform better when egocentric data are limited, whereas VLAs exhibit greater gains as the amount of egocentric data increases. Together, these findings provide practical guidance on processing and using egocentric data to train VLAs and WAMs, while clarifying the benefits and limitations of scaling these data.

title: Discrete adjoint method for the general synthetic iterative scheme for optimization of rarefied and continuum gas flows
abstract: A discrete adjoint method is developed for the general synthetic iterative scheme (GSIS) to enable efficient gradient-based optimization of gas flows across rarefied and continuum regimes. The primal GSIS is expressed as a fixed-point system of kinetic and macroscopic synthetic equations, and both sets of residuals are incorporated into a discrete Lagrangian. Imposing stationarity of this Lagrangian then yields a coupled mesoscopic-macroscopic adjoint system that directly inherits the primal acceleration structure, without a separate Chapman-Enskog or asymptotic analysis. The resulting system is solved by alternating kinetic and macroscopic updates analogous to those in the primal GSIS, with the inner subproblems treated using established discrete adjoint techniques for the discrete velocity method and Navier-Stokes equations. Tests on the NACA0012 airfoil show that adjoint sensitivities closely agree with central finite-difference estimates, while the adjoint solver achieves convergence efficiency comparable to that of the primal GSIS, with both solvers converging within tens of iterations in rarefied and near-continuum flows. The method is further validated by multi-objective shape optimization and boundary-flow-parameter optimization. For a three-dimensional re-entry capsule, shape optimization reduces peak wall heat flux by 14.17%, 10.68%, and 6.54% while achieving respective lift-to-drag gains of 10%, 20%, and 25%. For a fixed-geometry showerhead chamber, optimization of inlet-flow allocation reduces the coefficient of variation of wafer pressure from 1.49% to 0.06% at fixed total gas supply, while maintaining the mean pressure near its initial value. Beyond these applications, the formulation provides a systematic and extensible framework for constructing multiscale adjoint solvers directly from the fixed-point representations of their primal counterparts.

title: Policy Invariance Is Not Learning Invariance: Potential-Based Reward Shaping for Navigation with a Limited View
abstract: Potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) does not change the optimal policy, but how much it speeds up learning depends on the potential and on effects outside this guarantee. We analyse how PBRS changes the one-step reward while it preserves the discounted return: a per-step $(γ-1)Φ$ term, the terminal-state rule, a constant shift of the potential, and positive cycles in a bonus that is not potential-based. We then measure these consequences in pre-registered experiments with a PPO agent. The agent has a limited egocentric view and is tested on two MiniGrid navigation tasks (160 runs, 10 seeds per condition). On LavaCrossing, a geodesic (BFS) potential learned faster than both the sparse baseline and a Euclidean potential with a 7x7 and a 5x5 view (AUC difference +0.27 to +0.39, Holm p between 0.007 and 0.0499). The Euclidean potential did not differ from the baseline. In 20 runs with a non-potential bonus, none of the agents learned the task. The Euclidean potential caused more than twice as many deaths in lava during early training. View size did not detectably change the benefit of shaping. With a 5x5 view on SimpleCrossing, some BFS runs got stuck in loops and never learned; shifting the potential did not remove this, so the per-step term alone does not explain it.

title: Progress on finite temperature Sp(4) lattice gauge theory with matter fields
abstract: We explore the finite temperature behaviour of the Sp(4) lattice gauge theory coupled to two dynamical Wilson fermions transforming in the fundamental representation. The continuum theory provides a realisation of composite dark matter within the Strongly Interacting Massive Particle (SIMP) paradigm. Its thermal phase transition in the early universe might have generated an observable relic stochastic gravitational wave signal. Evaluating the sensitivity of future gravitational wave experiments to this signal requires knowledge of the strength of the phase transition. We explore the two dimensional parameter space of the theory, defined by the bare fermion mass and inverse gauge coupling. For this exploratory study we focus on lattices with a small number of sites in the temporal dimension. We analyse the finite volume scaling behaviour of Polyakov loop observables. Specifically the scaling of the peak of the susceptibility, informed by multiple histogram reweighting, is used to discriminate between the presence of a phase transition or crossover. In the light fermion mass regime we find strong indications of a crossover, while for heavy fermions we find preliminary evidence of a first-order phase transition. These findings motivate further studies of the continuum limit for this and other Sp(2N) gauge theories.

title: Revisiting LLMs as Context Engineers
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear \textbf{when and how} LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated ($r=-0.5, p\le 0.05$) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.

title: DexDuet: Learning Contact-Preserving Bimanual Dexterity from Human Demonstrations
abstract: Human demonstrations provide a rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Existing methods primarily optimize object trajectory tracking, often overlooking how human hands interact with the object. Even with accurate tracking, robots may contact incorrect object parts or slide their fingers, resulting in unstable manipulation. We present DexDuet, a framework that learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration. DexDuet employs two interaction rewards to preserve human hand-object configurations and contacts. To enable coordinated manipulation, we factorize the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies that condition on each other's states. We further propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts object assistance and training starts across demonstration segments to overcome difficult manipulation phases. Across four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, DexDuet improves object-tracking ADD-AUC by 11 to 41 points over the corresponding baselines while consistently achieving better contact preservation. Notably, among 122 paired runs with comparable object-tracking accuracy, DexDuet preserves the human's contacts better in 117 cases. Code and videos are available at https://rcl-robotics.github.io/Dexduet.io/

title: Fast Gradient-Based Framework for Spatial and Length Optimization of Geothermal Borehole Fields
abstract: Common analytical design tools for Borehole Heat Exchanger (BHE) fields size the total drilling length for a given layout but do not optimize the positions of the boreholes. We introduce a framework (OptiGeoS) for the simultaneous, gradient-based optimization of the borehole length and the continuous borehole positions under groundwater advection. It couples the Moving Finite Line Source model with local BHE equations and evaluates the temporal convolutions by Fast Fourier Transforms. The gradients with respect to the length and the positions are computed analytically. A flow-dependent Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation confines each borehole to its own cell, which enforces the spatial separation and provides advection-informed layouts. Under purely conductive conditions, the fluid temperature extremes of the forward model for a single borehole lie between those of EED and GHEtool, which differ by $0.32\,\mathrm{K}$. For a field of 120 boreholes, the hourly outlet temperature agrees with that of EED with an RMSE of $0.28\,\mathrm{K}$, while the peak temperatures deviate by up to $2\,\mathrm{K}$. For 25 boreholes simulated hourly over 20 years, one forward simulation takes less than $0.5\,\mathrm{s}$ and a full optimization about $8\,\mathrm{min}$ on a laptop CPU. In a case study with groundwater advection, the optimized layout requires $16.2\,\%$ less borehole length than a fixed grid. It reduces the length increase caused by the advected thermal plume from $20.9\,\%$ to $1.4\,\%$.

title: Two-Component Model for the Unidentified Extended Fermi-LAT Source 4FGL J1908.6+0915e / FL16Y J1908.6+0915e in the SGR 1900+14--W49A Sky Region
abstract: Galactic PeVatrons are expected to be powerful sources of non-thermal high-energy (HE, $E>100$ MeV) and very-high-energy (VHE, $E>100$ GeV) $γ$-ray emission as a manifestation of acceleration processes in supernova remnants (SNRs), star formation regions (SFRs), and pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe). In the sky region containing the magnetar SGR 1900+14 and the young massive star cluster (YMSC) W49A, there is one recently identified point-like source FL16Y J1910.2+0903, and there are three unidentified gamma-ray sources: the Fermi-LAT extended source FL16Y J1908.6+0915e, the HAWC extended source 4HWC J1908+0845, and the LHAASO point-like source LHAASO J1907+0913. We investigate the possibility of explaining the HE and VHE $γ$-ray emission from the SGR 1900+14--W49A sky region using a model of the Fermi-LAT extended source FL16Y J1908.6+0915e as superposition of two extended sources -- a potential SNR/PWN associated with the magnetar SGR 1900+14 and the stellar-wind superbubble adjacent to the YMSC W49A complex. To this end, we simulate the observed $γ$-ray emission in hadronic and leptonic models using the open NAIMA code and show that it consists of two extended regions: the stellar wind superbubble in W49A region -- an analog of the Westerlund 1 superbubble -- powered by the YMSC W49A (the southern part of the extended source FL16Y J1908.6+0915e); and the SGR 1900+14 region, powered by a potential SNR/PWN associated with the magnetar (the northern part of the extended source FL16Y J1908.6+0915e). However, due to the considerable distance to the magnetar ($d=12.5$ kpc), the required cosmic-ray energy budget in both hadronic and leptonic scenarios corresponds to a hypernova explosion and/or a powerful magnetar wind nebula created by a newly born millisecond magnetar with a rotational energy of the order of $10^{52}$ erg.

title: Generic Strong Regularity and the Branson--Gover Conjecture
abstract: On each closed smooth manifold of even dimension $2N\ge 4$, we prove that the Branson--Gover detour operators are strongly regular in every degree $k-1$, $1\le k<N$, on a $C^\infty$-open dense set of Riemannian metrics.
