The proof bounds one code's average performance across all loss patterns of a given size; binomial fluctuations then determine the Gaussian correction. It combines tests of correct and secret communication with tensor-product averaging and a classical polynomial identity. Arbitrary mixed encoders and collective decoders are allowed. Requiring the private error bound for every message preserves the Gaussian term. Fixing the ideal environment state to the actual marginal instead changes the quantile to $Φ^{-1}(1-\sqrt{1-\varepsilon})$. Thus the precise privacy criterion affects communication at second order.

title: PRC4D: Physical Relation-Constrained Persistent 4D Reconstruction
abstract: A faithful 4D reconstruction should capture both the shape and motion of objects, even when they disappear from view. Existing methods preserve previously observed geometry and extend motion through occlusion using local spatial and motion associations. However, treating short-term contact or shared motion as sufficient evidence of persistent rigidity can introduce incorrect motion constraints and distort overall reconstruction. To address this limitation, we present PRC4D, a physical relation-constrained framework that identifies reliable rigid relations and uses them to maintain spatial consistency through occlusion. PRC4D combines 3D contact and relative motion consistency with sequence-level verification to distinguish persistent couplings from transient interactions. The resulting graph guides observed-pose refinement and motion propagation from visible to occluded components without altering reconstructed geometry. Experiments on diverse real-world multi-object sequences and controlled occlusion simulations demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy, reduced relative pose errors, and more consistent object configurations under changing visibility.

title: Scaling Architectural Simulation to Giga Instructions Per Second
abstract: The cost of detailed architectural simulation constrains design-space exploration, while parallelization across simulated cores offers limited host concurrency for single-core and small multicore targets. We present GIPSim, an instruction-driven simulator that derives instruction timing from dependencies and resource constraints, reducing the overhead of updating pipeline state every simulated cycle. It applies synchronization-guided temporal decomposition to recorded execution, exposing host parallelism beyond the target core count. GIPSim replays the resulting segments in parallel and aggregates their durations through a dependency graph to estimate overall execution time, with replay contexts reconstructed using retained microarchitectural state, warmup, and synchronization-guided cache eviction. This accounts for synchronization waits without requiring host workers to follow target execution order. We evaluate GIPSim using QEMU traces of application and operating system execution on multi-core x86-64, AArch64, and RV64GC systems. GIPSim achieves an average single-node simulation throughput of 13.8 million instructions per second (MIPS) with one worker and 1{,}010 MIPS with 96 workers, peaking at 1{,}421 MIPS. The corresponding mean absolute percentage errors in execution cycles relative to gem5 are 7.52\% and 7.43\%, respectively.

title: A direct majorant and an improved Huber constant on cofinite Fuchsian groups
abstract: To obtain an effective upper bound for Huber's constant on cofinite Fuchsian groups, we introduce an algorithm that bypasses the quantitative Karamata Tauberian theorem in estimating spectral-counting growth by direct use of re-optimized Gaussian kernel instead. Further steps involve the different choice of a compactly supported test function, keeping linear and constant terms in the spectral estimate, optimizing the exact cusp geometry, and retaining the full explicit primitive-geodesic majorant in subsequent Chebyshev estimates. The more direct path is established to control the difference between the size of the hyperbolic term in the Selberg trace formula and the second Chebyshev function. Finally, the self-improvement device combined with a knowledge of low-lying spectral data leads to the sharpening that in the case of $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ reads $C_{\mathrm{Hub},\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{Z}) }<199$. The improvement factor is greater than $8.3\cdot10^{10}$ compared to what was claimed by the initial algorithm and greater than $1.1\cdot10^6$ compared to the currently known bound.

title: Not All Pairs Align: Caption-Guided Audio-Visual Contrastive Learning
abstract: We address the problem of learning audio-visual representations from co-occurring modalities. Multimodal contrastive learning typically assumes that paired observations provide shared views of the same underlying information. While this may be true for datasets collected in constrained environments, it does not always hold. For instance, co-occurring audio and visual signals can differ substantially in their content due to off-screen sounds. Nevertheless, standard contrastive objectives treat all paired samples as equally aligned. In this work, we propose Caption Guided Alignment Aware Loss (CGAAL), a model-agnostic objective that leverages modality-specific captions to estimate semantic agreement between audio and video. CGAAL uses these agreement scores to weight the contribution of each positive pair. A warm-up period and gradual thresholding strategy progressively introduce this alignment-aware training signal. We demonstrate the generality of CGAAL by applying it to three contrastive baselines, consistently improving their performance on audio-visual retrieval.

title: Verify then Steer: Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery for Continuous Vision-and-Language Navigation
abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow language instructions to reach a target in an unseen 3D environment. However, existing methods still struggle to recover from route deviations at test time. We investigate this limitation through the lens of instruction progress, and trace it to a phenomenon we term progress hallucination: agents misinterpret off-route observations as evidence of task progress, causing their internal instruction progress to advance beyond the actual task stage and hindering recovery based on earlier sub-instructions. To address this failure mode, we propose PHAR (Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery), a test-time recovery framework following a verify-then-steer paradigm. The verifier examines residual-stream representations of the Vision-Language Model (VLM) to identify mismatch of cross-modal evidence along the trajectories, and uses split conformal calibration to control false alarms. When an alarm is raised, the steering module uses a contextual bandit to adaptively select the rewind extent of instruction progress for online recovery. Through extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, our framework enhances the reliability of multiple state-of-the-art vision-language navigation methods at test time.

title: Contribution to the GdTe$_3$ magnetic phase diagram from electronic transport measurements
abstract: Magnetic phase diagrams of the three antiferromagnetic (AFM) transitions of GdTe$_3$ that occur at zero magnetic field at $T_{N1}=12$ K, $T_{N2}=10.5$ K and $T_1=7$ K are investigated by means of resistance measurements in a magnetic field oriented along the three crystallographic directions. With the magnetic field applied in the basal plane we found re-entrance of an intermediate phase which may be a result of the coupling between the $T_{N2}$ AFM and the charge density wave with possibly a ferroaxial order. A spin flop transition is also observed at a temperature that presumably converges towards a triple point in vicinity of 2.5-3.0 T and $T$ between $T_1$ and $T_{N2}$. Our results help complete a complex phase diagram of GdTe$_3$ and advance a method for investigating magnetic ordering via transport measurements -- a technique applicable to many other compounds.

title: Optimal Transport Meets t-SNE: Integrated Visualization without Batch Effects in OT-tSNE
abstract: Visual exploration is an integral step in understanding the structure of datasets. However, systematic variation between datasets collected under different conditions, known as batch effects, can obscure shared structure and complicate their joint visualization. Existing methods often rely on cross-batch nearest-neighbor relations to integrate the batches. Yet, these local correspondences can be unreliable for challenging cross-batch geometries. We propose optimal-transport t-SNE (OT-tSNE), which replaces nearest-neighbor-based matching with globally coupled affinities derived from entropic optimal transport. Controlled synthetic experiments demonstrated that nearest-neighbor-based methods can deteriorate, while optimal-transport affinities and OT-tSNE embeddings remain robust. Across seven real single-cell datasets, we benchmarked OT-tSNE against a broad range of integration and visualization methods and found that it achieves a Pareto-efficient trade-off between batch mixing and biological conservation, and integrates batches particularly well.

title: A Framework for Graph Node Symmetric Quantification under Dataset Shift
abstract: Graph node quantification is the supervised learning task of estimating the prevalence of different classes within an arbitrary sample of unlabelled nodes from a graph, subject to some form of dataset shift. Existing approaches to graph node quantification typically follow the standard aggregative paradigm, i.e., they use labelled nodes from the graph to train an intermediate node classifier, and obtain an estimated class distribution for the sample by aggregating the classifier's predictions for the individual nodes and then correcting the result via some adjustment strategy that accounts for dataset shift. In this work we propose a framework for graph node quantification that does away with both node-level supervision, since its training phase only requires node samples labelled by their class distribution, and node-level predictions, since it estimates class prevalence values directly, without the need of any intermediate node classifier. The framework thus allows symmetric quantification, since (unlike in standard ``asymmetric'' quantification methods) the labelled items used for training and the unlabelled items on which predictions must be issued are of the same type (i.e., node samples). This framework (that we dub GSQ, for Graph Node Symmetric Quantification) allows building pipelines consisting of a node encoder, an embedding pooler, a prevalence predictor, and an optional post-hoc scaling step. These components can be instantiated by choosing from different trainable and reservoir-based encoders, different pooling operators, and different prediction objectives. We evaluate the GSQ framework on binary and multi-class datasets with different levels of homophily, under prior probability shift and under structural covariate shift.

title: Noncommutative $\mathcal{R}(p,q)-$deformed beta functions of first and second kind : beta gamma relations, shift identities and symmetrisation
abstract: We develop the theory of the beta functions attached to the $\mathcal{R}(p,q)-$deformed quantum algebras of Hounkonnou and Bukweli Kyemba, for structure functions whose deformed numbers are generated by two deformation functions $ϕ_{1}>ϕ_{2}>0$. Working with the Jackson type series representation of the deformed integral, we define a first kind beta function on $[0,1]$ from the deformed power $(1\ominusϕ_{2}t)^{y-1}$, extended to complex exponents, and a second kind beta function on the half line from $(1\oplusϕ_{1}t)^{-x-y}$. The first kind function equals $ϕ_{1}^{(y-1)(2x+y-2)/2}Γ_{\mathcal{R}(p,q)}(x)Γ_{\mathcal{R}(p,q)}(y)/Γ_{\mathcal{R}(p,q)}(x+y)$ for all complex arguments with positive real parts; we derive its general shift identity, its exchange defect $ϕ_{1}^{(y-x)(x+y-1)/2}$, a commutative symmetrisation unique up to a constant, its asymptotics and a deformed Euler integral for a deformed Gauss hypergeometric function, which yields a deformed Gauss summation. The second kind function is evaluated through Ramanujan's ${}_{1}ψ_{1}$ summation and involves a second deformed gamma function, differing from the first one by a one periodic theta quotient, so that its exchange defect persists in the one parameter case. We prove a Bohr Mollerup type characterisation and a multiplication formula for the deformed gamma function, show that it is logarithmically convex on the positive half line if and only if $ϕ_{1}\geq1$, obtain the joint logarithmic convexity of normalised beta functions with a deformed Turán identity, and compute the moments of the associated deformed beta distributions. Gauge invariance covers the Jagannathan Srinivasa Rao, Chakrabarti Jagannathan, generalized $q-$Quesne and Hounkonnou Ngompe deformations, and every identity is confirmed numerically to thirty digits.

title: CPU-Eval: Evaluating Large Language Models for CPU Hardware Code Generation
abstract: Benchmarks such as VerilogEval have supported rapid advances in hardware description language (HDL) generation by large language models (LLMs). However, recent HDL-generation systems achieve pass rates above 90% on VerilogEval, leaving limited headroom for revealing further advances. To provide a challenging target for further progress on a practically important hardware-development task, we introduce CPU-Eval, a benchmark of 339 HDL-generation problems constructed from six CPUs. Drawn from practical CPU designs, including families fabricated in silicon, the problems span CPUs from small embedded cores to Linux-capable out-of-order cores and cover diverse CPU functions written in SystemVerilog, Chisel, and SpinalHDL. In each problem, an LLM performs the real CPU-development task of generating HDL. Across seven state-of-the-art LLMs, mean pass@1 is 45.14 percentage points lower on CPU-Eval than on VerilogEval v2 Spec-to-RTL, exposing capability differences obscured by VerilogEval's high pass rates. CPU-Eval reveals that pass@1 is lower for submodules with more source-code lines, which motivates fine-grained modular design for LLM-aided hardware generation. We also show that pass@1 is lower for CPUs written in less widely used HDLs, motivating designers to verify that an LLM is sufficiently proficient at generating code in the HDL they use before deployment.

title: BEACON: Learning Observation-Conditioned Starting Points for Guided Conditional Flow Matching in Microscopy
abstract: Fluorescence microscopy drives much of modern life science, but accessible imaging setups often yield images degraded by out-of-focus light, limited resolution, and strong signal-dependent noise. Computational restoration can recover high-quality images from such data, enabling cheaper and faster imaging at lower light dose, provided biologically meaningful structures are preserved. Guided conditional flow matching has recently shown strong results for microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution by learning distributions of plausible restorations. However, it pairs each clean target with an independent standard Gaussian sample, so the starting point of every training path does not leverage the degraded observation. This arbitrary noise--target coupling can produce conflicting velocity targets and makes the conditional velocity field harder to learn. We present BEACON, a $BE$st-of-$K$ $A$daptive learned coupling for guided $CON$ditional flow matching, which learns an observation-conditioned base distribution. During training, a lightweight conditional noise model proposes $K$ starting points for each degraded input, and the candidate with the lowest flow-matching loss supervises both networks, while a KL term keeps the proposal close to the Gaussian prior. At inference, a single draw from the learned proposal is transported along the velocity field, requiring neither candidate selection nor the target. We evaluate BEACON on ten datasets spanning microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution against 13 baseline families. BEACON achieves the best median perception--distortion rank for every pairing of a fidelity metric (PSNR, MicroMS-SSIM) with a perceptual metric (LPIPS, FID). Code and pretrained models will be released under a permissive license.

title: Every Edit Its Own Budget: Per-Instruction Token Freezing for Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-Edit Image Editing
abstract: Accelerating instruction-based image editing when one instruction requests several edits is challenging. Many training-free accelerators for flow-matching image editors skip tokens whose prediction has stopped changing, but decide this with a single threshold for the whole image. With several edits, such a threshold, tuned for speed, freezes small and slowly settling edits first, and requested edits disappear. We propose TIDE (Training-free Instruction-aware Drift-based Editing), which gives every instruction part its own compute budget. First, TIDE finds the region of each part in the editor's own attention by unbalanced optimal transport, without masks or external models. Second, it freezes a token once its drift is small relative to its own part and moves it along the straight path to its endpoint estimate. Third, a sparse engine computes only the remaining tokens. We prove that part-agnostic rules cannot guarantee per-part error budgets, characterize the optimal per-part threshold policy up to one tie class per part, and derive when our rule attains it. On FLUX.2 Klein, one global threshold breaks at least one edit's budget in 89% of MICE-Bench images, and TIDE drops up to 77% fewer edits at matched or higher speed (48% on MICE-Bench), a gap human raters confirm. On the many-step Klein Base, TIDE is the fastest compared method on six benchmarks (4.81-4.89x) and needs 5.3x fewer TFLOPs than vanilla, the largest saving we measure. With the same settings, it is also the fastest compared method on Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, a second model family (3.46-3.52x), and drops the fewest edits on all six benchmarks. Code will be made publicly available.

title: On the number of positive solutions of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation on compact star graphs
abstract: In this paper, we consider the number and the shape of positive solutions of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation on compact symmetric star graphs with Dirichlet condition at the exterior vertex and Kirchhoff condition at the central vertex.

title: Delay-Tolerant Formation Tracking for Multi-AGV Systems via Reference-Shift Coupling
abstract: Automated guided vehicles (AGVs) that transport a load together must keep a formation while each vehicle tracks its own reference, and they coordinate over wireless links with link-dependent, time-varying and jumping delays. We propose a cascade design for differential-drive AGVs modelled as kinematic unicycles: delayed data from the neighbours drive only a second-order filter that shifts each vehicle's own reference, and an unmodified gain-scheduled tracking law follows the shifted reference. A saturation keeps the shifted reference feasible, and the feed-forward is exact, so the tracking loop never sees the network. We prove that tracking and formation errors remain bounded for arbitrary delays and converge for every bounded delay and every directed, possibly switching, graph. We also construct a strict Lyapunov function with explicit constants and prove exponential convergence and a local input-to-state estimate with delay-independent gains. On undirected graphs, the coupling attenuates the formation error caused by persistent local errors by at least the factor lambda/(lambda+Lambda*lambda_2(L)) (leak lambda, coupling gain Lambda, algebraic connectivity lambda_2(L)), for any delay. Every inequality is verified with an event-driven, error-controlled simulation. A robustness study on a high-fidelity AGV model (drive dynamics, slip, localisation errors, clock offsets, lossy Wi-Fi) comprises 4,894 runs, including paired comparisons against tuned baselines. The cascade never failed, with latencies up to 4 s, 90% packet loss and up to 12 vehicles, whereas a direct delayed coupling failed when its gain saturated the drives. Coupling reduced the formation error after traction losses by 21-32% and after safety stops by up to 47%, at the price of tracking accuracy. Localisation bias and clock offsets, which no coupling law can observe, limit the achievable accuracy.

title: TESS: Query-Guided Temporal Event-Structured Frame Selection for Long-Video Understanding
abstract: Temporal localization in long videos is challenging because brief, question-relevant events are dispersed among extensive redundant content. Limited visual budgets increase the risk of omitting these events or their temporal context, undermining reliable reasoning. Existing frame selection methods emphasize semantic relevance or temporal coverage, often overlooking the complementary evidence needed to locate related events and establish their temporal relationships. To address this limitation, we propose TESS, a training-free framework for query-guided temporal event-structured frame selection. TESS selects frames that jointly show the reference event and the event asked about, in the required temporal order. Leveraging frozen vision-language representations, TESS integrates soft temporal gating, role-aware budget allocation, and within-role redundancy suppression to preserve complementary event evidence. Extensive experiments across four long-video understanding benchmarks and three multimodal backbones demonstrate that TESS consistently outperforms the strongest compared baseline by 4.0-5.5 percentage points under a fixed frame budget. Further analyses reveal greater improvements on longer videos and robust performance under tighter visual budgets, while independent evidence annotations confirm enhanced event and temporal-relation coverage. These findings establish explicit temporal evidence organization as an effective training-free strategy for preserving event relationships and supporting efficient temporal reasoning over long videos. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TESS_code.

title: Time-uniform bounds and long-time asymptotics for a three-species drift-diffusion model for memristors
abstract: The qualitative behavior of weak solutions to the two-dimensional drift-diffusion equations for memristors, incorporating Shockley-Read-Hall-type generation-recombination terms and time-dependent boundary conditions, is investigated. The model couples the electron, hole, and oxygen-vacancy densities to the electric potential through the Poisson equation. The global existence and uniqueness of weak solutions are established. If the boundary data converge to the thermal equilibrium at an integrable rate, the densities remain uniformly-in-time bounded above and below, and the solution converges exponentially fast to thermal equilibrium. For time-independent boundary data and sufficiently small applied bias, solutions converge exponentially fast to steady states carrying nonzero fluxes.

title: Continuum model for disconnection structures of hetero-interfaces
abstract: Hetero-interfaces, as planar defects between dissimilar materials, accommodate the lattice misfit through networks of line defects of disconnections (a combination of structural ledges/step and dislocation characters). We develop a continuum model that predicts the hetero-interface structures, including disconnection networks, the interface inclination and misorientation angles. The model is based on the interfacial energy minimization with respect to all possible disconnection modes, subject to the interface structure constraint of the generalized Frank-Bilby equation that describes the lattice correspondence across the interface including both dislocation and step characters of disconnections and the inclination and misorientation angles. Numerical simulations are performed to determine the equilibrium configurations of three different types of hetero-interfaces: the $α$/$β$ (orthorhombic/monoclinic) interface in ZrO$_2$, $α$/$β$ hetero-interfaces in Ti and Au/Pd (001) twist-misfit interfaces. Comparisons with experiments, atomistic simulations and theoretical predictions show that our continuum model provides excellent predictions of the hetero-interface structures including disconnection networks and inclination, misorientation angles. Furthermore, systematic analysis reveals the functional dependence of hetero-interface structural properties on inclination and misorientation angles.

title: A Face Robot which Imitates Human Musculoskeletal Skin System and Its Evaluation on Basic Movement of Facial Expression
abstract: Facial robots require many coordinated, smallamplitude motions, but accommodating these motions in a compact face remains difficult. This paper presents an anatomically inspired facial-robot platform that reproduces the layered organization of the human facial musculoskeletal system. The platform comprises bone, muscle, and skin components whose geometry, shape, and attachment locations are derived from three-dimensional anatomical data. Wire-driven, compliant muscle components are routed through PTFE tubes, allowing actuation to be placed away from the face. We describe the selection and fabrication of 65 muscles (34 muscle types) required to reproduce the 47 target action units (AUs) in the Facial Action Coding System (FACS). We then evaluate the reproducibility of individual AUs in two stages: muscle actuation without skin and actuation after the silicone skin is attached. Forty of the 47 target AUs were reproduced with the muscle components, and 30 were reproduced after skin attachment. These results demonstrate the feasibility of reproducing a broad range of FACS facial expressions using an anatomically inspired musculoskeletal structure. The proposed platform provides a foundation for the systematic development and evaluation of future anatomically inspired facial robots

title: Admissibility of Linear Time Series Models under Cone Constraints
abstract: Time series analysis extends beyond vector-valued observations to evolving probability densities, quantile functions, and covariance operators. These objects carry intrinsic constraints, raising questions about the admissibility of additive linear models, which have long served as a foundation for time series modelling and theory. We give a necessary and sufficient support condition for a stationary Hilbert-space linear process to remain in a closed convex cone almost surely. Innovations with unbounded lower tails, including Gaussian innovations, confine randomness to the cone's largest linear subspace. For fractional filters with convergent normalized cumulative coefficients, the leading stochastic directions obey the same restriction, even with bounded innovations. For real-line quantiles, variation under unbounded lower tails and leading fractional accumulation can occur only through location shifts. For cone-valued processes, partial sums of centred stationary increments remain bounded in mean square when evaluated by any linear functional that is nonnegative on the cone, in contrast to the growing variance of a random walk. We derive an exact slope criterion for locally absolutely continuous quantiles and construct nondegenerate additive models with bounded innovations for quantiles, densities, and covariance matrices. These findings clarify the scope of ordinary additive modelling under structural constraints.

title: Within-task hazards of AI agents: unidentified by time-horizon curves, identified by repeated runs
abstract: The time horizon of an AI agent is read off a curve: the probability that the agent completes a task, plotted against the time a human needs for it. Several recent analyses fit survival models to this curve and conclude that agents' hazard of failure declines as a task goes on. The curve cannot support that conclusion. Every log-logistic horizon curve with slope $β\le1$ is a mixture of constant-hazard curves, and in a proportional-hazards frailty model the same curve is produced by every within-task Weibull shape $k\geβ$. If runs of a task are conditionally independent, repeated runs restore identification within this model: the probability that two runs both succeed is the single-run curve shifted by $1/k$ on the $\log_2$ time axis. Without the Weibull form, the horizontal distance between these two curves still bears on the direction of the hazard: if the average within-task hazard is non-increasing, the distance is at least one, and so is the population limit of a two-step estimator when the cross-section is log-logistic. We decompose the bias of that estimator into a violation of the shift and a first-step misspecification term, and examine five mechanisms that can break the shift. On METR's public run-level data, under stated assumptions that the data cannot verify, no model's 95% interval for $1/k$ lies entirely above one, and for the five frontier models in the TH1.0 release every interval from runs in different batches lies below one. Under the same assumptions, taken interval by interval and given a log-logistic cross-section, these intervals reject a non-increasing average hazard for the five models, whereas in TH1.1 the result depends on how human times were obtained. Whether $k>1$ reflects a hazard that rises within a task or tasks whose difficulty human time measures only loosely needs experiments that observe the same task at several lengths.

title: On the Importance of Hidden-State Refinement in Masked Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked or corrupted token sequences, allowing token predictions to condition on bidirectional context and update multiple positions in parallel. While each denoising step produces a rich layer-wise hidden-state trajectory, prior work typically focuses only on token-level information and discards these continuous hidden states, leaving their refinement dynamics underexplored. In this work, we analyze hidden-state dynamics in MDLMs and find clear evidence of layer-wise and cross-step refinement: smooth evolution across adjacent layers, greater predictive power in deeper layers, gradual degradation under transformer block removal, and strong final-state alignment across consecutive denoising steps. Motivated by these observations, we propose Cross-Step Recurrent Refinement (CSRR), a mechanism that carries hidden-state information across denoising steps to enhance generation. Extensive experiments show that CSRR improves text generation quality, highlighting the critical role of continuous hidden-state refinement in MDLMs. Project page: https://zhongzero.github.io/Recurrent-DLLM/

title: Smyth completeness and nonexpansive iteration in $q$-hyperconvex $T_0$-quasi-metric spaces
abstract: We study the specialization order $\le_d$, defined by $x\le_d y$ if and only if $d(x,y)=0$, of a $q$-hyperconvex $T_0$-quasi-metric space $(X,d)$. We show that every nonempty bounded subset $A$ of $X$ has an infimum $\bigwedge A$ characterized by the metric formula $d(w,\bigwedge A)=\sup_{a\in A}d(w,a)$ for all $w\in X$, and dually a supremum, and that powers and copowers exist. For bounded $X$ this gives an elementary proof, with explicit metric formulas, of the known fact that Isbell-convex Lawvere metric spaces are complete in the sense of enriched category theory; the formulas themselves and the extension to bounded subsets of unbounded $q$-hyperconvex spaces are not covered by the enriched-categorical argument, which requires radii in $[0,\infty]$. Consequently no $T_1$-quasi-metric space with at least two points is $q$-hyperconvex, and the fixed points of every order-preserving self-map of a bounded $q$-hyperconvex space form a nonempty complete lattice. We show that the fixed point set of a nonexpansive self-map need not be a sublattice and that the specialization order need not be distributive. Our main result concerns the continuity of nonexpansive maps. Nonexpansive self-maps of bounded $q$-hyperconvex spaces need not preserve suprema of increasing sequences, and the supremum of the orbit of the least element need not be a fixed point. We prove that for a bounded $q$-hyperconvex $T_0$-quasi-metric space the following are equivalent: the space is Smyth complete; every increasing sequence converges to its supremum in the symmetrized metric; every nonexpansive self-map preserves suprema of increasing sequences; every nonexpansive self-map preserves suprema of directed sets; every nonexpansive self-map is Yoneda-continuous. In this case Kleene iteration from the least element converges to the least fixed point; this applies for instance when the symmetrized metric is compact.

title: Sequences for Flat-Top Beams
abstract: Flat-top beams have numerous applications in radar and communication systems. Sequences with diverging merit factors can approach the ideal omnidirectional beams but do not directly apply to flat-top beams, which require simultaneous control of passband ripple and stopband leakage. To bridge this gap, we study the asymptotic behavior of both quantities of flat-top beams by using tools of Fourier analysis. We establish contrasting results for sequences with finite or infinite alphabets. For sequences with finite alphabet, including binary and quaternary ones, their passband ripple and stopband leakage cannot simultaneously vanish as the sequence length grows to infinity. For sequences with infinite alphabet, however, both requirements are satisfied simultaneously by the generalized step-chirp (GSC) sequences if and only if the length-bandwidth product $Nγ$ goes to infinity and the distance of the step size $a$ from $\{0,1,\tfrac12,\tfrac13,\ldots\}$ goes to zero. Besides, both quantities vanish at rate $O((Nγ)^{-1/2})$ if $a\in \{1,\tfrac12,\tfrac13,\ldots\}$.These results broaden the scope of classical sequence design beyond full-band spectral flatness and provide a theoretical foundation for flat-top beam synthesis.

title: Notes for a seminar on vortex layer cascades
abstract: After the seminars I recently gave at New York University, the University of Chicago, Princeton University and the University of Bonn and after having been asked by some people to publish these notes, I decided to upload them to arXiv. In recent years, the method of vortex layer cascades has successfully been applied to construct finite-time singularities in multiple fluid equations (3D Euler, Boussinesq, IPM, g-SQG...). In this talk, I will motivate and describe the method and sketch how it can be applied to the 2D Boussinesq and 2D non-homogeneous Euler equations. In both systems, the growth of the vorticity is driven by an accumulated hysteresis effect triggered by the cyclic deformation of the density layers, whose dynamics is governed by an infinite chain of degenerate pendula. Our work also settles the previously open question about global existence of classical solutions of the (forced) 2D non-homogeneous Euler equations.

title: Grokipedia stretches the US political spectrum
abstract: Language models now write reference works that people and other AI systems consult. Grokipedia, written by xAI's model, presents itself as a less biased alternative to crowd-edited Wikipedia. We compare the biographies of 1,614 Democratic and Republican current and former politicians, from Andrew Jackson to members of the current Congress, on both encyclopedias in February and November 2026. For nine in ten Republicans, Grokipedia's biography reads as if written by a more conservative author than Wikipedia's. For Democrats, this holds only about half the time. We find the politicians' ideology explains this asymmetry. For 1,022 politicians with Congressional roll call voting records, how conservative the author seems rises linearly with the politician's ideology and about twice as steeply on Grokipedia as on Wikipedia. Republicans in races where Elon Musk's America PAC spent money show no extra bias. Rather than favoring a party, Grokipedia stretches the political spectrum, moving the biographies of the most liberal politicians further left and of the most conservative politicians further right.

title: Stability and periodic switching in feedback systems with sector-bounded hybrid integrators
abstract: We study stability of piecewise linear systems composed of the feedback interconnection of a linear time-invariant process and a sector-bounded hybrid integrator. Exploiting the observation that for such systems state-dependent switching sequences asymptotically exhibit periodic behaviour, we develop a spectral approach to stability analysis as an alternative to sufficient Lyapunov-based methods. We formulate a conjecture that asymptotic periodicity holds irrespective of the initial conditions and system stability, and provide a description of the limit system and propose an algorithm to obtain its parameters. We establish this rigorously for second-order linear-time invariant processes. Based on spectral properties of the resulting periodic limit system, we derive sufficient stability conditions. The results provide a novel viewpoint for accurate stability analysis of general state-based piecewise linear systems.

title: Invariant measures for stochastic heat equations with dissipative drift in the whole space
abstract: We study the long-time behavior of a nonlinear stochastic heat equation on the whole space $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, driven by a Gaussian noise that is white in time and spatially homogeneous. The equation features a reaction term $f$ satisfying a one-sided Lipschitz condition and a bounded, globally Lipschitz diffusion coefficient $σ$. Solutions are constructed in a scale of weighted continuous function spaces. Under an additional dissipativity condition on $f$, which covers reaction terms of the form $f(u)=u-u^{3}$, we prove that the transition semigroup admits an invariant measure on some weighted space $C_ρ$. This constitutes the first step toward a complete ergodic theory for dissipative stochastic heat equations on unbounded domains, a setting that has so far remained largely open in the literature.

title: Factorized Context Attention: From Emulated to Native Grid Probing
abstract: Models read a book, an hour of video, or an image in one forward pass. As the context grows, this pass slows down, loses accuracy, and stops at the context window. Sparse attention is efficient, but keeps the other two limitations. Grid probing, a recent training-free method, recovers the accuracy and extends the reach by asking a frozen model the same question about short local and strided spans of the input, but every question repeats the whole computation, since each span is encoded again. Our insight is that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through prompts, since each probe only restricts which part of the input the question can see. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA), a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern natively, as the attention of the model itself. FCA encodes the input once into a KV cache, reads all spans as masked sequences in one batched forward, and uses a stair position schedule to keep every span inside the trained position range. Across long video understanding, long-context text inference and image grounding, FCA matches the accuracy and the reach of grid probing at a fraction of its cost. It gains about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels, finds needles in videos of over a thousand frames and in texts four times the length of the window, and answers a later question about the same input in as little as a tenth of the time of grid probing. Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models.

title: One Subspace Is Not Enough: LocalSubspaceAD for Training-Free Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
abstract: Defect-free industrial samples can vary considerably in appearance, texture, and geometry. In few-shot anomaly detection, this variability has to be modeled from only a handful of images. SubspaceAD showed that a single principal subspace of foundation-model patch features is a strong training-free model of nominal appearance. However, a single subspace has to cover all of the nominal data's variability, so a deviation that is anomalous for one semantic region can be within the nominal variability of another. We propose LocalSubspaceAD, which extends SubspaceAD from a single subspace to a mixture of subspaces, assigning each group of patches with similar features its own subspace. The set of patch-features is partitioned using k-means, one subspace is fit per cluster, and each patch is scored by the minimum of re-projection residuals over all subspaces. The proposed method requires no training and no EM refinement. On MVTec AD, VisA and Real-IAD with 1, 2 and 4 shots, it improves over a single subspace (SubspaceAD) on both evaluated backbones: by 1.2 to 1.8 points image AUROC on DINOv2, and by 1.4 to 4.4 points in image AUROC, pixel AUPR and AUPRO on DINOv3. The gains are most pronounced on objects with heterogeneous nominal appearance, such as multi-instance categories and PCBs. Ablations show that the gains stem from a finer-grained model of variability through locally oriented subspaces, rather than from the subspace offsets (cluster means). We further show that the gains do not stem from added capacity alone: the local subspaces appear to capture the structure of coherent clusters in feature space, and the model does not merely act as a compressed memory bank.

title: Three combinatorial identities of the Rogers-Ramanujan type
abstract: The purpose of the present paper is to establish three combinatorial Rogers--Ramanujan type identities. Although their motivation comes from the representation theory of affine Lie algebra of type $A_2^{(2)}$, our proofs are entirely combinatorial and analytic. They follow the automata-theoretic approach introduced by Takigiku and Tsuchioka in their proof of Nandi's conjecture and adapt it to the present setting.

title: An Introduction to O-minimal Geometry
abstract: These lecture notes on o-minimal geometry comprise six chapters: 1 - O minimal Structures. 2 - Cell Decomposition. 3 - Connected Components and Dimension. 4 - Definable Triangulation. 5 - Generic Fibers for Definable Families. 6 - Smoothness.

title: Holographic Spread Complexity of a Probe Particle with General Initial Data
abstract: We investigate the holographic spread complexity of a massive particle probing global AdS$_3$ with general initial data. By constructing an adapted Hamiltonian, we map each bulk geodesic to a boundary Krylov dynamical pair, whose dynamics are governed solely by the conserved chiral charges. We find that, for generic initial data, the original identification $\dot{C}\sim p_ρ$ fails; instead, both the complexity and its growth rate depend nonlinearly on the bulk Noether charges. We systematically analyze this nonlinear encoding via several perturbative expansions. We further investigate two refined variants: the symmetry-resolved spread complexity, which restores the bulk radial $π$-periodicity, and the chiral spread complexity, which admits an exact closed form approaching the standard complexity at small angular momentum. Finally, by directly quantizing an effective AdS$_2$ theory, we obtain a new holographic interpretation of spread complexity in terms of the lapse function.

title: Exact Last-Iterate Bounds and Optimal Stepsizes for Proximal Stochastic Gradient Descent
abstract: Proximal Stochastic Gradient Descent minimizes the sum of an $L$-smooth convex function $f$, known through unbiased stochastic gradients of bounded variance, and a nonsmooth convex function $R$, known through its proximity operator. We derive the exact worst-case value of the expected objective gap of its last iterate, for every predetermined stepsize schedule in a broad class, which contains all the schedules with stepsizes at most $3/(2L)$. This extends to the composite setting a recent result of Grimmer and Shen for the smooth case $R=0$. The value is the sum of an initial-error term and of one term per iteration, which is the price of the noise injected at this iteration, damped by the stepsizes that remain after it. The upper bound is proved with a simple potential, the Moreau envelope of the objective with a smoothing parameter proportional to the remaining stepsize sum, and it is attained by an explicit instance. The formula shows that a logarithmic factor is unavoidable with a constant stepsize, and it gives the exact price of the proximity operator, relative to the smooth case. It also makes the choice of the stepsizes a tractable optimization problem: for a uniform variance bound $σ^2$, the best schedule is unique, decreasing, and computed by a scalar search, and it is minimax optimal among all predetermined schedules, unless the noise level is low. Asymptotically, the minimax value $M_T$ after $T$ iterations satisfies $(Dσ/M_T)^2=T+\log T+C_\star+o(1)$, where $D$ is a bound on the initial distance to a solution and $C_\star\approx1.768$ is a universal constant; unlike in the smooth case, $L$ plays no role at this order. This law is achieved by an explicit schedule, which is the optimal one when $f=0$.

title: Homothetic Copies of Polytopes and Binomial Barcodes
abstract: Let $X\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be a finite full-dimensional configuration, and put $F_X(N)=\max_{S\subset\mathbb{R}^d, |S|=N}\#\{(\mathbf{v},λ)\in\mathbb{R}^d\times(0,\infty):\mathbf{v}+λX\subseteq S\}$. Elekes and Erdős posed the problem of estimating $F_X(N)$. In this article, we determine its exact value when $X$ is the vertex set of a simplex. For several other classes of configurations, we obtain sharp asymptotic bounds and exact extremal values. We also introduce binomial barcodes for order polytopes and a recursive criterion for their effectiveness. In particular, if $X$ is the vertex set of the three-dimensional cube, then, for $n\ge 1$, $F_X(n^3)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}j^3=\left(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\right)^2$.

title: Cross-Order Information-Guided Estimation for Non-Uniform Hypergraphs
abstract: Many real-world interactions involve groups of nodes rather than pairs. A non-uniform hypergraph records such interactions as hyperedges of different orders, where the order counts the nodes in a hyperedge. Full estimation evaluates every candidate hyperedge, whose number grows exponentially with the order, and classical remedies sacrifice higher-order information or aggravate computation. The orders are not isolated: the lower orders, cheap to compute and rich in information, reveal where higher-order hyperedges are likely to occur. We propose CINE (Cross-order Information-guided Negative-sampling Estimation) under a latent space model in which all orders share latent positions. Starting from order two, CINE climbs one order at a time. At each higher order, CINE keeps all present hyperedges, samples a small subset of negative examples guided by lower-order scores, and corrects for the known inclusion probabilities to preserve the target of full estimation. CINE thereby lets users choose the trade-off between computation time and estimation accuracy: the retained orders and the sampling budget set the time, and the retained information provably approaches full-data information as the sampling budget grows. In simulations, CINE approaches the accuracy of full estimation at a small fraction of its computation time, and larger teams in MADStat reveal research associations.

title: NRG-Twins: Pixel-Level Ground Truth for Rigidity Violations in Generated Videos
abstract: Video generators now produce realistic clips of scenes and objects, which makes generated video an attractive source of 3D content. Yet generated video is not 3D consistent: static content slowly deforms or slides, 3D reconstruction degrades, and the errors are too subtle to label by hand. To make generators 3D consistent, or to build rewards and guidance that push them there, we need data that say where and by how much a generated video breaks rigidity, and these data must come from generated video itself. We obtain per-pixel ground-truth labels from real-generated twins: a real clip paired with its re-creation by a keyframe-conditioned video generator. After inserting real keyframes so that the twin camera roughly follows the real one, we measure per pixel, in degrees, how far the twin departs from a rigid scene seen along its own camera path. We release Non-Rigidly Generated Twins (NRG-Twins), 871 twins, the code that builds them for new generators, and a benchmark with an official test split. A detector trained on these data, the Non-Rigidly Generated Pixel Detector (NRG-PD), predicts the per-pixel angle from RGB alone. It separates inconsistent from consistent pixels with AUROC 0.85, against 0.40-0.74 for seven existing consistency and motion-segmentation methods, and its predictions improve 3DGS of video that contains generated content.

title: Video Models are Excellent Motion Models
abstract: Video foundation models have emerged as powerful generators of dynamic visual content, exhibiting remarkable capabilities in synthesizing complex actions and interactions. We argue that these models have also become excellent motion generators, with motion priors that are richer and more general than those learned by dedicated motion models. Their advantage extends beyond visual realism and is manifested in two important aspects: motion naturalness, including coherent body coordination, physical plausibility, and realistic interactions with objects and the environment; and motion scope, encompassing a much broader range of activities and semantic coherence, particularly uncommon, complex, and compound actions. To investigate this position, we introduce a common evaluation framework that compares video and dedicated motion models through three complementary settings: text-only motion generation, reconstruction of video-generated motion from sparse keyframes, and video-based enrichment of motion-model outputs. By converting all outputs into a shared 3D skeletal representation, we evaluate motion naturalness, semantic alignment, action coverage, physical motion characteristics, and fidelity to motion constraints. Our results suggest that video foundation models can generate more natural and semantically meaningful movements, particularly for complex and compound actions. Moreover, we investigate motion-conditioned generation through loose skeletal control, finding that dedicated motion models do not consistently improve video-generated motion, while video models can enrich skeletal animations using sparse motion guidance. Our findings suggest a shift in the role of specialized motion models, from generating complete animations to guiding and controlling the richer motion capabilities already embedded in video foundation models.

title: Dual-Pilot Design for OCDM Channel Estimation
abstract: Channel acquisition in orthogonal chirp division multiplexing (OCDM) over doubly-dispersive channels incurs a large pilot overhead, since delay and Doppler jointly shift the symbols in the chirp domain and separating them requires repeated pilots, each protected against the complete coupled displacement. This letter proposes a dual-pulsone pilot design that reduces this overhead in two steps. First, a pulsone occupies fewer chirp-domain bins than alias-free Doppler estimation requires, deliberately allowing Doppler wrapping. Second, a phase-offset pulsone is placed within the same protected region to observe a complementary part of the displacement, further reducing the shared guard. The phase offset also resolves the wrapping ambiguity, enabling low-complexity delay-Doppler estimation. Simulations show competitive estimation and BER performance, with the lowest complexity and highest payload efficiency among the considered OCDM estimators.

title: Computing expectations associated with McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equations via probability-flow ordinary differential equations
abstract: This work considers the numerical approximation of expectations of functionals of $d$-dimensional McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equations (MV-SDEs) with random initial conditions. Standard numerical schemes employ a stochastic interacting particle system of $P$ coupled $d$-dimensional SDEs, whose empirical measure converges to the MV-SDE law. However, naive Euler--Maruyama Monte Carlo (MC) estimators based on particle systems achieve a computational complexity of $\mathcal{O}\left( \text{TOL}^{-4} \right)$ to satisfy a prescribed error tolerance TOL. To reduce this complexity, this work reformulates the associated nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation as a Liouville equation describing the evolution of the law of a deterministic mean-field ordinary differential equation (ODE) with random initial conditions, sharing the same marginal distributions as the original MV-SDE. The resulting mean-field ODE eliminates the need to approximate Itô integrals and permits the use of higher-order integration schemes in time and stochastic space. However, simulating trajectories requires the score function of the MV-SDE's marginal law, which is approximated using a statistical estimator based on a system of $P$ coupled $d$-dimensional ODEs. The proposed estimator combines randomized quasi-MC in the stochastic variables and Runge--Kutta integrators in time, with efficient score estimation. Under assumptions on weak-error and variance convergence, the resulting estimator achieves a computational complexity of $\mathcal{O}\left(\text{TOL}^{-\left(\max\{β/α,2\} + 1/γ\right)}\right)$, where $α$ and $β$ denote, respectively, the weak-error and variance convergence rates with respect to $P$, and $γ$ is the order of the time-integration scheme.

title: Nonexistence of positive entire solutions to systems of semilinear elliptic inequalities
abstract: Consider the system $Δu \geq p(x)g(v)$, $Δv \geq q(x)f(|\nabla u|)$, with $u>0$ and $v>0$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $n\geq2$, $f,g\in C[0,\infty)$ and $p,q\in C(\mathbb{R}^n)$. If $f,g$ are non-decreasing and convex, using a comparison argument we prove a sufficient Keller-Osserman type condition for the nonexistence of entire solutions. This result is sharp for a wide class of systems. Similar results are also shown to hold for systems without gradient terms.

title: Trace-defined double covers of the $S_3$-involution graph of $PSL_2(2^n)$
abstract: For $q=2^n\ge 4$, we construct a family of Deza double covers $Γ(q,ξ)$ of the $S_3$-involution graph of $PSL_2(q)$, parametrized by $ξ\in\mathbb F_q^*$. We show that each resulting cover is connected, arc-transitive and amply regular with parameters $(2(q^2-1),q,Tr(ξ),1)$, where $Tr$ denotes the absolute trace. We also show that the trace-one covers are antipodal of diameter $5$ and girth $3$, whereas the trace-zero covers are non-antipodal of diameter $3$ and girth $5$. For $q=4$, these cases yield the well-known icosidodecahedral and dodecadodecahedral graphs, respectively. Then we determine the distance distributions and full automorphism groups of the covers and prove that, for fixed $q$, two covers are isomorphic if and only if their defining parameters lie in the same Frobenius orbit. We also express the Ramanujan property of a cover in terms of the spectral norm of a signed adjacency matrix of the base graph.

title: Romans Mass from a $\mathrm{GL}(1,\mathbb{R})$ Topological Field Theory with Boundary
abstract: We construct an eleven-dimensional topological field theory with boundary whose edge modes are the dilaton and form fields of type IIA supergravity, including the Romans mass. The bulk action is the Chern--Simons functional of the superalgebra of the doubled formalism, completed by two brackets that are invisible in ten dimensions; it is unique up to normalization, contains no potentials, and the metric enters only through a boundary term. The Romans mass is the boundary value of a zero-form, like the other field strengths: it is varied, and its equation of motion is an eleven-form Gauss law with no ten-dimensional counterpart. The boundary term breaks the $GL(1,\mathbb{R})$ gauge symmetry to $O(1)$: the dilaton is the edge mode on $GL(1,\mathbb{R})/O(1)$, and $(-1)^{F_L}$, which reverses the Romans mass, becomes a gauge symmetry. The holonomies of the flat connection are monodromies of the dilaton and of $(-1)^{F_L}$, fixed classically by the D8-brane charges when the mass is nonzero, and the hypersurface dual to the $O(1)$ holonomy can end on reflection seven-branes. Since no field is self-dual, the reduction gives Romans' action off shell, while other boundary conditions of the same bulk give massless type IIA and dual formulations.

title: Entanglement island and Page curve for one-sided rotating Kerr black holes
abstract: We investigate the information paradox for one-sided asymptotically flat rotating Kerr black holes formed through gravitational collapse using the island prescription. Near the horizon, the dynamics of a scalar field can be described by an effective two-dimensional theory, which provides the framework for our analysis. We study how rotation affects the location of the island boundary $\partial I$, the Page time, and the scrambling time, treating non-extremal and extremal Kerr black holes separately. For non-extremal black holes, the emergence of an island prevents the unbounded growth of Hawking radiation entropy at late times and restores the unitary Page curve. We further find that the island boundary depends on the location of the cutoff surface, in contrast to the behaviour found for eternal Kerr black holes. In the extremal case, the late-time entanglement entropy of Hawking radiation approaches the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of the extremal black hole. Our results demonstrate the important role of black hole geometry in determining the behaviour of entanglement entropy and suggest that the island prescription provides a semiclassical resolution of the information paradox for one-sided rotating Kerr black holes.

title: See the Answer, Learn to Embed: Learning Universal Multimodal Embeddings from Hindsight
abstract: Universal Multimodal Embedding (UME) models map heterogeneous multimodal inputs into a shared embedding space, where pairwise similarity supports diverse downstream tasks. Recent reasoning-driven UME approaches use intermediate reasoning to generate additional context for embedding, but often incur extra computation at inference. In this paper, we explore the matched candidate (i.e., the paired target) as an alternative source of context, asking whether a model can "see the answer" during training and "learn to embed" without it at inference. However, direct conditioning on this privileged context can introduce candidate-specific information unavailable from the query alone or cause the candidate-conditioned query representation to collapse toward the candidate embedding. To address this, we introduce Hindsight-Enhanced Multimodal Embeddings (HEME), which learns query-grounded hindsight representations from such candidate context. HEME first trains a hindsight teacher with a hindsight attention mask, mismatched-candidate conditioning, and query-token alignment to limit excessive reliance on the candidate. It then freezes the teacher and distills its hindsight representation and similarity distribution into a standalone student embedder. At inference, the student independently encodes queries and candidates without candidate conditioning or the hindsight teacher. Experiments on MMEB-V2 and the agent and text tasks of MMEB-V3 demonstrate the effectiveness of HEME and show that it enables more efficient inference than explicit reasoning-driven methods.

title: Joule is FLOP: Optimizing Tensor-Core Kernels Beyond Latency Hiding at the GPU Power Wall
abstract: For a tensor-core kernel whose average board power stays near the GPU's power cap, runtime is approximately the energy consumed per call divided by that cap. Data movement whose latency is hidden by computation still consumes energy; reducing this traffic can raise the sustained clock and shorten execution even without reducing cycle count. We introduce Joule, a framework that accounts for this energy-frequency coupling in tensor-kernel design and scheduling. Its cost model combines hardware event counts, physical data-path energy costs, and nonlinear voltage scaling across domains to solve for sustained frequency and runtime under a power cap. Combining the model with data-movement lower bounds across memory levels and dies yields a power-aware speed of light (PSoL) that quantifies structural and implementation gaps. This analysis guides wide-tile kernels that use the full tensor memory (TMEM) capacity on B200, with fine-grained asynchronous rotation to overlap accumulator readout with tensor-core computation. It also guides power-aware spatial and temporal tile scheduling that accounts for trade-offs among read sharing, locality, and load balance. Given measured event counts, the model achieves 0.69% mean energy prediction error on B200. Across 60 dense-layer shapes, our GEMM delivers geometric-mean speedups of 4.94%, 6.64%, and 2.12% over exhaustively selected cuBLAS algorithms on B200, H100 NVL, and RTX PRO 6000, respectively. For fused Mega-MoE on eight B200 GPUs, the resulting optimizations improve performance by 2.60% to 5.17% over the upstream DeepGEMM baseline with die-local expert weights. We will open source Joule upon publication.

title: Overparameterized Simulation-Error Minimization for Nonlinear System Identification: Horizon-Uniform Landscape and Identifiability
abstract: Simulation-error minimization is a standard criterion in nonlinear system identification, but its landscape is nonconvex and its conditioning can degrade geometrically with the data horizon N. We propose to lift the trajectory with a free, softly penalized per-step correction, which yields a fit loss that gradient descent provably minimizes: under a rank condition on the output map and a bound on the one-step Jacobian, it satisfies a Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality with an explicit constant independent of N. A zero-loss model leaves the physical parameter undetermined. Identifiability is restored by a minimal-correction selection principle: under structural identifiability, the global minimizer of the penalized loss returns the true parameters for every positive penalty weight, and under noise and unmodeled dynamics the parameter error grows at most linearly with the mismatch. The resulting estimator, gradient descent on the fit loss followed by a homotopy in the penalty weight, reconciles fit and selection, with a local convergence guarantee. In experiments, it recovers the parameters on long records of expanding and chaotic systems on which single shooting fails.

title: Interference-Free In-Symbol Pilots for High-Mobility DFT-s-OFDM Uplink
abstract: The 5G New Radio (NR) uplink uses discrete Fourier transform spread orthogonal frequency-division multi- plexing (DFT-s-OFDM) for its low peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR). Its demodulation reference signal (DMRS) occupies whole symbols, although channel estimation only needs channel samples. Since existing designs cannot place pilots inside a data symbol without interference on the data, or on both data and pilots, NR keeps whole DMRS symbols, which wastes spectral efficiency (SE), and adds more of them as the channel varies faster, lowering the SE further. We develop a technique that places pilots free of data interference inside the data symbols, for frequency-domain channel estimation in every symbol. Using the Zak transform, we show that leaving a set of equally spaced pre- DFT samples empty frees one column of the Zak grid of the DFT output. The data values of the pilot subcarriers are relocated into this column by adding a constant over a few subcarrier combs, which preserves the energy and keeps the NR DFT sizes. The receiver undoes it linearly with comb sums, without decisions or side information, and a symbol loses as few as one data sample beyond its pilots. Since the pilots raise the PAPR, we keep them few per symbol and hop their positions across symbols, so that a two-dimensional estimator over the slot resolves long delay spreads at high Doppler. On 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) channels, pilots in every symbol achieve a higher effective SE than all NR DMRS configurations from pedestrian to high- speed-train velocities, at a PAPR close to plain DFT-s-OFDM.

title: PVWander: 3D Memory-guided Panoramic Video Wandering with Path-Facing Canonicalization
abstract: Long-horizon panoramic video wandering aims to continuously synthesize scene-consistent $360^\circ$ observations along user-specified camera trajectories from an initial equirectangular projection (ERP) panorama. Existing panoramic video models have achieved promising results in camera-controlled generation, while recent 3D-guided approaches further provide geometric guidance for improving scene consistency. However, stable long-horizon wandering remains challenging due to diverse motion--orientation relationships and imperfect memory guidance induced by accumulated generation artifacts and depth inaccuracies. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PVWander}, a 3D-memory-guided framework that accumulates generated observations into an online point-cloud memory and reprojects it to guide subsequent generation, with two complementary designs: \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} for motion--orientation alignment and \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} for adaptive memory guidance. \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} exploits the horizontal cyclic symmetry of ERP panoramas to uniformly align each clip's ERP orientation with its principal translation direction, yielding more consistent, forward-like relative motions while preserving the prescribed camera path. \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} exploits the coarse-to-fine nature of diffusion denoising to adaptively regulate reprojected memory guidance through timestep-dependent channel-wise gates, preserving its structural benefits while mitigating visual artifacts from imperfect projections. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PVWander achieves improved long-horizon generation quality, while ablations validate the effectiveness of both designs.

title: Horizon dynamical entropies and phase space topology
abstract: We study phase space topologies induced by infinite-dimensional norms as a means to solve the problem of 'integrability' of Hamiltonian generators corresponding to diffeomorphisms of a null hypersurface, with the specific goal in mind to compare different prescriptions for the dynamical entropy of black holes, which replaces the area in non-stationary regimes. We first show that for a scalar field, there exists a family of norms that would provide integrability for different polarizations. We then show that a single member of this family applies to the gravitational field, and it is given by the Sobolev norm already considered in the literature. The obstruction to the other candidates lies in the semi-positivity of the metric.

title: A Mesh to Remember: Persistent Appearance for Interactive Video Worlds
abstract: Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object's frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).

title: When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents
abstract: Human annotations on documents (such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions) express corrective intent yet existing OCR and document understanding systems treat these marks as visual noise rather than semantic edit operations. We introduce intent-aware OCR, the task of generating corrected transcriptions by jointly reasoning over original document content and visual intent cues (handwritten or digital) that convey edit intent. To support this setting, we present DocIntent, a multimodal dataset of 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, each paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets. We further introduce IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark designed to evaluate model robustness under diverse real-world annotation conditions. Leveraging DocIntent, we fine-tune DocIntentOCR, a suite of 3B and 7B parameter vision-language models, under direct intent supervision on corrected transcriptions. On IntentBench, the fine-tuned 3B and 7B models achieve F1-scores of 0.81 and 0.83, respectively, substantially outperforming commercial closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.1 (0.626)), and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B (0.50)) demonstrating that intent-aware supervision enables compact domain-specific models to outperform substantially larger general-purpose systems on this task. This work establishes intent-aware OCR as a novel human-in-the-loop document understanding task and provides foundational resources (dataset, benchmark, models) to advance research in interactive document processing.

title: ObsBridge: Observation-Grounded Conditioning for Ego Trajectory Prediction
abstract: Pedestrian forecasting from ego-view observations is challenging because occlusion, limited visibility, and tracking errors corrupt observed motion histories. Such errors are particularly consequential for autonomous robot navigation. Existing paradigms typically either impute noisy history positions before forecasting or jointly train an auxiliary history reconstruction branch. However, predictors trained on clean histories may be sensitive to residual errors in recovered histories at deployment. Meanwhile, auxiliary reconstruction still computes inter-agent interactions over raw, corrupted coordinates. We investigate conditioning future prediction on both recovered historical states and raw observation evidence, with progressive training to accommodate imperfect recovery. Building on this insight, we propose ObsBridge, a flow-based trajectory forecasting framework with observation-grounded historical bridging. Specifically, ObsBridge first employs a frozen estimator to recover historical motion from agent-relative and ego-relative positions, image-plane locations, and visibility states. During training, we introduce an agent-wise curriculum that gradually replaces clean teacher histories with complete estimated histories before context encoding. This progressively exposes the predictor to estimated histories during training. Furthermore, we design a residual geometry adapter to fuse the encoded motion with original observation evidence. We aggregate the resulting representations through social attention to condition the flow-based trajectory generator. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that ObsBridge outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On EgoTraj-TBD, it reduces minADE@20 by 6.5\% and minFDE@20 by 8.7\%. The code will be provided at https://github.com/shawnliang420/ObsBridge.

title: Sharp Barycentric Costs in Teichmuller Space
abstract: The affine Beltrami fiber over a closed hyperbolic surface has a quadratic normal response whose least vertical $L^2$ energy equals the tangent norm dual to the hyperbolic cotangent supremum norm. We prove this calibration using a curvature identity and exact localized responses. Its strictness determines the energy measures of near-minimizers and, under an amplitude constraint, gives a positive excess with an explicit quadratic lower coefficient when the supporting differential has nondegenerate maxima. Pointwise Poincar'e barycenters of representatives in one fiber give a nonlinear realization: equal-weight pairs attain prescribed small outputs exactly, and their creation energy approaches the calibrated norm if and only if the output scale is negligible relative to the squared amplitude bound. Restoring the full local fiber graph has leading cost four times the squared Weil--Petersson norm. For degenerating surfaces, we identify the additive limit of the calibrated norm across persistent components and collar directions. The induced length metric completes to marked augmented Teichm"uller space and has distance $\fracπ{2}\sum_i \ell_i + O((\sum_i \ell_i)^2)$ to a fixed pinching stratum. Systole-dependent estimates also yield exact nonlinear realizations along degenerating families.

title: Shock formation in traffic flow models with Arrhenius look-ahead interactions
abstract: We study finite-time shock formation in a nonlocal traffic flow model with Arrhenius look-ahead dynamics. For the constant interaction potential, we derive a time-dependent lower bound for the minimum slope and obtain a sufficient condition with logarithmic dependence on the magnitude of the minimum initial slope. For the linear interaction potential with look-ahead distance $γ$, we show that the condition $u'_0(x_0)>\frac{1}γ$ at a single point is sufficient for shock formation, which is independent of the minimum initial slope. Our results strictly improve the corresponding conditions of Lee and Liu \cite{r17}.

title: Which Parameters to Update? An Instance-Specific Adaptation Framework for Real-World Pansharpening
abstract: Pansharpening aims to fuse a single observed image pair, comprising a low-resolution multispectral (LRMS) image and a panchromatic (PAN) image, to obtain a high-resolution multispectral (HRMS) image. Recently, deep learning-based methods have achieved significant performance due to their strong capability of extracting nonlinear features. However, distribution shifts between training data and test images can degrade the performance of pretrained pansharpening networks, limiting their generalization in real-world scenarios. In this work, we propose an instance-specific test-time adaptation framework that uses the observed PAN-LRMS pair to select and update only a subset of the pretrained network's parameters. Specifically, the framework uses cross-scoring to identify parameter groups whose updates improve reconstruction across image patches. It then updates the selected groups by minimizing a loss that combines a spectral consistency term with a newly designed spatial consistency term. Experiments show that the adapted networks perform better than their pretrained counterparts and outperform representative state-of-the-art pansharpening methods on GaoFen-2, QuickBird, and WorldView series datasets.

title: Electron spin relaxation and coherence times of silicon vacancies in 4H-SiC
abstract: Color defect centers carrying electron spins in solid crystals like diamond and silicon carbide (SiC) are promising candidates for qubits and quantum sensors, with SiC material being particularly interesting due to its compatibility with the existing semiconductor technology. Here we investigated the electron spin properties of silicon vacancy centers (V1 and V2) both electron spin $S = 3/2$ in 4H-SiC in the temperature range $T=80-300$~K using electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR). The EPR spectrum shows central and satellite lines, where the former ones originate from V1 and V2 centers, as well as from unknown defect center X. The analysis of continuous wave EPR measurements revealed a spin concentration of $c_{\mathrm{V1}}=1.47\pm0.3\times10^{14}$, $c_{\mathrm{V2}}=5.6\pm1.12\times10^{13}$ and $c_{\mathrm{X}}=1.03\pm0.21\times10^{13}$ spins/cm$^{3}$. Additionally, electron spin coherence $T_2$ and relaxation times $T_1$ have been measured on the central and on the satellite spectral lines, resulting in longer $T_1$ and $T_2$ for the satellite transition, compared to the central one, with maximum values of $42.8\pm1.3$~ms and $0.708\pm0.004$~ms respectively at $T=80$~K. We reveal, that decoherence is mainly caused by nuclear and electron spin diffusion.

title: The Teacher Is Already Inside: Self-Distilling Looped Language Models Beyond Their Last Loop
abstract: Looped language models apply one shared transformer stack several times per token, and every loop is readable through the shared language-model head. Post-training them is hard. Reward-only reinforcement learning needs a verifier and learns from one sparse signal per response; spreading the reward over loops collapses the entropy of every loop; and cross-loop self-distillation, as in LoopOPD, can only teach intermediate loops, because the last loop cannot learn from its own frozen copy: the loss is zero at initialisation. We observe that a looped model already contains a policy that decodes better than its last loop: the next-token distribution extrapolated from the first loop through the last. ELPSD (Extrapolated-Loop Policy Self-Distillation) turns this distribution into a self-distillation target: a frozen copy of the model computes it, and the model's own last loop is distilled towards it on its own rollouts, using the exact reverse KL at every visited prefix. Teacher and student are the same model, so ELPSD needs no reward, no external teacher and no privileged context, and it leaves rollouts and decoding unchanged. We show that the objective pulls the last loop towards the base model's last loop with weight 1+w and away from the base model's first loop with weight w, and that the teacher must stay frozen, since an idealised teacher recomputed from the current model extrapolates without bound. We evaluate ELPSD on Ouro-1.4B-Thinking across five math benchmarks against the base model, GRPO, RLTT and OPSD. Without any reward, ELPSD raises the average avg@8 from 61.15 to 63.69 and is the best method on all five benchmarks, ahead of GRPO (62.32), which uses a verifier, and the self-distillation method OPSD (61.77), which needs reference solutions.

title: Reflection positivity of discrete and Brownian loop-soup occupation fields
