However, these findings leave unresolved whether visual learning contributes beyond the spontaneous emergence of numerical selectivity. Human development provides a clue, as children become better at making judgments in which numerosity and proportion conflict. Here, we introduce a geometric framework to trace how representations of these two quantities change across learning. Although untrained and pretrained networks exhibited similar unit-level numerosity selectivity and basic comparison performance, natural-image pretraining increased the angle between numerosity and proportion subspaces while reducing their overlap, supporting more robust readout under conflict. Direct manipulation of these geometric properties further demonstrated their functional contributions to decoding accuracy and functional independence. Importantly, conventional supervised pretraining was not essential for quantity separation, which also emerged through self-supervised learning without category labels and synthetic-image training without natural-image exposure. Together, our findings suggest that structured visual learning can refine spontaneously emerging number sense into robust and functionally independent quantity representations without explicit numerical training.

title: Norm of the Generalized Hilbert Matrix Operator Between Some Spaces of Analytic Functions
abstract: We study the generalized Hilbert operator \[ \mathcal H_bf(z)=\int_0^1\frac{(1-t)^b}{(1-tz)^{b+1}}f(t)\,dt, \qquad b>0, \] on several spaces of analytic functions in the unit disk. For logarithmically weighted Korenblum spaces, we obtain an exact supremum representation and a lower estimate for the norm of the mapping from $H_{α,\log}^{\infty}$ to $H_α^\infty$. We then establish two-sided estimates and characterize the boundedness range of $\mathcal H_b$ on the $α$-Bloch spaces $\mathcal B^α$. We also derive norm bounds for the mapping from $H^\infty$ into the endpoint Zygmund-type space $Λ_1^{1,*}$. Furthermore, we give a norm representation for $\mathcal H_b:H_α^\infty\to\mathcal B^{α+1}$ and identify a norm-attaining function. In particular, for $0<α\leq2/3$, the norm is expressed explicitly in terms of a Beta function. Finally, we obtain an exact supremum representation of the norm of $\mathcal H_b$ on $H_{α,\log}^{\infty}$, together with explicit norm estimates. Our results extend those of Hao et al. [J. Geom. Anal. 35 (2025), Paper No. 184] for the classical Hilbert matrix operator ($b=0$) to the generalized case $b>0$.

title: Controllable CAD Generation and Interactive Editing of Fluid Rotors
abstract: Computer-aided design (CAD) provides the geometric foundation for rotors in fluid rotating machinery. However, creating models for different rotors requires different modeling processes, making it difficult to control geometry through design intent and reuse existing models. We introduce VaneCraft, an agent-driven framework for rotor generation, inverse recovery, and editing through a unified analytical representation. The agent interprets design requests and invokes geometric modeling operations. The representation defines geometric controls through meridional geometry and independent boundary angle laws. An anisotropic partial differential equation (PDE) maps these controls to the blade surfaces. Geometric parameter correction (GPC) uses a joint geometric encoder and a parameter decoder to refine controls initialized from rotor category and dimensions. Inverse recovery maps existing CAD to the same geometric controls for reconstruction and continued editing. Experiments demonstrate that VaneCraft supports anisotropy control and parameter editing and outperforms representative baselines in rotor CAD generation tasks. Project page is available on \href{https://github.com/shenchen333/vanecraft}{GitHub}.

title: Global self-organisation via driven interchange turbulence in a hard-core Z-pinch
abstract: Whereas most magnetic-confinement concepts seek to suppress turbulent transport, the levitated dipole exploits it, with plasma turbulently self-organising to concentrate into the stronger-field region near the levitating coil. In a sufficiently large device, this can create the conditions needed for fusion, despite stiff and vigorous transport. We study this process in global simulations of a driven hard-core Z-pinch using compressible ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) with self-consistent evolution of the magnetic field. The results reveal how plasma and field jointly settle onto a continuously turbulent, finite-beta interchange-marginal family. Across a wide drive scan in two-dimensional simulations, quasi-universal pressure and density profiles result, with the magnetic-field profile changing from a decreasing vacuum-like form to one with an interior minimum at increasing beta. These profiles are robust to large changes to the heat and particle sources (including moving both to the outside of the device) as well as to different exhaust and boundary prescriptions. A designer consequently has little direct control over the selected profiles, including the final separation between the pressure maximum and coil, which is set by a turbulent boundary layer. We show that such results persist in the presence of three-dimensional fluctuations at modest beta, but that high-beta states become unstable to a field-parallel m=1 instability that is the analogue of the ballooning instability in a true dipole; this evacuates the core, destroying confinement. Based on a near-marginal expansion and a geometrical remapping, we argue that many features of our results should apply to any shearless closed-field-line system.

title: Before They Were Cool: Do Early Fans Abandon Artists Who Suddenly Become Popular? Evidence from Online Music Listening
abstract: Identity-signalling theory, echoed in the hipster's "I liked them before they were cool", expects an artist's first fans to pull away once the artist becomes popular, by leaving or by avoiding what the newcomers play. A rival account expects the event that brings the crowd to renew existing listeners' attention to the artist. We test both in the Last.fm listening histories of 594,415 users (21.1 billion plays, 2005-2013), where every play appears on the user's profile. Study 1 detects 78 crowd arrivals: months in which the number of people discovering an artist tripled without a new album, single or EP, for example after a song appeared in a film. Study 2 compares Grammy and Mercury Prize winners with nominees who won nothing. We compare listeners who had played the artist before the crowd arrived (early fans) with early fans of comparison artists. Early fans did not withdraw. Those still listening stopped less often (25.8% vs. 29.1% over six months), and those who had drifted away returned more often (29.6% vs. 25.0%). Those who kept listening converged on the crowd: the song most newcomers played took a larger share of their plays, with no turn to deep cuts. More lapsed fans returned after larger surges, and neither fans with the most distinctive tastes nor fans facing a more mainstream crowd quit more. Award wins brought few new listeners and no clear change. Where listening is displayed by default, early fans moved towards the crowd after sudden popularity, not away from it.

title: The Dirac equation in arbitrary coordinate systems and curved spacetimes - An orthonormal frames approach
abstract: In this pedagogical article we discuss the Dirac equation in arbitrary coordinate systems. We explain the need for connections when dealing with spinor fields and present the practical steps needed to compute the Dirac operator in a general setting, allowing for arbitrary coordinate systems and position-dependent orthonormal gamma matrices, both of which can simplify computations in certain scenarios. The extension to include minimally coupled gravity is straightforward. Examples are provided, including constructing the Dirac equation in spherical and cylindrical symmetry (with or without gravity) and the Kerr spacetime. We also briefly comment on the advantages and disadvantages of various tetrads and orthonormal gamma matrices. This manuscript should be accessible to readers who have studied the Dirac equation at an introductory level (e.g., in Cartesian coordinates in flat spacetime with constant gamma matrices). The emphasis is on the use of orthonormal frames, since these correspond to the coordinate systems most familiar to readers when dealing with most field theories, and represent the physical frames where measurements are performed. The aim is to get the reader quickly to the point of being able to do calculations, so the presentation favors a concise, pragmatic approach over extended derivations.

title: Greedy Decoding Hides Good Plans: Sample-and-Verify Planning for Vision-Language Driving Models
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly adopted for end-to-end driving planning, yet their performance is typically evaluated based on a single greedily decoded trajectory. However, greedy decoding may overlook better trajectories within the model's output distribution. Experiments on WOD-E2E and NAVSIM reveal a consistent performance gap between greedily decoded trajectories and the best sampled candidates, showing that planning errors can arise from trajectory selection, rather than trajectory generation alone. On WOD-E2E, when the ego vehicle should start moving, the model often assigns probability to different possible start times, causing greedy decoding to repeatedly favor waiting and produce a stationary plan even though moving trajectories are available. Motivated by these findings, we propose Sample-and-Verify (SaV), which keeps the VLM planner frozen and samples multiple candidate trajectories. A lightweight verifier is trained from ground-truth futures to estimate the relative quality of these candidates. It uses trajectory kinematics, candidate-set agreement and likelihood, and ego-motion features to select the final trajectory. On WOD-E2E, SaV reduces ADE and FDE by approximately 15% across three VLM planners on the validation set. Changes in RFS are smaller: two planners show slight decreases on val-456, while Alpamayo-1.5 improves from 7.74 to 7.81 RFS on the official test set as ADE@5s decreases by 11%. On NAVSIM, SaV reduces ADE@4s by 10-24% across three VLM planners, while PDMS changes are less consistent. These results show that trajectory selection can substantially improve displacement accuracy without additional planner training. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/hzxbzp/sample-and-verify.

title: How Many Sources, Not Just How Many Problems: Planning the Precision of LLM Evaluations from Earlier Results
abstract: When benchmark problems share sources, such as variants of one template or tasks from one repository, an evaluation budget must fix the number of sources as well as the number of problems. We ask whether pilot data or earlier evaluation results can predict, before an evaluation is run, how much the standard deviation (SD) of the score grows when the same budget is concentrated on fewer sources. We use the classical design effect with an intraclass correlation estimated on data disjoint from those used to check the prediction. On GSM-Symbolic, 100 problems drawn as 10 templates x 10 variants have an SD of 9.2 pp against 2.7 pp from 100 templates; pilot data on 15 other questions predict the ratio as 3.49 against 3.52 measured on held-out questions (medians over 20 splits; single splits err by -13% to +16%), once the actual sampling plan is included. On SWE-bench Verified, 10 randomly selected public submissions predict the median ratio for 119 other submissions within 3% for 2 or more repositories, and 3 submissions are nearly as good. Dropping the finite-population terms from the design prediction gives errors of 13-21% on GSM-Symbolic, where it reduces to the textbook formula, and 25-35% on SWE-bench. Widening iid intervals by the square root of the pilot design effect brings pass@1 coverage on concentrated designs to 0.93-0.98, but not pass@16 (0.85, 0.76). We also report two lessons for anyone validating such predictions: split pilot and held-out data by question source, not by difficulty version, and do not read a good fit of the formula as evidence of source clustering (MATH-500). The method is not new; we contribute a held-out test of its advance predictions and a recipe for using them. Code: https://github.com/Guang627/deff-eval

title: Using waveform types, discrete Sobolev distances, and trend compatibility to cluster short time series of clinical data
abstract: Clinical tests, such as the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), perturb a physiological system at rest and record its excursion over a fixed protocol window as a short, undersampled time series. Such curves rarely allow parameter identification at the individual level, yet their trends carry physiological information that emerges at the population level as recurrent response patterns. Standard clustering methods aggregate differences globally and average out those trends, losing precisely the information about how the system regains control after the perturbation; identifying response patterns requires a method that preserves them. We present a nonparametric framework that factorizes each curve into unit waveforms, sorts them with a symbolic trend-compatibility filter, and compares compatible shapes using discrete Sobolev-type distances on finite differences up to order $k$. The number of clusters, i.e., distinct response types, equals the number of realizable trend patterns the cohort populates, validated by resampling. Applied to 1283 five-point OGTTs, the method identifies 7 glycemia and 8 insulinemia types. The count holds across a threefold range of resolution. In benchmarks against six classical clustering methods, ours alone never mixes opposite trends, with comparable reconstruction error and stability. Clinical normality, assessed after clustering, is graded, overlapping, and distributed unevenly across response types ($h=0.14$--$0.48$). Overall, our method distinguishes response types among curves too short for alignment-based methods yet too informative for reduction to summary values. It applies to any protocol recording a system's response to a standardized perturbation on a short grid.

title: JWST Reveals Contrast Overdensities around Two ALMA-CRISTAL Galaxies at $z\sim5.2$
abstract: The distribution of stellar mass between massive galaxies and their companions traces how galaxy assembly proceeds within early large-scale structure. We investigate the environments of two galaxies from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) CRISTAL survey: CRISTAL-19 (C19; $z=5.235$) and CRISTAL-21 (C21; $z=5.256$), using F444W slitless spectroscopy from the Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) on the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) in COSMOS-3D. A friends-of-friends analysis of H$α$ emitters identifies two distinct overdense nodes separated by approximately 25 comoving Mpc. Although C21 is the more massive galaxy, C19 has the more massive, actively star-forming companions. The companion populations around C19 and C21 have median stellar masses of $\log(M_\star/M_\odot)=9.43$ and 8.82 and median dust-corrected H$α$ star formation rates of 31 and $16~M_\odot~\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, respectively. Their star formation rate contrast largely reflects the difference in companion masses. C19 contains only $4.5^{+0.9}_{-0.7}\%$ of the combined measured stellar mass of itself and its selected companions; the corresponding fraction for C21 is $39^{+5}_{-5}\%$. Thus, stellar mass remains more widely distributed among galaxies around C19, whereas a larger share resides in C21. Resolved interacting companions around C19 and [C II] kinematics consistent with a late-stage merger in C21 support this contrast in assembly state. These findings support the phase-dependent picture of Zou et al. (2026), in which the surrounding star-forming population changes as interactions and mergers build up a massive galaxy.

title: State Space Attention: Learning Context-Dependent Memory Retention
abstract: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context length. Bounding it raises the question of what a sequence model should retain for long-context reasoning. We argue this choice should be learned, and introduce State Space Attention (SSA), which learns to keep a bounded set of past representations and reads them with standard attention. A learned scorer rescores every chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory. A fixed-context Transformer is then the special case that always keeps the most recent tokens. We train the scorer and reader jointly, either moving gradually from a differentiable soft weighting of memories to hard retention, or with hard retention from the start. To produce signal for the scorer, we generate supervised samples during training, a technique we call recovery. We compare SSA with recurrent models, bounded-memory attention methods, and full-attention Transformers across retrieval, variable tracking, multi-hop reasoning, and language modeling. On our retrieval and reasoning benchmarks, SSA matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks, far outperforms a Transformer with the same readable budget on every long-context retrieval task we evaluate, and matches or outperforms one with about 4 times that budget, while using constant inference memory. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language model scale is on RULER. SSA makes a fixed number of tokens useful over a longer context, and since it reads memory with standard attention, we propose that it can be stacked with KV cache eviction methods. We also pretrain and post-train 400M-parameter models and measure how SSA's training and inference costs scale with context length and model size. Together, these experiments examine the capabilities and limitations of learned memory retention for long-context sequence modeling.

title: PICE: Prototype-Informed Conditional Model Evolution Toward Self-Evolving Medical Image Recognition
abstract: Medical image classifiers in clinical practice must continually evolve to accommodate emerging disease categories while maintaining reliable classification of existing conditions. This is challenging because privacy and data-sharing restrictions limit access to historical patient data, while assigning dedicated capacity to each new diagnostic task causes linear model growth. Effective evolution requires preserving prior disease knowledge without retaining historical images while expanding model capacity only when necessary. To this end, we propose PICE, a Prototype-Informed Conditional Model Evolution framework organized around what to preserve, when evolution is needed, and how that evolution is realized. PICE preserves prior disease knowledge in a prototype-statistical memory. For each incoming task, it assesses compatibility with historical references reconstructed from memory, reusing the closest adapter when compatibility is sufficient and instantiating a new one when evolution is required. PICE then realizes evolution by updating the memory and recalibrating the unified classifier with Gaussian pseudo features, thereby integrating new knowledge into the cumulative diagnostic space. During inference, memory-derived similarities guide task-agnostic adapter selection and fusion, enabling prediction over all learned disease categories. Experiments on Skin8, Kvasir-V2, and Path16 demonstrate the effectiveness of PICE across diverse clinical scenarios. On Skin8, PICE achieves a 7.60\% improvement in accuracy over the SOTA method on new tasks, while maintaining 71.10\% accuracy on previous tasks. It also reduces additional learnable parameters by 18.51\%. These results indicate that PICE improves classification while balancing knowledge retention, adaptation, and parameter growth, supporting continual model evolution as new diagnostic categories emerge without access to historical images.

title: Welfare-Enhancing Mechanism Design for Agent Ecosystems
abstract: The emerging Agentic Web forms a multi-agent ecosystem: a decentralized service market where the user agent selects which content agents to query from their submitted profiles, before seeing any documents. Profiles therefore become a new target of optimization. Existing Generative Engine Optimization studies how a single supplier rewrites documents the engine can already retrieve, to improve their citation. In the Agentic Web, multiple content agents optimize profiles to compete for limited opportunities to deliver documents. To study this repeated interaction, we build WildRegistry, a simulation framework and benchmark based on a real agentic-search request stream, and model it as a dynamic game under private monitoring. Long-horizon experiments show that this competition lowers website-selection quality and settles at a harmful stable point, which our empirical criterion identifies as an approximate rewriting equilibrium. We therefore design a welfare-enhancing mechanism, DEC (Delivery-Evidence Credit), a platform-side policy that uses recorded delivery outcomes to reallocate later opportunities and reduce information asymmetry. DEC improves this endpoint, raising website-selection quality while preserving most of providers' exposure gains, for a Welfare Gain of +2.01 points and a healthier long-horizon outcome. More broadly, our findings highlight the importance of mechanism design in agent ecosystems: turning recorded delivery outcomes into evidence that endogenously shapes later user-agent selection and content-agent adaptation can steer long-horizon adaptation toward delivered capabilities.

title: Multi-Modal Causal Disentanglement for Multi-Domain Sequential Audio Recommendation
abstract: Modern music platforms expose users to heterogeneous audio content domains such as songs, playlists, and podcasts. Multi-domain sequential recommendation (MDSR) seeks to exploit such cross-domain behavior, yet two obstacles persist in practice. First, joint optimization across heterogeneous domains is prone to negative transfer, with high-traffic domains dominating the shared parameter space and suppressing weaker domains. Second, conventional ID-based collaborative signals fail to bridge domains that are semantically related but exhibit little behavioral overlap. This paper presents CAMAR, a multi-modal causal disentanglement framework for multi-domain audio recommendation. From a causal perspective, user behavior is modeled as the joint outcome of a domain-invariant preference and domain-specific preferences. Guided by this view, CAMAR factorizes user representations into domain-invariant and domain-specific components and enforces domain adversarial invariance together with orthogonality, restricting cross-domain interaction to the invariant subspace and suppressing harmful transfer paths. To strengthen cross-domain semantic coupling, CAMAR derives trainable semantic-ID embeddings from pre-trained text, vision, and audio features through residual quantization, yielding an end-to-end multi-modal adaptation tailored to recommendation. A transfer network imputes user representations for inactive domains, mitigating cross-domain cold start. Experiments on both public and industrial datasets demonstrate consistent gains over strong baselines. In online A/B tests on NetEase Cloud Music, one of China's largest music streaming platforms, CAMAR delivers consistent gains across all three domains in their main traffic scenarios, validating its effectiveness in multi-domain audio recommendation at scale.

title: Impact of the Performance of Autonomy and Communication Subsystems on the Level-of-Safety of Partially Autonomous Machine Systems
abstract: The level-of-safety of a partially autonomous machine system depends on two subsystems: the autonomy subsystem that manages the system between human interventions; and the communication subsystem that enables those interventions. These subsystems are typically evaluated independently. We model the level-of-safety analytically as a function of their joint performance. Three parameters characterize the autonomy subsystem: the Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI); the urgency $\mathcal{U}$ or mean time within which an intervention must be completed to avoid failure; and the complexity $\mathcal{C}$ or mean time to understand, decide on and execute it. Two characterize the communication subsystem: its availability $P_A$ and its latency $\varepsilon$. A dimensionless criticality ratio $ρ=(\mathcal{C}+\varepsilon)/\mathcal{U}$ prescribes the shape of the Pareto tradeoff between the MTBI and $P_A$ at a constant level-of-safety. At $ρ=0.01$, a perfect link lowers the required MTBI by two orders of magnitude. At $ρ=1$, it only halves it. Under exponential timing assumptions the model is in closed form, and compliance with a safety budget can be stated at a chosen assurance level. We illustrate it for remotely piloted aircraft with assumed parameter values and propose a simulation procedure to estimate them.

title: Graphical Rules for Zero-energy Quantum-Interference Patterns in Bipartite Lattices
abstract: Quantum interference(QI) plays an important role in electron transport in molecules, where conductance is determined by the coherent superposition of different quantum-walk paths connecting the source and drain sites. In some systems, the pronounced even-odd conductance oscillation with the walk length can be observed; meanwhile destructive QI can lead to a dramatic suppression of conductance, resulting in a huge on/off ratio. In this paper, we extend the investigation from individual molecules to bipartite lattice systems, providing an abstract framework for exploring QI in a broad range of two-dimensional systems. We propose a simple graphical rule for predicting the QI pattern-the conductance map obtained by varying the drain site while keeping the source site fixed-in bipartite structures with arbitrary boundaries and holes. The analysis can be completed in three steps. First, a unit-cell-replicated bipartite subset is constructed by removing a subset of atoms from the input network, and its Green's function map is efficiently obtained from a local recurrence relation. Second, the removed atoms and local structural modifications are coupled back as local degrees of freedom, generating zero-mode vectors through the same Green's function map. Finally, the surviving zero-mode combinations are selected by an effective coupling matrix, whose projectors correct the reference map to yield the final QI pattern. This rule applies to finite flakes with arbitrary boundaries and holes and extends naturally to infinite lattices and vacancy defects.

title: Extension complexity is not additive under Cartesian products
abstract: We prove that the linear extension complexity of a Cartesian product of polytopes can be strictly smaller than the sum of the extension complexities of its factors. This disproves Conjecture 1.2 of Grande, Padrol and Sanyal. We construct a rational 24-dimensional polytope $P$ with 50 facets and 150 vertices such that $P$ has extension complexity 40 and $P \times P$ has extension complexity exactly 79. We also prove that the saving can be arbitrarily large, even in a Cartesian square: for every $t$ there is a rational polytope $R_t$ whose square needs at least $t$ fewer inequalities than two separate copies of $R_t$. For two different factors, we construct a family whose product saves at least $\lceil 5n/27 \rceil$ inequalities while the two separate complexities sum to $O(n)$, so that the saving is a constant fraction of the total. The proofs rest on a transfer theorem: wedging over the omitted facets of a polytope turns a gap between the nonnegative ranks of partial slack matrices into a gap between extension complexities. The unbounded squares come from intersecting families of sets on successively larger alphabets. In the square the two copies of each coordinate share generators, while a counting lemma determines the exact cost of a single factor.

title: Interpreting Speckle Effects Through Neuron Interventions
abstract: Speckle, the multiplicative noise inherent to synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging, reduces the performance of pretrained SAR models. We use interpretability methods to examine its effects inside pretrained vision models. We identify neurons that respond selectively to speckle and test whether correcting their activations improves reconstruction. We study SARMAE, an Earth observation model pretrained on a million-scale SAR dataset. Synthetic scenes with known reflectivity allow us to measure recovery precisely. The model contains 38 speckle-selective neurons that track speckle's value distribution. Restoring these neurons to their clean values does not improve reconstruction. Activation patching across layers shows that the first MLP has the largest restoration and injection effects. Within this layer, a different set of 64 neurons recovers 44.1\% of the correlation loss on held-out scenes. When the speckle-selective neurons are held at their noisy values, 96.5\% of this gain remains, while holding the values of three decoder heads removes 37.4\%. In an ImageNet-pretrained MAE, restoration is most effective in the third MLP block. On manipulated Sentinel-1 and Capella images, the same 64 neurons also improve reconstruction, whereas for land-cover classification, only restoring the entire first MLP yields a clear gain. The neurons that respond most to speckle are therefore not the ones the model uses to recover the scene.

title: Determination of the strong coupling constant from the R ratio obtained in KEDR and BESIII experiments
abstract: The experimental data collected by the KEDR and BESIII collaborations at energies below the charm quark threshold are compared with the massless QCD expressions for the $e^+e^-$ annihilation R-ratio truncated at different orders of perturbation theory. The fits demonstrate the dependence of the extracted $α_s(M_Z)$ values on the orders of truncation of the corresponding approximations.

title: The evolution of extreme spatial heterochiasmy in amphibians: interactions between sex-specific meiotic program and chromosome architecture
abstract: Heterochiasmy, sex differences in meiotic recombination, is usually described in terms of genetic-map length, potentially obscuring more consequential differences in crossover location. Amphibians provide striking examples of extreme spatial heterochiasmy, with male recombination concentrated near chromosome ends and female recombination broadly distributed, yet the evolution and genetic basis of this pattern remains poorly understood. Here, we combine a review with a phylogenetic comparative synthesis of male chiasma location across 97 amphibian species. Male crossover localization is phylogenetically structured, and ancestral reconstruction favors predominantly interstitial recombination at deeper anuran nodes, although not conclusively. The strongest correlate of male terminal crossover location is chromosome morphology: telocentric-rich karyotypes retain more interstitial male chiasmata, whereas metacentric chromosomes show more terminal male chiasmata. Genome size and sex-chromosome system show little association. We propose a sequential model in which sex-specific meiotic regulation first establishes a crossover-precursor placement bias, while centromere position influences which precursors mature into crossovers. This model predicts that chromosome fusion, fission or centromere repositioning can alter male chiasma location without requiring changes to the underlying meiotic program. Our synthesis highlights crossover location as a distinct dimension of heterochiasmy with consequences for genome-wide linkage, adaptation, divergence and sex-chromosome evolution.

title: FreshVLA: Frequency-Regularized Time Scale Hierarchical Latent Actions for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Learning reusable latent actions from action-free videos offers an effective route to improving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies. However, reconstruction-oriented latent actions do not necessarily benefit policy learning: as they may encode task-irrelevant static appearance with scene identity, or entangle slowly varying task progress with fine-grained execution dynamics in limited discrete code. We propose FreshVLA, a VLA framework built on a frequency-guided, dynamics-sensitive learning paradigm for acquiring temporally hierarchical continuous latent actions. FreshVLA uses a high-pass prior to guide visual transition encoding toward dynamical regions, thereby reducing reliance on static appearance cues. It further organizes latent actions into coarse-grained task progress and fine-grained execution dynamics through cross-timescale sampling and frequency-domain regularization, enhancing their capacity to represent long-horizon behaviors. During policy training, we freeze the pretrained latent action encoder and transfer its representations to robot control through joint flow-matching of latent and robot actions. FreshVLA achieves 98.2% average success on LIBERO and 98.0% on LIBERO-Long, exceeding GR00T-N1.6 on the latter by 3.6%. It also reaches an average sequence length of 4.52 on CALVIN and strong overall success rate of 80.4% in the zero-shot LIBERO-PLUS evaluation. Furthermore, FreshVLA exhibits greater robustness to visual perturbations and a more distinct division of roles between two branches in modeling low- and high-frequency motion, respectively. In 35-step action regression, it achieves a 51.3-percentage-point higher relative error reduction than its hierarchical discrete counterpart. Real-world experiments demonstrate that FreshVLA improves the average success rate over $π_{0.5}$ by 7.5%. The FreshVLA project page is available at https://freshvla.github.io/.

title: What Is Redundant at High Resolution? Efficient Attention and Feed-Forward Design for All-in-One Image Restoration
abstract: Multi-scale architectures are widely adopted in all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) to capture larger-scale context at low-resolution stages and refine details at high-resolution (HR) stages. However, processing spatially large feature maps at HR stages incurs substantial computational costs and memory traffic, making efficient HR processing challenging. To address this challenge, we propose High-resolution Global-Local Restoration (HiGLR), an efficient multi-scale AIO-IR network grounded in an analysis of spatial redundancy in self-attention and convolutional feed-forward networks (ConvFFNs). Specifically, this analysis identifies three key redundancies: per-query readout at the finest-scale stage, key routing across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and spatial mixing in the expanded feature spaces of ConvFFNs. Accordingly, HiGLR replaces costly self-attention at the finest-scale stage with a learned input-independent kernel. At intermediate stages, we propose a Block-Routed Hybrid Attention, which combines coarse-scale dense attention with fine-scale block-sparse attention over value residuals relative to coarse summaries, and shares routing indices across neighboring queries. We further introduce a Dual-Space FFN that performs spatial mixing in a compact space and pointwise nonlinear transformation in an expanded space, enabling efficient kernel fusion. Combining these designs, HiGLR achieves state-of-the-art performance while delivering up to a $4.24\times$ inference speedup over existing methods.

title: Electron exchange matters in electron spectroscopy
abstract: Electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) conventionally considers classical Coulomb interactions between probe and material electrons, overlooking their fermionic exchange at relativistic energies. Here, we develop a relativistic theory of magnon EELS incorporating both magnetic dipole and electron exchange interactions. We show that the two channels leave distinguishable electron spin states, suppressing their interference in conventional EELS. However, spin-resolved detection erases this which-path information, revealing first-order interference despite the weak exchange amplitude. Remarkably, the same interference produces a left-right intensity asymmetry with a spin-polarized incident beam, without requiring outgoing-spin analysis. We demonstrate that this signal directly probes magnon angular momentum and distinguishes excitations of opposite handedness, opening a route to nanoscale measurements of chiral magnetic excitations.

title: Simple ordinary geometrically split abelian varieties over finite fields
abstract: In this paper we provide a partial classification (necessary conditions) for all possible simple ordinary geometrically split abelian varieties over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$. Let $A$ be such an abelian variety, i.e. $A$ is simple over $\mathbb{F}_q$ and splits as $A \sim B^s$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q^d}$ for some simple abelian variety $B$. Assume that $d$ is a minimal extension degree over which $A$ splits and $B$ has a minimal field of definition (up to isogeny) $\mathbb{F}_{q^e}\subseteq \mathbb{F}_{q^d}$. For dimension $2$, Howe and Zhu showed that the only possible degrees $d$ are $2$, $3$, $4$, and $6$. Moreover, for each such degree $d$, they provided explicit formulae expressing the isogeny invariant, namely the characteristic polynomial of the Frobenius endomorphism $χ_{A,q}$, in terms of the coeffients of $χ_{B,q}$. We extend this result to ordinary abelian varieties of higher dimension. For dimensions $3$--$10$, we provide complete lists of such varieties as components of the Weil restriction $W_{\mathbb{F}_{q^d}/\mathbb{F}_q}(B)$ together with all possible triples $(d, e, s)$ and restrictions on characteristic polynomial $χ_{A,q}$ of the form $χ_{A, q} \mid χ_{V, q}$. Here, $V$ is a component of Weil restriction $W_{\mathbb{F}_{q^d}/\mathbb{F}_q}(B)$ containing $A$ as an isogeny factor and having explicit expression of the characteristic polynomial $χ_{V,q}$ in terms of coefficients of $χ_{B,q^e}$. For higher dimensions, we propose an algorithm for enumeration of all possible cases for a given dimension of $A$. We also provide an implementation of this algorithm.

title: How Much Effort Does an AI Code Reviewer Need? Evidence from Claude 5.5 Models on Plausible-but-Wrong Patches
abstract: AI coding agents write code faster than people can review it, so teams add AI reviewers. Reasoning models let such a reviewer trade cost for diligence through an effort setting. We asked how much effort a reviewer needs to catch plausible-but-wrong patches, which pass a benchmark's tests but fail stronger ones. Claude Opus 5.5 (preregistered), Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 (exploratory) each reviewed the same 90 agent-written Django patches from SWE-bench Verified at low, medium and high effort. By strengthened SWE-ABS tests, 55 patches were wrong and 35 correct. In every model, high effort accepted fewer wrong patches than low (false success .45 against .67 for Opus, .49 against .65 for Sonnet, .51 against .78 for Haiku), a supported difference for Opus and Haiku. For Opus, medium was non-inferior to high within 15 percentage points (difference .018, 95% CI [-.065, .108]) and cost 20% less, short of the preregistered 30%. For Sonnet and Haiku, medium cost 39% and 51% less than high but was not shown non-inferior. Opus at medium or high agreed best with the labels; Haiku at high cost about 8% as much per review as Opus at medium, accuracy difference unresolved. Exploratory coding showed that most rejections named the tested defect and that effort added such rejections. No setting is a strong gate: each accepted at least 45% of wrong patches. For 32 of the 55 wrong patches the issue may not require what the failing test checks; without them, neither accuracy hypothesis holds for any model.

title: Sparse-to-Sparse Feature Learning for Cross-Layer Analysis and Steering
abstract: Understanding how models internally represent information is a central challenge in interpretation and control. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense hidden representations into sparse features, and cross-layer methods capture structure spanning multiple layers. However, existing objectives do not explicitly train the sparse code at one layer to predict the sparse code at the next layer. We propose sparse-to-sparse feature learning (S2S), where sparse features at each intermediate layer are trained to predict those of the immediately following layer, with the final layer anchored by an output-distribution loss and optimization proceeding sequentially from output to input. Experiments across eight language models show stronger adjacent-layer correspondence than matched sparse-feature baselines. We evaluate feature-based interventions at matched output-distribution shift, separating steering-induced effects from sparse-pathway reconstruction effects. Causal ablation provides complementary evidence beyond correspondence metrics.

title: On the rigidity of generalized cylinders
abstract: We prove pointed Gromov--Hausdorff rigidity of cylinders $N\times\mathbb R^d$ whenever $N$ is a compact Einstein manifold rigid as a Ricci shrinker.

title: High-Dimensional Single-Photon Frequency Conversion for Orbital Angular Momentum Comb State
abstract: The orbital angular momentum (OAM) degree of freedom provides an important resource for constructing high-dimensional optical quantum information systems. However, the generation of high-dimensional single-photon OAM comb state and its high-fidelity frequency conversion remain challenging due to limited spatial modulation resolution, imperfect mode matching, and finite nonlinear conversion efficiency. Here, we proposed and experimentally demonstrated a scalable scheme for the generation and frequency conversion of high-dimensional single-photon OAM comb state. We prepared a single-photon OAM comb state with a dimension of up to 128, achieving a fidelity of 0.787 between the reconstructed and target states and an effective dimension of 100. Furthermore, using the sum-frequency generation, we demonstrated the frequency upconversion of single-photon high-dimensional OAM comb state from the communication band to a visible wavelength of 520 nm, while verifying the preservation of both the OAM mode distribution and phase information through density matrix reconstruction. Our work established a versatile platform for the generation, manipulation, and characterization of high-dimensional OAM comb states, with potential applications in cross-band quantum information transfer, high-capacity quantum communication, and high-dimensional quantum networks.

title: CariesBench: A Hierarchical Multi-view Benchmark for Dental Caries Screening and Diagnostic Reasoning from 3D Intraoral Scans
abstract: Dental caries assessment is a structured clinical process requiring lesion localization, identification of the affected tooth and surface, and severity grading rather than simple image-level recognition. 3D intraoral scans (IOS) preserve detailed dental geometry and surface morphology and support standardized rendering from complementary viewpoints, enabling fine-grained visual assessment while introducing a distinct need for anatomically grounded multi-view reasoning. Despite recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and dental vision-language benchmarks, existing evaluations do not jointly assess hierarchical arch-to-tooth-to-surface reasoning, cross-view evidence integration, and surface-level caries assessment. To address this gap, we introduce CariesBench, a hierarchical benchmark constructed from 5,932 3D IOS, comprising 85,455 standardized multi-view renderings and 133,994 clinically grounded visual question answering instances with expert quality control. CariesBench comprises three complementary task families: Arch-level Clinical Screening (ACS), Tooth-level Diagnostic Reasoning (TDR), and Structured Clinical Decision-Making (SCD). Using the CariesBench training set, we further fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct to obtain IntraoralGPT. Extensive evaluation of 24 representative baseline MLLMs reveals a substantial benchmark-level performance disparity between arch-level screening and tooth-level diagnostic reasoning, with higher accuracy on ACS than on TDR. CariesBench-specific supervision substantially improves the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct baseline, increasing the 19-task macro-average clinical accuracy from 52.7% to 69.5% and TDR Overall from 34.4% to 44.7%.

title: Physics-Informed Learning for Multiplayer Differential Games
abstract: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.

title: Pretraining for Forecasting in Relational Databases
abstract: Real-world forecasting increasingly relies on asynchronous transaction logs in relational databases rather than uniformly sampled arrays. While relational deep learning (RDL) models can forecast from these complex histories, they are typically trained separately for each specific target and root entity type. We introduce Query-Conditioned Relational pretraining (QCRP), a self-supervised framework that enables a standard RDL backbone to act as a universal forecaster across a database. QCRP generates diverse forecasting objectives using a structured temporal query grammar and interleaves them through a shared conditional predictor. This produces a robust, frozen encoder reusable for downstream tasks via lightweight predictors or a zero-shot interface. Evaluated on large-scale RelBench databases, QCRP learns frozen representations that support competitive forecasting across tasks and entity types. Furthermore, a single unified QCRP model checkpoint is competitive with isolated, entity-specific specialists. We demonstrate promising results for reusing the learned representations from standard RDL backbones for forecasting tasks in relational databases.

title: On the sharp vanishing order of the Weyl tensor at a blow-up point for the Yamabe equation in all dimensions
abstract: We determine the sharp vanishing order of the Weyl tensor at a blow-up point of solutions to the Yamabe equation in every dimension $n\ge 25$. On every closed, connected, smooth $n$-dimensional manifold $M$ of positive Yamabe type and at any prescribed point $p\in M$, we construct a smooth metric $ \widehat g$ and a sequence of smooth positive solutions to the Yamabe equation blowing up at $p$, such that the first nonzero covariant derivative of the Weyl tensor at $p$ has any prescribed order $l$ satisfying $l\ge 6$ when $25\le n\le 29$, $l \ge 4$ when $30\le n\le 51$, and $l\ge 2$ when $n\ge 52$. Moreover, $|\nabla_{ \widehat g}^{l}W_{ \widehat g}|>0$ everywhere on $M$. Earlier constructions realize every strictly higher order as the first nonzero order, while the known Weyl vanishing results exclude every lower first nonzero order. Thus the endpoint cases $l=6,4,2$ were the only ones left open, and are settled here. In particular, the order-two examples show that the compactness criterion $|W|+|\nabla W|>0$ is sharp. At the endpoints, the construction arranges global and localized metric perturbations to interact at leading order in a limiting functional. For $l=2,4$, anisotropic polynomial ansatzes involving two orthogonal algebraic Weyl tensors remove a distinguished translation degeneracy and produce $C^1$-stable saddle points. For $l=6$, a different polynomial ansatz produces a nondegenerate local minimum. Higher prescribed orders are obtained by separating the perturbation that determines the limiting functional from the one that prescribes the Weyl derivative.

title: The Danger of Double Precision: Working Precision as a Hidden Constraint in Gaussian Process Maximum Likelihood
abstract: Gaussian process (GP) hyperparameters are routinely fitted by maximizing the marginal likelihood in IEEE double precision, although for smooth kernels and noiseless data the covariance matrix is often more ill conditioned than double precision can resolve. For a squared-exponential kernel on a design with a Bayesian-optimization cluster, refits over a range of significand widths, judged against a high-precision reference, show that the double-precision fit is a different model and that fits converge only once the width exceeds the base-2 logarithm of the covariance condition number, about 70 bits. Cholesky failure acts as an implicit conditioning constraint, caused mostly by rounding of the kernel entries; the constrained solution predicted from the working precision alone is within 20% of the best Powell fits at five of the six precisions from 40 to 64 bits, with a local expansion proved for the idealized problem. Across 43 kernels, designs and problem settings, including negative controls that double precision already resolves, the bits needed follow the log condition number at the reference optimum plus a tolerance-dependent offset, and at the loosest tolerance double precision suffices for the Matern 1.5 kernel but not for the squared-exponential kernel on clustered designs. Double-precision hyperparameters overstate the posterior standard deviation near the design cluster and, on a quadratic objective whose likelihood heads to the flat limit, stall closed-loop active learning. Promoting the whole likelihood to 80 significand bits recovers the reference accuracy on every fixed design tested, whereas a fixed jitter trades failures for a posterior bias.

title: PRIOR: Pre-Call Reasoning in SFT and Its Influence on Tool-Use Retention under RL
abstract: Tool use learned during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is not always retained during reinforcement learning (RL). We study how properties of SFT data may affect this retention by constructing Low, Medium, and High SFT datasets with approximately matched token budgets but different tool-call depths. Under the same RL recipe, the three initializations reach similar RL training accuracy yet exhibit markedly different tool-use dynamics: tool initiation increases in Low, declines in Medium, and collapses in High. We observe that these datasets also differ substantially in the amount of reasoning preceding each tool call. In particular, High trajectories contain considerably less pre-call reasoning, motivating the hypothesis that pre-call reasoning may affect how well tool use is calibrated and, consequently, whether the corresponding behaviors are retained during RL. An idealized theoretical analysis provides a selective-retention view of this process: advantages in overall and tool-conditioned accuracy can be preserved under outcome-only optimization, while tool initiation increases only when tool-using trajectories are more successful than the tool-free alternative. Guided by this analysis, we rank the original High trajectories by average pre-call reasoning length and retain the highest-ranked examples while approximately matching cumulative SFT token exposure. This simple filtering strategy improves post-RL accuracy and tool-conditioned final-answer success without consistently increasing tool initiation across multiple benchmarks. These results suggest that pre-call reasoning is a useful dimension of SFT supervision for understanding and improving tool-use retention under downstream RL.

title: Structure-Aware Multimodal Retrieval Under Data Scarcity, Privacy Constraints and Out-of-Domain Content
abstract: Purpose: Figure retrieval from reference atlases in expert domains like forensic pathology, dentistry and geology must work without labels or training pairs, on content that often cannot leave local hardware, and on images outside the training data of image-text encoders. This work proposes a structure-aware pipeline that satisfies all three, retrieving figures through the page structure recovered by layout geometry and a local open-weight 8B VLM. Methods: A geometry-based pairing method is introduced, in which the model receives a schematic of the detected boxes and selects each picture's caption without access to pixels or text. Caption retrieval is evaluated on three private corpora (29 books, 10,421 figures, 218 queries) with blind human grading, against a lexical baseline, generated descriptions and five image-text encoders. Results: Geometric pairing was correct for 96%, 92% and 77% of pictures in the three domains, against 76%, 45% and 53% for the better of two document parsers. A hosted model given the schematic was equally accurate, while coordinates as text lost 22 points. Caption retrieval obtained an nDCG@5 of 0.85, 0.87 and 0.76, against 0.54, 0.51 and 0.27 for the best cross-modal encoder and 0.41, 0.28 and 0.30 for generated descriptions. Pairing errors carried over to retrieval. Conclusion: The proposed pipeline achieves accurate figure retrieval with small local models and no in-domain training, where general and biomedical image-text encoders fall far behind. Its geometry-only pairing is the most accurate of five methods and exposes no content, even to a hosted model. Code and prompts are released.

title: Linear-Time Online Visual Geometry Transformer with Hybrid Architecture
abstract: Transformer-based 3D reconstruction models such as VGGT and $π^3$ predict cameras, depth and point maps directly from many input views. Causal attention models such as StreamVGGT extend them to online video but cache all past tokens, so their total compute grows quadratically with the stream length. Recurrent models such as CUT3R and TTT3R keep a fixed-size state at constant cost, but they progressively forget early geometry. We present LinearVGGT, a hybrid model distilled from StreamVGGT, which uses Mamba2 layers for efficient sequence modeling in three of every four global layers. The remaining layers use register-guided sparse attention to retrieve a few relevant past frames, compensating for the limited exact long-range recall of Mamba2. Our distillation needs only 9\% of the GPU hours and 31\% of the training frames that StreamVGGT uses to learn from VGGT. LinearVGGT keeps an almost constant latency of 27 ms per frame over 1,024 frames and is on average $12 \times$ faster than StreamVGGT. It outperforms its teacher and is competitive with the state-of-the-art streaming model LingBot-Map, while running $2.5\times$ faster and using $2.7\times$ less memory.

title: Symbol-Level Precoding With Microwave Linear Analog Computers (MiLACs): Performance Limits and Stem-Connected Hardware Design
abstract: Symbol-level precoding (SLP) improves multiuser transmission by exploiting constructive interference based on user symbols. A microwave linear analog computer (MiLAC) maps a reduced number of radio-frequency (RF) port input signals to a large antenna array through a tunable passive microwave network. Their combination enables MiLAC to reduce the RF-chain burden of SLP, while SLP offers symbol-dependent design flexibility that can alleviate the performance loss caused by a limited number of RF chains and practical circuit constraints of MiLAC. This work investigates the joint design of SLP and MiLAC and analyzes how a limited number of RF chains and practical circuit constraints affect performance. For ideal MiLAC networks, we characterize the condition for attaining fully digital SLP performance and quantify the associated performance loss otherwise. We propose the joint effective subspace MiLAC-SLP (JES-MiLAC-SLP) algorithm to jointly optimize the analog beamforming matrix and SLP signals over a symbol block. For stem-connected MiLAC networks with finite tuning ranges and quantized tuning states, we propose the hardware-constrained JES-MiLAC-SLP (HC-JES-MiLAC-SLP) algorithm. It identifies circuit state changes for which SLP can better compensate the errors caused by circuit limitations, and updates the circuit state accordingly. Numerical results validate the derived findings and show that joint design reduces errors relative to separate MiLAC and SLP designs. Under the considered configurations, HC-JES-MiLAC-SLP substantially narrows the gap to fully digital SLP.

title: Self-supervised Clipped-objective Reinforcement Leaning Framework for Risk-aware Portfolio Management
abstract: Portfolio management involves balancing diverse financial assets, a critical yet challenging task in quantitative trading. Although deep reinforcement learning has emerged as an active research domain for solving complex sequential decision-making problems over the past decade, deploying reinforcement learning frameworks in non-stationary financial markets raises formidable difficulties. Most existing reinforcement learning-based portfolio management models fail to account for tick-level intraday market dynamics (e.g., order flow imbalances and liquidity fluctuations), which reflect rapid capital movements. Simultaneously, these models suffer from unstable learning processes due to reinforcement learning's inherent high variance. This paper presents a Self-supervised Clipped-objective Portfolio management framework (SCP), which addresses these limitations through a two-phase architecture. Market feature integration phase (application contribution) integrates micro-level market microstructure patterns with macro-level financial indicators to enhance sensitivity to intraday asset trend dynamics. Policy optimization Phase (AI contribution) employs intermediate asset state representations to derive optimal portfolio allocations via a self-supervised clipped-objective policy-learner, ensuring both effectiveness and computational efficiency. Extensive evaluations on three major index datasets from China's A-share market demonstrate that SCP's superior performance in balancing risk-return trade-offs compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Exploratory and ablation studies further validate the contributions of SCP's key components.

title: OneQuery: Unified Sequence-to-Structure Generation for Multilingual E-commerce Query Understanding
abstract: Multilingual e-commerce search requires robust query understanding to convert cross-lingual user queries with varied linguistic patterns into standardized semantic representations that support retrieval and ranking. However, traditional Query Understanding systems suffer from error accumulation, separately optimized subtasks that ignore their mutual correlations, and high maintenance costs. To address these issues, this paper proposes OneQuery, a unified generative framework for multilingual query understanding based on domain-specific large language models in e-commerce. We reformulate four subtasks, namely Language Recognition, Spelling Correction, Translation, and Query Tagging, into a unified Sequenceto-Structure autoregressive generation process constrained by predefined schemas, and design a three-stage progressive training pipeline with multi-task reinforcement learning alignment. OneQuery demonstrates consistent gains over baselines across all tasks and remains effective across different backbone sizes, and online experiments in the AliExpress e-commerce search scenario further confirm its practical value for industrial deployment.

title: Fine-Grained Ego-Vehicle Action Recognition from Driving Video
abstract: Fine-grained ego-vehicle action recognition turns large-scale driving video into structured, searchable driving scenarios, providing a foundation for discovering critical maneuvers and systematically developing and evaluating autonomous driving models. However, large-scale driving videos often lack explicit ego-action labels, and existing datasets vary in action definitions, annotation granularity, and available supervision. We introduce EgoManeuver, a unified benchmark of 16 lateral and 6 longitudinal actions constructed from seven public driving datasets. Our multi-source labeling system leverages existing annotations and complementary evidence available in each source dataset, including vehicle signals, ego poses, HD-map topology, and captions, to assign labels under a unified fine-grained action taxonomy. We further standardize temporal action boundaries across datasets and validate the resulting labels through kinematic consistency checks and targeted human review. The resulting benchmark contains 86.6K segments spanning 190.8 h across 26 countries and provides a long-tail-aware evaluation protocol. We also introduce DenseEgo, a video-based baseline that combines spatially aware representations with dense per-step action supervision. On the EgoManeuver, DenseEgo achieves 82.7 lateral and 83.5 longitudinal mAP, outperforming the strongest existing video model by 1.5 and 5.0 points, respectively. Finally, we demonstrate one way to integrate DenseEgo with a language-model agent for retrieving driving videos that match user-specified actions and scenarios. All code, datasets, and model weights will be publicly released.

title: Recall4D: Forgetting, Not Misalignment, Limits Long-Horizon Feed-Forward 4D Reconstruction
abstract: Feed-forward 4D trackers recover camera motion, depth, and point trajectories from short video clips, but chaining windows over long videos degrades their accuracy. We find that replacing inter-window alignment with ground-truth transforms leaves tracking error essentially unchanged. Static-point error instead grows with time since last observation: repeatedly predicting a static point from windows that no longer observe it corrupts previously recovered geometry. We call this failure forgetting. Merely retaining the last observed positions of unseen points reduces error by 26% on PointOdyssey without modifying the tracker. We introduce Recall4D, a training-free framework that augments a frozen tracker with a persistent world state and sparse motion anchors. Static points retain their world-space positions outside the camera view and are refined by averaging observations decoded at sparse keyframes while in view. For dynamic objects, the tracker decodes sparse representative anchors, while geometric skinning propagates their displacements to dense queries. Across two long-horizon benchmarks, Recall4D improves the accuracy of its backbone while running 7.6-9.0$\times$ faster, and its accuracy gains carry over to five further backbones and three other long-sequence tasks, demonstrating its generality.

title: Online Identification Can Replace a Floor-Plan Prior on Unseen Buildings
abstract: The Smart Buildings Challenge asks for one HVAC control policy that runs office buildings and weather it has never seen, from the building's metadata and sensor streams alone. Our controller sees no data from the target building before it runs and is not tuned per building; its few global constants were set on development scenarios. Each zone has a first-order grey-box model that starts from coefficients computed from the floor plan and is updated online by recursive least squares, and a planner and a closed-form mapping turn the models into plant commands. On two sets of buildings and weather that we generated, a validation set and a stress set with real-year weather, it scores 0.145 and 0.159 times the starter kit's PID baseline, and 0.095 times on a holdout built after all versions were fixed and scored once. It improves on every building, also against our two implementations of ASHRAE Guideline 36: per set it scores 0.60 to 0.71 times a basic version and 0.83 to 0.96 times one partly tuned on the public leaderboard, which wins one of 54 scenarios; with a 5 °C frost target for empty zones on both, the margin over the tuned version shrinks to 1.4% on the stress set, where one of six buildings is 0.2% worse. In an ablation on a reduced-order model, removing both the floor-plan prior and online identification costs 28%, 20% and 42% on the validation, stress and holdout sets, far more than the two effects combined: either source of building-specific information recovers most of what is lost without both. On one office floor in a second simulator, BOPTEST, this does not carry over: with identification on, the two priors give similar results, but the floor-plan prior alone, with constants fitted on the competition's simulator, is the least stable arm. These simulation results motivate testing floor-plan-initialised adaptive control in buildings that have drawings but no operating data.

title: Time-resolved Polarimetry of the Type Ibn Supernova 2025kzr Suggests a Possible Ejecta-CSM Misalignment
abstract: Type Ibn supernovae (SNe) are rare interacting transients. The dense, helium-rich circumstellar material (CSM) surrounding these events provides insight into the final stages of massive-star evolution. The geometries of the ejecta and CSM provide complementary constraints on the explosion and pre-SN mass loss, yet their temporal evolution has remained largely unexplored by spectropolarimetry. Here we present the first spectropolarimetric time series spanning the interaction-to-ejecta transition of the Type Ibn SN\,2025kzr. Three epochs of Very Large Telescope observations, combined with two epochs of published $V$-band imaging polarimetry, span 5--34 days after explosion. Continuum polarization is low at the earliest epoch, then rises to $\sim$0.6\% by day\,11 as the SN ejecta sweep up the dense CSM. This rise, together with a rotating polarization position angle, indicates a significant change in the geometry of the emitting region. The polarization subsequently falls below our detection limit as the photosphere recedes into the ejecta. Radiation-hydrodynamic and Monte Carlo polarization models illustrate that this evolution can be reproduced by an oblate CSM and prolate ejecta, with the symmetry axis of the cold dense shell tilted relative to that of the CSM. Binary mass transfer can produce an equatorially enhanced CSM, although the polarization data alone cannot identify the progenitor's formation channel. Similar polarization signatures in other supernovae suggest that misaligned ejecta and CSM may be common, making time-resolved spectropolarimetry a powerful probe of the link between pre-explosion mass loss and explosion geometry.

title: Binary mass transfer fossil in the ancient GD-1 stellar stream
abstract: We report the discovery of J0930+2902, the first carbon-enhanced metal-poor star with s-process enrichment (CEMP-s) identified in the GD-1 stellar stream, which is widely believed to originate from the tidal disruption of an old, metal-poor globular cluster. Using high-resolution Subaru/HDS spectroscopy, we present a comprehensive chemical abundance analysis of this star. Stellar atmospheric parameters were re-derived using Gaia photometry and parallaxes, combined with an iterative non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) analysis of Fe lines. We determine abundances for 22 elements, including NLTE analyses of C, Na, Mg, Ca, Ti, Cr, Mn, Co, Sr, Y, Zr, Ba, and Eu. J0930+2902 exhibits pronounced enhancements of C, N, Na, and s-process elements, together with a low $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratio of 7.4, consistent with enrichment through binary mass transfer from a former asymptotic giant branch (AGB) companion. Large radial-velocity variations and a significant near-ultraviolet excess independently indicate the presence of a white dwarf companion, providing strong support for this scenario. Comparisons with FRUITY AGB nucleosynthesis models show that the residual neutron-capture abundance pattern is best reproduced by a low-mass AGB companion with an initial mass of approximately 3.0 $M_{\odot}$. Its enhancements of C, N, Na, and s-process elements make it chemically distinct from the other confirmed GD-1 members. These results identify J0930+2902 as a fossil record of binary mass transfer preserved in the ancient GD-1 stellar stream, demonstrating that binary interaction can leave long-lived chemical signatures in accreted stellar populations.

title: Cutting Bus Service Without Cutting Access: Persistent Homology of Service Deserts and Timetable Reductions
abstract: Japanese bus operators are withdrawing service for lack of drivers, and the choice of which trips to withdraw determines who keeps a bus. We measure service at each stop from vehicle GPS and smart-card records, without timetables, and use persistent homology of walking and walking-plus-waiting time to find enclosed service deserts: pockets surrounded by service but beyond walking distance from it. Around Tsukuba, 35 such pockets lie more than 800m from any station or hourly stop. The 17 that are fully ringed by walkable service hold 18,446 residents. We compare two 2020 timetable reductions by Kanto Railway with random reductions and a heuristic frontier of same-size, capacity-feasible alternatives. At two and four buses an hour, both reductions protected service better than random reductions. No alternative found by the sweep dominates the state-of-emergency timetable. The summer timetable is dominated: it withdrew hourly service from 5,253 residents around stops with almost no morning riders, whereas same-size alternatives kept it for all of them at equal waiting. Averages hide a tail: under the actual timetables, 5.9% and 3.9% of residents are at stops whose expected wait rises by 10 minutes or more, against 0.5% and 0.3% in the alternatives, and capping the increase at 10 minutes at every served stop is feasible at the operator's sizes. If half the removed hours become paid hours saved, the labor saving of both reductions and their main alternatives fall short of the fare revenue on the removed trips.

title: Towards three-dimensional dark matter mapping in the extended solar neighbourhood with Gaia Data Release 3 and deep learning
abstract: We investigate a method for inferring the local dark matter (DM) density in the solar neighbourhood using a deep learning framework that learns the mapping between stellar kinematics and the underlying DM density field from cosmological simulations. To this end, we construct a training set from 7 Milky Way-like galaxies in the FIRE-2 simulation suite. We use three-dimensional stellar kinematic components, consisting of the tangential velocities along the right ascension and declination directions ($v_{α*}$ and $v_δ$) derived from parallaxes and proper motions, together with radial velocity, as input features to predict the three-dimensional DM density field. Two distinct architectures, VNet (arXiv:1606.04797) and ViT-VNet (arXiv:2205.08534), are trained on identical datasets. Both models reproduce the large-scale DM density gradient, whereas small-scale fluctuations are systematically smoothed. Applying the trained models to Gaia DR3 data yields our best estimates of the local DM density: $0.80^{+0.10}_{-0.10}$ and $1.12^{+0.15}_{-0.13}$ GeV cm$^{-3}$ from VNet and ViT-VNet, respectively. The quoted uncertainties reflect the inference scatter across the training set. We further examine systematics from model dependence and the simulation-Gaia domain mismatch, providing an initial step towards a framework for reconstructing local DM maps from future multi-epoch astrometric measurements, including those expected from Gaia DR4.

title: DynaSeek: Large Language Model-Driven Hybrid Dynamic Model Discovery for Grid-Tied Inverters from Limited Measurements
abstract: Discovering the unknown governing equations of grid-tied inverters from limited measurements is essential for the stability analysis of modern inverter-dominated power systems. However, existing identification methods struggle to jointly resolve unmeasured internal control memory and saturation-induced mode transitions from accessible terminal waveforms. To address this challenge, this paper proposes DynaSeek, a large language model (LLM)-driven framework for discovering explicit hybrid differential-algebraic equations (DAEs) of current-limited inverters. The framework integrates physics-constrained symbolic skeleton synthesis with the joint numerical estimation of shared model parameters and record-specific latent initial states across multi-island experience archives. Furthermore, two complementary structural diagnostics evaluating cross-record state closure and cross-window consistency are established to detect structural deficiencies across distinct input histories and transient stages. Guided by diagnostic feedback, DynaSeek directs variable-dimensional latent-state expansion and current-limiting and anti-windup refinement to yield self-contained hybrid DAEs unifying unsaturated regulation, current limiting, and post-fault recovery. Controller-hardware-in-the-loop (CHIL) experiments and closed-loop system-level simulations demonstrate that DynaSeek reduces transient trajectory reconstruction errors by one to two orders of magnitude compared with symbolic and neural baselines while accurately preserving reference critical clearing times, enabling reliable large-signal stability assessment of inverters with inaccessible internal controls.

title: Introducing Parton-Level Fluctuations in the TRENTo-Sea Model
abstract: A variety of experimental and theoretical data suggest that initial condition models for heavy-ion collisions contain a degree of sub-nucleonic fluctuations. While current models fit the number and size of these fluctuations to data, we use nuclear parton distribution functions to constrain sub-nucleonic structure and fluctuations in TRENTo-Sea, an extension of TRENTo. Sampling the momentum fraction distributions of quarks and gluons in heavy ions, we use perturbative quantum chromodynamics to collide nuclei at the parton level, and we introduce an infrared center-of-momentum damping scale which is tuned to proton-proton cross sections. We find that our model successfully reproduces the $\varepsilon_2\{2\}$ of data-calibrated models except in central collisions, and an analysis of the power spectrum and granularity of the pre-equilibrium fireball shows that the number of low-$x$ partons in a nucleon has a significant effect on the local transverse geometry. Our model is largely insensitive to variations of the infrared parameters, as such changes are absorbed into the calibration of the infrared regulator. We expect that this work will aid future research on soft-hard correlations and constraining different nPDF sets.

title: Graded Monoidal Categories and Internalization
abstract: In stable homotopy theory, there are a variety of ways to construct a point-set level smash product of spectra, each with its own advantages and limitations. These constructions often involve internalizing some graded external product. In this paper, we aim to formalize this process through a general categorical framework, providing a common language for these constructions. We propose a general theory for internalizing a graded monoidal product, investigate its 2-categorical properties, and use this framework to recover both Day convolution and the smash product of $S$-modules.

title: SlicePlanner: Logic-Guided Agentic AI for Online QoS-Aware Network Slicing in Open RAN
abstract: Adaptive network slicing in Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) demands reconfiguration decisions that respond to live traffic conditions while remaining safe with respect to Service Level Agreement (SLA) constraints, a combination that purely data-driven controllers cannot reliably guarantee without continuous retraining. We present SlicePlanner, a logic-guided closed-loop framework that treats each RAN reconfiguration as a controlled hypothesis: proposed from live and historical KeyPerformance Indicator (KPI) evidence, filtered through explicit SLA constraints and mined RAN control rules, and committed only when post-action measurements confirm improvement. SlicePlanner comprises two cooperating agents: SliceSense, which monitors live KPIs, retrieves context-conditioned evidence, and ranks candidate RAN actions through a surrogate-guided admissibility filter; and SliceGuard, which validates post-action KPI responses, rolls back harmful configurations, and refreshes rules under distribution drift. Validated over the air using OpenAirInterface, FlexRIC, and commercial Sierra Wireless 5G devices, SlicePlanner reduces SLA latency violations by up to 86% over static slicing and 50% over Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based slicing, while maintaining comparable cell throughput and auditable decisions without online retraining.

title: Amatlas: A 2D Array Architecture for Union-Find Decoding Without Global Coordination
abstract: Real-time decoding of the surface code is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and scaling the decoder to large code distances in hardware remains a challenge. The locality of Union-Find (UF) decoding makes it a leading candidate for such a decoder in distributed hardware. Prior distributed UF decoders, however, map the three-dimensional decoding graph onto an array of processing elements (PEs) under a central controller that synchronizes all PEs at every stage, and a three-dimensional array of PEs scales poorly on planar hardware. This paper presents Amatlas, a two-dimensional PE array for UF decoding that operates without a central controller. Amatlas assigns one PE to each stabilizer on the two-dimensional qubit lattice and stores the states of all measurement rounds in the local memory of the PE, so every link connects adjacent PEs in the array. Every PE advances on every clock cycle without array-wide synchronization, and the clock is the only global signal of the array. Under circuit-level noise, the RTL implementation of Amatlas fits a VCU129 FPGA up to a code distance of 25, where the average decoding time is 462 ns per round at a physical error rate of 0.1%. Amatlas achieves a threshold of 0.72%, compared with 0.78% reported for UF decoding under the same noise model.

title: Bounding the security of the FALCON signature scheme in the quantum random oracle model
abstract: In 2016, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) announced their invitation for proposals of public key encryption and signature schemes that are resistant to attacks by quantum computers. Since then, several rounds of proposals and revisions have occurred resulting in the 2022 announcement that three signature schemes - CRYSTALS-Dilithium, FALCON, and SPHINCS+ - would be standardized. However, in 2024, work by Fouque et al. noted an oversight in the published security for FALCON, which they were only able to remedy in a classical computing setting, namely the random oracle model (ROM). In this paper, we provide the first complete security proof for FALCON in the quantum random oracle model (QROM). Specifically, we will prove a reduction to the security of FALCON from the ring inhomogeneous short integer solution (RISIS) problem and the NTRU learning problem utilizing known quantum reprogramming results. We then provide parameter sets which meet the security levels required by NIST under our reduction.

title: Symmetric identities and determinants for matrices composed of Legendre symbols
