To the best of the authors' knowledge, regular LF-spaces in particular provide the first natural example of a category that has all kernels but is not preabelian and whose maximal deflation-exact structure is neither two-sided exact nor equal to the class of all kernel-cokernel pairs.

title: Feed-Forward Adaptive Gaussian Splatting for Interactive Medical Volume Rendering
abstract: Path-traced rendering shows CT and MR volumes with realistic lighting, but it restarts after every change of view, clipping plane or transfer function (TF), the map from voxel intensity to colour and opacity, which limits the frame rate. Feed-forward Gaussian splatting models such as RenderFM predict the Gaussians directly from the volume instead of fitting them to each scan, and are fast. RenderFM, however, handles only CT, runs its network again after every TF edit, has no clipping operator, and places its Gaussians on a uniform 3-mm grid that blurs organ boundaries and cut faces. We present RenderFM-Next, a feed-forward model that addresses these limits. One network handles both CT and MR. Its Gaussians are predicted once per volume: a new TF needs no pass of this network, and a clipping plane cuts them exactly, using operators from prior work. The model predicts coarse 3-mm Gaussians for the whole volume and refines them to 1.5 mm only where refinement improves the image. A small score head ranks the coarse Gaussians by how much refining them would reduce the rendering error; at render time the user chooses how many are refined, and those next to a clipping plane are always refined, which sharpens cut faces. We build a benchmark of about 2,000 CT and MR scans with path-traced references under clinical presets, TF edits and clipping. Our RenderFM-Next improves over RenderFM retrained on this benchmark by 2.8 dB on CT and 2.4 dB on MR and renders a 1600x1600 view in 4-6 ms. Refinement adds 0.30 / 0.69 dB over the same model trained without it (0.51 / 1.17 dB on cut faces), and refining a learned 10% of the coarse Gaussians matches a random 50% with 2.4x fewer Gaussians. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/renderfmnext/

title: Backpropagation as Dirac-bracket dynamics of dissipative training
abstract: Gradient-based training of a parametric model is the motion of a damped particle in the potential set by the loss. Using the Bateman-Galley doubling of the degrees of freedom, which gives dissipative systems an action principle, we write gradient flow, the heavy-ball method and Nesterov's accelerated gradient method as Hamiltonian systems. We show that, within this Hamiltonian description, backpropagation is Dirac evolution. The activations of a feed-forward network are treated as coordinates of phase space, and the layer equations as constraints. These constraints are second class for every architecture, and Hamilton's equations with the resulting Dirac bracket reproduce training with the exact gradient of the loss, although the Hamiltonian contains only the cost of the network output. The Dirac bracket of an activation with the momenta of the parameters is its Jacobian, the inverse of the constraint matrix contains both the forward and the reverse modes of automatic differentiation, and the errors propagated by backpropagation are the Lagrange multipliers of the layer constraints: the constraint forces of a kinematic chain under the load of the cost. These results hold in the full doubled phase space, not only in the physical limit. The network's part of the constraint algebra is the same for every optimizer, Nesterov's look-ahead adds one layer of momentum-dependent constraints that couple the two copies of the doubled system, and gradient flow is obtained by constructing the Dirac bracket in stages. We confirm these statements numerically to machine precision and train a network by integrating the Dirac flow of its constraints, with no backward pass in the computation.

title: ProManO: Beyond Sim(3) for Metric Upgrade of Feed-Forward Geometry with Visual-Inertial Anchors
abstract: Upgrading feed-forward geometry to metric scale with visual-inertial odometry (VIO) raises the question of which correction should align dense feed-forward prediction with sparse metric VIO anchors. Existing methods use either a similarity transformation, which cannot represent depth-dependent distortion, or a projective transformation, which alters pre-calibrated intrinsics. We prove that the transformations compatible with pre-calibrated intrinsics form a ten-dimensional manifold. Beyond Sim(3), this manifold contains three degrees of freedom (DoF) that locate the plane at infinity and leave residuals growing quadratically with depth range after any similarity alignment. These DoF are invisible in the image and can be resolved only by metric depth along viewing rays or by multi-view constraints. To estimate them, we propose ProManO, a probabilistic manifold optimization framework in which every anchor is weighted by its along-ray uncertainty and inlier probability within a single expectation-maximization (EM) procedure. ProManO certifies the similarity synchronization and refines the plane at infinity only where it is observable, which guarantees an objective value no worse than that of the optimal similarity alignment. Experiments on EuRoC, CID-SIMS, Oxford Spires, and KITTI-360 demonstrate that ProManO achieves the highest mean F1 and outperforms Sim(3) alignment on all four datasets. The project page is available at https://h0xg.github.io/ProManO/.

title: High-Throughput GPU Decoding of Quantum Bivariate Bicycle Codes under Circuit-Level Noise
abstract: Bivariate bicycle (BB) codes reduce the physical-qubit overhead of quantum error correction compared to other codes such as Surface codes, but circuit-level faults create dependencies across measurement rounds that limit decoding throughput. We present a parallel-window GPU decoder that combines reusable fault patterns, compact shared-memory state, and persistent GPU workers using min-sum with Relay-BP recovery. On an RTX 5090, the proposed decoder keeps pace with one syndrome round every 1 $μ$s across all four evaluated codes, up to [[144,12,12]] with 63-144 $μ$s median commit delays. This rate has not been demonstrated in prior circuit-level GPU decoding studies and it provides $120\times$ higher decoding throughput than sequential sliding-window decoding. Checking neighboring detector rounds before accepting a decoding result reduces failure rates by up to 65%. For [[144,12,12]] at $p=0.002$, our proposed decoder achieves $7.58\times 10^{-6}$ failures per round, 36% lower than the published belief propagation (BP) with syndrome flipping (BP-SF) result.

title: Seebeck and Hall effects in charge-neutral ballistic graphene as probes of electron-electron interactions
abstract: Electron-hole asymmetry of the Coulomb velocity renormalization is responsible for finite Seebeck and Hall coefficients in charge-neutral graphene. In the ballistic regime the thermopower is small, $0.1$--$1~μ$V/K, because the chemical-potential shift required by $n_e{=}n_h$ cancels its leading part. When the electron-electron scattering length falls below the sample length, the thermopower crosses over to a collision-dominated value of $4$--$10~μ$V/K, that is an order of magnitude larger. This crossover is a direct thermoelectric marker of the breakdown of ballistic transport and a baseline for identifying the Dirac fluid.

title: Fast Fluid Antenna Multiple Access: Exact Analysis and Fixed-Aperture Asymptotics
abstract: In this paper, we investigate the interference-limited outage performance of fast fluid antenna multiple access (FAMA), in which the receive port is selected according to the instantaneous symbol-based signal-to-interference energy ratio. For any positive-definite spatial covariance matrix and an arbitrary finite number of candidate ports, we show that constant-modulus multiuser interference admits an exact reduction to the comparison of two independent correlated exponential random vectors. This representation leads to a nonnegative double multi-index series for the outage probability, a recursive coefficient evaluation, and a certified truncation-error bound. We then study the distinct asymptotic regime where the number of candidate ports goes to infinity while the physical aperture remains unchanged, assuming exponential spatial correlation. For this model, we derive an explicit finite-port series requiring no numerical integration, and characterize continuous port selection through a convergent one-dimensional series for arbitrary thresholds. The analysis further yields an exact expression relating the maximum supportable number of users to the antenna aperture size and target outage probability. Numerical results validate the finite-port and asymptotic analyses, and illustrate that given sufficient aperture size, a user utilizing fast FAMA can overcome a massive number of interferers for decent communication performance.

title: Mode-resolved spin-wave spectroscopy by a single paramagnetic center
abstract: We demonstrate mode-resolved ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) spectroscopy using optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) of a single nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in (111)-oriented diamond. A two-tone drive couples the magnetization dynamics to the NV spin resonance via the magnon Kerr effect. We show that the NV can detect the static stray field produced by this effect down to precession cone angles $θ\approx \SI{1}{\degree}$, providing a generic scheme to measure the linear FMR spectrum with the spatial resolution of an atomic-size probe. We validate the approach on a normally magnetized yttrium iron garnet (YIG) microdisk, resolving its intrinsic quantized spin-wave modes. Scanning the probe across the surface, we map the spatial profile of the modes and find quantitative agreement with analytical models.

title: SkySearcher: High-Altitude Onboard VLM Reasoning for Aerial Semantic Search
abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have improved semantic and visual reasoning, enabling UAVs to search for open-vocabulary queries in unstructured environments at high altitude. However, existing systems mainly follow low-altitude strategies, focusing on close-range iterative exploration, requiring storage-intensive dense 3D metric-semantic reconstructions or relying on large cloud-serviced VLMs assuming constant internet access. We propose SkySearcher, an aerial semantic search navigation method designed for large outdoor scenes. SkySearcher integrates onboard VLM reasoning with a lightweight probabilistic representation that guides an information-driven exploration. The VLM extracts semantic information at high altitude about the target or cues informing about its location. This information is projected to the ground using the camera frustum instead of limited-depth sensors, actively exploiting the expansive field of view offered by elevated sensing. The information regarding the presence or absence of semantic cues is then integrated into a probabilistic map by modeling the spatial belief of the query, maintaining a task-driven memory for the mission and guiding the exploration towards semantically promising regions. Extensive simulations for Aerial Object Goal Navigation on public benchmarks demonstrate that SkySearcher significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in success rate, flight time, and navigation precision, while a deployment of SkySercher running fully onboard a drone demonstrates the applicability of our approach.

title: Resource theory of pi-ordered imaginarity and its resource quantifiers
abstract: Conventional resource theory of quantum imaginarity takes real density matrices as free states without ordering constraints on their diagonal populations. Motivated by the role of population ordering in the incoherent ergotropy of quantum batteries and the recently proposed framework of $π$-ordered coherence, we develop the resource theory of $π$-ordered imaginarity. In this refined framework, free states are required to be real in the reference basis and to obey a prescribed permutation order $π$ for their diagonal populations. This theory thereby identifies two independent quantum resources: complex phases and population misordering, where the latter is inaccessible within the standard imaginarity resource theory. We characterize the structure of free states using majorization and the Schur-Horn theorem, define admissible $π$-ordered real operations, and examine their intersection with $π$-ordered incoherent operations. We further construct resource quantifiers for the $π$-ordered imaginarity based on relative entropy, fidelity and robustness, and derive inequalities relating the robustness of $π$-ordered imaginarity and that of $π$-ordered coherence. The present framework generalizes the standard resource theory of imaginarity to incorporate population ordering and is naturally suited for thermodynamic settings such as quantum batteries.

title: Superconformal Index Identities for Dual Gauge Theories
abstract: We study superconformal index identities for three classes of dual four-dimensional gauge theories. For $\mathcal N=4$ super-Yang--Mills theory with gauge groups $SO(2n+1)$ and $USp(2n)$, we prove at every rank the equality of flavored Schur indices predicted by $S$-duality, using Rains's diagonal trace transformation. For Kutasov--Schwimmer duality with adjoint superpotential $\textrm{Tr} X^{k+1}$, we prove the index identity between $SU(k+1)$ and $SU(k-1)$ with two flavors at independent elliptic nomes $p,q$, in the ultraviolet assignment $R(Q)=0$. On the locus $p=q^k$, we reduce the identity to that of ordinary supersymmetric QCD whenever the specialized expressions are generically regular. Finally, we test the dualities conjectured by Cho and Song between quiver and single-group descriptions of four families of Argyres--Douglas theories. For the rank-one $H_1$ theory we prove equality of the two full flavored indices, and for each family at arbitrary rank we evaluate the generalized Coulomb index in both descriptions, obtaining the product formula conjectured by Buican and Jiang.

title: Computing Feasible EF1 Allocations under Generalized Assignment Constraints
abstract: We study the fair allocation of indivisible goods under generalized assignment constraints, where each agent's bundle must fit within her budget, the sizes of goods may differ across agents, and unallocated goods go to a charity. A natural fairness notion here is feasible envy-freeness up to one good (FEF1), which requires an agent's envy towards any feasible subset of another bundle to disappear after some good is removed from this subset. While FEF1 allocations always exist, they could previously be computed efficiently only when sizes are common to all agents. We show that FEF1 allocations can be computed in strongly polynomial time, and more generally whenever each agent's value can be almost exactly maximized over her feasible bundles, a requirement that cannot be relaxed substantially. Our analysis relies on an essentially tight quadratic bound on how often each agent's bundle is repaired. Moreover, the allocation can be made approximately envy-free up to any good while retaining nearly half the Nash welfare of any given allocation. In contrast, requiring a single good to eliminate an agent's envy towards all feasible subsets of another bundle at once, which makes no difference without constraints, renders the problem NP-hard and may halve the attainable Nash welfare.

title: Who Is Ego? Scaling Cross-View Camera Wearer Identification and Segmentation beyond Humans
abstract: A first-person (ego) image reveals what a camera sees, but not who or what carries it. Given a synchronized third-person (exo) image, camera wearer identification asks who is ego: which candidate carries the ego camera? We extend this task beyond humans to robots, vehicles, animals, and drones, and broaden its spatial scope (where is ego) from selecting a provided candidate mask to wearer segmentation with absence prediction and mutual camera localization across ego-exo views. We introduce FindEgo-1M, comprising 1.16M real and simulated ego-exo pairs across 12 wearer types, 17 domains, and 111 test settings. Our approach exploits a geometric relation: the ego camera's projection into the exo image, i.e., the epipole, lies on or near its wearer. We introduce EgoRay-ZS, the first method to turn a frozen feed-forward 3D reconstruction model, VGGT-$Ω$, into a training-free solution for wearer identification and segmentation. Its geometric readout ranks candidate masks or segmentation proposals by angular offset and distance to the ego camera, while the relative pose provides mutual camera directions. We then develop the full EgoRay model through pose-supervised training on FindEgo-1M and label-free test-time adaptation constrained by candidate masks. Without task-specific training, EgoRay-ZS achieves 78.0% identification accuracy on TF2023's original labels, versus 52.9% reported for the dataset-trained PEN. On FindEgo-1M, EgoRay achieves state-of-the-art chance-corrected accuracy of 87.1 and 77.7 on seen and unseen settings. On matched queries, EgoRay also outperforms GPT-6 Astra by 31.6 and 21.3 points on seen and unseen settings, respectively, while running $18\times$ faster. Data, code, and models will be released.

title: An Exact Branch-Price-and-Cut Algorithm for the Vehicle Routing Problem with Floating Targets
abstract: The Vehicle Routing Problem with Floating Targets (VRPFT) is a generalization of the capacitated vehicle routing problem where targets may actively move to locations ''convenient'' for the vehicles. In particular, each target may leave its home location at a bounded speed. A solution to the VRPFT is a sequence of targets for each vehicle to visit and a meeting point in space-time for each target. In this paper, we solve the VRPFT exactly with a branch-price-and-cut algorithm. Our key contribution is a dominance criterion for the pricing labeling algorithm that utilizes closed-form lower and upper bounds on a vehicle's trajectory cost given a fixed sequence of targets. We prove that the criterion preserves optimality, and the algorithm has smaller computation time than the exact dynamic program of prior work on identical hardware. We also provide a relaxed criterion that prunes more aggressively; the resulting heuristic is faster than our exact algorithm and matched every certified optimum on the benchmark.

title: Where Does the Asymmetry Enter? Staging a Fairness Audit Across a Fused Multimodal Moderation Pipeline
abstract: Almost every short-video upload now passes through a classifier that fuses video, speech, and on-screen text into one decision about whether it may be seen. It moderates every language community on the platform at once, and fairness across them is judged, if at all, from one accuracy score. That score is compatible with error falling almost entirely on one language group. An audit that goes looking reads the model's decisions, the last stage of a long pipeline and the one whose test has the fewest items. We ask where in a fused pipeline a subgroup asymmetry can be detected at all: in what the classifier may read, in what its branches encode, or in what it decides. We answer this with a post-hoc audit of a published TikTok classifier, holding all three stages to one significance standard using only its logged decisions, labels, and pre-fusion features, with source language as the subgroup axis. The asymmetry is significant at the stage deciding what the model may read, and again in what the text branch encodes. At the earlier stage, a language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English one, for reasons of segmentation, not verbosity. The asymmetry is undetectable at the decision, where the smallest subgroup leaves twelve items to test. An audit reading only decisions looks where its evidence is thinnest; the same test staged upstream recovers a disparity the decision-level view returns as noise.

title: FlyingStart: Learned Cross-Token Warm Starts for Fixed-Point Decoding in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
abstract: Recurrent-depth language models generate each token by iterating a shared block of layers until its hidden state converges. Inference methods for these models decide when to stop the iteration, yet every token still starts from random noise and pays the full cost of converging. We show that where the iteration starts is a second, independent lever. A token's fixed point is predictable from the state at which the previous token stopped, after a learned change of coordinates, and we introduce FlyingStart, a linear warm start that is fitted in closed form on the frozen model and costs under 5% of one loop. The iteration and its stopping rule are unchanged, so the exit criterion certifies the same distance to the fixed point from any start: a better start removes loops at unchanged accuracy. On Huginn-0125, FlyingStart matches the accuracy of the strongest training-free baseline with 14--19% fewer decoding layers, raises batched throughput by 16--18% in two serving engines, and adds a further 10--14% on top of self-speculative decoding. A contraction analysis predicts the number of loops saved on all four models we study, including one where the prediction was recorded before any evaluation, and token by token on Huginn, and it identifies when a warm start pays off: the saving grows with the number of loops a model needs to converge.

title: Auditing Identity and Timing Signals in Operational Logs
abstract: Models that predict events from operational logs, such as sepsis in ICU records or failures in hard drives, can score well by recognizing which patient or drive a record came from, or when it was recorded, instead of predicting the event. I introduce two simple audits that measure how much of this information a dataset carries before any event-prediction model is trained, and apply them to seven public datasets in six domains. One asks whether a classifier can tell that two records came from the same unit; the other asks which of two records from the same unit came later. Under the stated nulls, both have expected AUC 0.5. In ICU data, the identity audit flags a common preprocessing step: carrying the last measurement forward raises identity AUC from 0.916 to 0.993. On a 12-hour sepsis forecasting task, carrying forward makes a model look 0.163 AUC better than raw values when a patient's hours are split between training and test, but only 0.046 better when patients are held out. The exaggeration under patient overlap also appears in a second ICU dataset with mortality as the outcome. On the sepsis task, a chronological control with complete follow-up, in which training sees only a patient's earlier, resolved hours, shows no positive mean overlap gap. Timing is a strong predictor: with complete follow-up, hour of stay and measurement counts alone, with no clinical value, score 0.761 on held-out patients, and adding the raw clinical values changes that by +0.018. Outside the ICU, 95% of drives and 75% of loans have records on both sides of a calendar cut, and the overlap gap persists under a calendar split. The audits show which features and preprocessing choices to check; the evaluation protocol decides the consequences. I release the code, a library that runs the audits on any table with a unit column and a time column, and a guide to using the audits.

title: The Monge Optimal Transport Barycenter Problem with Adaptive Features
abstract: The data-driven Monge optimal transport barycenter problem seeks a map $y=T(x,z)$ that minimally perturbs an outcome $x$ while removing its statistical dependence on covariates $z$. Numerical implementations approximate the independence constraint through finite-dimensional test-function spaces, making the effectiveness of dependence removal sensitive to the choice of features. This article develops a procedure whereby the features themselves are optimized throughout the procedure. In particular, we adopt a feature space for $f$ consisting of Gaussian radial basis functions (RBFs) with adaptive individual centers and bandwidths. Synthetic experiments show that while fixed nonlinear RBF features can capture dependence structures that are poorly represented by linear features, adapting the RBF centers and bandwidths can further improve dependence removal within a limited feature space and achieve residual dependence comparable to that obtained with a larger fixed basis. We further extend the formulation to multidimensional covariates and evaluate its applicability to real-world problems, including removing age-related dependence in biomedical measurements and dependence on temperature and humidity in bike-sharing demand.

title: Efficient Data Fusion in Distributionally Robust Optimization
abstract: Decisions under uncertainty increasingly rest on fragmented evidence, such as samples from related but different populations, privacy-protected summary statistics, or complementary statistical descriptions of the same data. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) can fuse such evidence by constructing one ambiguity set per source and hedging against all distributions in the intersection of these sets. This fusion approach is less conservative than aggregating the sources into a single ambiguity set, but it is computationally demanding. Exact reformulations grow exponentially with the number of sources, and even deciding whether the intersection is nonempty is NP-hard. We show that fusion DRO admits an exact reformulation in which the ambiguity sets are coupled only through functional Lagrange multipliers. Restricting these multipliers to affine decision rules yields upper bounds that decompose across the ambiguity sets, are exact for quadratic losses over Wasserstein balls around Gaussian references, and provably dominate aggregation-based relaxations such as Minkowski sums and balls around mixtures. The approximations admit finite conic reformulations in important special cases and subgradient methods for weakly convex losses, which makes fusion DRO applicable to neural network training. In portfolio, newsvendor, and binary classification experiments, the affine approximation stays close to the exact value wherever the latter is computable, scales far better than exact methods, and outperforms aggregation-based benchmarks out-of-sample.

title: A search and multi-frequency study of curved parsec-scale jets in active galaxies
abstract: Very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations show that a fraction of active galactic nucleus (AGN) jets exhibit pronounced apparent bending on parsec scales, potentially strongly enhanced by projection effects. While individual sources have been studied in detail, the statistical properties of curved jets and the physical mechanisms responsible for their morphology remain poorly constrained. We aim to select a statistically robust sample of AGNs with significantly curved parsec-scale jets and to constrain the physical mechanisms responsible for jet bending. We analyse 123 456 VLBI images of 17 478 AGNs collected by the public Astrogeo database. After filtering for extended structure, we extract and stack multi-epoch, multi-frequency (1.2--86 GHz) ridge lines. We fit linear and logarithmic helices representing jet precession and resonant Kelvin--Helmholtz instability mode. We combine model-fits and Monte Carlo simulations to further constrain these physical models. We robustly identify 586 AGNs (7.4% of sources with resolved jets) with curved parsec-scale jets. Compared to straight jets, curved ones are less common at low redshifts, possibly due to the sample-related selection effects. In the precession scenario, the inferred periods span $P \sim$10--10 000 yr, with a logarithmic mean of $\sim 220$ yr. Solid-body disc precession in supermassive black hole binaries is broadly consistent with these periods, whereas geodetic precession requires extremely tight, near-equal-mass systems. Lense--Thirring precession remains viable for both thin and thick discs. Kelvin--Helmholtz instability also provides a potential explanation. However, identifying the preferred model for each individual source requires further investigation, including temporal analysis and jet kinematics.

title: The inductive Galois-McKay conjecture for groups of Lie type C
abstract: We prove the inductive Galois-McKay conjecture for the symplectic groups. A key result is the determination of the character fields of the irreducible characters of the extensions of the symplectic group by field automorphisms. Two main ingredients for this are the theory of Brauer trees and the generalized Gelfand-Graev characters.

title: On dual varieties of smooth projective varieties
abstract: For a smooth irreducible nondegenerate complex projective variety $X\subsetneq\mathbb P^N$, we prove that its projective dual $X^\vee$ is a hypersurface whenever $\operatorname{dim} X\ge3\operatorname{codim}X-2$. This result may be regarded as further evidence for Hartshorne's complete intersection conjecture. We also prove the duality defect conjecture of Landman in codimension at most five. Finally, we complete Ein's classification of smooth nondegenerate complex projective varieties with smooth projective dual. The list consists of smooth quadrics, the Segre varieties $\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^m$ with $m\ge2$, the Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}(2,5)$, and the spinor tenfold in $\mathbb P^{15}$.

title: StePPO: Adaptive Step-Size Control for Initial-Value Problems Using Proximal Policy Optimisation
abstract: ODE solvers are used to model, simulate, and analyse continuous-time systems found in many signal processing applications. Time integration of these initial-value problems is traditionally performed using adaptive embedded Runge--Kutta methods. For proper time-step selection, adaptive solvers accept or reject each candidate step according to a local error estimate. Their efficiency is therefore controlled by the rule that selects the next step size. Classical proportional--integral--derivative (PID) controllers are computationally inexpensive per decision and reliable, but their reactive design can lead to costly numerical solves near stiff transitions. We formulate step-size selection for parametrised IVPs as a Markov decision process and train a continuous-action policy using proximal policy optimisation. The policy processes its observation signals using a deep network while maintaining the embedded solver logic. We evaluate on a decay function, the Van der Pol system, and the Brusselator system at matched tolerances, and compare against a standard PID controller and a multi-scale DeepONet network. We find that the proposed learned policy remains within prescribed error tolerances while reducing the required number of solve steps by up to 60%, achieving a wall-clock time reduction of 58%, for both in- and out-of-distribution settings.

title: LetzElPhC: an electron-phonon code for efficient exciton-phonon workflows
abstract: We present \texttt{LetzElPhC}, an open-source software package that computes electron-phonon matrix elements from the output of density functional perturbation theory calculations performed with the \texttt{Quantum ESPRESSO} code. By interfacing directly with the \texttt{Yambo} code and exploiting crystal symmetries, \texttt{LetzElPhC} enables a scalable workflow for evaluating exciton-phonon matrix elements while enforcing strict gauge consistency between one-electron Bloch states and Bethe-Salpeter excitonic wave functions across the full Brillouin zone. This symmetry-preserving approach avoids phase ambiguities and significantly reduces both computational costs and memory requirements. To support large-scale simulations on dense momentum grids, the package incorporates Fourier interpolation of dynamical matrices and perturbed Kohn-Sham potentials, accounting for long-range dipole and quadrupole interactions in both two- and three-dimensional materials, combined with multi-level parallelization and efficient parallel I/O. Together, these capabilities seamlessly complement the \texttt{Yambo} code to enable first-principles simulations of phonon-assisted optical spectroscopies, which we demonstrate through applications to resonant Raman scattering in monolayer $\text{WSe}_2$ and phonon-assisted luminescence in cubic AgBr.

title: New Insights into the Parameterized Complexity of Cutwidth
abstract: The Cutwidth problem asks for a linear ordering of the vertices that minimizes the maximum number of edges crossing between two consecutive positions. The problem is proven to be NP-hard by Gavril [CISS '77], which motivated research in parameterized complexity. A previously claimed FPT result for Cutwidth and Imbalance parameterized by twin cover by Gorzny and Buss [COCOON '19] was later invalidated. Misra and Mittal [Theor. Comput. Sci. '21] clarified this issue, proved that Imbalance is in XP parameterized by twin cover and in FPT parameterized by $ω$-bounded twin cover, i.e., where the size of the cliques outside the twin cover are bounded by $ω$. The analogous questions remained open for cutwidth. In this work, we answer one of them by showing that Cutwidth is FPT parameterized by $ω$-bounded twin cover. Additionally, we present an XP algorithm for Cutwidth parameterized by vertex integrity and prove W[1]-hardness for the parameter treedepth.

title: Recent Developments in Colibri: A Neural-Network PDF Model and Improved Bayesian Sampling
abstract: We present recent developments in Colibri, an open-source framework for flexible fits of parton distribution functions (PDFs). Colibri allows the implementation of any PDF functional form as well as Bayesian, Monte Carlo, and Hessian inference methods, making it particularly well suited for systematic comparisons of model architectures and uncertainty propagation treatments. In these proceedings, we report on two key updates to the framework: the release of colibri-n3fit, an open-source implementation of the neural-network model used by the NNPDF collaboration, and the integration of an upgraded, highly efficient Bayesian sampler, bridging the gap between the computational cost of Bayesian PDF fitting and other uncertainty propagation treatments. Combined, these updates extend Colibri's capabilities to neural-network PDF fits, enabling direct, quantitative Bayesian analyses of the n3fit architecture and opening new avenues for comparative studies.

title: Nuclear Modification of $π^0$ Production in pO and OO Collisions with ALICE
abstract: Energy loss of high-momentum partons is one of the key signatures of the quark--gluon plasma formed in heavy-ion collisions. Through measurements of the nuclear modification factor, $R_{\rm AA}$, where a strong suppression of high-$p_{\rm T}$ particle yields is observed, parton energy loss has been confirmed in Pb--Pb collisions at the LHC. However, in small collision systems, like pp and p--Pb, energy loss has not yet been confirmed. In this contribution, a measurement of the $π^0$ $R_{\rm AA}$ in OO and pO collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.36$ TeV and $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 9.62$ TeV, respectively, is presented. These results are based on the measured $π^0$ $p_{\rm T}$ spectra in OO, pO, and pp collisions using the ALICE electromagnetic calorimeter. The measurement of the $R_{\rm pO}$ allows for precise constraints on cold-nuclear matter effects. In combination with the $R_{\rm OO}$, this allows for a separation of cold and hot nuclear matter contributions and enables a quantitative determination of partonic energy loss in OO collisions. The measurements are compared to theoretical model calculations that include both cold and hot nuclear matter effects.

title: Majorana Neutrino Exchange in Free-Baryon $B_1B_2\to ppe^-e^-$ Reactions
abstract: The free-baryon reactions $B_1B_2\to pp e^-e^-$ are studied for six nonstrange and strange initial states, with light- and heavy-Majorana-neutrino exchange treated in the same baryon-level framework. For light-neutrino exchange, the cross sections scale with the square of the effective Majorana mass $m_{ββ}$. The calculated cross sections increase as the off-shell cutoff $Δq^2$ is reduced, especially near threshold and in the hyperon channels, because more of the phase-space region where the squared four-momentum of the exchanged neutrino is close to zero is retained. At $\sqrt{s}=5.1~\mathrm{GeV}$, the six light-neutrino cross sections span $9.28\times10^{-49}$--$1.78\times10^{-45}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-2}$ for $m_{ββ}=30~\mathrm{meV}$ and $Δq^2=10^{-2}~\mathrm{GeV}^2$. For heavy-neutrino exchange, the cross sections scale with $η_N^2$, where $η_N=|U_{eN}|^2/m_N$. The leading propagator correction remains below one percent for $m_N\gtrsim50~\mathrm{GeV}$ over the phase-space region considered. At $\sqrt{s}=5.1~\mathrm{GeV}$, the heavy-neutrino cross sections span $7.55\times10^{-45}$--$1.98\times10^{-41}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-2}$ for $η_N=4.0\times10^{-9}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$. At higher energies, the two exchange cases give the same CKM-driven channel ordering, with the $nn$ cross section largest. At fixed $\sqrt{s}$, compared with the light-neutrino spectra calculated with $Δq^2=10^{-2}~\mbox{GeV}^2$, the heavy-neutrino peaks occur at a smaller squared invariant mass for the proton pair and a larger one for the electron pair. These results extend the free-baryon analogue of neutrinoless double-beta decay to strange initial states and provide theoretical reference results for comparing light- and heavy-Majorana-neutrino exchange.

title: Know the Design, Pick the Attack: Sentence-Keyed Watermarks for LLMs
abstract: A watermark lets the provider of a language model recognise the text its model wrote, which matters more as generated text becomes hard to tell from human writing: provenance underpins academic integrity, the fight against misinformation and new regulation. Providers have started to watermark the text of their models, and to explain how their watermarks work. Explaining a watermark, however, also tells an attacker how to break it, and there are two ways to do so: reword the text to erase the mark, or learn the mark and copy it onto text the model never wrote. Each attack has been studied on its own. We study an attacker that reads the published design to choose between them: it erases the watermarks that are hard to learn and forges the ones that survive rewording. Against it, every existing watermark we compare fails. We propose KeyedLex, which reads its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and whose detector does not need to recover the key exactly. It outperforms every watermark we compare on both models we test, losing about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds, at no extra cost in text quality over the best-known watermarks.

title: Selecting $2 \times 2$ submatrices with optimally bounded inverses
abstract: For a matrix $U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$ ($n \ge k$) with orthonormal columns, the Goreinov--Tyrtyshnikov--Zamarashkin (GTZ) conjecture asserts that there exists a $k \times k$ submatrix $U_I$ with $\|U_I^{-1}\|_2 \le \sqrt{n}$. The conjecture remains open for $3 \le k \le n - 3$. The existence of such a submatrix in the case $k = 2$ was proved for $n=4$ by Nesterenko (2023) and recently for general $n$ by Sengupta and Pautov (2026). In this paper, we give a short, elementary, constructive proof of a weighted strengthening of this result, which yields a single-pass streaming algorithm that selects a row pair satisfying the $\sqrt{n}$ bound in $\mathcal O(n)$ operations and $\mathcal O(1)$ auxiliary memory. We further give an explicit matrix representation of all equality cases for $k = 2$ characterized by Nesterenko (2026) and use it to construct a single matrix family on which standard selection strategies (including global and local maximum-volume selection, Bischof--Stewart pivoted QR, column-pivoted QR, and LU with partial pivoting) simultaneously fail to attain the $\sqrt{n}$ bound.

title: AFM metrology for 3D high aspect ratio semiconductor structures
abstract: Transistors have long been the foundation of the semiconductor industry, with continuous architectural innovations enabling the scaling of integrated circuits while maintaining high performance. Advancements in deposition and lithographic techniques have further expanded design possibilities, while increasing structural complexity demands stricter process control. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) offers a rapid and reliable metrology solution, providing high-resolution measurements and robust statistical analysis of critical parameters. In this work, we present clearly resolved individual profiles of lines and spaces in high aspect ratio (HAR) gate all around FET (GAAFET)-type structures on both the nanosheet (NS) region and in the isolation region between the nanosheets and we present a comprehensive statistical evaluation of their critical dimensions.

title: Angular Interpolation in Sparse-View Low-Dose CT Reconstruction: Placement Effects and Data-Consistency Step-Size Scaling
abstract: Dual-domain networks combine projection and image processing for sparse-view low-dose computed tomography (CT). We quantify the contribution of angular interpolation before learning and distinguish its roles in sinogram initialisation and the image residual base. On synthetic parallel-beam data, parameter-free interpolation reduces noise-free missing-view mean absolute error by 99.7% relative to zero filling at 60 views. Full-view filtered back-projection (FBP) of the jointly learned completed sinogram adds 1.27 dB of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) over interpolated FBP. In a data-consistency dual-domain network (DC-DuNet), a 2x2 configuration ablation controls branch width, depth and training schedule while varying these placements and their associated input channels. After 20 epochs, the PSNR contrasts are +1.98 dB for sinogram initialisation and -2.16 dB for the interpolated image base; the image-base ranking also reverses during training. The sinogram-initialised variant exceeds an image-only U-Net by 0.96 dB at 60 views and 10% dose, and by 1.28 dB on independently generated synthetic data. The U-Net leads at higher view counts and with a shared interpolated image base. Without retraining, the variant retains a 0.12 dB advantage on held-out CHAOS abdominal CT under simulated degradation; the image-base contrast rounds to zero. The implemented projection/backprojection pair has empirical dominant gain of approximately 0.85NK, where N is image-grid width and K acquired view count. These results distinguish interpolation placement from network architecture and support NK normalisation for step calibration.

title: Long-Horizon Planning with Latent World Models via Graph Anchors
abstract: Latent world models plan in a compact latent space by predicting the outcomes of actions. Their planners judge a plan by the latent distance between its predicted end state and the goal image. We show that this distance fails in two distinct ways. First, it loses directional signal a few steps from the goal, causing distant goals to fail. Second, it weighs the robot arm over the manipulated object, causing manipulation to fail at contact. We measure both failures directly on recorded data by asking whether a lower latent distance corresponds to true progress toward the goal. Across five environments, six visual representations (including raw pixels and V-JEPA 2), and nine Meta-World tasks, this ranking test cleanly separates the two failures, and the graph distance to a goal predicts where closed-loop planning breaks down. Both failures share a single remedy: replacing the distant goal with a nearby target that lies on a recorded trajectory. We realize this principle with Graph Anchors, a training-free planner for frozen latent world models. It builds a sparse graph once over the model's own training frames and aims each planning step at a node a few moves ahead along the shortest path to the goal, keeping paths on recorded transitions wherever contact matters. On goals up to 400 steps away, Graph Anchors raise LeWM's success from 13% to 85% on PointMaze-Medium, from 8% to 87% on PointMaze-Large, and from 5% to 71% on Push-T, where stronger search toward the goal fails and where prior training-free planners break down under missing step horizons, subsampling shortcuts, or fragmented contact.

title: A Monolithic Fully Eulerian Lattice Boltzmann Framework for Fluid--Structure Interaction with Neo-Hookean Elastic Solids
abstract: We present a fully Eulerian, monolithic lattice Boltzmann method for fluid--structure interaction with incompressible neo-Hookean solids at unequal densities, and use it to compute the Turek--Hron FSI2 and FSI3 benchmarks on a single Cartesian grid. A pressure-based kinetic scheme advances the mixture momentum, a polynomial MTHINC reconstruction transports the solid volume fraction with closed-form fluxes, and the left Cauchy--Green tensor gives the elastic stress; all updates are explicit and local. Because the density is transported independently of the populations, two corrections are introduced. A lattice-link correction makes uniform translation an exact discrete solution for any density ratio, which is verified to round-off up to $ρ_s/ρ_f=1000$. A pressure-mode correction, derived from an asymptotic analysis of the scheme, removes the frame-dependent defect that otherwise causes a secular drift of the solid mass. The verification separates the two sources of error: the scheme is second-order accurate towards the diffuse-interface solution at fixed interface thickness, and first-order towards the sharp-interface solution when the thickness scales with the grid, as predicted by an estimate of the interfacial truncation error. The method reproduces a deformable disk in Taylor--Green and lid-driven-cavity flows, and the FSI3 and FSI2 benchmarks at density ratios of one and ten.

title: SMOTE 25 Years of Magic: What Has Been Done, What the Evidence Shows, and Whom It Reached
abstract: Background. SMOTE was published in this journal in 2002 and reviewed here at its fifteenth anniversary in 2018. At twenty-five it is cited by more than 34,000 indexed works, half of them outside computer science. Objectives. To establish what the methods built on SMOTE change, how strong the evidence for them is, and whom the technique has reached. Methods. We audited a curated corpus of 76 papers, 37 of which propose a SMOTE-family generator, and tested its coverage with a systematic search of 22,426 records in the PRISMA 2020 format. From the corpus we collected 1,756 dataset entries, 1,511 published comparisons with SMOTE and the evaluation design of 71 studies; from the search we drew 300 applications of SMOTE at random. We used an agentic AI approach to extract, screen and code under our written rules, and we report how each step was checked. Results. Every variant re-decides some of the six decisions of the SMOTE rule, and 24 of the 37 are only ever run on two classes. In their own papers, proposed methods beat SMOTE in 79.0% of the decided comparisons, but independent studies find that the gains shrink with strong learners and tuned thresholds, and that resampling damages calibration. The corpus holds 52 of the 3,097 records that pass the screen and covers the early years closely, the recent ones thinly. The reach is very wide, but a benefit at the level of outcomes is undemonstrated, four harms are documented, and an estimated 37% of applications resample the whole data set before splitting it. Conclusions. For tabular classification, a new SMOTE variant should no longer count as a contribution in itself: a new generator should be tested one decision at a time against class weighting and a tuned threshold with a strong learner, with calibration reported. We close with a selection guide, a reporting checklist of fifteen items and a research agenda.

title: A Genetic Algorithm Approach to Reconstructing Scalar-Tensor Lagrangians
abstract: Recent DESI baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data, combined with cosmic microwave background (CMB) and Type Ia supernovae observations, have been interpreted as evidence for dynamical dark energy whose equation of state crosses the phantom divide $w=-1$. Such a crossing cannot be realized smoothly by a minimally coupled scalar field $φ$, but can arise naturally in scalar-tensor theories. We present a data-driven framework that reconstructs the scalar-tensor Lagrangian directly from observations, using a genetic algorithm to evolve the symbolic expressions for the nonminimal coupling $F(φ)$ and the scalar potential $U(φ)$. Each candidate is evaluated through a forward model that self-consistently determines the expansion history, the effective gravitational coupling, and the growth of structure. Candidates are ranked by a joint likelihood of DESI DR2 BAO, Pantheon+ supernovae calibrated with SH0ES Cepheids, compressed CMB distance priors, and redshift-space distortion measurements of $fσ_8$. We restrict to the unscreened branch of the theory and impose Solar System constraints on the post-Newtonian parameter $γ$ and on the time variation of the gravitational coupling, together with a Big Bang nucleosynthesis bound on its evolution. Across 64 independent runs, the best reconstruction improves the fit relative to $Λ$CDM by $Δχ^2=-16.6$, compared with $Δχ^2=-10.6$ for the CPL dark-energy parametrization. The preferred coupling is well described by $F(φ)=c_1φ^2+e^φ(1-c_2φ)$. The reconstructed theory shows phantom behavior at $z\gtrsim0.5$, but it remains close to $w=-1$ at low redshift.

title: Magnetic Reconfiguration Controls Spin Splitting and Spin-Orbit-Coupled Responses in Compensated Magnets
abstract: Compensated magnets provide a versatile platform for spin-dependent electronic and transport phenomena. Here, we show that magnetic reconfiguration, i.e., selective reversal of local moments without changing the underlying crystal structure, can profoundly transform the nonrelativistic spin splitting and spin-orbit-coupled responses of spin-degenerate antiferromagnets (AFMs), altermagnets (AMs), and compensated ferrimagnets (cFIMs). Strikingly, magnetic configurations with nearly degenerate energies can exhibit qualitatively different spin-split band structures and anomalous Hall responses, allowing a small magnetic-energy scale to produce large changes in physical properties. Combining tight-binding models, oriented spin space group analysis, and first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that converting an AM configuration into cFIM states activates staggered onsite-potential contributions to spin splitting, complementing the anisotropic-hopping mechanism of AMs and removing symmetry-enforced degeneracies. Moreover, cFIM symmetry permits an anomalous Hall response at first order in spin-orbit coupling, in contrast to the higher-order or orientation-constrained responses of corresponding AM states. We demonstrate this regime in Mn2Mo3O8, one of 12 cFIM candidates identified in the MAGNDATA database, and further demonstrate its generality by designing cFIMs from collinear AFMs, exemplified by MnGeO3 and Co2Mo3O8. Our results establish magnetic reconfiguration as a powerful symmetry-guided strategy for dramatically reshaping electronic and transport responses in compensated magnets.

title: Limit laws for Siegel theta sums
abstract: Siegel theta sums are exponential sums over the integer lattice whose phases are determined by a quadratic form. For a random choice of quadratic form, we prove a limit law for the modulus of the normalised sum as the summation range tends to infinity. The limiting distribution depends on the space from which the quadratic form is sampled. We prove precise heavy-tail asymptotics for random sampling from (a) the full space of quadratic forms and (b) the space of diagonal forms. This study extends classic results by Jurkat and Van Horne for one-variable theta sums and by Götze and Gordin for theta series on Siegel half-spaces. Our approach uses the Shale--Weil representation of the metaplectic group and the ergodic theory of unipotent flows.

title: Decoder-as-a-Probe: Verbalizing and Steering Visual Representations in LVLMs
abstract: It is commonly accepted that high-level concepts are represented linearly in the representation space of large neural networks. For Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs), finding those interpretable directions in visual representations is important for interpretability. To find them, the classical approach is to train a linear classifier on the representations, but it needs a large amount of labels and only recovers what can be read from the representations, not what the model actually uses. In this paper we start from the following insight: The LLM Decoder of an LVLM is also a classifier whose classes are the possible next tokens. So we use its first-order Taylor expansion as a linear classifier. Hence, we introduce Decoder-as-a-Probe (DaP), which significantly outperforms classical probing and steering baselines especially when training data is sparse. (1) It verbalizes what an LVLM perceives in a given image. (2) It can surgically change the perception of the LVLM about specific attributes (e.g. change only the color, the clothes worn or the action done). Due to its simplicity and data efficiency, we believe DaP can serve as a plug-and-play tool for LVLM research, such as interpretability, hallucination mitigation or instruction tuning.

title: Feasibility-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for O-CU and O-DU Mapping in 6G O-RAN
abstract: This paper studies the mapping of the virtual network function components (VNFCs) of the O-RAN central unit (O-CU) and O-RAN distributed unit (O-DU) onto virtual machines (VMs) in sixth-generation (6G) open radio access networks (O-RAN). The problem is formulated as a feasibility-aware sequential decision process that maximizes the number of placed VNFCs and, secondarily, favors fewer active VMs and lower residual resource wastage. Although conventional optimization techniques can solve this problem, their computational cost becomes prohibitive for larger instances or when optimization must be repeated. To address this limitation, we explore two neural reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods: a deep $Q$-network (DQN) and a double deep $Q$-network (Double DQN). Whereas DQN uses the same target network to both select and evaluate the bootstrap action, Double DQN decouples these two operations to mitigate maximization-induced overestimation. We compare both methods against six baselines: random feasible placement, first-fit, first-fit decreasing, best-fit, a resource-wastage-aware heuristic, and a time-bounded mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solver. We conduct a controlled experimental evaluation across four problem sizes with $30$ independent instances each, together with capacity-stress, distribution-shift, and reward-ablation experiments. For the $16 \times 8$ VNFC-to-VM scenario, DQN and Double DQN achieve mean placed-VNFC fractions of $0.990$ and $0.996$, respectively. However, first-fit decreasing and the resource-wastage-aware heuristic match this placement quality with lower efficiency cost and lower decision time, whereas the MILP attains the lowest efficiency cost at a much higher runtime. The results clarify the strengths and limitations of neural placement for this static problem, without establishing superiority over conventional methods.

title: Nonpolynomial entire solutions of the special Lagrangian equation with critical phase
abstract: In this paper, we construct smooth nonpolynomial entire solutions of the special Lagrangian equation with critical phase $(n-2)π/2$ for every $n\ge4$. Together with the nonquadratic example in dimension two and Warren's example in dimension three, our construction shows that the supercritical condition $|θ|>(n-2)π/2$ in the Bernstein theorem proved by Yuan is sharp in every dimension $n\ge2$.

title: Site-Resolved Optical Spectroscopy of Thulium in Solid Argon
abstract: We utilize the high resolution of the ground state transition ${}^2\mathrm{F}_{7/2} \leftrightarrow {}^2\mathrm{F}_{5/2}$ in thulium atoms isolated in solid argon to perform excitation-emission spectroscopy. Decomposition of the excitation-emission spectrum reveals 6 absorption-emission profiles, which are attributed to multiple trapping sites in the host matrix. Comparison with vacuum transition energies shows large matrix-induced shifts for $\mathrm{s}\rightarrow\mathrm{p}$ transitions, whereas $\mathrm{f} \rightarrow \mathrm{d}$ transitions remain close to their free-atom energies. A single site exhibiting strong emission at 560nm is investigated and a three-photon excitation pathway is determined as a possible origin of the high energy 560nm light. Additionally, for long-lived levels belonging to the $\mathrm{f}^{12}\mathrm{d}$ configuration, narrow, crystal-field split absorption lines are identified. Matrix effects are important for establishing the mechanism behind the observed spectra and long $\mathrm{f}^{12}\mathrm{d}$ lifetimes.

title: AGLR: Attribute-Guided Latent Refinement for Fine-Grained Humanoid Motion Generation and Editing
abstract: Humanoid motion generation must accommodate evolving task requirements, where localized adjustments should satisfy new geometric constraints without disrupting desired motion details. However, language-based control lacks geometric precision, while joint-level constraints require explicit spatial targets. Local geometric constraints are also underdetermined, complicating target satisfaction and source preservation. We present AGLR (Attribute-Guided Latent Refinement), a unified framework for fine-grained humanoid motion generation and editing through source-anchored refinement. A compact geometric interface supports composable, time-varying control of limb extents, torso orientation, and root trajectories. Given a generated or encoded base latent, an Attribute Residual Adapter predicts a single-pass correction, with dual-level supervision enforcing target matching and selective preservation across attributes and motion coordinates. On HumanML3D-G1, AGLR achieves the highest controllable-generation and preservation-constrained editing success rates among evaluated methods. Editing take only 9.1 ms for a cached 500-frame motion, without additional sampling or test-time optimization. Zero-shot evaluation on BONES-SEED-G1 further demonstrates transfer without fine-tuning.

title: Dynamics of a Charged Particle on a Conformal Helicoidal Surface
abstract: We study the classical and quantum motion of a charged particle on a conformal helicoidal surface embedded in four-dimensional Euclidean space. A uniform ambient magnetic field pulls back to a nonuniform surface field. The cyclic longitudinal coordinate permits an exact transverse reduction. The ordinary helicoid in the same axial field shares the effective potential and the turning points, while the conformal metric increases the physical period at matched energy and longitudinal momentum. We classify the single- and double-well regimes and obtain the exact transverse periods in the two double-well sectors. The periods diverge logarithmically at the separatrix, with twice the leading coefficient above the barrier as below it. The zero-field limit allows transverse escape, and the weak-twist limit is locally free but nonuniform across the surface. Intrinsic quantization gives an exact weighted transverse eigenvalue problem. Fixed-momentum eigenvalues test the harmonic approximation in a central well and resolve the tunneling splittings in a double well.

title: PURA: Video Token Pruning via Unified Spatiotemporal Redundancy Assessment
abstract: Video large language models incur substantial inference costs from long visual token sequences. Existing video token compression methods mitigate these costs by exploiting spatial redundancy within frames and temporal redundancy across frames. However, many approaches impose predefined processing orders or fixed allocation ratios for spatial and temporal compression, limiting their ability to adapt to the varying balance of spatiotemporal redundancy across videos. To address this limitation, we propose PURA, a training-free method that prunes visual tokens through unified spatiotemporal redundancy assessment. For each token, PURA constructs spatial and temporal reference candidates and selects the reference with the lowest representation error across the two dimensions. The representation error is combined with token importance to determine each token's removal cost. To avoid the time overhead of removing the lowest-cost token one by one, we introduce Coordinated Pruning, which iteratively groups mutually compatible low-cost removals into batches for simultaneous execution and updates the pruning state after each batch until the target budget is reached. Extensive experiments on three video large language models and five video understanding benchmarks demonstrate that PURA achieves a favorable trade-off between task performance and inference efficiency.

title: Inverse scattering transform for the $N$-component Gerdjikov-Ivanov equation with nonzero boundary conditions
abstract: This paper investigates the inverse scattering theory of the $N$-component Gerdjikov-Ivanov equation with nonzero boundary conditions. The analyticity of the Jost eigenfunctions is analyzed, and auxiliary eigenfunctions are constructed using tensor products and generalized cross products, thereby yielding a set of analytic eigenfunctions required to formulate the inverse problem. Three fundamental symmetry relations satisfied by the eigenfunctions and scattering data are established, and the asymptotic behavior of both is examined. We provide a complete characterization of the discrete spectrum and derive the corresponding residue conditions by analyzing the ranks of the relevant matrices. The inverse problem is then formulated as a matrix Riemann-Hilbert problem whose solution is used to reconstruct the potential. In the reflectionless case, an explicit solution formula is obtained. Finally, taking the four-component case as an example, we illustrate the structural features of solitons, breathers, and their interactions.

title: Rank Before You Encode: Reading a Few Percent of a Whole-Slide Image
abstract: Classifying a whole-slide image requires encoding thousands of high-resolution tiles with a pathology foundation model, which accounts for most of the inference cost. Existing efficient methods reduce this cost by selecting fewer tiles, but typically train a new model around their selection strategy. A largely unexplored alternative is to keep an existing full-bag model frozen and run it on selected tiles at the same encoder cost. We introduce this comparison, alongside random tile sampling at matched cost. To select tiles, we fit a lightweight selector with 3.3K parameters to the attention of a frozen model, without additional slide labels. The selector ranks regions from a slide thumbnail, encodes the top K regions at 5x magnification, and selects b for processing at 20x. We evaluate seven frozen MIL aggregators on six tasks and compare them with nine efficient methods trained on the same features and splits. At a budget of (K,b)=(1000,10), encoding costs about 6.6% of the full bag and is 10-14x faster, excluding tiling. The AUROC drop is no more than 0.005 in 33 of 36 aggregator-task pairs. At (500,10), the cost falls to about 4% and inference is 13-22x faster, but AUROC drops by up to 0.035 on CAMELYON17, where small metastases are easily missed. Selection improves over random sampling by about 0.10 AUROC on tasks with focal lesions, while random sampling performs well on diffuse tasks. In our comparisons, the frozen model at (500,10) is ahead of nine efficient methods in 55 of 60 paired comparisons. Giving an existing WSI model fewer tiles is thus a baseline that a new efficient model should be compared with at matched encoder cost.

title: Lone Wolves and Lattices in Bayesian Matching with Transfers
abstract: I study the Lone Wolf and lattice properties of stable outcomes in one-to-one matching with transferable utility and one-sided incomplete information, using the Bayesian stable market states of Liu (2020) and Chen and Hu (2024). With transfers, the wage in a blocking offer screens the worker's types, so it determines both whom the firm attracts and what the firm learns. I show by example that the firm-side and matched-set versions of the Lone Wolf property, as well as the lattice property, can fail even when outcomes are compared under the same information structure. I then assume that each worker's matching value is additively separable in his type and the firm's identity. Under this condition, a firm that is unmatched in some stable outcome earns zero in every stable outcome with the same type profile and information structure. Workers can retain information rents, so the worker-side property can fail. Nevertheless, outside a finite union of affine hyperplanes in the space of firm values, all such stable outcomes leave the same agents unmatched. Whenever they do, the stable payoff vectors form a lattice, and worker-optimal and firm-optimal outcomes exist. The results extend to comonotonicity of relative preferences when posterior beliefs are independent across workers.

title: Confronting $b \to (s, d)μ^+ μ^-$ and $\mathcal{L}_{K^{*}\bar{K}^{*}}$ puzzle in a $U(1)_{B-3L_μ}$ framework with neutrino phenomenology
abstract: Current data on several observables in $b \to (s,d)$ $μ^+ μ^-$ transitions reveal certain discrepancies with Standard Model (SM) predictions. Considering the possibility that these deviations stem from new physics, we explore a $Z^{\prime}$ framework based on $U(1)_{B-3L_μ}$ model. The parameter space is examined in light of existing constraints from $b \to (s,d)$ $μ^+ μ^-$ transitions. Within this framework, we show that the quark couplings accommodating $b \to (s,d)$ $μ^+ μ^-$ anomalies, imprint correlated signatures on the non-leptonic puzzles $\mathcal{L}_{K^{*}\bar{K}^{*}}$ in $B_{s(d)} \to K^{*}\bar{K}^{*}$ decays. We find that the scenario with both vector and axial-vector contributions of opposite sign is favored by the data compared to pure vector contribution, offering a correlated probe of the underlying new-physics scenario. We further explore the neutrino phenomenology within the same framework in light of current data.

title: Existence of complete singular solutions of the Yamabe equation at prescribed points
abstract: Let $(M^n,g)$ be smooth, connected and closed, with $n\ge3$, and let $P$ be a prescribed nonempty finite set. We characterize the conformal classes $[g]$ that admit a complete metric of positive constant scalar curvature on $M\setminus P$. Such a metric exists precisely when $Y(M,[g])>0$ and either $[g]$ is nonround or $|P|\ge2$. In a nonround positive conformal class, the metrics can be chosen with Fowler asymptotics and arbitrary fixed ratios of their small asymptotic neck sizes. As the neck sizes tend to zero, every sequence of these metrics has a subsequence converging smoothly away from the punctures to a smooth Yamabe minimizing metric. The construction allows degenerate Yamabe minimizers and arbitrary curvature jets at the prescribed points. For nonempty closed singular sets $Λ\subset M$ with empty interior, we also announce the same existence criterion with the additional requirement that the Bessel capacity $C_{1+2/n,n/2}(Λ)$ vanish.

title: Resilience Analysis Through Automated Stage Identification and Quantitative Assessment
abstract: This paper introduced an ML-based approach, designed to be domain- and threat-agnostic, for automated recognition of PARA (Plan/Prepare, Absorb, Recover, Adapt) resilience stages in system-performance time series, enabling subsequent quantitative resilience analysis across different systems. We investigate four ML models for resilience stage recognition: Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). We then use the ML models' predictions to quantify system resilience by computing corresponding resilience metrics from system-performance data observed before, during, and after disruptive events. We evaluate the proposed approach using datasets from two distinct operational domain network systems and an airport transportation system, demonstrating its domain-agnostic applicability to resilience assessment. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of resilience stage classification, with the best F1-scores ranging from 74.3% to 99.4% across all resilience stages. The overall resilience metrics R_t and RL are estimated, with the best models' MAPE ranging from 0.35-0.82% on IEEE 802.11 and LTE to 1.65-9.56% for the airport. These results provide a basis for threat-agnostic resilience analysis of complex engineering systems, enabling further assessment of how effectively a system withstands, absorbs, and recovers from disruptive events and stress conditions.

title: On infinite torsion of abelian varieties over large algebraic fields of positive characteristic
abstract: Let $A$ be a non-zero abelian variety defined over a finitely generated field $F$. A conjecture of Geyer and Jarden [GJ78] asserts that for every $σ\in \mathrm{Gal}(F^{sep}/F)$ outside a set of Haar measure zero, there exist infinitely many primes $\ell$ such that the $\ell$-torsion subgroup of $A(F^{sep}(σ))$ is non-zero (or equivalently, the torsion subgroup of $A(F^{sep}(σ))$ is infinite), where $F^{sep}(σ)$ denotes the subfield of $F^{sep}$ fixed by $σ$. While this conjecture remains open when $\mathrm{Char}(F)>0$, we establish a new case under the assumptions of $\mathrm{End}(A)=\mathbb{Z}$ and the connectedness of the algebraic monodromy groups attached to $A/F$.

title: AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base
abstract: We present AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base, a mixture-of-experts language model with 80 billion total parameters and approximately 3 billion active parameters per token, trained from scratch at Yandex and released under the Apache 2.0 license. The model combines Kimi Delta Attention with full attention, uses Attention Residuals, and is trained with Muon. Training comprises general pretraining on 17.5 trillion tokens, two context-extension stages, and a dedicated stage for reasoning and agentic interaction. We describe the data collection and augmentation pipelines, evaluation protocols, architectural ablations, and scaling-law experiments. We identify the limitations of held-out training loss as a proxy for downstream performance and introduce an auxiliary loss on mixture-of-experts outputs to stabilize training at the predicted learning rate. Domain-specific data selection and augmentation improve factual knowledge, mathematics, and programming skills, while agent trajectories introduced during pretraining improve performance on agentic benchmarks after supervised fine-tuning. In zero-shot reasoning evaluation, the model achieves leading results among open base models of comparable size, with 88.7% pass@8 on IMO-AnswerBench and 82.9% pass@8 on LiveCodeBench v5-v6. To evaluate Russian-language factual knowledge, we introduce and release two benchmarks with their evaluation protocols: WikiWebFacts, which tests short factual questions drawn from encyclopedic sources and search queries, and HardMultiQA, which tests more demanding factual questions inspired by user interactions. Our model scores 86.5% on WikiWebFacts and 67.9% on HardMultiQA, compared with 83.2% and 65.4% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B total and 13B active parameters) and 72.8% and 54.5% for Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base (120B total and 12B active parameters), outperforming both larger models on these benchmarks.

title: Convergence of Residual-driven Adaptive Kernel-based Multilevel Approximation
abstract: Kernel-based multilevel methods combine compactly supported radial basis functions with a residual correction scheme and are known to converge linearly in the number of levels. In this paper we study an adaptive version of the multilevel method, in which the interpolation on each level only uses those sites at which the residual of the preceding level exceeds a given threshold. Although this method has been proposed some time ago and converges in all numerical tests, a convergence proof has been missing so far. We close this gap. We derive an a priori error bound, an a posteriori error bound valid for arbitrary point selections, and extend the analysis to penalized least-squares approximation and to target functions outside the native space of the kernel. For a variant with an additional check-loop per level, we show convergence with the rate of the classical multilevel method. We illustrate our findings with three numerical examples.

title: Rational terms and UV counterterms of the SMEFT at next-to-leading order in QCD
abstract: We compute the rational terms $R_2$ and the ultraviolet counterterms of the dimension-six Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) at next-to-leading order (NLO) in QCD without any flavour assumption, for complex Wilson coefficients, massive quarks and a general CKM matrix. We also compute the on-shell renormalisation factors of the quark fields in the presence of flavour mixing. We work with an anticommuting $γ_5$ and read closed fermion loops with a single $γ_5$ at the operator insertion. The results, also for common flavour assumptions, are provided in electronic form and in a Mathematica package attached to the paper. We use them to build example models for MadGraph5_aMC@NLO and give NLO predictions for representative processes.

title: Diffusion Effects on a Stochastic Amplifier Driven by the Square of a Gaussian Field: Discontinuous Transition to Intermittency
abstract: We study the effects of diffusion on the transition to intermittency in stochastic amplification driven by the square of a Gaussian field. The transition is characterized by an order parameter quantifying the spatial uniformity of the amplification. We consider a model in which the diffusion-amplification process is embedded in a random lattice of point absorbers in such a way that the Feynman-Kac formula is restricted to Brownian paths with a range not exceeding a finite cut-off. In this setting, with the Gaussian driving field in a wide class of physical interest, we show that diffusion-induced damping of the amplification is sufficiently strong to change the nature of the transition: from continuous in the absence of diffusion, to discontinuous in the presence of diffusion.

title: Viscosity solutions for integro-differential equations with gradient and source terms
abstract: We address global well-posedness for integro-differential equations with gradient and source terms. This naturally results from establishing the comparison principle for viscosity solutions and existence via Perron's method. There are many earlier results for similar equations, and our work attempts to give a unified approach and improve upon some recent examples. There is a natural juxtaposition of earlier results in the usual framework of viscosity solutions which rely on a min-max structure, with some more recent implementations coming from the free boundary literature in which a min-max is not apparent initially, but does appear a posteriori due to certain rigid structural constraints. Here we give a presentation that combines ideas from both situations. The most important feature of the operators in our equations is what we call the global comparison property. This is combined with a natural local Lipschitz assumption on the operator defining the equation.

title: DéjàVu: Plurality Consensus by First Repetition
abstract: We analyze DéjàVu, a simple protocol for plurality consensus: in each synchronous round, each agent samples one uniformly random agent and adopts the first opinion it observes twice, resetting its memory after every adoption. The rule requires neither frequency counters nor knowledge of the population size or the number of opinions. It relies only on repetition detection, an ability documented in single neurons and reflected in the mere-exposure effect. For a population of $n$ agents with $k$ initial opinions, let $M_0$ be the initial count of the plurality opinion (so $n/M_0 \le k$) and $Δ_0$ its bias, the difference between $M_0$ and the count of the second most popular opinion. We prove that, whenever $Δ_0 = Ω(\sqrt{M_0 \log n})$, DéjàVu reaches consensus on the initial plurality opinion within $O(\sqrt{n/M_0} \log(e M_0 / Δ_0) + \log\log n)$ rounds with high probability. Moreover, we show that, for the same bias regime, DéjàVu is asymptotically never slower than the $h$-majority protocol, collecting its $h$ samples one per round, for every fixed choice of $h$, even one chosen optimally for the initial configuration. There are also initial configurations for which DéjàVu is asymptotically faster for every $h$. The opinion counts alone do not determine the dynamics: each adoption depends on a hidden memory filled over many rounds while the population changed, and agents with older (hence fuller) memories tend to reset sooner, so an advantage held mostly by them can be lost. The few rigorous convergence results we are aware of for such dynamics concern only two opinions. We derive the exact law of the memories given the history of opinions and resets, and track how the plurality opinion's advantage is distributed across memory ages, giving more weight to recently reset agents as they are less likely to reset again soon.

title: Square-root comparison, Turnpike, and exact semidefinite feasibility
abstract: Given positive integers $a_i,K$, put $S=\sum_{i=1}^k\sqrt{a_i}$. We construct a realizable Turnpike instance in which the minimum spacing of distinct distances and the smallest nonzero addition residual are both at most $|S-K|$ when $S\ne K$. With approximation oracles, one three-distance realizability query decides $S\le K$. For unordered lists of radical sums with nonnegative rational coefficients, a polynomial-time substitution by integers preserves every normalized ruler. We give the classical reduction of square-root comparison to exact semidefinite feasibility in both threshold directions. The comparison enters through numerical separation and marked sorting; the integer recoding needs no such comparison for unordered reconstruction.

title: Kant-Q: A Q-Learning Algorithm for Kantian Equilibrium in Symmetric Markov Games
abstract: AI agents increasingly interact with one another, and many of these interactions are mixed-motive games, which have posed a persistent challenge for learning algorithms. Most multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms are designed to reach Nash equilibria, yet in many such games these equilibria are Pareto-inefficient. We instead study Kantian equilibria, an economic solution concept in which each agent plays the action it would want all agents to adopt. In symmetric games, this corresponds to an optimal common policy. We propose Kant-Q, a Q-learning algorithm in which each agent learns action profiles where all agents play the same action. Each update is then a sample from a single-agent MDP, so Kant-Q inherits the convergence guarantees of standard Q-learning. We show that every symmetric Markov game has a pure Kantian equilibrium.
